artigo.texto: India’s shift towards renewable power is expected to create a major requirement for energy storage, with over Rs 4 lakh crore of storage-related investment estimated to be needed by FY32, according to CareEdge Ratings. The report said India’s power sector is moving from a challenge of adding generation capacity to a new challenge of integrating increasing renewable capacity into the electricity system. While non-fossil sources account for around 50 per cent of India’s installed power generation capacity, they contribute around 29 per cent of actual electricity generation. This gap makes energy storage, transmission infrastructure and flexible generation increasingly important as the share of renewable power rises. The report highlighted that India’s energy storage requirement is expected to reach around 411 GWh by FY32, compared with operational storage capacity of around 54 GWh as of June 2026. It stated, “CareEdge Ratings estimates storage-related capex of over Rs 4 lakh crore to meet FY32 requirements”. It also added that the rise in storage requirements reflects the need to integrate renewable generation into the power system and ensure that electricity produced from variable renewable sources can be managed effectively. Battery and pumped storage gain importance The report also pointed to a sharp increase in standalone storage-based tenders. Such tenders rose to around 21 GW in FY26 from 7 GW in FY25, indicating growing activity in the energy storage segment. The agency highlighted the complementary roles of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and Pumped Storage Plants (PSPs) in supporting India’s power transition. Both technologies are expected to have an important role as the country adds more renewable generation capacity. Coal power retains a role in the transition At the same time, CareEdge Ratings said coal-based thermal power is entering a multi-year phase of improved credit stability and renewed investment relevance. Well-contracted coal-based thermal power assets are likely to remain important for meeting growing electricity demand while also providing the flexibility required to integrate increasing renewable capacity, the report said. This indicates that the expansion of renewable energy is likely to be accompanied by investments in other parts of the power system rather than replacing conventional generation immediately. Storage and flexible generation would help manage renewable power, while transmission infrastructure would be required to move electricity across the grid. Transmission investment to rise The transmission sector is also expected to see significant investment. The report estimates a capex outlay of around Rs 5.19 lakh crore during FY27-FY31. However, the agency identified several execution-related challenges for the transmission sector, including right-of-way issues, forest clearances and coordination requirements. Despite these challenges, it said the stable cash flow profile and long concession tenures of operational transmission assets continue to support the sector’s credit profile. Published on September 28, 2026

artigo.texto: CATL's Hungarian Gigafactory Enters Trial Production as eVTOL Battery Clears Key Safety Hurdle Published on 09/25/2026 at 14:52 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL has cleared a pair of operational milestones that extend well beyond the electric-car market it dominates, even as its Shenzhen-listed shares hover within a hair of their yearly floor. In Debrecen, Hungary, trial production has officially begun at the company's newly built cell plant after all regulatory requirements were satisfied, CATL announced Tuesday. With a projected annual capacity of 100 gigawatt-hours, the facility is slated to become the group's largest manufacturing site outside China. The move is central to management's push to build local capacity overseas, reducing reliance on the home market and allowing direct supply to major customers on their doorstep. Separately, CATL's aerospace battery system for crewed electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft (eVTOL) has passed a decisive safety test. The review confirmed that a thermal runaway does not propagate to neighboring cells. According to the company, it is the world's first aerospace battery system using prismatic cells to reach this safety threshold at an energy density of up to 350 watt-hours per kilogram. During testing, overheating was triggered simultaneously in two adjacent cells without setting off a chain reaction within the pack — a benchmark the aviation industry treats as a critical gate for certifying electric aircraft. Home-Market Pressures Mount The twin advances land against a shifting customer landscape in China. Automakers are increasingly pursuing greater independence or bringing in additional cell suppliers. Li Auto has said it will move to self-developed batteries across the group, meaning the new generation of its Li Mega model will no longer carry CATL cells. Electronics group Xiaomi, for its part, agreed on September 4 to partner with rivals CALB and Sunwoda for its Pengcheng vehicles. Premium models from many Chinese manufacturers continue to rely on CATL cells, but volume-model contracts are increasingly going to competitors. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? Chief technology officer Lin Jiubiao struck a calm tone Monday on China's consumer tax on batteries, which took effect September 1. While the company has seen volume cuts and fluctuations on individual orders, it has simultaneously opened up new demand potential, he said. Business for the current year remains unchanged overall, with the effects so far contained. His remarks followed a stretch of noticeable market jitters: in mid-September the stock logged its sharpest multi-day decline in more than a year, driven by speculation over production cutbacks and growing investor caution ahead of the third quarter. Buyback, Charging Network and a Norwegian Beachhead CATL has been putting capital to work at home as well. On September 11, it acquired 604,293 of its own A-shares on the Shenzhen exchange for a total of exactly 199,978,827.46 yuan. To shore up its market position, the group is widening its ecosystem around battery charging and swapping. Yang Jun, who heads CATL's battery-swap business, presented a network of combined fast-charging and swap stations. The installations share transformers and charging modules, cutting electricity losses by more than 13 percentage points compared with conventional stations. Together with partners such as Nio, the company aims to establish uniform national standards for swap stations. International service is advancing in parallel. CATL's new facility in Norway — its largest customer-service site outside Asia to date — arrives in a market where pure electric cars accounted for 98.7 percent of new registrations in August. The Norwegian operation is designed to handle complex repairs within 48 hours. On the energy-infrastructure front, a mandatory filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission shows the company signed a cooperation agreement with the VNET Group on August 18. The partners plan to jointly build a three-tier ecosystem linking computing power and electricity supply at gigawatt scale. Shares Stay Pinned Near the Low None of the operational news has lifted the stock. In Thursday trading, the shares fell 2.5 percent in Shenzhen to close at 293.50 CNY, leaving them just 0.2 percent above their 52-week low. artigo.texto: India to add up to 50 GWh battery storage capacity over next 2 yrs: Crisil Battery storage deployment is set to rise sharply from 1 GWh in FY26 as renewable energy expands and storage-linked projects gain a larger share of government auctions Listen to This Article India’s renewable energy sector is set for a significant surge in battery energy storage system (BESS) deployment, with 45-50 gigawatt-hour (GWh) of capacity expected to be commissioned over the current and next financial year, compared with just 1 GWh as of last fiscal, according to Crisil. The ratings agency said the growth is attributed to a strong pipeline of projects under implementation and continued policy support. Capacity additions could have been even higher, but 8-9 GWh of awarded capacity faces a higher risk of delay, moderating the overall deployment outlook. The analysis covers bids awarded between FY24 and FY26 across 100 renewable energy developers. Crisil said the growing need for storage is a consequence of the rising share of renewable energy (RE) to 39 per cent of India’s installed power generation capacity and 15 per cent of energy generated last fiscal. As RE generation is intermittent, it has increased the need for firm and peak-hour power supply. This has elevated the importance of energy storage solutions, particularly BESS. The requirement is especially acute for solar projects because electricity demand peaks in the evening, when solar generation is negligible and BESS can address this mismatch. In line with its objective of integrating a larger share of RE into the national power grid in a sustainable manner, the government has accelerated storage-linked auctions. Projects incorporating BESS accounted for nearly 40 per cent of total auctioned capacity in FY26, up sharply from about 5 per cent in FY24 and FY25. Also Read “As a result, 50-55 GWh of BESS capacity is scheduled for commissioning across FY27 and FY28. Of this, around 40 GWh has been awarded through government-led auctions, where distribution utilities are the offtakers, while the remaining 10-15 GWh is expected to serve commercial and industrial consumers directly or be deployed in the merchant market,” Crisil said. However, 21 per cent of the under-construction BESS capacity, equivalent to about 12 GWh, faces weak return potential, which may lead to some delays in commissioning. The risk has emerged because battery prices have hardened in 2026, while tariffs bid out for these projects were relatively low. “Developers typically procure batteries about a year after securing project bids. Consequently, most projects awarded in 2025 are now exposed to higher battery prices, which have rebounded from the lows witnessed in 2025. As battery prices were consistently coming down till 2025, developers appeared to have bid aggressively on the assumption that prices would continue their downward trajectory,” said Manish Gupta, senior director and deputy chief ratings officer at Crisil. However, in reality, battery prices have increased and, at these prevailing levels, project returns may be insufficient to achieve a typical target internal rate of return of 12-14 per cent, according to Crisil. Consequently, developers may defer implementation in anticipation of more favourable battery pricing. Further, around 8-9 GWh out of this 12 GWh of planned capacity is exposed to an additional challenge: limited implementation experience among project sponsors. While BESS projects typically face relatively lower land acquisition and connectivity-related challenges compared to conventional renewable energy projects, equipment procurement remains a key risk given the sector’s continued dependence on overseas suppliers for batteries and other critical components. The global market for solid state battery silicon carbon negative electrode is entering a pivotal commercialization phase, with demand fundamentals strengthening as automotive OEMs and cell manufacturers accelerate roadmaps toward higher-energy-density solid-state batteries. Silicon-carbon composite anodes, which combine silicon's high theoretical capacity with carbon's structural buffering, are positioned as a critical enabler for extending EV range and enabling fast charging without compromising cycle life. While the market remains in early-stage industrialization, the forecast horizon to 2035 points to a steep adoption curve, supported by gigafactory investments, tightening emissions regulations, and the premium pricing that advanced anode materials can command in performance-driven applications. This report provides a structured, commercially grounded analysis of the market, covering demand architecture, supply chain bottlenecks, pricing dynamics, competitive positioning, and geographic production shifts. It is designed for battery manufacturers, material suppliers, investors, and strategic entrants seeking a clear view of where value will accrue as solid-state batteries move from pilot lines to mass production. The baseline scenario for the solid state battery silicon carbon negative electrode market through 2035 assumes a gradual but accelerating transition from laboratory and pilot-scale adoption to commercial-scale deployment, primarily driven by the automotive sector's push for longer-range and faster-charging electric vehicles. In the near term, demand will be concentrated in premium EV models and high-performance consumer electronics, where the cost premium of silicon-carbon anodes can be justified by performance gains. As solid-state battery technology matures and manufacturing yields improve, costs are expected to decline, enabling broader adoption across mid-range vehicles and stationary storage applications. The supply chain will face multi-layered bottlenecks, including constrained upstream capacity for high-purity nanostructured silicon, limited availability of specialized coating and compounding equipment, and a scarcity of dry-room manufacturing capacity. These constraints will ease gradually as investments flow into dedicated production facilities, but qualification cycles with cell makers will remain long and capital-intensive. Pricing models are expected to evolve from simple per-kilogram material pricing toward value-capture mechanisms tied to cell performance, such as contributions to energy density and royalty fees per gigawatt-hour of cell output. Geographically, Asia-Pacific will maintain dominance in production and consumption, while North America and Europe will see rapid capacity build-out supported by local content requirements and government incentives. The market index is projected to reach 480 by 2035, reflecting a compound annual growth rate of 18.5% from 2025 to 2035. Electric vehicles represent the dominant end-use sector for solid state battery silicon carbon negative electrodes, accounting for the majority of current and forecast demand. Automotive OEMs are under increasing regulatory and competitive pressure to extend driving range and reduce charging times, which directly translates into demand for higher-energy-density anode materials. Silicon-carbon anodes enable cells with significantly higher capacity than conventional graphite, making them a critical enabler for next-generation EV platforms. Currently, adoption is concentrated in premium and performance models, where the cost premium is offset by superior performance. Through 2035, as solid-state battery technology matures and manufacturing scales, silicon-carbon anodes are expected to penetrate mid-range and mass-market vehicles. Key demand-side indicators include EV production volumes, average battery pack size, and the proportion of vehicles offering fast-charging capabilities. The shift toward solid-state batteries will further accelerate adoption, as these batteries require silicon-carbon anodes to achieve target energy densities. Current trend: Rapid adoption driven by range and fast-charging requirements. Major trends: Increasing EV range targets pushing battery energy density requirements above 300 Wh/kg, Fast-charging capability becoming a key differentiator for EV models, Solid-state battery commercialization timelines accelerating among major automakers, Government incentives and emissions regulations favoring higher-performance batteries, and Vertical integration by OEMs into battery cell production. Representative participants: Tesla, Panasonic Energy, LG Energy Solution, CATL, Samsung SDI, and QuantumScape. Consumer electronics, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and drones, represent a significant and high-margin end-use sector for silicon-carbon negative electrodes. Device manufacturers are continuously seeking to extend battery life and reduce charging times, which drives demand for higher-capacity anode materials. Silicon-carbon anodes offer a compelling solution, enabling thinner and lighter batteries without compromising capacity. Currently, adoption is limited to premium flagship devices, where the cost premium is acceptable. Through 2035, as production costs decline and technology matures, silicon-carbon anodes are expected to penetrate mid-tier devices and new form factors such as augmented reality glasses. artigo.texto: Oregon’s second largest investor-owned electric utility could soon directly assign the costs of new energy projects and infrastructure needed for data centers to data center operators. Pacific Power last week agreed to the deal following months of negotiations with staff of the Oregon Public Utility Commission, the watchdog Citizens’ Utility Board and a handful of environmental and community advocacy groups. The Citizens’ Utility Board in a news release Tuesday called the agreement “the strongest from a for-profit electric utility yet” under Oregon’s new POWER Act, which mandates the state’s monopoly electric utilities create a separate rate class for data centers to ensure other customers aren’t subsidizing the massive energy demand from the server farms. Both Pacific Power and the state’s largest electric utility, Portland General Electric, have raised customer rates 50% since 2020, while most customer classes became more energy efficient, and data centers grew to make up nearly one-quarter of all retail electricity sales statewide. The three-member Public Utility Commission is expected to approve Pacific Power’s deal on Nov. 13, according to Charlotte Shuff, a spokesperson for the Citizens’ Utility Board. Shuff expects the Data Center Coalition, an industry group representing the tech companies, will attempt to appeal. The coalition also appealed a recent PGE proposal to assign costs based not on how much each rate class is driving “peak demand” on the system, which is moments when usage is at its highest point. The state utility commission rejected the appeal, but the citizens’ board expects the coalition will bring the case to the Oregon Court of Appeals. While Pacific Power’s plan assigns costs based on who is driving overall demand, PGE’s plan assigns costs based on how much each customer class is growing and adding to the system’s highest demand periods. After the state’s Public Utility Commission approved PGE’s proposal in July, the company announced rates for data centers would increase by nearly 30% while residential payers would see their bills decline slightly. Pacific Power’s proposal goes further than PGE’s by requiring new data centers that receive electricity from Pacific Power to cover the costs for all new energy generation and storage projects needed to power them, including new power plants and batteries, even if those additions also benefit other customers. Data centers would also pay for any upgrades that are needed to serve them, even if those same upgrades benefit other customer classes. Data centers would be responsible for the cost of all wires and poles built for them to receive distributed power, and all costs related to energy purchased on the market from other companies to power them. If a 100 megawatt transmission line is needed to serve a 50 megawatt data center as well as other residential and industrial customers, the data center would pay for 50% of the transmission line, directly corresponding with its overall demand, according to the citizens’ board. New transmission lines can cost several million dollars per mile to build, and the West is in need of more than 12,000 miles of new transmission according to one recent estimate. Shuff said Pacific Power’s proposal came a long way in recent months and “to their credit they (Pacific Power) worked really hard to get to this. We’re really pleased with where we landed,” she said. The utility serves more than 650,000 Oregon customers, and has seen energy demand grow by 8% between 2013 and 2023 due to data centers, according to a Sightline Institute analysis of U.S. Energy Information Administration data. PGE is the state’s largest electric utility, serving 930,000 customers, and has absorbed the most data center load growth of any private utility in the state during the last decade, according to that analysis. PGE’s system of charging customers based not on overall demand growth but “peak demand growth” is driven in part by the fact that they serve a higher number of small data centers in densely populated counties, according to Bob Jenks, executive director of the Citizens’ Utilities Board. Pacific Power’s data center customers are mostly large facilities in more rural parts of the state. It’s easier to make the case that building a new transmission line in Washington County could benefit all customer classes, who are all using more air conditioning in the summer, he explained, “whereas if you build a data center in Madras, it’s pretty clear whether or not new energy investments and infrastructure costs associated with that are for the data center or not,” Jenks said. Drew Hanson, a PGE spokesperson, reiterated in an email the different challenges the two utilities face. “(Pacific Power’s) service area is larger and more spread out, so a single data center may require infrastructure built specifically for that customer, such as a new transmission line, substation, or power resource. In those cases, costs can be tied more directly to the customer creating the need,” he said. Pacific Power’s plan applies to future data centers, while PGE’s applies to future and existing data centers. Pacific Power will need to address costs associated with its current data center customers and their demands next spring. The company has just a handful of data center customers at present “but dozens want to get onto their system, and some of them are massive,” Jenks said. artigo.texto: INDIANTOWN – The Village Council here voted unanimously Sept. 10 to direct its legal counsel to began drafting a data center moratorium and transparency ordinance, a week and a half after the recently-elected Board majority fired the village manager and replaced its long-term attorney in a quest to fulfill campaign promises of pausing such applications. In addition to replacing Village Manager Taryn Kryzda with former Stuart City Manager Michael Giardino on Sept. 1, the Council replaced Village Attorney Wade Vose with one of his colleagues because he’d acknowledged his reluctance to recommend Indiantown’s participation in a data center moratorium. Two days afterwards, Community Development Director Deana Freeman tendered her 30-day notice, realizing her work on at least three data center applications had put her in the cross-hairs of an angry group of area residents. Giardino told the Hometown News that he tried to persuade Freeman to stay on, but when she declined, he told her to make her resignation immediate. The interim village manager has now assumed Freeman’s responsibilities as well. Interim Village Attorney Janet Smith launched the moratorium discussion during the latest meeting. “What we would like to proffer to the Council is two ordinances,” she said. “They will both have to go through planning and zoning and come before you on two separate readings. You will have public comment at each of those meetings. The first one is the moratorium that we feel will be legally defensible. The second one is the transparency ordinance.” The last ordinance was in response to public outcry that Freeman had allegedly signed a non-disclosure agreement with a potential data-center developer, which caused much of the opposition to believe it was a common practice in Village Hall in order to keep residents in the dark. Smith admitted that she had not personally seen the NDA in question but had since submitted a public records request for a copy. Around the Sept. 3 date of Freeman’s resignation letter, a purported copy of that NDA began circulating on Indiantown Facebook pages. The Hometown News could not authenticate that document, however. “I’ve only been told that there was one NDA,” she continued. “I’m still waiting to see about getting it, so that’s in the process. I did hear that NDAs were frowned upon by the Council and the community.” Smith acknowledged there were other methods utilized by municipalities to protect industry trade secrets that could still be implemented in the future. “I have statutory exceptions that the Council can use for trade secrets,” she explained. “If someone is bringing forward a proposal considered a trade secret and they’re willing to indemnify the Village while they speak to us so we can protect their records, then we have that opportunity. So, an NDA should not be needed.” The interim attorney hopes to begin the ordinance process with the Planning, Zoning & appeals Board on Oct. 1, followed by the Council’s first reading Oct. 8. “On Oct. 22, we would have it back before you for second reading and adoption,” she concluded as she read her draft language to the Board. “This would become an ordinance for the Village.” Mayor Phyllis Waters Brown was the first to comment afterward, repeating her concerns of potentially clashing with developers over Senate Bill 180 and other Florida statutes. “This is not a surprise to anyone – I do not want wish to go to court,”she said. “What is wrong with having an open house for all of them, [so] we learn what we need to learn. Let them show us and teach us what we’re asking for and do a moratorium on the ones that may come after.” “Nothing in what I’m proposing would stop you from doing that,” Smith responded. “There’s nothing against having a workshop or a town hall. I’m not giving you any solution that can’t be stopped. If you want to do anything in-between working with the interim manager, you still have that opportunity.” After Councilman Anthony Dowling made a motion to follow Smith’s recommendations -- which was seconded by Councilwoman Janet Hernandez -- a handful of public speakers addressed the Board. Clemenstville resident Linda Byczko started them off. Like several others who’ve actively pushed for the moratorium, Byczko does not live within the Indiantown Village limits and could not vote in the last election. Instead, those county residents lobbied Village residents to vote to make a change. “I think you need time to write regulations to protect the Village,” she said. “The land development regulations right now are very weak: They do not address what you have going on here.” Rory Greenberg has submitted a data-center application for the former Florida Steel Corp. site and stressed his desire to collaborate with the community. “This industry’s moving very fast,” he said. “I think working together and being self-regulating is the best approach. We’re not looking to move fast; we’re just looking to move in earnest. You guys pick the expert, I’ll hire them.” The face of the local opposition, Eric Miller, followed Greenberg to the podium. Like Byczko, he couldn’t vote, but it was of his own doing. During the incorporation movement, he successfully lobbied to keep his Little Ranch area outside of the Village limits. “Mr. Greenberg is right,” he said. “What you’re proposing and you’re going to vote on here is what could have started last February had there been open dialogue and everything not kept in dark rooms. We wanted a seat at the table to make sure what was coming in here was going to be safe. This gives us a framework to work in. You’ve been given another opportunity to work with us, the people that live in this area.” The attorney for the Silver Fox 606 data center applicant, Ethan Loeb subsequently advised the Council of potential litigation. “Certain organizations from our perspective have private property rights that are vested,” he said. “My client’s one of them. artigo.texto: Up to ₹50 lakhs | Starts at 9.99% The World Trade Organization’s Dispute Settlement Body on September 25 agreed to establish a panel to examine Russia’s challenge to the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and an alleged export subsidy linked to the EU’s emissions trading system, opening a new dispute over one of the bloc’s key climate-trade policies. Russia argues that the EU’s CBAM package creates significant barriers to trade in goods covered by the mechanism. It also alleges that the allocation of emissions allowances to certain companies under the EU’s Emissions Trading System amounts to an export subsidy that strengthens the competitiveness of European industries. The EU rejected Russia’s allegations and said it was confident that both CBAM and the ETS comply with WTO rules. Brussels said it would participate in the proceedings to support the rules-based multilateral trading system, while separately criticizing Russia’s actions in relation to Ukraine. The panel was established after Russia submitted its second request, following the EU’s objection to the first request at the DSB’s July meeting. The case, DS639: European Union and its Member States — Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, has attracted broad interest among WTO members. Argentina, Brazil, Canada, China, India, Indonesia, Japan, Saudi Arabia, South Korea, Malaysia, Norway, Paraguay, Singapore, Switzerland, Chinese Taipei, Thailand, the United Kingdom and the United States reserved their rights to participate as third parties. The DSB also agreed to postpone consideration of a panel report in a separate dispute between China and Türkiye over measures concerning electric vehicles and other vehicles originating in China. The report, circulated on 28 July, will now be considered by the DSB by 27 October 2026. Appellate Body deadlock reaches 100th proposal The meeting also underscored the continuing impasse over the WTO’s dispute settlement system. Colombia, speaking for 130 members, introduced for the 100th time a proposal to begin selecting candidates to fill vacancies on the WTO Appellate Body. The United States again opposed the proposal, saying it does not address Washington’s fundamental concerns about the WTO dispute settlement system and that members remain divided over the reforms needed. More than 20 members subsequently voiced support for the joint proposal and called for the restoration of a fully functioning dispute settlement system. Several also encouraged greater participation in the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement (MPIA), an alternative mechanism under Article 25 of the Dispute Settlement Understanding for participating members. Colombia said the group regretted that the selection process had once again not been launched, arguing that ongoing reform discussions should not prevent the Appellate Body from operating fully or members from meeting their obligations to fill vacancies. The DSB Chair, Brazilian Ambassador Guilherme de Aguiar Patriota, also reported on an information session aimed at preserving institutional knowledge of the dispute settlement reform process. The session covered the history and use of the WTO dispute settlement system and reform efforts following the WTO’s 12th and 13th Ministerial Conferences. artigo.texto: NIMBY digital e a conta de energia da inteligÃªncia artificial e datacenters A inteligência artificial não mora na nuvem. Ela ocupa terrenos, usa equipamentos, consome eletricidade, rejeita calor e exige redes de transmissão e fibra ótica. É legítimo perguntar quem pagará por essa infraestrutura e o que receberão as comunidades que a abrigarem. Uma pesquisa divulgada em 22 de setembro pelo Fórum Econômico Mundial registra a expectativa de seus economistas-chefes de que os data centers contribuam para o crescimento, mas também tragam pressão sobre serviços públicos, poucos empregos diretos e resistência local. É um alerta importante. Não é, porém, uma lei da física nem uma sentença para todos os países e projetos. A demanda por energia já cresce por razões muito mais amplas. Queremos casas mais confortáveis, ar-condicionado, mobilidade elétrica, serviços digitais, equipamentos de saúde e processos produtivos mais sofisticados. A Agência Internacional de Energia estima que os data centers responderão por cerca de um décimo do crescimento mundial do consumo elétrico até 2030: uma parcela relevante, mas inferior à de motores industriais, climatização de edifícios e veículos elétricos. Culpar exclusivamente a IA por toda alta da conta de luz seria tão impreciso quanto afirmar que ela não terá impacto algum. Também precisamos distinguir duas coisas que frequentemente aparecem misturadas. Uma família pode pagar mais porque passou a consumir mais eletricidade e, portanto, a usufruir mais serviços e conforto. Pode pagar mais, também, porque subiu o preço de cada quilowatt-hora. Nesse segundo caso, importam os custos da geração, das redes, dos encargos e dos tributos, assim como as decisões sobre quem financia novos investimentos. Chamar tudo isso de “efeito dos data centers” encobre escolhas de política energética e distribuição de custos que devem ser transparentes. Uma grande instalação mal localizada pode, sim, disputar capacidade elétrica e água com a população. Se a rede precisar ser ampliada para atendê-la, não é aceitável simplesmente espalhar a conta entre consumidores residenciais sem demonstrar os benefícios correspondentes. Mas o resultado pode ser diferente quando o empreendedor paga pelas instalações que provoca, contrata geração renovável adicional, ajuda a viabilizar armazenamento e flexibilidade e se instala onde há capacidade ou geração hoje restringida. No Nordeste, essa possibilidade merece estudo projeto a projeto: energia renovável sujeita a curtailment não equivale automaticamente a suprimento firme, disponível 24 horas por dia. O mesmo rigor vale para a água. Um circuito fechado dentro do data center não assegura consumo hídrico próximo de zero: é preciso saber como o calor será finalmente rejeitado. Em regiões de escassez, a localização e a tecnologia de refrigeração devem ser escolhidas antes da licença, com divulgação de captação, consumo efetivo, origem da água e desempenho verificado. Reúso, refrigeração seca e sistemas híbridos são alternativas a comparar, não promessas genéricas. Quanto aos empregos, não devemos vender um data center como uma fábrica que manterá milhares de trabalhadores em seu interior. Seu valor potencial está também na construção, nos serviços especializados e, sobretudo, no que uma região consegue desenvolver ao redor da infraestrutura: pesquisa, formação, computação, aplicações de IA e empresas locais. Esse efeito não nasce sozinho. Requer contratos, investimento em pessoas e instituições capazes de ligar a capacidade computacional à economia regional. A resistência das comunidades tampouco pode ser descartada como medo do futuro. Uma pesquisa da Universidade da Pensilvânia encontrou oposição à instalação de data centers próximos entre 61% dos adultos consultados nos Estados Unidos. Esse dado não descreve automaticamente o Brasil, mas ensina algo: as pessoas percebem quando os custos são locais e os benefícios, distantes. Reprimir ou execrar data centers não resolve a demanda por processamento. Afastá-los sem critério pode apenas transferir consumo de energia, impactos e oportunidades para outros lugares. A resposta é estabelecer condições para recebê-los: conexão planejada; custos de expansão atribuídos com justiça; energia progressivamente menos emissora; metas auditáveis de eficiência elétrica e hídrica; participação das comunidades desde o início; e contrapartidas proporcionais, verificáveis e duradouras. Feito assim, um data center pode deixar de parecer um grande consumidor que chegou para disputar recursos e tornar-se parceiro na expansão da infraestrutura local. As comunidades não têm obrigação de acolher qualquer projeto. Têm o direito de exigir que ele melhore, em vez de encarecer, suas condições de vida. Portanto, a questão é menos sobre quem pagará essa conta, e mais sobre quem colherá os benefícios e quem fará regras impedirão que o futuro dos datacenters seja construído às custas dos seus vizinhos. Jean Paul Prates é advogado e economista com mais de 40 anos de experiência internacional, reconhecido como um dos principais especialistas no setor energético e de recursos naturais. Foi Presidente da Petrobras, Senador da República, Secretário de Estado de Energia e fundador do Centro de Estratégias em Recursos Naturais e Energia – CERNE. Atualmente é sócio da Altiva Inteligência Estratégica, Head do LIDE Energia e conselheiro de empresas e associações setoriais.

artigo.texto: Zeon Corporation Key supplier for automotive and industrial seals According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Hydrogenated Nitrile Rubber (HNBR) Compounds market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global market for hydrogenated nitrile rubber (HNBR) compounds is entering a period of accelerated transformation, with demand projected to expand at a compound annual growth rate of 9–13% through 2035. This growth is not merely a continuation of historical trends but a structural shift driven by the rapid build-out of battery manufacturing capacity and grid-scale energy storage infrastructure. HNBR compounds, known for their superior chemical resistance, high-temperature stability, and mechanical durability, are increasingly specified for sealing and gasketing applications in equipment that handles aggressive electrolytes, thermal management fluids, and high-voltage insulation environments. While traditional industrial sealing segments continue to provide a stable demand base, the energy sector is emerging as the primary growth engine, particularly in Asia-Pacific and Europe. However, the market faces supply-side constraints: 5–8 major producers control an estimated 65–75% of nameplate capacity, leading to extended lead times of 6–10 weeks for specialty grades. Qualification cycles for energy-grade compounds have lengthened to 12–18 months as OEMs demand rigorous aging and chemical-exposure validation. Despite these challenges, the outlook to 2035 remains robust, with capacity additions targeting clean-room compounding and twin-screw extrusion lines purpose-built for energy-sector specifications. This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the market size, growth trajectory, demand structure, supply capability, trade flows, pricing, and competitive landscape, offering a data-driven view for manufacturers, distributors, investors, and procurement teams navigating this dynamic market. The baseline scenario for the global HNBR compounds market anticipates a compound annual growth rate of 9–13% from 2026 to 2035, with the market index reaching 240–280 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook is underpinned by the accelerating deployment of battery gigafactories and grid-scale energy storage systems, which require high-performance sealing solutions capable of withstanding aggressive electrolytes and thermal cycling. In the baseline, Asia-Pacific remains the largest and fastest-growing region, accounting for an estimated 45–55% of global HNBR consumption in the energy domain, driven by gigafactory construction in China, South Korea, and Southeast Asia. Europe and North America follow, supported by renewable integration projects and data-center backup power investments. Supply-side dynamics are expected to remain tight through the early forecast period, as capacity expansions are concentrated among a few major producers and qualification timelines for new entrants stretch to 12–24 months. Price premiums for HNBR over standard NBR are projected to persist in the 60–100% range, with energy-grade compounds commanding an additional 15–25% premium. Feedstock cost volatility for acrylonitrile and butadiene poses a risk to margin stability, though quarterly contract resets provide some flexibility. Overall, the baseline scenario assumes no major demand-disrupting technological substitutions, but acknowledges that alternative elastomers or sealing technologies could capture niche applications if qualification bottlenecks persist. The market is expected to remain structurally concentrated, with strategic partnerships and capacity investments shaping competitive dynamics through 2035. The battery manufacturing and energy storage sector is the primary growth engine for HNBR compounds, driven by the global build-out of gigafactories and grid-scale storage projects. HNBR seals are critical in electrode coating and electrolyte filling equipment, where resistance to aggressive electrolytes and thermal cycling is essential. As battery production capacity expands, particularly in Asia-Pacific and Europe, demand for energy-grade HNBR compounds is projected to accelerate. Qualification cycles of 12–18 months ensure that once specified, HNBR compounds remain in place for the equipment's lifecycle, creating a stable aftermarket. Key demand indicators include gigafactory construction announcements, battery production volumes, and grid storage installations. By 2035, this segment is expected to account for the largest share of HNBR consumption, supported by ongoing innovations in battery chemistry and manufacturing processes. Current trend: Rapid growth. Major trends: Gigafactory expansion in China, South Korea, and Southeast Asia, Increasing adoption of solid-state batteries requiring new sealing solutions, Grid-scale energy storage projects for renewable integration, Rising demand for electrolyte-resistant compounds, and Shift toward local sourcing of battery components in Europe and North America. Representative participants: Zeon Corporation, LANXESS AG, NOK Corporation, Trelleborg AB, and Freudenberg Sealing Technologies. Demand indicators include vehicle production volumes, EV penetration rates, and regulatory mandates for emissions and safety. artigo.texto: A ABB anunciou o lançamento do Infinitus, um portfólio de soluções de Corrente Contínua (CC) projetado para gerenciar as crescentes demandas de energia dos Data Centers de IA. O portfólio acelerará a adoção de arquiteturas CC em Data Centers, melhorando a eficiência energética e reduzindo a pegada da infraestrutura de energia, ao mesmo tempo em que aumenta a capacidade de computação disponível. A ABB espera que outros setores de alto consumo energético façam a mesma transição. A Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA) prevê que a demanda global de eletricidade dos data centers mais que dobre até 2030, e a ABB estima que aproximadamente 25–40% da nova capacidade instalada em 2030 poderá utilizar distribuição CC. Espera-se que os chips de IA de próxima geração consumam 1 MW por rack ou mais, um aumento em relação aos quase 200 kW atuais, exigindo uma mudança para uma arquitetura CC capaz de sustentar o desempenho e, ao mesmo tempo, impulsionar a eficiência energética. Com a distribuição em 800 VCC, a pegada é mais compacta, eliminando etapas redundantes de conversão e reduzindo as perdas de calor dos sistemas convencionais de corrente alternada (CA). Um relatório recente da BCG/ABB calculou que a distribuição CC gera ganhos de eficiência energética superiores a 5% e aumenta o espaço disponível para racks de computação. Para um Data Center de 500 MW, um ganho de eficiência de 5% pode significar 25 MW adicionais de energia para cargas de TI geradoras de receita e mais de US$ 300 milhões em receita adicional potencial por ano. Com ganhos de eficiência de 5% em um campus de data center de 500 MW, a economia de energia ao longo de um ano seria equivalente a abastecer Washington D.C. por quase uma semana inteira. Giampiero Frisio, presidente da área de negócios de Eletrificação da ABB, afirmou: “A ABB é pioneira em tecnologia CC há mais de 25 anos em diversos segmentos. Estamos trabalhando em estreita colaboração com fabricantes de chips, clientes hyperscale, parceiros de fornecimento e entidades do setor para definir os padrões e o ritmo da implementação de arquiteturas CC de alta eficiência. O Infinitus é o primeiro portfólio a fornecer os blocos de construção para qualquer arquitetura de Data Center — seja CC nativa ou híbrida CA/CC — para alimentar com eficiência os chips de IA de próxima geração. Essa tecnologia trará ganhos de eficiência energética semelhantes a outros setores de alto consumo, como manufatura em larga escala, energias renováveis e operações marítimas.” O Infinitus é o primeiro portfólio integrado Source-to-rack de CC do setor. Em seu núcleo está a inovadora tecnologia de transformador de estado sólido Infinitus da ABB, que permite que as instalações operem com uma pegada menor e maior eficiência energética. Como o único grande fornecedor de eletrificação com o primeiro disjuntor de estado sólido totalmente certificado pela IEC do mundo e um UPS estático de média tensão pioneiro no setor em produção, a ABB oferece uma amplitude de tecnologia incomparável no mercado. O portfólio CC Infinitus da ABB inclui cinco blocos de construção principais: Powertrains de Média Tensão fornecem energia estável e resiliente da rede elétrica ou de geração no local; Fontes CC e Qualidade de Energia convertem CA em CC, eliminando a conversão do white space; Distribuição de Energia CC entrega energia de forma segura e confiável, permitindo maior densidade de potência em uma pegada menor; Proteção de Energia CC fornece proteção para operadores, servidores de IA e hardware contra sobrecorrentes CC; Otimização de Resfriamento reduz o consumo de energia no grey space e no white space com acionamentos de velocidade variável e motores conectados em CC. A ABB trabalha com os clientes para projetar soluções adaptadas às suas demandas específicas de energia, layout das instalações e matriz energética. Essa abordagem de parceria garante que cada implantação seja otimizada para máxima eficiência e confiabilidade. O portfólio Infinitus complementa os sistemas CA tradicionais com a flexibilidade da CC, apoiando os clientes em todas as arquiteturas de energia e, ao mesmo tempo, permitindo eficiência, confiabilidade e escalabilidade sem precedentes para os Data Centers da era da IA. Para Data Centers de próxima geração, essa arquitetura integrada permite a entrega de energia de alta densidade e alta eficiência que os futuros chips de IA exigem. Com vários componentes principais produzidos nos próximos doze meses, espera-se que as primeiras instalações nativas em CC que utilizam o portfólio Infinitus completo sejam instaladas e operacionais em dois a três anos. O lançamento do portfólio amplia o apoio à colaboração contínua da ABB com a Nvidia, anunciada pela primeira vez em outubro de 2025, para desenvolver arquiteturas de energia de 800 VCC para instalações de IA em escala de gigawatts. A ABB traz mais de 25 anos de experiência em CC e mais de 700 patentes abrangendo energias renováveis, geração de energia, armazenamento de energia, motores e acionamentos.

artigo.texto: 26/09/2026 08:18 26/09/2026 11:30 Redação com Ascom - Prefeitura de Delmiro Gouveia Compartilhe nas redes sociais Delmiro Gouveia recebeu nessa sexta-feira (25) a apresentação do projeto Eco Polo Nordeste, iniciativa que prevê a implantação de um novo complexo industrial no município, com foco em bioenergia, tecnologia e mobilidade elétrica. Projeto apresentado nessa sexta-feira (25) prevê complexo industrial com bioenergia, reaproveitamento de calor e caminhões elétricos. Foto: Assessoria Entre os empreendimentos anunciados está uma usina de etanol de milho do Grupo Milenium Bioenergia. A expectativa apresentada é de geração de empregos diretos e estímulo ao cultivo de milho na região. O projeto também prevê a instalação de um polo de data centers de hiperescala voltados à inteligência artificial. Conforme a proposta divulgada, o complexo deve funcionar de forma integrada ao parque de bioenergia nos próximos seis anos, com reaproveitamento do calor gerado pelos servidores nos processos térmicos da biorrefinaria. Outra previsão é a instalação de uma montadora de caminhões elétricos da FNM, associando a proposta a tecnologias de energia limpa e produção automotiva. Os empreendimentos anunciados ainda deverão avançar pelas etapas de planejamento, licenciamento, infraestrutura e implantação. A expectativa é que o Eco Polo Nordeste amplie a atividade industrial, tecnológica e agrícola no município. Recent developments show project owners and developers having a bad time while the trading space booms, he argues. Australia: developer model is dead The Australian market has matured and simply developing and selling projects is no longer a viable business, writes Sheng Fang, global strategy at EV infrastructure firm StarCharge. “The venture-capital-style returns that once came from securing land, approval and a connection offer have evaporated,” he said. What affects BESS ROI Ever wondered why two BESS with almost the same data sheet can have completely different return on investmetn (ROI) timelines? Angie Z, director of strategic partnerships for supplier Gooree dived into this in a much-commented post. artigo.texto: The Bulgarian battery boom: From zero to global leader September 25, 2026 The international energy sector currently has a curious case study in an unlikely place: Bulgaria, a country in southeastern Europe with a population of just 6.4 million, now has one of the world's highest ratios of battery storage to total power capacity, outpacing markets like California, Germany and China. In less than two years, Bulgaria's battery storage capacity has gone from zero to making up nearly a quarter of the country's total installed power capacity, fueled by EU funding and private capital worth close to €3 billion ($3.4 billion), according to calculations by Bulgaria's leading business publication Capital. Bulgaria was lucky enough to escape the worst of the heatwaves and droughts that forced a cut in nuclear and hydro output in Hungary and Romania this summer. During that period, it turned its batteries into a key grid stabilizer for neighboring markets and profited by storing cheap solar power and selling it in the evening when prices spike. And while experts say the Bulgarian battery boom went "under the radar," it remains to be seen how this rapid development will affect the other generators of power, whether the current business model is sustainable and whether private investment will dictate a shift in the national strategy for the country's energy transition. What is the Bulgarian battery boom? In January 2026, a report by the energy think tank Ember estimated Bulgaria's battery capacity — both operational and in the pipeline — to be 1.66 GW. Eight months later, capacity had more than tripled to 5.4 GW, according to data from ENTSO-E. Bulgaria's Ministry of Energy told AFP it had already reached 5.7 GW. "Two years ago, no one imagined we would have even half of this capacity," Ivaylo Stanchev, editor-in-chief of the business publication Capital, told DW. Stanchev compiled one of the country's most comprehensive lists of battery projects, filling a gap left by the absence of an official public database. The list itself reflects investment levels that have outpaced official forecasts. While the rapid battery buildout was sparked by the Next Generation EU recovery fund and the subsequent RESTORE programs, which approved €700 million ($797 million) in funding for 113 projects, Stanchev estimates that private investment amounted to almost three times that figure: roughly €2 billion. Although most of the lithium batteries come from China, the investors are mostly from Bulgaria or from other European countries, which see potential in the growing niche. How much can the batteries store? "When fully charged, the batteries can store enough energy to power the whole country for several hours," said Stanchev, drawing a comparison that, although practically impossible, illustrates the scale of the development. Its effects are already tangible: Bulgaria produces a large amount of solar energy and buys more from Greece and Romania. Daily prices during the summer tend to be low or even negative during the sunniest hours of the day, allowing batteries to buy cheap energy, store it and discharge it in the evening, when local and international markets need it, at a higher price. The main export destination is Romania, which was particularly badly hit during the summer as it had to reduce nuclear capacity because of the drought along the Danube. Bulgaria, historically a net exporter, has thus turned into a regional battery hub, with an operational storage capacity that is now greater than that of Greece and Romania combined. What is the impact of this rapid development? There is no measurement that isolates the batteries' specific electricity price contribution, but Bulgaria's average price fell relative to other countries in the region during the first summer of large-scale battery operation. And while households in Bulgaria are subject to fixed electricity prices set by the state and have not yet seen a reduction in their electricity bills, industrial companies benefited from the change. "Between August 1 and August 16, the average day-ahead electricity price per MWh in Bulgaria was €132.2 — almost €14 lower than the price in Romania, even though they used to be almost equal," said Stanchev, adding that the difference comes mainly from the evening hours where the batteries' effect is most at play. Additionally, the batteries bring more security to the grid both domestically and regionally — as well as more revenue from exports and potential tax revenue from the company profits, he explained. Yet, these effects are part of the summer period snapshot, raising questions about the sustainability of the model throughout the year. Is this all good news? "Such record development should always be taken with a pinch of salt," said Kaloyan Staykov, chair of the Management Board of the Energy Management Institute in Bulgaria, adding that the year-long effects of the vast battery buildout "are yet to be seen." Staykov argues that, while a positive development for the market overall, the shift has come at a cost for conventional energy generators. "While the electricity price during the evening peak is now down, the generation that used to be more profitable during those hours needs to make up for the lower revenue stream, which pushes up the baseload price," he said. This issue points to a broader one. "Investments in batteries go beyond any national strategy for what the sector will look like in 10 or 20 years' time," he said, adding that "the role of national strategic roadmaps is changing from a leading one, to a following one." This comes at a time when Bulgaria is slowly pursuing a transition away from coal, including the expected phase-out of coal mining. At the same time, the country is advancing the rehabilitation of a massive pumped-storage hydropower plant (Chaira) and intends to build two new nuclear reactors at the Kozloduy Nuclear Power Plant in the years to come. artigo.texto: A Hyundai testa baterias E-GMP em segunda vida como armazenamento de energia para carregadores rápidos O Hyundai Motor Group e a LG Energy Solution estão testando um sistema de armazenamento de energia com baterias usadas (UBESS). O projeto de demonstração analisará se as baterias dos veículos E-GMP podem ser reutilizadas em estações de recarga rápida. Aqui estão os principais fatos: - A primeira instalação de teste em Hwaseong, na Coreia do Sul, possui 200 kWh de capacidade de armazenamento. - O teste utiliza baterias de veículos E-GMP, como o Hyundai Ioniq 5 e o Kia EV6. - Será testado o nivelamento de picos de demanda para reduzir os picos de consumo durante o carregamento ultrarrápido. Tecnologia e desempenho: Testando baterias de segunda vida O projeto-piloto avaliará a viabilidade técnica do uso de baterias de veículos aposentados em sistemas de recarga estacionários. Seu sistema de armazenamento de 200 kWh contém conjuntos de baterias usadas provenientes de veículos fabricados com a plataforma modular E-GMP. Os testes se concentrarão em algoritmos de carga e descarga, segurança térmica e na capacidade de retenção das baterias à medida que envelhecem em condições reais de operação. Ao armazenar eletricidade da rede durante horários fora de pico, o sistema tem como objetivo absorver picos de demanda e reduzir a sobrecarga na rede local. Contexto e infraestrutura: Testando uma economia circular de baterias As montadoras estão cada vez mais testando formas de reutilizar baterias antes de reciclar suas matérias-primas. Assim como a BMW, com sua instalação de armazenamento na fábrica de Leipzig, e a Mercedes-Benz Energy, a Hyundai está analisando como as baterias usadas de veículos elétricos podem entrar em uma segunda fase de vida útil. Enquanto grandes sistemas comerciais de armazenamento, como o Megapack da Tesla, utilizam células novas, o projeto-piloto UBESS se concentra em avaliar se as baterias usadas são economicamente viáveis em estações de recarga rápida. Entre os obstáculos a uma implantação mais ampla estão a avaliação precisa do estado de saúde dos módulos usados e a falta de padrões de certificação finalizados. O projeto-piloto UBESS é um teste prático para verificar se uma economia circular de baterias pode funcionar. Seus resultados mostrarão se os sistemas de armazenamento que utilizam baterias E-GMP desativadas podem ser ampliados de forma segura e econômica a longo prazo. Fonte(s) Imagem da Hyundai: Hyundai

artigo.texto: BYD will unveil its first vehicle fitted with a solid-state battery in 2027. It has not yet disclosed the specific model or a mass-production timetable. On Sept. 27 (local time), IT outlet Engadget reported that BYD said it is in a "leading position" in solid-state battery technology and commercialisation. Stella Li (스텔라 리), BYD executive vice president, said in a recent interview with Spanish edition of Carwow that BYD leads the solid-state battery field and is ahead in both commercialisation and technology. She added that BYD will unveil 1 model that first applies the technology in 2027 to back up that claim. It has not been confirmed whether the 2027 vehicle will be a mass-produced model for general consumers. Li did not disclose the specific model, launch date, battery capacity or performance. So far, the disclosed information is closer to a plan to apply solid-state battery technology to an actual vehicle and present it. The remarks also align with a roadmap disclosed by Sun Huajun (쑨화쥔), chief technology officer (CTO) at BYD battery subsidiary FinDreams, at a battery conference in February 2025. Sun presented a plan to begin demonstrations and vehicle fitment of solid-state batteries in 2027 and move into large-scale production and deployment around 2030. BYD is developing sulfide-based solid-state batteries in particular. BYD does not expect solid-state batteries to immediately replace existing lithium-ion batteries. Lian Yubo (롄위보), BYD chief scientist, said at the time that solid-state batteries will mainly be used in premium models and be applied alongside lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries depending on vehicle price ranges. That means LFP batteries will not disappear in the short term but will be used in parallel with solid-state batteries. Solid-state batteries replace the liquid electrolyte in existing lithium-ion batteries with a solid electrolyte. Solid electrolytes may enable higher energy density, which could reduce battery size and weight while increasing driving range per charge. Lower fire risk and possible operation in extreme temperatures are also cited as advantages. The sulfide-based solid-state batteries BYD is developing are also presented as offering potential improvements in fast charging, safety and lifespan. Cost is the biggest obstacle for the current technology. As a result, solid-state batteries are discussed as likely to be applied initially to premium models that are relatively expensive. Models such as the Denza Z have been mentioned as candidates, but BYD has not confirmed specific models for application. Competition among automakers over solid-state batteries is also continuing. Toyota aims to launch a solid-state battery vehicle in 2027 to 2028, and Mercedes has been testing an EQS equipped with a solid-state battery. Stellantis began road tests in 2026 of a development vehicle for the Dodge Charger Daytona fitted with a solid-state battery. Honda signed a joint research agreement on solid-state batteries with QuantumScape this year. With BYD's announcement, the solid-state battery race has moved a step further beyond the laboratory and into actual vehicle application. But with 2027 presented as the technology application and demonstration stage and around 2030 as the large-scale production stage, key factors for actual commercialisation are expected to be future vehicle performance, production costs and the scope of deployment.

artigo.texto: Image/CBAK Energy Technology According to CBAK Energy Technology, on September 23, CBAK Energy Technology and Nanjing Gaochun Economic Development Zone officially signed an investment agreement, and a 12 GWh sodium-ion battery cell project is about to land in Gaochun, Nanjing, Jiangsu. It is reported that the project has a planned total investment of approximately 3 billion yuan. Once fully completed and reaching full production, it is expected to add 4.8-5 billion yuan in sales revenue for the company. The company plans to advance the implementation of project construction-related work in H2 2027. The new production line will enable large-scale manufacturing of 32140-series sodium-ion battery cells, continuously iterate and optimize cell performance, and drive sodium-ion batteries from small-batch sampling to large-scale commercial application, providing the market with cost-effective energy storage and power battery solutions beyond lithium batteries. On the technical front, CBAK Energy Technology's self-developed 32140-series sodium-ion battery cells have completed multiple rounds of rigorous performance validation, featuring excellent wide-temperature-range performance, high safety, and long cycle life. The discharge retention rate remains outstanding even in low-temperature environments of -40°C, making the cells adaptable to complex operating conditions across different regions with significant temperature differences between north and south. The products are targeted at diversified scenarios including residential ESS, portable energy storage, light transportation vehicles, and backup power supplies. According to public information, CBAK Energy Technology, as a mainstream enterprise in China's large cylindrical battery sector, has long been deeply engaged in R&D and manufacturing along both lithium battery and sodium-ion battery technology routes. Leveraging the mature industrial supporting facilities, business environment, and locational advantages of Gaochun, Nanjing, the landing of this major project represents an important achievement of two-way empowerment and coordinated development between government and enterprise. The project focuses on sodium-ion battery cell R&D, large-scale production, and system integration business. Upon completion, it will supply sodium-ion battery products to diversified markets including energy storage, light power, and specialty power supplies, serving as another important technology route in the new energy sector and helping accelerate global electrification.

artigo.texto: Hitachi Energy’s battery energy storage system qualifies as NVIDIA DSX Ready BESS Features | 22.09.2026 | 3 min read Battery energy storage helps address the growing power demands of AI factories with resilient and flexible energy infrastructure Artificial intelligence is transforming industries at an unprecedented pace. Behind every AI model, data center, and digital service lies a growing challenge: access to reliable electricity. As AI factories increase in scale and complexity, battery energy storage is becoming essential for delivering the resilience, flexibility, and reliability that AI workloads demand. Hitachi Energy's battery energy storage system (BESS) has qualified as NVIDIA DSX Ready BESS as part of the inaugural DSX Ready launch, meeting the applicable reference design requirements for AI factory power infrastructure. The program helps customers identify qualified infrastructure building blocks and evaluate BESS solutions for resilient, reliable and scalable power systems. AI factories, the facilities that power the training and deployment of advanced AI models, are driving electricity demand while placing increasingly complex requirements on power systems. As these facilities grow in size and computing capacity, data center operators need energy infrastructure that can respond quickly to fluctuations in demand while maintaining continuous operations. Beyond storing energy, Hitachi Energy’s BESS serves as a flexible energy platform, supporting power continuity, power quality and operational flexibility while helping facilities respond to changing load conditions and applicable grid requirements. By rapidly absorbing or supplying power, the system supports demand response, energy cost optimization and the stabilization of dynamic AI workloads. These capabilities help data centers integrate renewable power, support grid code compliance and operate more effectively within available grid capacity. A core aspect of the NVIDIA DSX Ready program is ensuring compatibility with the NVIDIA DSX reference architecture, which helps standardize the design of power infrastructure for AI factories. The program enables customers to identify qualified technologies that can simplify deployment planning and support reliable operations across interconnected systems, including power, cooling, monitoring, and facilities management. As AI factories continue to scale, customers need power systems that can be deployed, integrated, and expanded quickly while maintaining reliability and resilience. As one of the first qualified BESS solutions in the NVIDIA DSX Ready program, this recognition reinforces Hitachi Energy's position at the forefront of AI factory electrification combining advanced technologies, power quality solutions and systems expertise to support end-to-end power infrastructure for the next generation of AI applications. Hitachi Energy's qualified solution combines energy storage, power conversion, automation, and digital technologies in an integrated architecture designed to support the dynamic energy requirements of AI-driven operations. The qualification encompasses Hitachi Energy's power converters and industry-leading power plant control capabilities that provide the responsive and reliable power conversion needed for next-generation AI data centers. By enabling precise power balancing, grid support, and energy optimization, the solution helps align BESS deployments with the performance, efficiency, and reliability objectives of the NVIDIA DSX Platform while seamlessly connecting energy storage systems with data center electrical infrastructure. The NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform brings together compute, networking, power, cooling, facilities and software to support AI factory design and operations. The DSX Ready program helps customers identify qualified power and cooling solutions that meet applicable NVIDIA DSX reference design requirements. The achievement reflects a broader trend across industries: as digitalization accelerates and AI adoption expands, energy infrastructure is becoming a critical enabler of innovation. Technologies such as Hitachi Energy’s BESS, alongside advances in grid infrastructure and digital solutions, will play an increasingly important role in ensuring that the growth of AI is supported by reliable, resilient, and sustainable power systems.

artigo.texto: Anthropic, OpenAI Keep Expanding the AI Data Center Map — and the Financing Gets Harder Key Highlights - Major AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI are securing multi-billion dollar compute commitments and expanding their infrastructure footprints globally. - The infrastructure buildout now involves complex financing, permitting, and construction challenges, moving beyond simple demand forecasting. - Gigawatt-scale campuses are being developed in diverse regions, emphasizing inference workloads and regional deployment strategies. - Nscale’s IPO disclosures reveal the scale and financial intricacies of the AI infrastructure boom, highlighting the gap between demand contracts and actual operational capacity. - Financing structures, including large private investments and bonds, are becoming central to enabling the massive infrastructure projects needed for frontier AI. September has offered one of the clearest pictures yet of what the frontier AI race looks like when translated from models and tokens into physical infrastructure. Anthropic has moved aggressively to lock down dedicated compute in the United States while establishing its first major data center foothold in Australia. OpenAI, meanwhile, has expanded into Malaysia through Nvidia-backed Firmus as the financing behind its much larger infrastructure ambitions continues to grow more complicated. All in all, the developments suggest that competition between the leading AI labs is entering another phase. Securing GPUs remains essential, but the harder problem is increasingly assembling the entire chain around them: land, power, cooling, networks, project finance and counterparties capable of delivering capacity measured in hundreds of megawatts — and increasingly gigawatts. That distinction is important for the data center industry. The AI infrastructure story is no longer simply about projected demand. It is increasingly about which commitments can actually become operating megawatts. Anthropic’s $45 Billion Bet Gets More Concrete The most revealing new detail came not from Anthropic itself, but from Nscale. The Nvidia-backed AI infrastructure provider filed for a U.S. initial public offering on Sept. 18, providing new financial and technical detail around a massive compute agreement first reported in August. Nscale’s SEC filing says it entered four GPU services agreements with Anthropic on Aug. 25 that could generate approximately $44.6 billion in aggregate payments. The agreements call for Nscale to provide Anthropic with dedicated infrastructure built around Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems at the company’s planned Monarch Compute Campus in Mason County, West Virginia. The deployments are structured in four tranches with multiyear service terms. Reuters previously reported the agreement at roughly $45 billion over six years, covering about 460 MW of compute capacity at Monarch. (The agreement follows Anthropic’s $19 billion, 401-MW lease with TeraWulf in Kentucky, another enormous commitment that illustrates how aggressively the AI developer is securing dedicated infrastructure ahead of demand). That alone would make the project notable. But Nscale’s IPO prospectus reveals the scale of the larger campus around it. Monarch sits on approximately 2,250 acres and is planned with more than 8 GW of gross power capacity, including an initial 2 GW of gross generation supporting roughly 1.37 GW of IT load targeted for the first half of 2028. Nscale has increasingly described itself as a vertically integrated infrastructure platform stretching from behind-the-meter generation through data centers, GPUs and cloud software. There is, however, an important caveat. Nscale disclosed that it must obtain qualifying financing for the GPU equipment and data center infrastructure required under the Anthropic agreements — and that as of the IPO filing it had not secured binding commitments for that financing. The disclosure reinforces a challenge DCF has been tracking as the gigawatt AI buildout faces its execution test: enormous contracted demand does not by itself secure the financing, power, equipment or construction capacity needed to deliver operating megawatts. The agreements also remain subject to specified delivery and service-availability requirements. That qualification may be as significant for the data center market as the $44.6 billion headline. The demand signal is extraordinary. But contracts of this magnitude increasingly represent the beginning of the infrastructure challenge rather than its conclusion. Nscale Illustrates the New AI Infrastructure Math Nscale itself offers a useful snapshot of how dramatically that equation has changed. The company reported $140.6 million in revenue for the first six months of 2026, up from $10.4 million a year earlier, while posting a net loss of approximately $1.02 billion. It now claims more than $103 billion in active and contracted total contract value and a power pipeline exceeding 10 GW. Reuters noted that its largest customer represented 52% of first-half revenue, while Microsoft and Anthropic are expected to become major customers going forward. This is increasingly characteristic of the AI infrastructure market: enormous contracted demand sitting against businesses that must spend staggering sums before much of the associated capacity can generate revenue. Nscale is hardly alone. What makes its filing valuable is that it exposes the machinery behind the boom unusually clearly. Another $35 Billion Compute Commitment Nscale is not Anthropic’s only enormous infrastructure commitment. At the beginning of September, Reuters reported that Anthropic had signed a roughly $35 billion cloud computing agreement with Nvidia-backed Lambda, securing access to infrastructure at a roughly 350-MW data center being developed by Hut 8 in Nueces County, Texas. artigo.texto: Data centers podem gerar 'boom' de negócios internacionais no Ceará Projetos no Pecém ampliam oportunidades em comércio exterior, logística e atração de capital estrangeiro A expansão dos data centers no Complexo do Pecém pode posicionar o Ceará em uma cadeia global que envolve tecnologia, energia, logística e comércio exterior. O movimento ganhou escala com a aprovação do projeto da Voltalia na ZPE do Pecém, com investimento previsto de R$ 181,7 bilhões, que se soma ao empreendimento da ByteDance, controladora do TikTok, cujas obras já estão avançadas. Acrescenta-se a esta equação ainda o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), sancionado pelo Governo Federal neste mês. O regime concede incentivos tributários e exige contrapartidas em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação, além de critérios de sustentabilidade. Comércio exterior em alta Para Augusto Fernandes, especialista em comércio internacional e empresário, os efeitos vão além dos próprios data centers. "Quando falamos em data centers, não estamos falando apenas de tecnologia. Estamos falando de uma cadeia internacional que envolve importação de equipamentos, serviços especializados, logística, energia, infraestrutura e capital estrangeiro", afirma. Segundo ele, o Estado reúne a estrutura do Pecém, a ZPE, energia renovável e cabos submarinos com conexão internacional. Exportação e importação Os projetos na ZPE são voltados à exportação de serviços de processamento de dados. Informações de usuários de outros países são processadas no Ceará e "exportadas" digitalmente, gerando divisas. A maior parte dos equipamentos vem do exterior, sobretudo da Ásia. A lista inclui: • Servidores de alta performance, GPUs para IA e unidades de armazenamento; • Switches, roteadores e componentes eletrônicos; • Sistemas de refrigeração, geradores de backup e cabos especiais. A previsão é de cerca de 15 voos cargueiros por mês vindos da China a partir de 2027. ZPE e Redata suspendem ou isentam Imposto de Importação, IPI e PIS/Cofins. São esses equipamentos que constituem grande parte do investimento previsto dos data centers, superando a casa dos R$ 100 bilhões, enquanto a construção gira em torno de R$ 10 bi a R$ 12 bi.
