artigo.texto: Last March, I helped pass HB1834, the bill that helped start the conversation about data center protections, through the State House. Unfortunately, it died in the Senate. As State Policy Manager for an environmental advocacy group, I spearheaded an advocacy movement to inform legislators in Harrisburg just how vital these protections were for Pennsylvanians. While the bill earned support on both sides of the aisle, my opponent Shelby Labs sided with data center developers and utility companies over her constituents. She voted against these guardrails, continuing her support for data centers after voting to give them millions in tax breaks. I’m grateful for the Shapiro administration’s latest executive order (EO2026-05) establishing some of the protections we fought for with HB1834, but I’m running for State House because our community needs a Representative in Harrisburg who will codify those protections, not do the bidding of AI companies. One of the most important data center guardrails I’ve fought for is protecting ratepayers from utility cost increases by requiring data centers to supply their own energy. Ratepayer protections act as a road block for utility companies: they can’t raise your bill just because a data center has added to demands on the grid. Energy supply requirements ease that demand. They require data centers to bring energy from outside or fund the infrastructure development necessary to pull their weight. These measures work to prevent everyday working families from shouldering the intense demands of power hungry data centers, but they won’t stop costs from going up on their own. The PJM grid supports the energy usage of thirteen states, and already we’re seeing the edges of what the framework can handle. Part of the reason behind electricity rates climbing year after year is the constant upgrades necessary to keep our infrastructure up and running. Regardless of the protections we attempt to place around data centers, their existence will further strain our energy supply and eventually raise our rates. We must invest in improvements to our existing grid while looking toward renewable, clean energy supplies as a solution. Our grid is sagging under its responsibility, and it’s time to work on offloading that pressure. Legislators are looking into best practices in distributing energy demand during non-peak hours, but this only lessens the issue. Increasing our clean energy capacity and fixing our power grid’s infrastructure can divert pressure from our grid entirely and lower our utility costs while creating good union jobs. HB1834 required data centers to partially power themselves with clean energy, but EO2026-05 only encourages it. Mega corporations, big tech, and the billionaires behind data centers need Pennsylvania. They need our land, our space, our developed infrastructure, but it’s time they pay for it. Our community should see the benefits, not simply the downsides, of data centers if they want to call our state home. Far from a tax break, I support requirements to ensure data centers bolster our renewable energy availability. Let’s ensure the costs of data centers are paid for by the billionaires who insist on building them, while Pennsylvanians reap the benefits of an unburdened energy grid and the advantages afforded by investments in our clean energy capabilities. In my role as State Policy Manager, I worked on solutions to bring labor, affordability, and the environment together, like when I wrote the VETSS Act connecting veterans with jobs in the sustainability sector. I saw firsthand what Pennsylvanians needed to keep their open spaces beautiful and green while helping the state’s hard workers, and I also saw which representatives weren’t willing to let go of a campaign donation to protect their constituents. I have extensive experience working on the most pressing issues in the state. I’ll take that same approach to data centers and energy policy as your next State Representative. When I get to Harrisburg I promise to pursue the solutions that will not only keep costs down in the near future, but benefit Pennsylvania for generations to come.

artigo.texto: WEG anuncia investimentos para ampliação do projeto da fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) Publicado às 8h57 A WEG (WEGE3) anunciou nesta sexta-feira, 25, a ampliação do projeto de sua nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), em construção em Itajaí, no estado de Santa Catarina. Anunciada em fevereiro deste ano, a nova fábrica terá um investimento total estimado de R$ 330 milhões e capacidade anual de 4 GWh, atendendo à demanda crescente por soluções associadas à transição energética, com início das operações previsto para o segundo semestre de 2027. “Reforçando a estratégia da companhia de apoiar o crescimento do mercado de armazenamento de energia no Brasil, na iminência do primeiro Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade Armazenamento Nacional, a ser realizado em dezembro de 2026, o projeto atualizado incorpora maior nível de automação e ganhos de eficiência industrial que permitirão ampliar a capacidade produtiva”, afirmou a WEG em um comunicado. O BESS desempenha papel fundamental nos sistemas elétricos modernos, principalmente na integração das fontes renováveis como solar e eólica, permitindo armazenar energia nos momentos de maior disponibilidade e disponibilizá-la quando necessário. Essa flexibilidade contribui para a estabilidade do sistema elétrico, maior eficiência operacional e aproveitamento dos recursos energéticos.

artigo.texto: The Instalco company Enervion begins work two large-scale battery storage projects in Finland The Instalco subsidiary Enervion Oy has commenced work on two battery storage systems in Kittilä in northern Finland. Work on site has now begun with groundworks and initial installations. The projects comprise turnkey delivery followed by ten years of operation and maintenance services. The assignment comprises two parallel battery energy storage projects, Sirkka and Köngäs, each with a power of 10 MW and a storage capacity of 20 MWh. The systems are based on Enico Jupiter Nova technology, developed specifically for demanding Nordic and Arctic climate conditions. Enervion is responsible for turnkey EPC delivery covering design, procurement, construction, installation and commissioning, followed by ten years of operations and maintenance services. The customer is wattss Services AG, a Swiss-based battery storage specialist with over six years of experience. "These projects are a clear testament to what Enervion and the Instalco Group can achieve within large-scale battery storage. Sirkka and Köngäs are two technically demanding projects carried out in parallel under challenging Arctic conditions in Lapland. By combining expertise from across the Group and our partner network, we are capable of undertaking increasingly large and advanced energy projects," says Anssi Laaksonen, CEO of Enervion. The contracts were signed in May 2026 and the order value of approximately EUR 10 million was included in Instalco’s order backlog at the end of the second quarter of 2026. The facilities are scheduled for completion and commissioning in summer 2027. Enervion is an Instalco subsidiary in Finland specialising in large-scale battery and energy storage projects. For further information, please contact: Fredrik Trahn, Head of Communications and Sustainability, Instalco +46 70 913 67 96 fredrik.trahn@instalco.se Instalco is one of Northern Europe’s leading installation companies in the areas of electrical, heating and plumbing, ventilation, industry, and tech & consulting. We design, install, service and maintain properties and facilities in Sweden, Norway, Finland and Germany. Operations are conducted through more than 175 subsidiaries with strong local presence, supported by a small central organisation. Instalco is listed on Nasdaq Stockholm under the ticker INSTAL. For more information, visit www.instalco.se. Image Attachments Attachments The Instalco company Enervion begins work two large-scale battery storage projects in Finland

artigo.texto: The people of northern Virginia have been living with data centers for many years. The area is home to the world’s largest concentration of data centers. In a survey we conducted, we found northern Virginians support development restrictions that could make data centers more transparent and accountable to the public. But they care about some types of regulations more than others. artigo.texto: High energy costs, data centers take center stage at Lt. Governor Hashmi's listening tour ROANOKE, Va. (WSET) — High energy costs are becoming a major topic as Virginia heads toward the midterm elections. Virginia Lieutenant Governor Ghazala Hashmi held a listening tour in Roanoke Thursday night, giving residents an opportunity to voice concerns about rising energy bills, data center development and a proposed merger between NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy. RELATED: - Gov. Spanberger unveils accountability framework for data centers, launches AI task force - Virginia lawmakers split on Gov. Spanberger’s new data center executive order The lieutenant governor also brought Delegates Lily Franklin and Sam Rasoul, as well as Roanoke Mayor Joe Cobb, to listen and respond to concerned residents. The event drew protesters who gathered outside Melrose Plaza before Hashmi's appearance. “NextEra’s got to go, hey, hey, ho, ho, NextEra’s got to go,” protesters chanted. One protester said the issue goes beyond the size of the companies involved. “This is not just some big business company coming in. This is a monopoly,” the protester said. The Dominion-NextEra Merger is valued at just under $67 billion. Of the over 100 people who attended, all of them mentioned they are concerned that the merger will cause their power bills to rise. "It is now time for you to throw the money changers out of the temples of our democracy," one man said. "You must protect Virginians as this merger will harm us," another man said. "This is not about bringing more power; it's about control and money." But energy costs were not the only issue protesters brought to the event. “We don’t know what they’re gonna do except they will want data centers,” one protester said. “They’ve already spoken, and they wanna profit from data centers.” Many people near Roanoke, Roanoke County, and Botetourt County shared concerns about higher energy costs due to data centers coming to the area. In Botetourt County, Google is building a data center, and many families are now concerned a data center could be coming to the Woodhaven Technology Park in Roanoke. During the listening session, residents asked what state lawmakers could do to address data center development across Virginia. “While we fight on the ground here to stop construction of data centers that are being passed without our consent, what are your plans in the next legislative session to help us out on the statewide level and stop those things?” one person asked. Delegate Sam Rasoul, a Democrat representing Virginia's 38th District, said he would support a moratorium if legislation came before him. “If I have an opportunity to vote on a moratorium, you know it’s a yes,” Rasoul said. “I’m ready to co-sponsor that kind of legislative motion.” Delegate Lily Franklin, a Democrat representing the 41st District, also called for a moratorium. “I just think it’s a full stop. We need a moratorium in Virginia on data centers,” Franklin said, drawing applause. Following the event, ABC13's Hayden Robertson spoke with Lieutenant Governor Hashmi to see where she stood on the moratorium debate. "You just heard from two members of your own members of your party and Republicans also calling for a moratorium on data centers, as Virginia is the data center capital of the world right now; if somebody brought that forward, would you vote in favor of a moratorium," Robertson asked. “In order to determine what we’re going to do next, I’m going to be reviewing every item of legislation that’s being proposed, most especially around our energy issues, and having read the language, I will be making my decision on should there be a tie in the Senate, then how I will take that vote," Lt. Governor Hashmi replied. The Lieutenant Governor also said data center developers should be responsible for paying for their own water and energy use rather than putting those costs on taxpayers. She also said that comments made during the Roanoke event concerning the Dominion-NextEra merger will be submitted to the Virginia State Corporation Commission for them to review as they discuss the merger.

artigo.texto: Having been in the information technology field since 1969, I have been reading about data centers in Lancaster County and how candidates for political office are responding to questions about them. Data centers consolidate computer power in one place to process massive amounts of information for multiple businesses. If everything goes well, large corporations will not only be saving money but also making large amounts of money. However, these centers are risky. When servers of multiple corporations are housed under one roof, even one breach of security can open opportunities for private information to cascade from business to business. Data centers will result in the elimination of jobs. They often need a huge amount of water to cool the servers, draining water from the community rivers, lakes and wells while raising the temperature in rivers and other waterways, killing fish and other water life. In addition, the air conditioning needed to cool the buildings will demand high levels of electricity, raising electricity costs and creating significant noise. I support state Sen. James Malone saying that we must pause building data centers until we have a clear understanding of how they will impact our communities. I approve of Gov. Josh Shapiro’s statement that businesses must be responsible for the costs of operation. I am pleased to hear that Jess Branas, candidate for the 97th Pennsylvania House District, is speaking up against data centers, pledging to work across the aisle and with townships to attract businesses that help communities to flourish — while bringing down energy costs. Richard Wilson West Earl Township

SÃO PAULO, Brazil, Sept. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A LG Electronics anuncia o lançamento da nova LG xboom Stage 501 no Brasil, ampliando seu portfólio de soluções de áudio com uma caixa de som portátil para a festa, desenvolvida para transformar qualquer ambiente em uma experiência completa de entretenimento. Para consumidores que procuram uma caixa de som bluetooth potente e com bateria de longa duração, a nova LG xboom Stage 501 chega como uma opção completa para festas e uso portátil. Combinando potência sonora, inteligência artificial, portabilidade e bateria de longa duração, o novo modelo foi projetado para acompanhar diferentes momentos de lazer, desde encontros casuais até celebrações de maior porte. A IA identifica e remove as vozes da música em tempo real, e cria uma experiência de karaokê prática e intuitiva, sem necessidade de aplicativos adicionais. Além disso, o recurso Key Changer permite ajustar o tom das músicas para diferentes vozes, tornando as apresentações ainda mais confortáveis e divertidas. Já o AI Lighting sincroniza os efeitos luminosos com o ritmo das músicas, criando uma atmosfera visual que acompanha cada momento da reprodução. A certificação IPX4 garante resistência contra respingos d’água e chuva leve, oferecendo mais tranquilidade para o uso em ambientes externos. Já a tecnologia Auracast(TM) permite conectar múltiplas caixas de som compatíveis para ampliar a cobertura sonora e criar experiências ainda mais imersivas em eventos de diferentes tamanhos. artigo.texto: The World Trade Organization will appoint experts to examine a complaint from Moscow over the European Union’s carbon border tax, a Geneva-based trade official said Friday. The decision was reached during a WTO Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) meeting, the official said on condition of anonymity. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official. The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) aims to ensure foreign producers pay a carbon cost similar to what European companies already pay under the bloc’s internal emissions trading system. Importers of carbon-heavy goods produced abroad like steel, aluminum and fertilizer must declare the CO2 emissions embedded in their products and pay a levy if they exceed EU standards. The EU has promoted the key environmental policy, which took effect at the start of the year, as a “virtuous” tool that encourages greener practices worldwide. But the policy has faced strong opposition amid charges that it restricts trade and favors European manufacturers. Arguing that the CBAM breaches the rules of global trade, Russia filed its initial complaint with the WTO over the policy in May last year. At that point, Moscow requested consultations with the EU and its member states regarding this issue, as well as on the two-decade-old Emissions Trading System (ETS), which enables certain industries to benefit from free carbon allowances. Brussels swiftly rejected the consultation request, insisting such discussions could not be fruitful given the circumstances created by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine since February 2022. Russian Drones, Missiles or Troops Could Test NATO Within Months, Danish Intelligence Says Moscow then asked the WTO this past July 10 to establish a panel of experts to examine the case, but the EU blocked the request. The DSB granted the second request on Friday, the trade official said. Under WTO regulations, parties in a dispute can block a first request for an arbitration panel, but if the parties make a second request, it is all but guaranteed to go through. In a communication sent to the WTO this week, the EU said Russia’s renewed panel request had created “an extraordinary situation” in which a country “that for more than four and a half years continues to wage a war of aggression... in violation of the most fundamental rules of international law” was asking for an assessment of the “international law compatibility of a regulatory, climate-oriented, environmental measure.” Brussels said it would agree to take part in the process due to its “firm support for the rules-based multilateral trading system,” but stressed that it would “only engage with the panel and not directly with the Russian Federation.” As long as Russia “is waging its war of aggression against Ukraine, it cannot expect to be able to rely on WTO rules for improved access for its exports to the market of the European Union,” the bloc said. artigo.texto: OVID TOWNSHIP, MI (WTVB) – Apex Clean Energy has officially commenced construction on its 75-megawatt Coldwater Storage battery facility in Branch County. Located east of Sanford Road in Ovid Township, adjacent to the ITC substation, the project is designed to capture and store power generated by the neighboring 150-megawatt Coldwater Solar farm, which went online last winter. The energy storage solution is being supplied by Canadian Solar’s subsidiary, e-STORAGE, which will integrate its proprietary lithium-ion phosphate-based SolBank 3.0 system to discharge electricity during peak demand hours. Commercial operation of the new battery facility is targeted for mid-2027. The official construction launch coincided with a celebration hosted by Apex Clean Energy, where company executives presented over $1 million in initial summer tax revenue payments to Coldwater and Ovid Townships. Local officials noted that while the existing solar installation is projected to inject nearly $30 million into the community over its lifetime, the newly started battery facility is estimated to contribute an additional $1 million annually during its first decade of operation. The continuous funds are slated to bolster vital public institutions, including local school districts, 911 emergency dispatch services, transit systems, and senior programs. Ovid Township Planning Commission Chair Andy Acmoody said grant funding from Apex has already paid for a tanker truck for the Lakeland Fire Department, a marine patrol boat for the Branch County Sheriff’s Office, and tornado warning sirens throughout the township.

artigo.texto: Zhang Yuegang, Professor of Tsinghua University: Solid-state batteries are stuck at the "two interfaces", while lithium metal batteries are trying to bypass this hurdle | Frontline Solid-state batteries are not necessarily the only answer for next-generation lithium batteries. Recently, at the 2026 Lithium Metal Battery Frontier Forum (LMBF 2026) held in Beijing, 36Kr had an exchange with Zhang Yuegang, the forum chairman and tenured professor at Tsinghua University. In the past few years, solid-state batteries have almost become one of the most popular technical directions in the power battery industry. However, in Zhang Yuegang's view, the industry first needs to clarify a basic concept: solid-state batteries and lithium metal batteries are not two technical generations that can be directly compared in the first place. The reason is that the two belong to different classification dimensions. The energy density of batteries is mainly determined by cathode and anode materials. The cathode can be lithium iron phosphate, high-nickel ternary, lithium-rich manganese-based or even sulfur, while the anode has evolved from graphite to silicon-carbon and lithium metal; the so-called solid state and liquid state distinguish the form of electrolyte. In other words, solid-state batteries change the electrolyte, while lithium metal batteries change the anode. It is still the cathode and anode that fundamentally determine how much energy a battery can store. Therefore, lithium metal anode batteries are also a key evolutionary branch of next-generation battery technology. In Zhang Yuegang's view, the currently booming solid-state battery route in the industry still has a number of material technical difficulties to overcome. As introduced, Zhang Yuegang is a tenured professor at Tsinghua University, an internationally renowned materials scientist with more than 30 years of experience in materials research at home and abroad. He has successively worked at the Nippon Electric Basic Research Institute, Stanford University in the United States, Intel, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Chinese Academy of Sciences and other institutions, and has achieved a number of important research results in the fields of nanomaterials, energy storage technology and other fields. Solid-state batteries are stuck at two "interfaces" The most attractive part of solid-state batteries for the industry is that they use solid electrolyte to replace flammable organic liquid electrolyte, so as to apply more cutting-edge cathode and anode materials and push the energy density up to the 500Wh/kg level. However, the interface problem of solid electrolyte still plagues the industry today, and Zhang Yuegang explained these difficulties in detail to 36Kr. Zhang Yuegang believes that the core problems can actually be attributed to two "interfaces". The first is the microscopic interface inside the cathode. The battery cathode is not a whole dense material, but composed of a large number of particles, with a large number of nano-scale pores inside. Liquid electrolyte can penetrate into these tiny spaces like water and fully contact with the cathode material; but solid electrolyte can hardly do this. If more solid electrolyte is added to improve ion transmission, it will take up the space of active materials that actually store energy, and eventually drag down the energy density of the whole battery. The second problem is the interface between the anode and the solid electrolyte as well as the lithium dendrite problem. A common judgment in the past was that solid electrolyte has higher mechanical strength and can physically block lithium dendrites. However, Zhang Yuegang believes that after more than ten years of research, various solid electrolytes still do not truly solve this problem at present. Solid materials naturally have microscopic defects, along which lithium will continue to grow. Once a penetration channel is formed, it may even quickly lead to internal short circuit. In addition, unlike liquids, solids cannot be fully wetted with each other, which is essentially closer to "point contact". In order to reduce the interface impedance, it is necessary to increase the proportion of electrolyte and the working pressure, but this contradicts the goal of improving energy density. Therefore, another evolutionary idea for the next generation of battery technology is to temporarily retain the liquid electrolyte and replace the anode with lithium metal first. The biggest obstacle for this route in the past was also lithium dendrites. It is difficult for lithium to always remain absolutely flat during the repeated deposition process, and it will gradually grow a structure similar to branches. Once the dendrites continue to grow and pierce the separator, it may cause an internal short circuit. Zhang Yuegang introduced that an important solution idea at present is to use additives in the liquid electrolyte to form a SEI protective film on the surface of lithium metal. When cracks appear in this film during the charging and discharging process, the additives can continue to react to dynamically repair the damaged area. In this way, dendrites can be controlled at the micron scale, which greatly reduces the risk of short circuit caused by their continuous growth. But the cost is also obvious: the continuous damage and repair of the SEI film means that the electrolyte will be continuously consumed. According to the progress given by Zhang Yuegang, relevant lithium metal batteries can now achieve hundreds of cycles, some high-specific-energy products at the 500Wh/kg level have exceeded 300 cycles, and products at the 400Wh/kg level can reach 600 cycles, but there is still a gap from the thousands of cycles generally required by new energy vehicles. The first batch of lithium metal batteries may "fly to the sky" first Zhang Yuegang judges that the more realistic commercialization path for lithium metal batteries is to enter drones and eVTOL

O que é BESS e por que a WEG está investindo R$ 330 milhões nesse mercado? WEG ampliou para R$ 330 milhões o investimento na nova fábrica de sistemas BESS em Itajaí (SC) Resumo completo A WEG ampliou para R$ 330 milhões o investimento em sua nova fábrica de sistemas BESS em Itajaí. A unidade terá capacidade produtiva de 4 GWh por ano, o dobro do inicialmente anunciado, e deve começar a operar no segundo semestre de 2027. Guardar a energia produzida pelo sol durante o dia para utilizá-la à noite ou armazenar parte da eletricidade gerada por um parque eólico quando há vento em abundância para liberá-la quando a geração diminuir. É para fazer esse tipo de gestão que existem os sistemas conhecidos pela sigla BESS, uma tecnologia que ganha espaço conforme aumenta a participação das fontes renováveis na geração de energia. E a WEG está aumentando sua aposta nesse mercado. A companhia anunciou a ampliação do projeto da nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias que está construindo em Itajaí, Santa Catarina. O investimento total estimado agora chega a R$ 330 milhões, enquanto a capacidade prevista para a unidade foi ampliada para 4 GWh por ano. A operação está prevista para começar no segundo semestre de 2027. Nova fábrica terá o dobro da capacidade anunciada inicialmente Quando o projeto da nova fábrica da WEG foi anunciado em fevereiro de 2026, a companhia informou que a unidade permitiria alcançar capacidade de produção de sistemas de armazenamento de energia equivalente a até 2 GWh por ano. Agora, antes mesmo de a fábrica entrar em operação, essa previsão passou para 4 GWh anuais, o dobro do anunciado inicialmente. Mas o que significa 4 GWh na prática? Para ter uma ideia da escala, 4 GWh correspondem a 4 milhões de kWh de energia. Uma residência da região Sul consome, em média, cerca de 213 kWh por mês, segundo dados da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE). Assim, a capacidade dos sistemas que a fábrica poderá produzir em um ano equivale, em quantidade de energia armazenável, a aproximadamente um mês de consumo de 19 mil residências. A comparação serve apenas para dimensionar a quantidade de energia. A fábrica não produzirá eletricidade, mas sistemas capazes de armazená-la para utilização posterior. Segundo a WEG, o projeto atualizado terá maior nível de automação e ganhos de eficiência industrial, permitindo atingir a nova capacidade produtiva. Afinal, o que é BESS? BESS vem de Battery Energy Storage System, ou Sistema de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias. Uma maneira simples de entender a tecnologia é imaginar uma bateria em escala industrial: em vez de armazenar energia para alimentar um celular ou movimentar um carro elétrico, esses sistemas guardam grandes quantidades de eletricidade para que ela possa ser utilizada posteriormente. Isso se torna especialmente importante com o crescimento de fontes renováveis como solar e eólica. Uma usina solar, por exemplo, produz eletricidade enquanto há incidência de sol, mas o consumo não necessariamente acontece no mesmo momento. O BESS permite armazenar parte dessa energia e disponibilizá-la mais tarde, inclusive em períodos em que a geração diminui. O mesmo princípio pode ser aplicado à energia eólica. Além de aproveitar melhor a eletricidade produzida, esses sistemas podem contribuir para dar mais flexibilidade e estabilidade à rede. A própria WEG explica em sua página dedicada ao BESS que a tecnologia também pode atuar no controle de tensão, regulação de frequência e capacidade de reserva do sistema elétrico. Por que a WEG está aumentando a aposta? Segundo a companhia, o mercado de armazenamento de energia vive um período de expansão impulsionado principalmente pelo crescimento das fontes renováveis e pela necessidade de maior flexibilidade e segurança no sistema elétrico. Outro fator observado pela empresa é a expectativa em torno do primeiro leilão de reserva de capacidade específico para armazenamento de energia no Brasil, previsto para dezembro de 2026. “O mercado de armazenamento de energia vive um momento de forte expansão, impulsionado pelo crescimento das fontes renováveis e pela necessidade crescente de maior flexibilidade e segurança para o sistema elétrico”, afirma Manfred Peter Johann, vice-presidente de Automação e Sistemas da WEG. Segundo o executivo, a ampliação demonstra a capacidade da companhia de adaptar seus investimentos às necessidades do mercado e apoiar o desenvolvimento do setor energético brasileiro. Tecnologia já começa a aparecer em aplicações reais Embora o nome BESS ainda seja pouco conhecido do grande público, a tecnologia já aparece em projetos brasileiros. Um exemplo ajuda a entender melhor sua utilidade: um projeto da WEG já combina energia solar e armazenamento em baterias em uma agroindústria, permitindo reduzir a dependência de geradores a diesel e aproveitar a eletricidade produzida pelos painéis solares. A lógica é relativamente simples: em vez de depender exclusivamente do momento em que o sol está gerando eletricidade, parte dessa energia pode ser guardada nas baterias e utilizada posteriormente. É justamente essa possibilidade de separar o momento da geração do momento do consumo que torna o armazenamento uma peça importante em um sistema elétrico com participação crescente de fontes renováveis. Nova fábrica terá alto nível de automação Desde o anúncio inicial, o projeto da unidade de Itajaí prevê linhas automáticas e semiautomáticas de montagem, além da utilização de robôs móveis autônomos na movimentação interna de materiais. A estrutura também contará com laboratório para testes, desenvolvimento e qualificação dos produtos e uma subestação preparada para simular condições reais de operação dos equipamentos. Na atualização do projeto, a WEG informou que decidiu incorporar um nível ainda maior de automação e ganhos de eficiência industrial. Com

artigo.texto: Shinsung E&G said on Sept. 28 that it will unveil its new All In One (AIO) data center cooling platform at Data Center World Asia (DCWA) 2026. DCWA is an event held in Singapore that showcases trends and technologies across the data center industry, including cooling, security and cloud infrastructure. Shinsung E&G will display a model of the AIO at its booth. AIO is an integrated server module combining servers and cooling equipment. The system can significantly reduce space requirements and construction time compared with conventional designs. Conventional data centers separately build data halls for servers, mechanical rooms and air-conditioning systems. For a 2.4-megawatt (MW) data center, AIO can reduce data hall floor space by 22% and floor-to-floor height by 20%. Equipment installation time can also be cut by about half. Each module can accommodate up to eight server racks. It supports power consumption ranging from 16 kilowatts (kW) per rack to as much as 140kW for graphics processing unit (GPU) servers. The system can combine In-Row cooling with direct liquid cooling (DLC), providing cooling performance designed for artificial intelligence (AI) server environments where heat generation is rising sharply. In-Row cooling places cooling units between server racks to remove heat, while DLC places cooling plates directly on heat-generating components and circulates liquid coolant to absorb the heat. The company will also install a kiosk at its booth to help visitors explore its products. It will present detailed specifications and deployment cases for key products including fan wall units (FWUs), which maintain consistent temperature and humidity inside data centers, and fan filter units (FFUs), which filter dust at the ceiling and blow clean air downward. "As the AI industry grows, data centers increasingly require precision cooling solutions optimized for high-heat, high-density environments," said Kim Tae-hyung, vice president at Shinsung E&G. "We will expand our data center business using the precision environmental control technologies we have accumulated in semiconductor and display cleanrooms." Shinsung E&G became the first Korean company to locally develop an FFU in 1991. It supplies equipment to Korean semiconductor and display companies including SK hynix and Samsung Display. More recently, the company has applied its precision cleanroom environmental control technology to data centers and is supplying infrastructure solutions for AI data centers.

artigo.texto: General Motors (GM), the largest U.S. automaker, is making extensive use of Korean companies as it prepares to mass-produce next-generation batteries. Its newly operational Battery Cell Development Center (BCDC), an entirely new battery cell production line, uses equipment from Korean battery equipment makers including PNT, Wonik PNE, Mplus and SEC across key processes ranging from electrode production and assembly to inspection. According to industry sources on Sept. 28, GM is conducting trial operations of battery cell production equipment at the BCDC located at its Technical Center in Warren, Michigan. Battery materials have also been introduced into some processes. GM plans to use the BCDC to develop next-generation battery cells, including lithium manganese-rich (LMR) batteries, and validate their production processes. GM already operates the Wallace Battery Cell Innovation Center (BCIC) at the Warren Technical Center. The BCIC is a research and development (R&D) facility that studies new battery materials and cell designs and produces prototypes. Its cell production capacity, however, is limited, making it difficult to identify process issues that may emerge when production is scaled up ahead of mass production. That is also why GM invested separately in the BCDC. While the BCIC can produce only dozens of prototype battery cells a week, the BCDC can produce thousands. The facility is also about 10 times larger than the BCIC. The BCDC has production capacity of 500 megawatt-hours (MWh), about one-hundredth that of a roughly 50-gigawatt-hour (GWh) Ultium Cells plant, GM's joint venture with LG Energy Solution. The BCDC's role is to conduct final validation of newly developed battery cells and production processes before they are deployed at mass-production plants. The BCDC produces prismatic battery cells. GM will initially validate LMR battery cells that it is developing for mass production in 2028. Sodium-ion batteries could also eventually undergo production-process validation at the BCDC. GM has been developing the technology by producing sodium-ion battery prototypes at the BCIC since June. GM adopted Korean battery equipment for key processes while building the BCDC production line. Korean equipment makers began shipping equipment late last year and installed it at the facility this year. PNT participated in the electrode process. The process involves coating battery materials, including cathode and anode materials, onto metal foil to produce the electrodes that form the basis of a cell. PNT had previously supplied equipment to Ultium Cells, establishing a business relationship with GM. The company is also known to have worked with GM on production equipment for key hydrogen fuel-cell components. Wonik PNE and Mplus supplied equipment for the assembly process, where electrodes are processed and assembled into battery cells. SEC supplied inspection equipment used to check the cells' internal condition and detect defects. In particular, Wonik PNE supplied notching and stacking equipment in addition to its core back-end process equipment. Notching cuts electrodes to a specified size, while stacking layers the cut electrodes. GM marks the first customer for which Wonik PNE has won and fulfilled orders for such equipment. Mplus equipment is used in the subsequent stage, where processed electrodes are inserted into prismatic cases and assembled. Mplus, which had focused primarily on equipment for pouch-type batteries, expanded into prismatic batteries and secured the GM supply deal. The BCDC supply track record could give the Korean equipment makers an advantage when GM invests in mass production of next-generation batteries. Because production processes are validated at the BCDC, the performance of the equipment can also be evaluated there. LMR batteries are likely to be the first target. GM is jointly developing LMR batteries with LG Energy Solution and plans to begin mass production at Ultium Cells in 2028. If the LMR battery production process validated at the BCDC is scaled up to the GWh level, additional investment in new equipment is expected to follow. "In the past, GM focused on researching the batteries themselves, primarily at the Wallace center, but with the BCDC it has moved to the stage of directly validating the actual production process," a source familiar with GM's battery business said. "As it gradually scales up production, it will validate both performance and cost competitiveness."

artigo.texto: The data center debate Weâve been warned in the past two weeks that artificial intelligence (AI) may kill us all in the next five to 10 years. Industry leaders have suggested there are dangerous developments in the works with AI models and how they are finding ways to self-adapt. Itâs a bit scary, and itâs overshadowing the positives that AI can provide for our personal lives and businesses. Data centers are at the core of this AI revolution, and they are mission-critical to our technological future. If you have a computer or cellphone, youâll be reliant on these new multibillion-dollar data centers to help you search, shop, compare and plan your life. These data centers will also drive business growth in many industries. From banking to manufacturing to healthcare and beyond, data centers will power business to provide the products or services in some sort of fashion. Their processing of data may more quickly identify your health emergency; it could streamline your factory production line; or it could spearhead the security to keep you protected from financial fraud or identity theft. For the data industry, specifically the companies that own and rely on these data centers, a word of caution: You have a huge public perception problem. Data centers are wildly unpopular with the general public. Recent polling conducted by Talk Business & Politics, in conjunction with Hendrix College, revealed that public opinion of data centers is âupside down,â as we say. With over 1,100 respondents, the poll asked: Would you strongly favor, somewhat favor, somewhat oppose, or strongly oppose the construction of a data center in your area to support artificial intelligence, or AI, technology in the U.S.? A little over 7% (7.1%) âstrongly favorâ the building of a data center in their community, while another 12% (11.9%) âsomewhat favor.â Conversely, 19% (18.9%) said they âsomewhat opposeâ the building of a data center in their region, while 51.5% said they âstrongly oppose.â About 10% (10.5%) had no opinion. Citizen concerns range from land and water usage, secrecy of rates and transactions, noise pollution, energy demand and potential rate increases for locals just to name a few. The backlash against data centers has risen quickly and is widespread. When you analyze the polling data, the first takeaway is the size of the âstrongly disapproveâ number. More than 51% is a huge negative number. Also, when a respondent answers a question in the âstronglyâ category, changing their opinion is extremely difficult to do. People donât go from âstrongly approve/disapproveâ in the opposite direction without significant persuasion. Other takeaways in the crosstabs show the strong opposition is found in all age groups, across party lines (Republicans are least strongly opposed), among men and women, and regardless of education levels. The one exception was in the breakdown of ethnicity. Asians, who were a very small sample size, were supportive of data centers. So why is the data center debate raging in Arkansas and America? The opposition is organized and loud and has found a variety of issues that unite opponents to speak out. Supporters of data centers are isolated â they tend to be solo companies â and quite frankly, they havenât been proactive enough in describing the advantages they can bring to communities and how they are mitigating concerns being raised by opponents. Data centers arenât going away. Artificial intelligence isnât going to disappear. The industry and the public are going to have to find some ways to coexist and be OK with their relationships. I donât know what those answers are, and Iâm not sure who or what institution should lead on this. For me, for the time being, Iâm calling on people with concerns to continue to raise them but to also be open-minded enough to have your concerns addressed. For the data center industry, I hope to see a more proactive approach to addressing those concerns and providing the information needed to reduce the skepticism. Finally, I call on all stakeholders in this debate to search for common ground. Data and its power have become an integral part of our lives. We have to find a way to make sure it doesnât kill us, kill progress or kill our hopes for a better future.

artigo.texto: Kuehne+Nagel and CATL partner to advance battery logistics and fleet electrification - Support Scope 3 emissions reduction across both companies value chains - Collaborate on electrified transport, battery logistics and battery storage initiatives - Explore battery swapping solutions in Asia Kuehne+Nagel and Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL), a global leader in new energy technologies, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to establish a strategic collaboration in battery logistics, transport electrification and emissions reduction initiatives. The partnership will initially focus on practical initiatives including the electrification of CATL transport flows in Europe and a battery-swapping pilot (provided by Qiji) for heavy-duty trucks, which is set to launch in China this year. Additional areas of collaboration include battery recycling and aftersales support, as well as energy storage and charging solutions for logistics sites. Together, these activities support both companies Scope 3 emissions reduction ambitions across their logistics and transportation value chains. As global leaders in our respective industries, CATL and Kuehne+Nagel share a commitment to accelerating the energy transition and achieving a net-zero emissions future, said Akin Li, Executive President of CATL Overseas Business. Our elevated partnership will not only contribute to both parties sustainability targets, but also help advance a greener future. Battery-electric vehicles are essential to decarbonising road freight, said Søren Schmidt, Executive Vice President Road Logistics at Kuehne+Nagel. Accelerating the transition requires solutions that are both high-performing and operationally viable. By combining CATLs battery expertise with our logistics capabilities, we can advance initiatives that help reduce our own emissions and those of our customers. The partnership comes at a time of rapidly growing demand for electric vehicles and energy storage solutions. In 2024, demand for electric truck batteries increased by more than 75%, while battery manufacturing capacity continues to expand through a growing network of gigafactories worldwide. About Kuehne+Nagel With approximately 88,000 employees across over 1,300 sites in close to 100 countries, the Kuehne+Nagel Group is one of the worlds leading logistics providers. Headquartered in Switzerland and listed on the Zurich stock exchange, it is the global number one in Air and Sea Logistics and holds strong market positions in Road and Contract Logistics. Supporting around 400,000 customers worldwide, the Group draws on its global network, logistics expertise, and data-driven insights to deliver end-to-end supply chain solutions for global companies and industries. About CATL Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL) is a global leader in zero-carbon new energy technology, committed to providing premier solutions and services for new energy applications worldwide. In 2025, CATLs EV battery consumption volume has ranked No.1 in the world for nine consecutive years, and it has ranked first in the market share of global energy storage battery shipments for five straight years. CATL enjoys wide recognition by global EV and energy storage partners. So far all the 20 battery factories under the Companys core operations have achieved carbon neutrality, and it aims to achieve carbon neutrality across the battery supply chain by 2035. artigo.texto: A expansão do mercado de armazenamento de energia está abrindo novas oportunidades para empresas e integradores do setor elétrico. Mas levar para o BESS a mesma lógica comercial usada na venda de sistemas fotovoltaicos pode resultar em propostas mal dimensionadas e projetos que não atendem à necessidade real do cliente. Esse foi um dos principais pontos discutidos no episódio #194 do Papo Solar, apresentado por Ericka Araújo e Gustavo Tegon, com a participação de Renan Casadei, gerente comercial de BESS da BelEnergy. Durante o programa, os participantes discutiram o que muda na venda de sistemas de armazenamento e quais informações precisam ser levantadas antes da elaboração de uma proposta. Entre as aplicações abordadas estão arbitragem de energia, backup, controle de demanda e atendimento a operações que precisam de maior segurança energética. Copiar proposta de concorrente pode aumentar risco em projetos de BESS Durante o episódio Casadei relatou o caso de um integrador que procurou a BelEnergy com uma proposta elaborada por um concorrente e solicitou uma solução equivalente, sem antes validar o dimensionamento do projeto. Ao aprofundar a análise das necessidades do cliente final, porém, foi identificada uma demanda que não estava contemplada na proposta original: o sistema também deveria fornecer backup para cargas críticas durante interrupções no fornecimento de energia. O projeto atendia um frigorífico, operação em que a continuidade do fornecimento pode ser determinante para conservar e evitar perdas dos produtos perecíveis. O caso foi utilizado para chamar a atenção para os riscos de replicar uma solução de armazenamento sem realizar uma análise técnica própria. Segundo Casadei, a definição dos equipamentos também deve partir das necessidades e da aplicação de cada cliente. “Muitos fazem o dimensionamento apenas com base na fatura. É possível fazer uma análise preliminar e identificar, por exemplo, que a principal necessidade do cliente é a arbitragem. Mas é importante deixar claro que se trata de uma avaliação inicial e que será necessária uma análise mais minuciosa. À medida que a negociação evolui, a proposta também precisa ser refinada”, disse Casadei. Na avaliação de Casadei, o problema surge quando uma análise preliminar passa a ser apresentada ao consumidor como uma solução definitiva, sem que o projeto tenha avançado para uma avaliação mais detalhada. ‘Um projeto de BESS não tem margem para erro, é preciso minimizar o máximo para eventuais problemas que podem acontecer”, disse Falta de segurança técnica pode comprometer a venda Outro ponto destacado por Renan Casadei é a necessidade de o integrador transmitir segurança sobre o funcionamento da solução oferecida. Como o mercado de BESS ainda está em processo de amadurecimento no Brasil, dúvidas sobre dimensionamento, operação, backup e desempenho podem surgir ao longo da negociação. Segundo ele, o problema ocorre quando o profissional não consegue explicar com clareza se o sistema será capaz de cumprir aquilo que está sendo apresentado ao cliente. Em projetos de maior valor, essa insegurança pode pesar na decisão de contratação. A atenção também deve chegar ao contrato. Casadei ressaltou a importância de definir de forma clara as responsabilidades do integrador, da distribuidora e do fabricante, além das condições relacionadas à garantia dos equipamentos e da solução. Casadei observou que, para o cliente, é importante saber quem será responsável pelo atendimento caso o sistema não apresente o desempenho esperado ou ocorra algum problema após a instalação. Nesse cenário, a garantia não deve ser tratada apenas como uma característica comercial do equipamento, o integrador precisa conhecer as condições estabelecidas pelo fabricante, os limites de cobertura e os procedimentos de acionamento, além de deixar claro ao cliente quais responsabilidades cabem a cada empresa envolvida no projeto. Casadei também chamou atenção para as consequências de erros de dimensionamento em sistemas de armazenamento. Em uma aplicação de arbitragem ou backup, por exemplo, uma solução incapaz de entregar a autonomia, potência ou funcionalidade prevista pode ter seu desempenho percebido rapidamente pelo cliente. Fatura de energia é apenas o começo Outro ponto discutido no Papo Solar foi o uso da conta de energia como base para dimensionar um BESS. A fatura pode ajudar em uma análise preliminar, mas não apresenta todas as informações necessárias para definir a solução. Dependendo da aplicação, o integrador pode precisar avaliar memória de massa, demanda contratada, perfil de consumo, cargas críticas, motores, compressores, sistemas de refrigeração, horários de funcionamento e impactos causados por interrupções no fornecimento. “É preciso entender a operação do cliente, como ele trabalha e qual é o seu perfil de carga. Isso inclui identificar a presença de cargas indutivas, motores, sistemas de refrigeração e compressores, além de avaliar o comportamento dessas cargas ao longo do dia e verificar se existem quedas de energia”, explicou. Casadei acrescenta que é necessário avaliar como o sistema será carregado, em que um cliente pode, por exemplo, querer utilizar baterias para reduzir o consumo no horário de ponta, mas não possuir margem suficiente em determinados períodos para carregar o BESS sem ultrapassar sua demanda contratada. Projetos de BESS podem ter retornos muito diferentes O episódio também mostrou por que comparar projetos de armazenamento apenas pelo investimento inicial ou por um payback padrão pode levar a conclusões erradas. Durante a conversa, Tegon citou o caso de um resort no Nordeste com aproximadamente 5 MWh de armazenamento, cuja operação dependia de geradores a diesel. Segundo ele, o projeto teria alcançado um payback estimado em cerca de oito meses devido ao perfil específico da operação. Casadei também citou projetos em que o armazenamento atende a outras necessidades. Em uma localidade do Amazonas abastecida por geradores a die

artigo.texto: China and the U.S. may be competing for dominance in artificial intelligence, but some Chinese manufacturers are eyeing the U.S. data center buildout as an opportunity. "We can see very big potential in the U.S. market," said S.K. Lee, a global vice president with Singapore-registered Brightray, an AI infrastructure company. "The China market is equally important, but we can see that there's a stronger demand in the U.S." Brightray's sole manufacturer is Chinese firm PrefabDC, which makes prefabricated data centers. Brightray manages the construction of the buildouts. Even with public backlash over the AI data center buildout growing, the U.S. boasts more AI data centers than any other country, with 5,427 in 2025, according to data published by the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence. China had 449, according to the same report. U.S. tech giants like Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon are estimated to spend around $765 billion combined this year on AI infrastructure. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon recently said that figure could hit $1 trillion next year. Chinese companies like Alibaba have committed far less. But the Chinese government has outlined plans to invest $295 billion to build data centers over the next five years, though it's still a far cry from U.S. private-sector investment. "Chinese companies just are not generating as much revenues from their AI services," said Jeffrey Ding, AI expert and assistant professor at The George Washington University. "And that's one of the reasons why they're not able to invest in these enormous data center buildouts that their competitors in the U.S. are doing." Ding said the deeper issue is "there is not as much demand for the AI services." Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington has brought renewed focus on the China-U.S. trade dynamic, and AI was a prominent part of talks between Xi and President Donald Trump. But the relationship between the rivals remains fraught. American policymakers and the security establishment fear cybersecurity risks and worry the U.S. could become reliant on China for critical infrastructure, potentially giving leverage to its main AI competitor. The Trump administration is considering bans on Chinese open-weight AI models as well as new types of Chinese data center components. "It is a very challenging environment between the geopolitics recently between the tariffs we've been seeing and the recent bans," said Benjamin Boucher, principal analyst on supply chains for Wood Mackenzie. "I think it is just going to depend on what we see at a political level over the coming years in terms of how it evolves." Boucher explained that the U.S., which is facing shortages in key components such as electrical equipment, doesn't have a lot of what it needs domestically. And while the U.S. has some components, there are long lead times, and China "can offer those at a much more favorable timing." "China is definitely very important towards the U.S. supply chain for data centers at the moment," Boucher said. China, the world's largest manufacturer, is already deep in the U.S. supply chain and has been for years. Chinese companies supply transformers, batteries and fiber-optic cables, among other products. At a factory in the eastern Chinese trading city of Yangzhou, Brightray's Lee explained how it benefits from China's extensive supply chain. "These materials, equipment are sourced from different parts of the world and a very big portion come from China because China's supply chain is very integrated and comprehensive. That's the reason why we have the factory here in China," Lee said. Prefabricated construction is used in the U.S., but mainly for the modules inside a building rather than modules that include the exterior of the building, as Brightray says it does. The method allows a company to build most of the data center inside a controlled environment to protect against weather and unexpected events at a site. In the U.S., data centers take on average about two to three years to build, industry analysts told CNBC. Brightray said its prefabricated data centers with PrefabDC can cut construction time by at least half.

artigo.texto: A Koller Alimentos, empresa brasileira fabricante de vinagres, colocou em operação uma solução de armazenamento de energia da Hoymiles, com 125 kW de potência e 261 kWh de capacidade, em sua unidade de Erechim (RS). Desenvolvido em parceria com a integradora Rossi Energia, o projeto busca reduzir o consumo de eletricidade da rede no horário de ponta, quando a geração solar da indústria já não está disponível. Entre 18h e 21h, a empresa poderá utilizar parte da energia armazenada para atender à demanda da operação e diminuir a exposição às tarifas mais elevadas desse período. A companhia já conta com um sistema de geração solar fotovoltaica, responsável pelo fornecimento de energia renovável durante boa parte do dia. A instalação do BESS acrescenta armazenamento à infraestrutura existente, permitindo gerir o uso da energia solar, da bateria e da rede elétrica conforme as necessidades da unidade. De acordo com a Hoymiles, além da gestão dos custos, o armazenamento também poderá, futuramente, desempenhar um papel importante para a continuidade da operação por meio de uma solução de backup. Na produção de vinagre, por exemplo, processos como a fermentação dependem do fornecimento de energia e podem ser impactados por interrupções. Para a Koller, a decisão de investir no BESS considerou a redução dos custos no horário de ponta e também a possibilidade futura de diminuir os impactos provocados por quedas de energia. “Optamos por comprar o BESS, primeiro pela redução de custo do horário de ponta e segundo para evitar a parada em quedas de energia do sistema das vinagreiras de fermentação. Acreditamos que com isso não teremos mais tempo de parada e as bactérias não sentirão os 15 ou 20 segundos que demora até o gerador transferir a energia” expressou Ronald Bernardo Coller, CEO da Koller Alimentos. O modelo utiliza resfriamento líquido, possui componentes com proteção IP55, sistemas de segurança em múltiplas camadas e gerenciamento em nuvem. Segundo a fabricante, o equipamento mantém a potência nominal de 125 kW em temperaturas de até 50 °C.” Após a instalação, o sistema passou pela etapa de comissionamento, acompanhada pela equipe da Hoymiles. O trabalho ocorreu sob a gestão de André Issa, gerente de Pós-Vendas, com participação do engenheiro Leo Moraes e de Philipe Espostes, além do suporte da matriz da companhia.” Fabiano Rossi, CEO da integradora, ressalta que o suporte oferecido pela fabricante pesou na escolha do equipamento. “Entre as diferentes marcas disponíveis para o projeto, a escolha pela Hoymiles levou em consideração a solidez da empresa, sua experiência no mercado e, principalmente, o suporte e a parceria que construímos ao longo dos anos. Esses fatores foram decisivos para seguirmos com a marca neste projeto”, afirmou. “Sabemos que o mercado brasileiro de armazenamento está em uma fase importante de maturação e que a tecnologia precisa vir acompanhada de conhecimento e suporte”, disse Issa. “Nosso time está comprometido em trabalhar lado a lado com integradores e distribuidores, desde o planejamento até o comissionamento e o pós-venda. Acreditamos que é construindo essa experiência em conjunto, compartilhando conhecimento e dando segurança aos nossos parceiros, que vamos contribuir para o desenvolvimento sustentável do mercado de BESS no Brasil”, acrescentou Issa. Desenvolvido para aplicações comerciais e industriais, o HoyUltra 261A reúne armazenamento, conversão e gerenciamento de energia em uma solução integrada. Na aplicação da Koller, o sistema permite coordenar a geração fotovoltaica, o armazenamento e o consumo da rede elétrica de acordo com as necessidades da indústria. O foco atual é a gestão do consumo no horário de ponta, com possibilidade de integração futura a uma solução de backup. Para Ariel Martins, gerente comercial da Hoymiles, o armazenamento amplia as possibilidades de gestão de energia pelas empresas. “O nosso compromisso é construir esse mercado de forma consistente, combinando tecnologia, suporte local, capacitação e proximidade com parceiros. Queremos que o armazenamento de energia seja entendido não apenas como uma solução de backup, mas como uma ferramenta estratégica para gestão de energia, eficiência operacional e maior controle sobre os custos das empresas”, pontuou Martins,. Outros projetos em andamento O projeto de Erechim não é uma iniciativa isolada, a companhia já trabalha em outros projetos BESS no país, ampliando gradualmente a aplicação de suas soluções em diferentes cenários comerciais e industriais. “Ver o primeiro HoyUltra 261A instalado e entrando em operação no Brasil representa a concretização de um trabalho que envolve produto, parceiros, equipe técnica e desenvolvimento de mercado. É um marco importante, mas também o início de uma etapa maior da nossa estratégia de armazenamento no país”, ressaltou Débora Garcez, Marketing Manager LATAM da Hoymiles. artigo.texto: Dispute Settlement Body Panel to review EU carbon border adjustment mechanism and emissions trading scheme Note This summary has been prepared by the WTO Secretariat’s Information and External Relations Division to help public understanding about developments in WTO disputes. It is not a legal interpretation of the issues, and it is not intended as a complete account of the issues. These can be found in the reports themselves and in the minutes of the Dispute Settlement Body’s meetings. More DS639: European Union and its Member States - Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism The Russian Federation submitted its second request for the establishment of a dispute panel to determine whether the European Union's CBAM and alleged export subsidy under the EU scheme for trading greenhouse gas emission allowances are consistent with the EU's WTO commitments. The EU had objected to Russia's first request for a panel at a DSB meeting on 24 July. Russia said the CBAM package creates significant trade barriers for covered goods imported into the EU. Russia added that the EU's allocation of allowances to certain companies under the Emissions Trading System (ETS) amounts to an export subsidy intended to strengthen the competitiveness of certain domestic industries. The EU said it was extraordinary that Russia - which the EU said continues to "wage its war of aggression against Ukraine" - is seeking to rely on international law to improve access for exports into the EU market. The EU said it would take part in the proceedings, not to legitimize Russia's actions, but to reaffirm the EU's strong support for the rules-based multilateral trading system. It also expressed confidence that both the CBAM and the ETS are consistent with WTO rules. The DSB agreed to the establishment of the panel. Argentina, Brazil, Canada, China, India, Indonesia, Japan, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the Republic of Korea, Malaysia, Norway, Paraguay, Singapore, Switzerland, Chinese Taipei, Thailand, the United Kingdom and the United States reserved their third-party rights to participate in the proceedings. DS629: Türkiye - Measures Concerning Electric Vehicles and Other Types of Vehicles from China China and Türkiye said they sought to continue engagement with each other for a resolution of this dispute. They requested additional time for the DSB to consider for adoption the panel report circulated on 28 July 2026 in the case initiated by China regarding measures adopted by Türkiye concerning electric vehicles and certain other types of vehicles originating in China. The parties asked that the DSB further delay consideration of the panel report until 27 October 2026. The DSB agreed to the request. Appellate Body appointments proposal Colombia, speaking on behalf of 130 members, introduced for the 100th time the group's proposal to start the selection processes for filling vacancies on the Appellate Body (AB). The extensive number of members submitting the proposal reflects a common interest in the functioning of the Appellate Body and, more generally, in the functioning of the WTO's dispute settlement system, Colombia said. The United States said that it does not support the proposed decision. The US reiterated that it has set out its fundamental concerns on WTO dispute settlement and that the proposal does not address those concerns. The US stated that, despite efforts by the US and other members in recent years to identify suitable reforms, there remains a wide divergence in views among members regarding the necessary changes. Over 20 members then took the floor and reiterated their support for the joint proposal and for the urgent need to restore a fully functioning dispute settlement system. Several of the members that took the floor encouraged others to consider taking part in the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement (MPIA), which provides the possibility of resorting to arbitration under Article 25 of the Dispute Settlement Understanding (DSU) in case of an appeal in disputes between any two or more participating members. Several members welcomed Cambodia as the newest member to join the MPIA. The list of current members of the MPIA is available here. Colombia, on behalf of the 130 members, said it regretted that for the 100th occasion members have not been able to launch the selection processes. Ongoing conversations about reform of the dispute settlement system should not prevent the Appellate Body from continuing to operate fully, and members shall comply with their obligations under the DSU to fill the vacancies as they arise, Colombia said for the group. Information session on dispute settlement reform The DSB Chair, Ambassador Guilherme de Aguiar Patriota of Brazil, said members' statements at an informal meeting held on 24 July broadly supported information sessions to preserve institutional memory on DS reform. The first information session, held after the DSB meeting on 25 September, consisted of two parts: the first on the history of the DS system, including trends in dispute activity and use of different means of dispute resolution; the second on DS reform processes following the 12th and 13th Ministerial Conferences. artigo.texto: WEG investe R$ 330 mi em fábrica de baterias A WEG, multinacional catarinense do setor eletroeletrônico, anunciou nesta sexta-feira (25) a ampliação do projeto de sua nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, denominado BESS, em construção em Itajaí, no Litoral Norte de Santa Catarina. O investimento total foi elevado para R$ 330 milhões, consolidando a aposta da companhia no mercado de armazenamento de energia no Brasil. A decisão ocorre em um momento estratégico, às vésperas do primeiro Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade de Armazenamento Nacional, previsto para dezembro de 2026. A empresa destacou que a ampliação do projeto da planta em Itajaí faz parte da estratégia da companhia de apoiar o crescimento do mercado de armazenamento de energia no Brasil. O movimento reflete a confiança da WEG na expansão da demanda por soluções que integrem fontes renováveis à matriz elétrica, um desafio crescente para o setor energético nacional. Investimento reforça aposta em armazenamento O novo aporte eleva o compromisso financeiro da WEG com a unidade fabril, que já estava em construção. A atualização do projeto incorpora maior nível de automação e ganhos de eficiência industrial, o que permitirá ampliar a capacidade produtiva da planta. Com isso, a companhia busca se posicionar de forma competitiva para atender à demanda projetada pelo leilão de reserva de capacidade e por outros segmentos do mercado. O BESS (Battery Energy Storage System, ou Sistema de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias) é uma tecnologia essencial para os sistemas elétricos modernos. Ele permite armazenar energia nos momentos de maior disponibilidade — como em dias ensolarados ou com ventos fortes — e disponibilizá-la quando a geração é insuficiente ou a demanda é alta. Essa flexibilidade contribui para a estabilidade do sistema elétrico, maior eficiência operacional e melhor aproveitamento dos recursos energéticos. A decisão da WEG de ampliar o projeto também sinaliza uma leitura positiva do ambiente regulatório brasileiro. O Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade de Armazenamento, marcado para dezembro de 2026, é apontado como um marco para o setor, pois deve criar um mercado formal para sistemas de armazenamento em larga escala. A empresa, no entanto, não detalhou projeções de receita ou participação esperada nesse certame. Impacto para a indústria e comércio Para empresários e comerciantes do interior paulista, o movimento da WEG pode ter reflexos indiretos relevantes. A expansão da capacidade produtiva de baterias tende a impulsionar a cadeia de fornecedores de componentes eletrônicos, serviços de engenharia e logística, gerando oportunidades de negócios para pequenas e médias empresas. Além disso, a consolidação do armazenamento de energia pode reduzir custos operacionais para indústrias e comércios que buscam maior previsibilidade no fornecimento elétrico. Especialistas do setor apontam que o armazenamento em baterias é peça-chave para a integração de fontes renováveis, como solar e eólica, que são intermitentes por natureza. Com sistemas BESS, empresas podem armazenar energia excedente gerada em horários de pico de produção e utilizá-la em momentos de tarifas mais altas, otimizando a conta de luz. Esse benefício é especialmente atrativo para o agronegócio e a indústria de transformação, segmentos fortes na região noroeste paulista. A WEG não divulgou cronograma atualizado para a conclusão das obras da fábrica em Itajaí, tampouco a capacidade produtiva final após a ampliação. A fonte não detalhou se haverá geração de empregos diretos adicionais em decorrência do novo investimento. No entanto, a elevação do aporte sugere um compromisso de longo prazo com a produção local de sistemas de armazenamento, o que pode fortalecer a competitividade da indústria nacional no setor. Contexto do leilão de reserva O primeiro Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade de Armazenamento Nacional, previsto para dezembro de 2026, é aguardado como um divisor de águas para o mercado de baterias no Brasil. O certame deverá contratar potência e energia de sistemas de armazenamento, criando um fluxo de receita previsível para os investidores. A WEG, ao ampliar sua fábrica antes do leilão, demonstra intenção de participar ativamente desse novo mercado. Para as empresas do interior paulista, o leilão pode abrir espaço para projetos de armazenamento associados a usinas solares e eólicas, muitos deles localizados no estado de São Paulo. A redução de custos de baterias, impulsionada pela produção local, pode viabilizar sistemas de menor porte para comércios e indústrias, ampliando o acesso a essa tecnologia. A fonte não detalhou, porém, se a WEG pretende comercializar soluções BESS diretamente para o varejo ou apenas para grandes geradores e utilities. Em resumo, o aumento do investimento da WEG em sua fábrica de baterias em Itajaí reforça a tendência de crescimento do armazenamento de energia no Brasil. A iniciativa deve gerar efeitos positivos na cadeia produtiva e abrir novas oportunidades para negócios que dependem de energia confiável e de custo competitivo. Perguntas Frequentes Qual é o valor do investimento da WEG na megafábrica de baterias em Santa Catarina? A WEG elevou o investimento para R$ 330 milhões na megafábrica de baterias em Itajaí, Santa Catarina. Onde a WEG está construindo sua nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias? A nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, chamada BESS, está em construção em Itajaí, no Litoral Norte de Santa Catarina. Qual é o papel do BESS nos sistemas elétricos modernos, segundo a WEG? O BESS permite armazenar energia nos momentos de maior disponibilidade e disponibilizá-la quando necessário, contribuindo para a estabilidade do sistema elétrico, maior eficiência operacional e aproveitamento dos recursos energéticos, especialmente na integração de fontes renováveis como solar e eólica.

artigo.texto: NH Investment & Securities Signs Carbon Credit Cooperation Agreement with Trinity Aviation for Domestic and International Markets Cooperation in Supplying CORSIA Credits and Consignment Trading of Domestic Emission Permits Collaborating to Support Airlines Responding to Carbon Regulations NH Investment & Securities and Trinity Aviation signed a carbon market business agreement on the 21st at Trinity Aviation headquarters located in Gangseo-gu, Seoul. After the signing ceremony, Gunhoo Park, Head of Client Solutions Division at NH Investment & Securities (right), and Dongbin Seo, Executive Director of Management Support at Trinity Aviation (left), took a commemorative photo. Photo by NH Investment & Securities View original image NH Investment & Securities announced on September 28 that it had signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Trinity Aviation on September 21 for "mutual cooperation concerning the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) and the Emissions Trading Scheme for greenhouse gases." This agreement marks the first case in which a domestic securities firm and an airline company have established a strategic partnership encompassing the supply of CORSIA credits and consignment trading of domestic greenhouse gas emission permits. Trinity Aviation plans to align with the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport’s aviation sector carbon reduction policy and the implementation direction of CORSIA, by linking NH Investment & Securities’ expertise in the carbon market and financial capacity to its own needs for procurement of emission permits. The company emphasized that the significance of this MOU lies in connecting airlines’ acquisition of emission credits and cost management for procurement to the specialized services of a financial institution. Purchasing emission credits requires not only consideration of the necessary quantity and timing, but also a careful review of market prices and trading conditions. Both companies will collaborate to establish stable and efficient procurement plans based on demand information and market analysis. As part of the collaboration, Trinity Aviation will first secure 20,000 tons of CORSIA credits through NH Investment & Securities, and plans to obtain at least 10% of the emissions that need to be offset, in stages, before the Phase 1 settlement deadline in January 2028. The two companies will use this transaction as a starting point for cooperating on CORSIA credit supply, sharing information such as projected mandatory quantity and procurement timing to strengthen the foundation for mid- to long-term procurement. The companies will also cooperate on establishing and operating a consignment trading framework for the domestic Emissions Trading Scheme (K-ETS). NH Investment & Securities will support Trinity Aviation’s smooth trading of carbon credits through its proprietary consignment trading system for emission permits, and provide specialized information on market analysis and policy trends. As a result, Trinity Aviation will be able to establish a systematic support system that covers both domestic emissions trading and procurement of CORSIA credits. Gunhoo Park, Head of Client Solutions Division at NH Investment & Securities, stated, "This agreement is meaningful as a strategic collaboration model that connects a securities company’s expertise in carbon finance with the real emission credit needs of airlines. We will support airlines’ stable acquisition of emission credits based on the supply of CORSIA credits and consignment trading of domestic credits, and expand customized carbon finance services that help respond to procurement costs and market fluctuations."
