artigo.texto: BYD unveils its first heavy-duty electric semi and it packs 1,000HP, charges in 20 minutes and carries a huge battery warranty Published on Sep 27, 2026 at 6:04 PM (UTC+4) by Ben Thompson Last updated on Sep 27, 2026 at 6:04 PM (UTC+4) Edited by Mason Jones BYD has unveiled its first heavy-duty electric semi, and it can be charged in 20 minutes. And that’s not the only impressive stat attached to the ET44. Capable of hauling 44-ton combinations and packing 1,000HP, there’s no questioning the power of this new offering from BYD. It’s enough to make us ask – should Tesla be worried? How BYD is on the rise If you’ve spent any length of time reading automotive news these past few years, the rip-roaring success of BYD won’t have passed you by. The Chinese carmaker has been flexing on its competitors for a long while now, whether it’s charging EVs in freezing cold temperatures or getting its SUVs to drive on three wheels. And that’s not forgetting their sales figures, which have been soaring around the world, from South America to Australia. With their back-to-back successes, it’d only make sense that the company would be looking to expand. And what better way to take on its primary rival – Tesla – than by putting out a semi truck? As you will undoubtedly know, the Tesla Semi has been making headlines all over the place, whether it’s being driven by Jay Leno or generating buzz for the weight of its battery. But after all that, is it about to get upstaged by the ET44? Let’s take a closer look. The ET44 is a heavy-duty semi to be reckoned with BYD has said the ET44 is capable of hauling a full 44-ton combination. It can’t be a coincidence that this is the maximum payload allowed on European roads. It also surely can’t be a coincidence that this is four tons more than what the Tesla Semi is capable of. Powered by an LFP Blade Battery, the ET44 can reach a peak power of 735kW (just under 1,000HP). It’s not just in physical capabilities that this semi poses a threat to Tesla – it’s also expected to be cheaper. It’s anticipated to arrive in Europe by 2027, with expansion in Canada, Australia, and the UK likely to follow. But it’s not such a clear-cut clean sweep for the ET44, as noted by YouTuber The Electric Viking. “[The Tesla Semi] charges at up to 1.2 megawatt with 548 or 822 kWh packs. So [BYD] has the charging edge and Tesla clearly has the bigger battery and will get significantly more range,” he explained. “The headline here is BYD’s own megawatt chargers. This truck pulls more than 1.5 megawatt and goes from 20 to 80% in about 20 minutes. So, it’s the fastest charging truck. “The real story here though, is BYD turning up with the truck, the battery, the megawatt charger, and the financing all under the same roof. Every other truck maker is waiting on someone else to build the chargers.” When asked whether he thought the ET44 posed a threat to the Tesla Semi, he gave a nuanced answer. “The short answer is that the ETT44 is the first serious competitor the Tesla Semi has faced in Europe and no threat at all in America — and even in Europe I expect the Semi to sell better. Tariffs decide the American half of that before the trucks do,” Sam Evans, The Electric Viking, told Supercar Blondie. “The ETT44 is a brand-new truck with no track record anywhere, no European factory named, and no customer deliveries until the second quarter of 2027. “Add the fact that the Semi enters Europe duty-free and BYD’s truck doesn’t, and I expect the Tesla Semi to outsell the ETT44 in Europe, not the other way round. “What BYD has really done is give Tesla its first proper competitor — a cheaper truck with a longer warranty and a one-stop package — and that will keep Tesla’s European pricing honest. “That’s good for every haulier in Europe, but it doesn’t make the ETT44 the better truck.” Timeline of BYD 1995: Founded by Wang Chuanfu with 20 employees, initially manufacturing nickel-cadmium batteries to compete with Japanese suppliers. 2000 – 2002: Becomes China’s first lithium-ion battery supplier to Motorola and Nokia. The company is listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. 2003: Acquires Xi’an Tsinchuan Auto, to pair its battery technology with vehicle manufacturing. 2005: Releases its first mass-produced ICE vehicle, the F3 2008: First plug-in hybrid, the F3DM, is launched. 2013 – 2015: Introduces the ‘Dynasty’ line of plug-in hybrid and electric vehicles. 2022: The company stops producing ICE vehicles to focus on BEVs and PHEVs, while launching global expansion across Europe, Asia-Pacific, and Latin America. 2023 – 2024: Surpasses 3 million NEV sales and overtakes Tesla in quarterly global pure-EV sales. 2025 – 2026: Expands further, opening manufacturing hubs across Brazil, Thailand, and Europe. Ben joined Supercar Blondie in February 2025 after being published by international organizations including LADbible, The Sun, the New York Post, and the Daily Mail. He covers supercars, rare and collectible vehicles, aviation, luxury assets, and the fascinating people behind them. His reporting has explored everything from seven-figure supercars and historic Ferrari collections to unusual aircraft adventures and extraordinary automotive discoveries from around the world. Ben has also gained first-hand insight into vehicle craftsmanship and customization, including visiting specialist workshops to see bespoke vehicles up close.

artigo.texto: Arevon Energy marks construction milestone at 250 MW Cormorant battery storage project in Daly City, California Arevon Energy hit a construction milestone at its Cormorant Energy Storage Project in Daly City, California, on September 16, 2026. The celebration brought state and local officials, project partners, labor and business leaders, and community members to the site of what will become a 250 MW/1,000 MWh battery storage facility — big enough to power 321,000 homes for up to four hours at peak demand. Commercial operations are expected to begin in 2027. Arevon marks construction progress at Daly City battery storage site The September 16 milestone wasn’t just a photo op. It pulled together a genuinely broad group — state and local officials, California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) representatives, labor and business leaders, community members — all there to recognize how far the project has come since construction kicked off in March 2026. Arevon CEO Justin Johnson put the project’s purpose plainly: “Cormorant represents the kind of critical energy infrastructure California needs to meet growing electricity demand while strengthening grid reliability.” Store power when there’s plenty of it, deliver it when the grid needs it most. That’s the whole idea. Cormorant is a 250 MW/1,000 MWh battery storage project in Daly City, California, developed and operated by Arevon in partnership with Primoris Services Corporation. Daly City Mayor Glenn Sylvester echoed that framing, noting the project positions the city as an active contributor to statewide infrastructure goals — not merely a host community. Commercial operations remain on track for 2027. Project expanded and backed by long-term power agreement with MCE Cormorant didn’t start out at its current scale. Originally designed at 188 MW/752 MWh, it was later bumped up to 250 MW/1,000 MWh. That expansion came with a key partner: MCE, a community electricity provider serving more than 1.8 million residents and businesses across Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, and Solano counties, which contracted for the additional capacity under a long-term offtake agreement. The partnership goes beyond buying power. MCE’s Acting CEO Vicken Kasarjian noted that more than $500,000 from the contract will flow directly to local community programs. “This project has a direct community benefit,” he said — pointing to built-in funding for initiatives supporting Bay Area residents. On the construction side, Arevon is working with Primoris Services Corporation’s Renewables group, and at peak the project employs around 175 workers. Grid reliability and environmental benefits expected over project lifetime Battery storage projects like Cormorant absorb electricity during off-peak hours — when solar generation is high and demand is lower — then release it when the grid is under stress. That charge-and-dispatch cycle is what makes storage a reliability tool, not just a clean energy one. Cormorant uses lithium iron phosphate battery technology, which carries a strong safety record and a long operating life. Both matter for a project expected to run for decades. Over its lifetime, the facility is projected to avoid 191,800 U.S. tons of CO₂ annually and save more than 4.2 billion gallons of water — figures that reflect displaced emissions and the water savings compared to conventional thermal generation. The CPUC sees projects like this as essential. Energy Division Director Molly Sterkel said the agency expects more than 20 GW of new clean resources to come online by 2032, with battery storage described as “a critical part of that effort” — particularly for filling the reliability gap when solar drops off in the evening and demand stays high. Economic impact and community investment in Daly City Beyond the grid, Cormorant is expected to generate more than $73 million in property tax revenue over its lifetime, flowing to local schools, infrastructure, and public services. That’s a long-term fiscal benefit that outlasts the construction phase by a wide margin. Arevon has built relationships with more than a dozen local organizations throughout the project’s development. Partners include Bayshore Elementary School District, Jefferson Union High School District, Daly City Partnership, Pilipino Bayanihan Resource Center, Bayshore Community Center, Pacific Islands Together, and John’s Closet, among others. The company’s involvement has spanned donations, sponsorships, scholarships, memberships, and volunteer work — a range that signals sustained engagement rather than a one-time check. Mike Stancil, Executive Director of the Daly City Partnership, described Arevon as “a caring and compassionate corporate partner.” Arevon itself operates more than 6.3 GW of solar and energy storage projects across 18 states and holds the No. 1 developer ranking in Solar Power World’s 2026 Top Solar Contractors List for California. Cormorant is one of several recent California storage projects the company has brought through development and into construction. A long-term agreement with MCE Cormorant is a 250 MW/1,000 MWh battery storage project in Daly City, California, developed and operated by Arevon in partnership with Primoris Services Corporation. It operates under a long-term agreement with MCE, which serves the broader Bay Area, and is expected to reach commercial operations in 2027. The project can power 321,000 homes for up to four hours during peak demand. Projected outcomes include avoiding 191,800 U.S. tons of CO₂ annually, saving more than 4.2 billion gallons of water over its lifetime, and generating more than $73 million in local property tax revenue. More than $500,000 from the MCE contract is earmarked for community programs in the region. artigo.texto: - China has prioritized breakthroughs in all-solid-state technologies to accelerate the roll-out of next-generation batteries. - The plan also calls for improving sodium battery performance and supporting corporate mergers and restructuring. China aims to achieve initial large-scale use of all-solid-state batteries by 2030, accelerating the transition of next-generation battery technology from research to commercialization. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) on Monday released its new battery industry development plan for the fifteenth five-year period, setting a roadmap for 2026 through 2030. The document, dated September 14, was jointly issued by 7 government agencies, including MIIT, the National Development and Reform Commission and the Ministry of Transport. The plan calls for steady growth in China's new battery industry through 2030, alongside breakthroughs in advanced electrode materials, new electrolytes and high-end auxiliary materials. Beyond the all-solid-state battery deployment target, it sets goals for long-life lithium batteries to reach 15,000 charge-discharge cycles and for leading manufacturers to achieve product defect rates at the parts-per-billion (PPB) level. All-solid-state batteries are a key technological priority. The document calls for faster breakthroughs in commercialization technologies, focusing on improving ionic conductivity and cycling stability while optimizing costs. Specific measures include improving interfacial contact, extending cycle life, advancing pressure-system engineering and scaling up production of high-performance solid electrolytes. The plan also calls for combining high-voltage, high-capacity cathode materials with new lithium-metal-based anodes and anode-free designs, while developing manufacturing equipment such as isostatic presses for solid-state batteries. China plans to build a supply system centered on lithium batteries, complemented by sodium and flow batteries, while strengthening its ability to commercialize all-solid-state and ultrafast-charging batteries. For sodium batteries, the document emphasizes cost, safety and resource availability advantages, calling for the development of cold-resistant, high-energy-density power batteries and energy storage batteries with long cycle lives. Industry consolidation and supply chain security are another focus. The document supports corporate mergers and restructuring and calls for faster exploration and development of domestic lithium, cobalt and other mineral resources. On recycling, the plan requires companies to establish used-battery collection systems aligned with their sales volumes. It also encourages them to build recycling capacity in major export markets where conditions permit. The document proposes a digital identity management system for products including new energy vehicle (NEV) power batteries, exploring internationally accepted battery passport arrangements and promoting mutual recognition of carbon footprint data. The battery plan follows China's September 11 release of its fifteenth five-year development plan for the intelligent connected NEV industry, which targets a 70% share for NEVs in domestic new passenger vehicle sales by 2030. The earlier automotive plan also called for tighter management of power battery production capacity. The latest battery plan further defines priorities for technology development, manufacturing upgrades and broader applications.

artigo.texto: Li Auto's Li Xiang Responds to "De-CATL" Debate: In-House Development Isn't About Opposing Suppliers, But Deep Collaboration Li Auto (02015.HK) Chairman and CEO Li Xiang published a public statement on September 28 responding to the recently heated industry debate over "de-CATL-ization." He stated clearly that interpreting in-house development as "de-XX-ization" and positioning oneself against suppliers reflects zero-sum thinking, and that Li Auto has never used such an approach to define its self-development strategy. Li Xiang emphasized in his post that outstanding Chinese smart EV companies would never define their strategies with such a narrow mindset. He cited examples: Apple's A-series chips, Nvidia's and Qualcomm's flagship chips are mostly designed in-house and manufactured by TSMC; Tesla's self-developed batteries are produced in collaboration with CATL (300750.SZ), LG, and Sunwoda (300207.SZ). This model has not weakened TSMC, CATL, or Sunwoda—it has made them stronger. "Automakers define product experience, system architecture, and quality standards more deeply, while partners leverage their professional capabilities in engineering, manufacturing processes, and scaled delivery," Li Xiang wrote. "A good OEM-supplier relationship is not about who replaces whom, but about making products better through deeper collaboration." The Threefold Logic of Self-Development Li Xiang further elaborated on three core reasons Li Auto insists on deep battery self-development. First, to deliver user experiences that lead industry standards and build solutions for unmet needs first. He noted that users don't care about underlying electrochemical terminology—they care about whether range holds up, how long long-distance charging takes, whether performance stays stable in extreme heat or cold, and how safety baselines are guaranteed. From the industry's first extended-range large battery to the physics-defying 5C ultra-fast charging, to improvements in LFP battery low-temperature performance, state-of-charge accuracy, and longevity, these hardcore battery metric breakthroughs often have no ready-made solutions on the market. Second, to make the battery an integrated part of the intelligent vehicle, achieving a "1+1>2" whole-vehicle experience. Li Xiang believes the battery is by no means an isolated component—it and the vehicle must form a complete living organism with full end-to-end connectivity. Deep integration of cells, PACK, BMS, thermal management, electric drive, and vehicle control not only improves system-wide safety and quality, but also enables continuous OTA evolution years after delivery—charging strategies can be optimized, energy management can be refined, and low-temperature performance can keep improving. Third, full-lifecycle data connectivity so users don't have to pay for supply-chain division of labor. Li Xiang stated that the physical battery must ultimately become a data battery; connecting battery and vehicle data represents a higher level of battery specialization. The value of this data connectivity lies in: any微小 anomaly during production can trigger early warnings and be resolved before installation and delivery; problems can be solved before users even sense potential risks. This also ensures absolute consistency in after-sales service and repair standards. Thanking "Comrade-in-Arms" CATL In his post, Li Xiang specifically mentioned the partnership with CATL. He revealed that Li Auto established its battery R&D team back in 2015, and when certain product definitions were doubted by everyone, it was CATL that collaborated on joint development and turned the impossible into reality. "Here, I want to especially thank our comrade-in-arms CATL. It was Li Auto's deep product definition, our joint development, and CATL's strong support that helped Li Auto create products that continue to lead the industry," Li Xiang wrote. The context for this statement is that as more automakers begin in-house development and manufacturing of core components like batteries, views such as "de-CATL-ization" have emerged in the market, sparking considerable controversy. Li Xiang's response aims to clarify: self-development does not mean cutting ties with suppliers, nor does it mean replacing them. "Li Auto never wants to 'de-XX-ize' anything. On the contrary, we welcome every outstanding partner to achieve deep integration with Li Auto and together push user experience to the extreme," Li Xiang stated. "Times are changing, and the only standard by which we evaluate change is whether it can create greater value for users: delivering better products, providing better services, and bringing better experiences. Changing for users is the ultimate starting point of all of Li Auto's choices." The Pace of Self-Developed Battery Rollout Li Auto plans to equip all models with self-developed batteries once production capacity successfully ramps up. Li Xiang previously stated that in the long term, batteries and chips will be the company's most important technological barriers and moats. "Self-development represents our hope to hold future-facing core technology barriers in our own hands, like Apple and Huawei." From an industry perspective, Li Xiang's statement reflects the deep restructuring currently underway in China's new energy vehicle supply chain. The trend of automakers extending upstream and self-developing core components is increasingly evident, and how to balance self-development with external supply chain relationships is becoming a strategic question every automaker must answer. Li Xiang's answer: self-development is not about becoming an island, but about pulling the best partners closer and together making the user experience better. artigo.texto: Geely Unveils Battery That Charges in Under 9 Minutes, Intensifying BYD-CATL Ultra-Fast Charging Race China's Geely Auto has unveiled a next-generation ultra-fast charging battery that completes charging from 10% to 97% in 8 minutes and 40 seconds. Built on 2.2-megawatt (MW) charging infrastructure, the technology represents the fastest charging solution Geely has readied for mass production and is expected to mark a new watershed in the ultra-fast charging race in China's EV market, long dominated by BYD and CATL. Geely showcased the "Shendun Golden Battery" on the 23rd at its automotive safety center in the Hangzhou Bay New Zone in Ningbo, Zhejiang Province. At the safety testing facility—built at a cost of 2 billion yuan (approximately $298.0 million) and billed as the world's largest—the company demonstrated the battery charging from 10% to 70% in 4 minutes and 30 seconds, and from 10% to 97% in 8 minutes and 40 seconds. Taking the stage, Geely Auto CEO Gan Jiayue said, "The faster rapid charging gets, the greater the safety concerns become," adding, "Through AI-driven innovation, Geely has captured safety, timeliness, and convenience in charging all at once." To ensure stability during ultra-high-power charging, Geely also unveiled the "Xingrui PowerMind," a smart energy AI model co-developed with Chinese AI company StepFun. The system uses algorithms to predict battery temperature up to 30 seconds in advance and adjusts charging output in real time accordingly. It is designed to maintain average battery temperature below 55°C and cap peak temperature at 65°C. A liquid cooling system that manages heat across the entire chain—from the charging station's energy storage system (ESS) to the charger, cable, charging port, and battery pack—was also applied to reduce heat concentration in specific sections during high-power charging. CEO Gan said, "Through AI technology innovation, we manage the battery simultaneously with charging, meeting the needs of users who want both fast charging and long battery life." Geely also offered an AI-based solution to address the impact of repeated rapid charging on battery life. The system applies micro-current pulses to "reactivate lithium ions accumulated on the anode during repeated rapid charging," extending battery life by 20%. The battery pack has completed testing in the Zeekr 001 and Lynk & Co 10. The Ultra-Fast Charging Gap with Competitors Geely's announcement surpasses the ultra-fast charging figures from BYD and CATL. Earlier this year, BYD unveiled its second-generation Blade Battery, capable of charging from 10% to 97% in 9 minutes, with 10% to 70% taking 5 minutes. CATL, the world's No. 1 battery maker, still maintains a technological edge. CATL's third-generation Shenxing battery, unveiled in April, completes charging from 10% to 80% in 3 minutes and 44 seconds, and from 10% to 98% in 6 minutes and 27 seconds. Geely's new battery outpaces BYD in the 10–70% range but falls short of CATL. However, Geely's announcement is noteworthy because it goes beyond mere technological showmanship and ties into supply chain strategy. According to local media tallies, among batteries installed in Geely vehicles from January to July this year, the share of its in-house battery brand Jiyao Tongxing reached 28.50%, up sharply from 18.46% in 2024. CATL's share over the same period still stood at 63.21%, indicating supply chain diversification remains in its early stages, but the trend of rapidly increasing in-house battery share is unmistakable. Automakers Move to Reduce CATL Dependence Behind Chinese automakers' intense focus on battery and charging technology competition lie sluggish domestic demand and deteriorating profitability. As the price-cutting war drags on, profits across China's auto industry fell approximately 20% year-over-year in the January–July period. To cut costs and strengthen pricing power, automakers are accelerating efforts to reduce dependence on CATL—which holds overwhelming market dominance—and develop their own batteries while diversifying supply chains. The imbalance in profit structure is confirmed by the numbers. CATL's first-half net profit this year was 43.284 billion yuan (approximately $6.4 billion), more than double the combined net profit of 21.048 billion yuan (approximately $3.1 billion) posted by 15 major listed Chinese automakers over the same period. With profits continuing to concentrate among battery makers, observers note that automakers face a growing imperative to secure core technology and cost leadership. The Widening Technology Gap with the United States The ultra-fast charging race among Chinese companies further highlights the technology gap with the U.S. EV market. The most powerful passenger-vehicle chargers in the United States deliver only a fraction of megawatt-class output. Tesla Superchargers, except for the latest models, cap out at 250 kW and 400V, while Electrify America offers 350 kW, IONNA's new units deliver 400 kW, and ChargePoint has brought 600 kW chargers to market. The gap is equally stark on the vehicle side. Hyundai and Kia's 800V EVs (Ioniq 5, EV6, etc.) actually max out at around 240 kW on 800V DC fast chargers, while the Porsche Taycan accepts only up to 320 kW. Recently launched 800V German EVs such as the BMW iX3 and Porsche Cayenne have begun supporting 400 kW DC charging, but this remains a far cry from China's 2.2 MW-class charging. In the United States, megawatt-class charging remains the exclusive domain of medium-duty EVs such as buses and heavy trucks. ChargePoint CEO Rick Wilmer recently stated that connecting two of the company's 600 kW chargers via a common DC bus could deliver 1.2 MW through a single port. However, he explained that NACS or CCS1 connectors cannot handle that level of power, requiring an MCS connector instead. Megawatt-class charging for passenger EVs in the United States remains at the roadmap stage. Once added, BigGo Finance appears first in Google Search

artigo.texto: Seven Chinese ministries issue 15th Five-Year Plan for next-gen batteries: accelerating all-solid-state battery industrialization, improving recycling systems Seven Chinese government agencies led by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology jointly issued the "15th Five-Year Plan for the New-Type Battery Industry" on September 28, laying out arrangements across two main fronts—technology breakthroughs and recycling utilization: on one hand accelerating breakthroughs in all-solid-state battery industrialization technology and making forward-looking arrangements for next-generation battery systems; on the other hand improving the spent battery recycling and utilization system to promote efficient use of recycled resources. The plan calls for deepening research on fundamental and forward-looking scientific questions in new-type batteries, and strengthening original innovation and disruptive technology breakthroughs. It promotes collaborative process innovation across battery materials, structural design, manufacturing technology, and system integration, aiming to improve intrinsic safety, energy and power density, structural strength, and lightweighting. For all-solid-state batteries, the plan explicitly focuses on improving ionic conductivity and cycling stability, optimizing costs, and other key directions to accelerate breakthroughs in industrialization technology. It also makes forward-looking arrangements for next-generation battery systems including new alkali metal-ion batteries, multivalent-ion batteries, metal-air/sulfur batteries, multifunctional composite structural batteries, and nuclear batteries. In the recycling segment, the plan requires implementation of the extended producer responsibility system, pushing companies to establish spent battery recycling systems—whether self-built or commissioned—that match their product sales volumes, and accelerating the construction and operation of recycling service outlets. Specific measures include: supporting R&D and industrial application of technologies and equipment for refined dismantling of new-type batteries, low-cost utilization, and efficient extraction of valuable elements; improving the refinement and automation levels of spent battery dismantling, crushing, sorting, and smelting processes; guiding localities to rationally allocate processing capacity commensurate with regional spent battery generation volumes, and promoting resource concentration toward competitive enterprises. Additionally, the plan proposes guiding companies to deploy spent battery comprehensive utilization capacity in major export markets for new-type batteries where conditions permit, in order to enhance resource security capabilities. artigo.texto: POSTECH Researchers Uncover Mechanism Behind Manganese-Based Cathode That Gains Capacity With Repeated Charging South Korean researchers at POSTECH have for the first time uncovered the operating principle behind a next-generation battery material that gains usable capacity as it undergoes repeated charge and discharge cycles. The team demonstrated experimentally that internal structural changes—long viewed solely as a culprit in battery degradation—can be precisely controlled to simultaneously boost both performance and lifespan. POSTECH announced on the 28th that a research team led by Professor Hong Ji-hyun of the Department of Battery Engineering and Professor Park Kyu-young of the Department of Battery Engineering and Department of Materials Science and Engineering has identified the structural transformation mechanism of manganese-based cathode materials, which are drawing attention as a next-generation EV battery material. Dr. Lim Guk-hyun of the Department of Battery Engineering and Lee Ho-jun, an integrated program student in the Department of Materials Science and Engineering, also participated in the research. The material at the center of the study is lithium-rich layered oxide (LMRO). This substance has been considered a leading next-generation battery candidate because it can store roughly 20% more energy than conventional nickel-based cathodes while reducing the use of expensive nickel and cobalt. However, it has suffered from a critical weakness: capacity and operating voltage both decline with repeated charge-discharge cycles. Moreover, studies on the underlying cause had produced conflicting findings about the battery's final internal structure, leaving the precise mechanism shrouded in uncertainty. The research team focused on the phenomenon of oxygen escaping from within the cathode during charge-discharge cycles. LMRO originally has a structure in which lithium and metal atoms are arranged in orderly layers, like a brick wall. But with repeated charging, the oxygen that holds this arrangement firmly in place gradually escapes, and the lithium and metal atoms intermix, eventually transforming the material into a disordered rock-salt structure with almost no regularity. The key discovery is that the amount of oxygen released determines the degree of structural change. The higher the voltage to which the battery was charged, the greater the oxygen loss—and correspondingly, the more the internal structure became disordered. The team confirmed that oxygen release can be precisely controlled by adjusting the depth of charge. This is where an unexpected result emerged. While oxygen loss might at first glance appear to damage the battery, when the structure becomes appropriately disordered, the pathways available for lithium transport actually increase, boosting usable capacity. A material with finely tuned oxygen loss demonstrated durability, retaining 98.4% of its initial performance after more than 200 charge-discharge cycles. "By controlling the battery's operating temperature or surface environment, we can regulate oxygen loss and structural change," said Professor Hong. "This can be applied to designing next-generation EV batteries tailored to specific applications." The significance of this research lies in reframing structural change—previously dismissed as an aging phenomenon to be avoided at all costs—as a design tool. By controlling the degree of disorder through either promoting or suppressing oxygen loss, the findings open a path to designing application-specific optimized materials: high-capacity batteries for long-range driving, or long-lifespan batteries for commercial vehicles where durability is paramount. The research was published in Energy & Environmental Science, an international journal in the energy field. The paper was included in the journal's "Hot Articles"—the top 10% of papers selected by the editorial board—and was also selected as a front inside-cover paper. The study was conducted with support from the Korea Institute for Advancement of Technology and the Korea Institute for the Advancement of Technology under South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy; the National Research Foundation of Korea under the Ministry of Science and ICT; and the Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute. The EV battery market is currently being rapidly encroached upon by Chinese-made lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, which compete on price. LFP batteries offer low cost, but their lower energy density translates to shorter driving range, and repeated charge-discharge cycles cause permanent loss of available lithium and increased internal resistance, gradually reducing capacity. LMRO is viewed as an alternative that targets both LFP's price competitiveness and nickel-based batteries' performance, as it can achieve higher energy density while reducing nickel and cobalt usage. That said, since this study establishes the principle at the laboratory level, additional validation is needed before commercialization. Long-term reliability at the actual battery cell level, reproducibility in mass-production processes, and integration with thermal management systems remain as follow-up tasks. Nevertheless, as the first study to quantitatively explain the fundamental mechanism of battery degradation and convert it into a design strategy, it is regarded as research that charts the direction for next-generation high-energy-density cathode development. artigo.texto: Fabricantes chineses enxergam na corrida por data centers de inteligência artificial nos Estados Unidos uma janela de oportunidade, segundo reportagem da CNBC. A avaliação ocorre mesmo com a disputa entre as duas maiores economias do mundo pelo domínio da tecnologia. Aposta no mercado americano A Brightray, empresa de infraestrutura de IA registrada em Singapura, vê “um potencial muito grande no mercado americano”, afirmou à CNBC S.K. Lee, vice-presidente global da companhia. Sua única fabricante é a chinesa PrefabDC, que produz data centers pré-fabricados, enquanto a Brightray gerencia as obras. Segundo a empresa, o modelo reduz em ao menos metade o tempo de construção, que hoje leva de dois a três anos nos EUA, de acordo com analistas do setor ouvidos pela CNBC. Os EUA concentravam 5.427 data centers de IA em 2025, ante 449 na China, segundo dados do Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence citados pela CNBC. Gigantes como Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon e Meta devem gastar cerca de US$ 765 bilhões combinados neste ano em infraestrutura de IA. O CEO do JPMorgan, Jamie Dimon, disse recentemente que o valor pode chegar a US$ 1 trilhão no próximo ano. Já o governo chinês planeja investir US$ 295 bilhões em data centers nos próximos cinco anos. Para Jeffrey Ding, especialista em IA e professor da George Washington University, as empresas chinesas geram menos receita com serviços de IA, o que limita investimentos e reflete uma demanda menor por esses serviços. Tensão geopolítica A relação entre os países, porém, segue complicada. A visita do presidente chinês Xi Jinping a Washington trouxe novo foco à dinâmica comercial, e a IA foi tema destacado nas conversas com o presidente Donald Trump. Autoridades americanas temem riscos de cibersegurança e dependência da China em infraestrutura crítica, e o governo Trump avalia proibir modelos chineses de IA de pesos abertos e novos tipos de componentes chineses para data centers. Benjamin Boucher, analista de cadeias de suprimentos da Wood Mackenzie, disse à CNBC que o ambiente é desafiador por causa das tarifas e das restrições recentes. Ele lembra que os EUA enfrentam escassez de componentes essenciais, como equipamentos elétricos, e prazos longos de entrega, enquanto a China oferece prazos mais favoráveis. Maior fabricante do mundo, o país já fornece transformadores, baterias e cabos de fibra óptica ao mercado americano. Na fábrica da Brightray em Yangzhou, Lee explicou que os materiais e equipamentos vêm de várias partes do mundo, com uma fatia grande da China por causa da integração de sua cadeia produtiva.

artigo.texto: Este texto decorre do artigo aprovado para o Congresso Mundial de Direito Agrário (Congresso Mondiale di Diritto Agrario), com sede em Verona e Alpego (Itália), e discute a titularidade dos créditos de carbono nos contratos de arrendamento e parceria rural. A promulgação da Lei nº 15.042/2024 deu novos contornos normativos aos mercados voluntário e regulado de carbono no Brasil, mas deixou em aberto controvérsias centrais sobre a titularidade desses ativos quando gerados em áreas rurais exploradas mediante contratos agrários típicos. Ao instituir o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SBCE), a legislação excluiu a produção primária agropecuária das obrigações do mercado regulado, o que não impede, contudo, a participação voluntária do setor por meio da geração de Certificados de Redução ou Remoção Verificada de Emissões (CRVE) e de outros ativos ambientais do mercado voluntário. Nesse cenário, o artigo 43, caput, da Lei nº 15.042/2024 estabelece que a titularidade dos créditos pertence àquele que efetivamente executa, gerencia e certifica o projeto de descarbonização, enquanto o seu inciso IV reconhece a titularidade originária aos proprietários ou usufrutuários do imóvel rural. Essa dualidade cria relevante incerteza jurídica para o planejamento produtivo e contratual no campo. Para compreender o alcance dessa ambiguidade, cumpre analisar inicialmente a regra geral em que o proprietário do imóvel rural é também o responsável direto pela exploração da atividade agropecuária e pela implantação das práticas sustentáveis. Nessa situação, pela própria redação da lei verifica-se que a titularidade pertencerá ao proprietário do imóvel rural, uma vez que ele mesmo executa o projeto de sequestro de carbono. Quando há perfeita convergência de identidades em uma só pessoa, a definição do direito sobre o ativo não apresenta maior complexidade, pois.o potencial abstrato de sequestro de carbono deriva do próprio direito real sobre a terra. Ademais, o proprietário-produtor arca sozinho com os investimentos iniciais, os custos de Monitoramento, Reporte e Verificação (MRV), a certificação e os riscos biológicos e climáticos inerentes ao ciclo produtivo rural, retendo de forma legítima e integral a titularidade originária dos créditos e as receitas deles advindas. No entanto, essa titularidade é mais complexa quando a terra pertence a uma pessoa, mas a atividade produtiva e a implementação do projeto sustentável são conduzidas por outra. Nesses casos, propõe-se que a atribuição da titularidade adote de um critério jurídico composto e funcional, estruturado a partir de três pilares: (1) o título que fundamenta o acesso e uso da terra, (2) a identificação do agente que efetivamente implementa as práticas de descarbonização e, (3) a matriz de alocação de riscos produtivos e econômicos estabelecida pela legislação. Distinção Ao aplicar esse critério aos contratos agrários típicos, verifica-se uma distinção marcante entre o arrendamento e a parceria rural. No contrato de arrendamento rural, a legislação aloca a matriz de riscos de maneira estritamente unilateral sobre o arrendatário. Por força do artigo 95, inciso I, do Estatuto da Terra (Lei nº 4.504/1964) e do artigo 29 do Decreto nº 59.566/1966, o arrendador faz jus a uma retribuição financeira fixa pela cessão do uso e da posse temporária do imóvel, mas não participa dos lucros ou prejuízos decorrentes de frustrações de safra, pragas ou eventos climáticos. Como cabe ao arrendatário suportar integralmente as oscilações do mercado, as intempéries climáticas, os investimentos em manejo sustentável do solo e os custos de estruturação e certificação do projeto, a titularidade dos créditos de carbono gerados deve pertencer exclusivamente a ele. A contraprestação devida ao proprietário permanece limitada ao valor do aluguel cadastral legalmente estipulado, sem direito a parcela sobre a receita dos créditos de carbono. No caso da parceria rural, a estrutura legal determina o compartilhamento compulsório dos resultados e dos riscos da exploração econômica, nos termos do artigo 96, inciso VI, e § 1º, do Estatuto da Terra, combinados com os artigos 35 e 36 do Decreto nº 59.566/1966. Nesse caso, o parceiro-outorgante (proprietário) e o parceiro-outorgado (produtor) repartem, segundo percentuais estipulados em lei e no contrato, os riscos de caso fortuito, força maior, perdas biológicas e variações de preços do mercado. Havendo participação simétrica nas incertezas e nos prejuízos da atividade produtiva que dá suporte ao projeto ambiental, a titularidade dos créditos de carbono e os proveitos econômicos obtidos com a sua alienação devem ser compartilhados entre ambos. A divisão da receita desses ativos deve observar estritamente a mesma proporção estabelecida para a partilha dos frutos da produção principal, conforme estabelece a legislação agrária. A titularidade dos créditos de carbono em imóveis rurais explorados por terceiros não é uma decorrência automática e exclusiva do domínio formal sobre a terra. Nas situações em que o risco produtivo e financeiro é suportado solitariamente pelo produtor, como no arrendamento, a titularidade dos créditos pertence a ele. Por outro lado, quando o risco é dividido entre proprietário e produtor, como na parceria, a titularidade traduz-se em um direito compartilhado, a fim de refletir o equilíbrio econômico-financeiro estabelecido pela legislação para esta espécie contratual. Nas hipóteses em que o projeto de descarbonização, por razões fora da vontade das partes, perdurar para além do prazo inicialmente previsto, entende-se que o contrato de arrendamento ou parceria também deverá ser prorrogado, por interpretação analógica do artigo 95, I, do Estatuto da Terra.

artigo.texto: A Rússia ataca o centro de dados da Vodafone em Kyiv. TPO - O Ministério da Defesa russo anunciou que suas forças atacaram uma série de alvos de infraestrutura logística, de comunicações e militar na Ucrânia, incluindo um centro de dados da Vodafone em Kiev. O Ministério da Defesa russo anunciou que, durante a noite, suas forças realizaram ataques com drones contra múltiplos alvos na Ucrânia , incluindo centros de logística, infraestrutura portuária e de transporte, e centros de comunicação. "Na noite passada, as Forças Armadas Russas continuaram a realizar ataques com drones visando centros de logística, infraestrutura portuária e de transporte, centros de comunicação e navios operados pelas forças armadas ucranianas", diz o comunicado. De acordo com a versão russa, um dos alvos do ataque foi um centro de dados da Vodafone em Kiev. Moscou acusa a empresa de ser uma das principais fornecedoras de serviços de telecomunicações móveis e internet para as forças armadas ucranianas, incluindo a transmissão de dados de inteligência. Você também pode gostar O Ministério da Defesa russo afirmou que as tropas russas também atacaram um centro logístico da Zammler na vila de Krasilovka, na região de Kyiv, que armazena e distribui ajuda militar ocidental para a Ucrânia. Na região de Odessa, a Rússia afirma ter atacado o centro logístico de drones Kalinsh em Ilyichovka, que se acredita armazenar drones interceptores FPV. O lado russo também afirmou ter atingido vários alvos no porto de Kiliya, incluindo o quartel-general da base naval de Vostok da Marinha ucraniana, um posto avançado da Guarda de Fronteira ucraniana, quatro depósitos de equipamentos militares e parte da infraestrutura portuária. Segundo um comunicado do Ministério da Defesa russo, os ataques também tiveram como alvo dois armazéns contendo drones e componentes de combate em Nikolayev, bem como um navio cargueiro no mar que, segundo Moscou, transportava equipamentos militares e bens de dupla utilização para o porto de Odessa. artigo.texto: Industry steps up with lithium-ion battery storage guidance Lewis Tyler Share this content UKWA and UKMHA publish guidance to help warehouse operators manage the risks associated with lithium-ion battery storage The UK Warehousing Association (UKWA) and the UK Material Handling Association (UKMHA) have published new guidance to help warehouse operators manage the risks associated with the growing use and storage of lithium-ion batteries. The two trade bodies have worked in parallel to provide practical advice covering both smaller batteries and larger traction batteries used to power warehouse equipment. The guidance was launched at a UKWA Member Connect event in Felixstowe, where Clare Bottle from UKWA and David Goss from UKMHA discussed key highlights for warehouse operators. Lithium-ion batteries are increasingly used across the economy, from laptops, e-bikes and scooters to industrial machinery such as forklifts. While batteries are an important part of the transition away from fossil fuels, the organisations note that unmonitored batteries can, in rare circumstances, enter thermal runaway and cause fire. The new guidance includes recommendations on storing batteries in cool, dry conditions, limiting long-term storage and separating battery types. It also provides advice on monitoring stock, preparing emergency plans and training staff. Clare Bottle, Chief Executive of UKWA, said: “Developments in battery technology are having a huge positive impact, making our lives more convenient, changing the way we move around, and helping the transition away from fossil fuels. All of these batteries move through the supply chain before ending up in businesses or people’s homes, so it is vital we get the storage and handling of them right. “There’s no reason, with proper precautions, that batteries can’t be stored safely. Many warehouses are doing so already. This guidance will help others get to grips with the issue and understand how they can manage the risks. It is a market that will only grow, so it’s important the UK has a wide range of warehouse operators equipped with this knowledge.” David Goss, Technical Director of UKMHA, said: “Lithium-ion batteries have been transformative, not only for consumers but also for powering the equipment essential to today’s fast and efficient logistics sector. “As with any technology, sensible precautions are necessary to minimise the risk of an incident. Whilst lithium-ion batteries have proven safe and reliable, effective risk management requires an understanding of the potential for hazards due to the release of stored energy or chemicals. “Through this collaboration, UKWA and UKMHA have developed complementary guidance addressing the storage of both industrial truck traction batteries and the smaller batteries in warehouse environments.” Both guidance documents are available from UKWA.

artigo.texto: Liftoff: Google is realizing Elon Musk's dream of AI data centers in space Next week, Google will be living out Elon Musk's dream of putting AI data centers in space — and they'll be doing it with help from Musk's space exploration company. On Thursday, October 1, 2026, Google will load an experimental satellite on SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket and launch it in space. The satellite is part of Google's Project Suncatcher initiative, which seeks to set up AI data centers in space. The experimental satellite will be able answer simple A.I. prompts from space, according to the New York Times. In a blog post about Project Suncatcher, Google explained the potential benefits of sending data centers into orbit: You May Also Like Cooling orbital data centers is a crucial research challenge. TPUs generate a large amount of heat in a small area, which needs to be diffused safely or the chips are at risk of overheating. But in space, there’s no airflow. In a vacuum, you can only diffuse heat via radiators, which requires a totally different approach to cooling electronics. As the New York Times reported, Google isn't sending a full-on orbital data center this time; it's sending the potential precursor to one. The satellite, named MVP, contains four “tensor processing units,” which are specialized chips with the computing power of one server in a data center here on Earth. The computer chips will be powered by the satellite's solar panels, which will provide one kilowatt of power to the chips. Google says that this is all it needs for this particular experiment, which will test how the hardware fares in outer space. The satellite is expected to operate in space for a period of one year. While in orbit, the computer chips will be able to process short queries for up to 15 minutes while Google's Gemini AI responds. After a 15-minute period, the chips will need to shut down to cool with a special cooling system, as fans typically used in computer systems don't work in space. After that one-year period, the satellite will stop operating but will continue to orbit the Earth for a total of six years before the planet's gravitational pull brings the satellite down, burning it as it falls through the atmosphere. When Musk's SpaceX acquired Musk's AI company xAI earlier this year, Musk explained that one of the main reasons for the companies to combine was so that they could work on putting AI data centers in space. "Current advances in AI are dependent on large terrestrial data centers, which require immense amounts of power and cooling," Musk said in a statement at the time of the acquisition. "Global electricity demand for AI simply cannot be met with terrestrial solutions, even in the near term, without imposing hardship on communities and the environment." In the long term, space-based AI is obviously the only way to scale," Musk continued. Google seems to agree with Musk. Shortly after Musk shared his orbital AI data center goals, Google announced Project Suncatcher, which the company greenlit in May 2025. It's important to note, however, that these are very early days for the orbital data center ambition. If these experiments prove that the project is at all feasible, it would likely be years, if not decades, before Google and Musk's vision comes to fruition. But Thursday's launch is certainly a first step in potentially building out AI data centers in space. Want more science and tech news delivered straight to your inbox? artigo.texto: This article was originally published by Mother Jones While tech oligarchs grandstand about the existential danger AI superintelligence poses to humanity, former Environmental Protection Agency officials say we should be worried about a more immediate threat to our health: the data centers that power those AI models. The former EPA researchers, now working with the nonprofit Environmental Protection Network, are warning in a new report that since January 2025, Donald Trump’s EPA has embarked on a systematic weakening of pollution safeguards, permitting processes, inspection norms, and other guardrails—at least 30 different actions—that could increase the health risks associated with the data center boom. There are currently about 3,000 data centers in the United States, and more than 1,500 new centers are in the planning stages. But as developers build out this vast, energy-hungry infrastructure, the country is losing the government regulatory safeguards that are needed to ensure that expansion is done safely, the ex–EPA officials say. Dan Costa, who spent 35 years at EPA studying air pollution, noted that for decades the environmental agency, which was established in 1970, had a large and committed cadre of researchers who investigated emerging sources of pollution and new environmental threats. “Over the decades, toxicologists, chemists, atmospheric scientists, modelers and engineers worked in concert with academic colleagues on behalf of the American people—not on behalf of industry,” Costa said in a press briefing last week. “We wanted to carry out EPA’s mission of protecting people’s health from industrial air pollution.” Now, though, that work force has been gutted. The Trump administration has dismantled EPA’s main research office, and the agency’s priorities have shifted away from strict enforcement of pollution standards. “Transforming the nation’s energy system, while diminishing its scientific capacity to understand what the impacts are going to be, makes no sense,” Costa said. But that appears to be the direction the country is heading in. President Donald Trump is “positioning America as the global leader in AI,” EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin wrote in a memo last year. The agency is “committed to bolstering” those efforts, Zeldin said, by “cutting heavy-handed regulations to ensure America can build and power the data centers essential to Making America the AI Capital of the World.” Since Trump returned to the White House, data center developers have seized the opportunity to expand at a rapid pace, helped by the administration’s moves. In some cases, that deregulation has involved keeping old coal-fired plants online past their planned decommissioning times in order to power data centers; other times, it has meant easing regulations on the use of onsite fossil-fuel-powered turbines to power hyperscale data centers like xAI’s Colossus. The agency has proposed a rule change that would let developers begin constructing data centers and their associated power plants before they get air pollution permits. And it has directed the agency’s enforcement staff to avoid any action that could “unduly burden or significantly disrupt” energy production or power generation. According to one study the former EPA researchers cited in their new report, pollution associated with the AI boom may lead to 1,300 additional deaths per year. Physician and former EPA administrative official Lynn Goldman said some health impacts of increased data center pollution might be felt quickly—for example, heart attacks or premature births associated with particulate exposure. Others, such as cancer, might take years to emerge. “The AI industry’s race for advantage should not be a matter of life or death,” Goldman said at the press conference. “Families shouldn’t have to pay for the AI boom with their health.”

artigo.texto: Last week, I walked my fields at Trails End Farm in Bradford as the sun came up over the hills. It’s the kind of quiet that reminds you why people move to New Hampshire — and why those of us lucky enough to live here fight so hard to protect it. That’s why I strongly support Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s proposed moratorium on new data centers in New Hampshire. Across the country from Colorado to Virginia, from Texas to right here in New Hampshire, massive new data center facilities are popping up. Recently proposals for new data center projects in Nottingham and Bow have received a lot of attention and public scrutiny — rightfully so. Here’s what the data shows. Data centers are among the most power-intensive facilities ever built. A single large-scale facility can consume as much electricity as a small city. When those facilities plug into New Hampshire’s grid, they drive up demand. When demand outpaces supply, ratepayers pay more. Every family heating their home. Every small business running its equipment. Every farmer keeping the lights on in the barn. They all pay more so that a data center — excuse me, an “innovation hub” — can run its servers around the clock. New Hampshire has a brand. We call it the New Hampshire Advantage. Low taxes. Common sense regulation. A quality of life worth protecting. That advantage doesn’t survive if we allow our energy infrastructure to be overwhelmed by facilities that offer almost nothing to our communities in return — no meaningful jobs, no tax base that justifies the strain, no benefit to the Granite Staters who actually live here. Gov. Ayotte is right to pump the brakes. A moratorium isn’t anti-business. It’s pro-New Hampshire. It says: we will think carefully before we commit our grid, our ratepayers and our communities to something we cannot easily undo. That is conservative governance. That is good stewardship. Any farmer will tell you — you don’t exhaust the land for a single season’s profit. Because apparently, “data center” has become a dirty word — and when a dirty word starts costing you a permit, the instinct in some corners is simple: find a cleaner word. So now, Granite Staters, you may start hearing about proposed “server farms” or “innovation hubs” coming to a town near you. Don’t be fooled. An innovation hub that requires hundreds of megawatts of power, consumes millions of gallons of water for cooling, generates little local employment and plugs directly into our electrical grid is not an innovation hub. It’s a data center. Calling it something else doesn’t change what it draws from our communities — or what it leaves behind. I’ve spent my career in business and academia studying how markets work. I’ve run hotels. I’ve taught marketing. And I know a rebranding campaign when I see one. This is one of the most transparent examples I’ve encountered in public life. The product hasn’t changed. Only the label has. And the label is designed to get past the very guardrails that Gov. Ayotte and this legislature are trying to put in place to protect New Hampshire’s ratepayers and energy grid. My message to those who want to sneak a data center past a moratorium by slapping a new name on it is simple: we see you. The people of New Hampshire see you. And we are not going to let a branding exercise substitute for honest policy. If you have a facility that draws industrial-scale power from our grid, it will be evaluated as what it is — not what you’ve chosen to call it this week. New Hampshire’s energy future is too important to leave to clever marketing. Our ratepayers deserve honesty. Our grid deserves protection. And our communities deserve leaders who won’t be talked out of common sense by people with a thesaurus and a permit application. I’m one of those leaders. And I’m not going anywhere. Sen. Dan Innis, from Bradford, represents District 7 in the New Hampshire Senate.

artigo.texto: Os projetos de data centers previstos para o Ceará para os próximos anos podem sustentar 112,3 mil empregos quando estiverem em operação, mas apenas 551 seriam postos diretos dentro dos próprios complexos. Os outros 111,7 mil estariam distribuídos pela cadeia de serviços e fornecedores ligada à atividade. Na prática, menos de 0,5% dos empregos dos data centers projetados seriam diretos, enquanto mais de 99% do efeito estimado sobre o mercado de trabalho dependeria da cadeia movimentada pelos empreendimentos. A projeção faz parte de estudo realizado pelo Observatório da Indústria, ligado a Federação das Indústrias do Estado do Ceará (FIEC) e divulgado pelo O Povo. Data centers no Ceará concentram empregos fora dos complexos Entre os 111,7 mil empregos sustentados na cadeia durante a operação, calculados pelo Observatório, estão atividades demandadas pelos empreendimentos, como manutenção de infraestrutura, conectividade, refrigeração, energia e outros serviços. O economista-chefe do Observatório, Guilherme Muchale, explicou durante o Proenergia Summit 2026 que os projetos exigem grandes volumes de capital e infraestrutura, enquanto a operação direta demanda menos trabalhadores. É essa característica que faz a maior parte do efeito estimado sobre o emprego no Ceará aparecer fora dos complexos de Data Centers Os 112,3 mil postos, portanto, não representam contratações diretas pelos operadores. O total resulta da soma dos 551 empregos previstos dentro dos data centers com as 111,7 mil ocupações que o estudo estima serem sustentadas na cadeia associada à operação. Projetos previstos mostram diferença entre obras e operação Além de Data Centers, essa característica também aparece em empregos nos empreendimentos já anunciados no Ceará. Em agosto, o Conselho Nacional das Zonas de Processamento de Exportação (CZPE) aprovou um projeto ligado à Voltalia Energia do Brasil para a Zona de Processamento de Exportação do Ceará. Com investimento previsto de R$ 181,7 bilhões, o empreendimento estima 2.300 empregos diretos na implantação e 400 durante a operação. Outro exemplo está em Fortaleza. A ampliação do data center Mega Lobster prevê aproximadamente 400 postos diretos e indiretos durante as obras, enquanto cerca de 30 empregos devem permanecer após a conclusão da expansão para 20 MW. Os dois projetos têm escalas e características diferentes e não validam, isoladamente, a projeção agregada da Fiec. Servem para mostrar uma característica relevante dos data centers no Ceará: o volume de investimento e de trabalhadores mobilizados na implantação pode ser muito superior ao quadro necessário para manter os equipamentos funcionando posteriormente. Projeção depende da expansão prevista para os data centers no Ceará Os empregos também não constituem um resultado já contratado. O estudo utiliza como referência um cenário de 2,7 GW de capacidade de data centers, além de informações do Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE 2035), referências acadêmicas e premissas relacionadas ao Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata). A própria apresentação não estabelece uma tarifa específica de energia, não detalha individualmente a disponibilidade futura da infraestrutura elétrica e não fixa um cronograma anual para que toda a capacidade considerada entre em funcionamento. Essas limitações importam porque o efeito calculado pelo Observatório da Indústria para o mercado de trabalho depende da instalação e da entrada em operação dos projetos considerados no cenário. Para os data centers no Ceará, portanto, a projeção ocupações está ligada não apenas aos 551 postos dentro dos complexos, mas principalmente à capacidade de a atividade sustentar demanda por fornecedores e serviços ao redor deles.

artigo.texto: Segundo o New York Times, o Google está se preparando para lançar um satélite de teste em órbita no dia 1º de outubro, marcando o início de sua ambição de construir centros de dados de IA operando no espaço, usando energia solar para processar tarefas de inteligência artificial. O satélite, chamado MVP, será lançado pelo foguete Falcon 9 da SpaceX a partir da Base da Força Aérea de Vandenberg, na Califórnia. Este ainda não é um centro de dados completo, mas sim o primeiro teste do projeto Suncatcher. Em testes realizados em solo, o satélite, com tamanho aproximado de uma geladeira, foi submetido a testes de vibração e teve seus processadores de IA acionados. O Google marcou cada parafuso do dispositivo para monitorar alterações sutis após o processo de teste. De acordo com o The Guardian , o MVP está equipado com quatro Unidades de Processamento Tensorial (TPUs), equivalentes à capacidade computacional de um servidor em um centro de dados. Painéis solares fornecem cerca de 1 kW de energia, o suficiente para o satélite realizar consultas simples de IA. O Google prevê que o satélite poderá processar consultas em cerca de um ano e permanecer em órbita por até seis anos antes de retornar à atmosfera. O problema da energia e do custo A ideia de instalar centros de dados no espaço surge da crescente demanda energética da inteligência artificial. Enquanto os centros de dados terrestres exigem quantidades enormes de eletricidade, os satélites podem acessar uma fonte de energia solar mais abundante e consistente. O Google não é a única empresa interessada nessa ideia. Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos e Sam Altman também manifestaram apoio à construção de centros de dados fora da Terra. No entanto, o projeto ainda enfrenta obstáculos significativos. Os satélites ficam expostos à radiação no espaço, e o custo de seu lançamento permanece elevado. Embora os custos possam diminuir com o desenvolvimento da indústria espacial, a construção de uma rede de centros de dados em órbita continua sendo um problema a ser resolvido. O Google estima que o custo de operação de um centro de dados orbital poderá se aproximar do custo de um centro de dados terrestre em meados da década de 2030, à medida que os custos de lançamento diminuírem. O professor Brandon Lucia, da Universidade Carnegie Mellon, acredita que a expansão de um satélite de teste para uma rede massiva exigiria muitos anos e um capital enorme. Segundo ele, esta ainda é uma área com poucos precedentes. James Manyika, um executivo sênior do Google, também se mostrou cauteloso quanto ao cronograma. Ele citou o processo de desenvolvimento da tecnologia de carros autônomos do Google, que levou cerca de 15 anos desde a pesquisa inicial até a implementação prática. O maior desafio é a dissipação de calor. Um dos maiores desafios enfrentados pelo Google foi o resfriamento dos chips. Na Terra, os data centers utilizam ventiladores e sistemas de refrigeração para dissipar o calor dos processadores. No espaço, os ventiladores não funcionam da mesma maneira. Portanto, o Google precisou desenvolver um sistema de condução térmica multicamadas para transferir o calor dos chips para um dissipador de calor externo no satélite. No projeto experimental, as TPUs foram colocadas na placa de circuito impresso, conectando-se ao material de transferência térmica e, em seguida, às camadas de alumínio e cobre, antes que o calor fosse transferido para o dissipador de calor. Atualmente, esse sistema permite que o chip opere por cerca de 15 minutos antes de precisar esfriar. Esse tempo é suficiente para lidar com consultas Gemini relativamente curtas. O Google planeja lançar mais dois satélites no próximo ano. A longo prazo, a empresa quer construir grupos de satélites que operem em formação, com mais de 80 satélites em uma rede. Se o projeto avançar, o Google poderá até mesmo projetar satélites dedicados maiores, aproximadamente do tamanho de um campo de futebol . Uma aposta a longo prazo O projeto Suncatcher teve origem numa ideia de Blaise Agüera y Arcas, que acreditava que as necessidades energéticas da IA poderiam impulsionar uma abordagem completamente nova para a infraestrutura computacional. Em fevereiro de 2025, o Google realizou testes de resistência à radiação em seus chips em um laboratório nuclear. Os processadores foram expostos a radiação equivalente a aproximadamente cinco anos de operação no espaço. Pequenos erros de dados causados pela radiação geralmente podem ser corrigidos reiniciando o chip. Em maio de 2025, a equipe do projeto apresentou sua ideia ao CEO Sundar Pichai, com a presença do cofundador Sergey Brin. O projeto recebeu então sinal verde. Inicialmente, o Google planejava lançar dois satélites em 2027. No entanto, a empresa decidiu antecipar o lançamento para este ano e assumir um risco maior. A Planet Labs foi contratada para construir os satélites, enquanto os chips foram instalados em uma plataforma de satélite pré-existente. Com o MVP, o objetivo do Google não é provar que data centers em órbita estão prontos para substituir instalações terrestres. A empresa está testando se os componentes mais críticos do conceito podem funcionar em um ambiente espacial. Travis Beals, líder do projeto, acredita que, mesmo que tudo corra bem nos próximos cinco anos, os resultados iniciais podem não ser significativos o suficiente para gerar mudanças imediatas. Mas, a longo prazo, ele vislumbra um futuro em que o processamento de consultas Gemini a partir do espaço possa se tornar uma prática comum. artigo.texto: Aderco's 2055G+: Emissions Performance with Shared, Verifiable Data Shipping companies can now harvest data on enhanced fuel performance as verified CO₂ reductions that they convert into Gold Standard carbon credits using Aderco’s ‘measure-as-you-go’ program, 2055G+, writes Gérald Baiwir, Head of Environment, Aderco. Looking beyond compliance with environmental regulations, shipping companies are discovering that savings from onboard energy-efficiency measures can be converted into valuable, Gold Standard-backed carbon credits, allowing them to benefit financially while reducing emissions. Until very recently, doing so has been labour-intensive and resource-heavy. Operators have had to reconstruct their vessels’ performance data retroactively, often working with incomplete or inconsistent datasets. This has resulted in lengthy validation timelines, significant uncertainty around data accuracy and, in worst-case scenarios, disputes over performance improvements. On the flipside, genuine efficiency gains have often gone uncertified: not because they weren’t real, but because the data was simply not structured for certification. Verifiable Data To address this, Aderco has rolled out a new ‘measure-as-you-go’ program, 2055G+, which operators can use to ensure steps they take to improve energy efficiency are reflected in accurate data. 2055G+ offers a single, transparent data framework that is continually updated, audit-ready and accessible to stakeholders, including shipowners, operators and charterers. Performance data is influenced by various factors, including different routes, weather conditions and load profiles, for example. 2055G+ addresses these differences through vessel-specific baseline modelling, advanced benchmarking and continuous data normalization, ensuring performance is measured fairly and accurately, regardless of fleet profile. Its methodology follows an approach similar to the EU Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) and applies rigorous filters – linked to minimum sailing hours, sea state conditions and ‘laden condition only’ – to ensure data quality and comparability. In this way charter party discussions over voyage performance are backed by verified data rather than estimates, and users can be sure of their position with respect to the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII), the EU MRV and the ETS, among other regulatory frameworks. Ownership of emissions reductions – and, by extension, the Voluntary Carbon Credits they generate – is clearly defined from the outset. In short, 2055G+ replaces debate with shared, verifiable data. Transparent Process In the first instance, the 2055G+ process is being applied to offer full transparency on the impact of Aderco’s 2055G additive in enhancing fuel performance and reducing CO2. It establishes a fuel and emissions baseline using noon reports collected over the vessel’s full dry dock cycle as the starting point for 2055G use under real operating conditions for a minimum of six months to optimise fuel efficiency and reduce emissions. Pre- and post-treatment fuel consumption is compared, using operational data that is also verified by Adi Terra, an independent project developer. The resulting CO₂ savings are converted into certified carbon credits, delivering both financial returns and verifiable environmental impact reductions. These credits are validated under the Gold Standard Retrofit Methodology providing high liquidity and strong market value. The potential gains are far from theoretical. Even before qualifying for Voluntary Carbon Credits, adopters can realize instant fuel-related savings. Classification societies have independently verified how 2055G+ reporting consistently reports reductions to fuel consumption and corresponding CO₂ emissions by 3-5%. Examples include a 3.25% reduction on a Capesize vessel, verified by RINA, and a 4.84% reduction on a reefer vessel, verified by ABS. In many cases, this improved fuel efficiency is enough to raise a vessel’s rating by one band (for example, from C to B, or from D to C), preventing a vessel downgrade as IMO requirements tighten. Because CII impact is highly vessel- and operation-specific, 2055G+’s ability to continuously monitor performance is especially useful. Data and Certification Backbone The primary value of efficiency measures lies in reducing fuel consumption and associated emissions. However, under many commercial charter arrangements, these fuel savings are realised by the charterer rather than the vessel owner, creating a well-recognized split-incentive that can discourage investment in decarbonization measures. The ability to generate Gold Standard voluntary carbon credits addresses this by creating a new revenue stream for the party making the investment. Fuel savings therefore remain the operational foundation of the program, while certified carbon credits provide an additional financial return that helps unlock investments that might otherwise not proceed. Given today's voluntary carbon market conditions, these credits benefit from strong demand and attractive liquidity. The commercial logic is straightforward: fuel savings improve operational efficiency, while carbon credits create an additional source of value for vessel owners, aligning commercial incentives with decarbonisation. These measures can take many forms, including (but not limited to) propeller optimization, anti-fouling hull coatings and waste heat recovery systems. Today, 2055G+ certifies fuel treatment. Tomorrow, Aderco's ambition is broader: any retrofit measure that demonstrably improves vessel efficiency is a candidate for generating certified carbon credits. We are building the data and certification backbone that strengthens the business case for reducing emissions, whether stakeholders benefit through lower fuel consumption or via the parallel revenue stream from tradable carbon credits. artigo.texto: NineDot Adds 20 MW Battery Energy Storage Site NineDot Energy has opened its largest battery energy storage site to date in Hunts Point, New York. The new system adds nearly 20 MW of capacity to the local electricity network. NineDot expects it to become fully operational before next summer. The project shows how community scale battery energy storage can help grids handle peak demand. It can also improve grid resilience during heat waves and other periods of high electricity use. Battery Energy Storage Supports Peak Demand The Hunts Point system can deliver nearly 20 MW of power when electricity demand rises. According to NineDot, this is enough to supply nearly 20,000 homes during peak grid hours. The system can also reduce the need for nearby gas fired peaker plants. Utilities typically rely on these plants when electricity demand reaches high levels. Batteries offer another option by storing electricity and returning it to the grid when demand increases. “We’re honored to bring this battery storage site to the Hunts Point community,” said Adam Cohen, NineDot’s Chief Technology Officer and Co-founder. “Hunts Point has historically been overburdened by high-emitting fossil fuels, and this battery storage facility marks an inflection point in improving the local environment and grid reliability.” NineDot built the project on the former site of a fuel oil trucking company. The company expects the battery to support further electrification in Hunts Point. Future demand could include electrified markets and truck fleets. NineDot Targets 400 MW in 2026 NineDot has already used its battery fleet to support the grid during periods of high demand. During New York’s July 1 to 4, 2026 heat wave, nine NineDot projects exported nearly 34 MW at peak times. The batteries supported Con Edison’s local distribution network as well as the wider state transmission system. Currently, NineDot operates 11 projects across six locations in Staten Island and the Bronx. Together, they provide 39 MW of battery capacity. Meanwhile, the company continues to expand its battery energy storage portfolio. More than 60 additional projects are now in development. Its total project pipeline exceeds 1 GW. By the end of 2026, NineDot aims to have 400 MW of battery storage in operation, under construction or in development. Electricity networks face growing demand from electrification and renewable energy deployment. Distributed battery storage can help networks respond to those changes. In particular, batteries can supply power during peak periods and reduce pressure on existing grid infrastructure.
