artigo.texto: O risco de falta de energia e os perigos dos aparelhos que consomem muita energia. Um relatório recente do Ministério da Indústria e Comércio indica que o andamento de alguns projetos de geração e transmissão de energia está atrasado, enquanto a demanda por eletricidade continua a aumentar e novos tipos de carga estão surgindo. O Ministério da Indústria e Comércio propôs a revisão, atualização e ajuste do Plano de Desenvolvimento Energético 8 para responder proativamente ao risco de escassez de eletricidade no período de 2026 a 2030. De acordo com o Plano de Desenvolvimento Energético 8 revisado, a demanda comercial de eletricidade em 2030 está projetada em 500,4 a 557,8 bilhões de kWh, com produção e importação de eletricidade entre 560,4 e 624,6 bilhões de kWh, enquanto a capacidade máxima do sistema poderá atingir 89.655 a 99.934 MW. O consumo de eletricidade deverá aumentar entre 10,5% e 12,9% ao ano durante o período de 2026 a 2030. O funcionamento real deste ano também demonstra que a pressão da escassez de eletricidade está aumentando. A capacidade máxima do sistema elétrico nacional atingiu aproximadamente 58.500 MW durante o pico da onda de calor no final de junho. FOTO: HOANG HY Na cidade de Ho Chi Minh, a Companhia de Energia Elétrica da Cidade de Ho Chi Minh (EVNHCMC) prevê que a capacidade de pico de carga para toda a região poderá atingir 10.059 MW no cenário de alta demanda de energia deste ano. Notavelmente, a rede de transmissão que fornece eletricidade à cidade está atualmente operando em plena carga, chegando até mesmo a ficar sobrecarregada em alguns momentos, enquanto a Companhia Nacional de Transmissão de Energia (EVNNPT) e outras empresas do setor elétrico estão implementando simultaneamente dezenas de projetos de transmissão e distribuição para o período de 2026 a 2030. Entretanto, os centros de dados estão se tornando um tipo de carga muito diferente em comparação com as cargas tradicionais. Ao contrário de uma fábrica, onde o horário de funcionamento pode ser ajustado ou algumas cargas podem ser transferidas para fora dos horários de pico, os centros de dados precisam operar continuamente. Servidores, sistemas de armazenamento, conectividade de rede e, principalmente, sistemas de refrigeração precisam funcionar 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana. De fato, mesmo a escala de um único projeto demonstra o altíssimo consumo de eletricidade dos data centers. Dados do Ministério da Ciência e Tecnologia mostram que o Vietnã possui 41 data centers comerciais com uma capacidade instalada total de 221 MW. A capacidade instalada operacional total estimada do mercado deverá atingir aproximadamente 524,7 MW em 2025 e poderá chegar a 950 MW em 2030. Na cidade de Ho Chi Minh, a dimensão dessa demanda começa a se tornar evidente. A EVNHCMC estima que, a curto prazo, a cidade precisa preparar aproximadamente 200 MW para quatro projetos de data center que já receberam aprovação de investimento. A longo prazo, a demanda de eletricidade para esse grupo de projetos poderá chegar a 1.000 MW. Por exemplo, o data center no Parque Industrial Tan Phu Trung (cidade de Ho Chi Minh) tem uma capacidade projetada de 140 MW, permitindo a instalação de aproximadamente 10.000 racks. Quando totalmente concluído, este será o primeiro projeto de data center do Vietnã com capacidade superior a 100 MW, colocando-o entre os 10 maiores do Sudeste Asiático. Atualmente, a cidade possui 14 centros de dados operados por 9 empresas, com uma capacidade total de aproximadamente 33 MW. A EVNHCMC estima que, com uma reserva geral de cerca de 35% do fornecimento de energia da cidade, a demanda imediata pode ser atendida, mas o principal desafio reside na necessidade de sistemas de backup adicionais para garantir o fornecimento contínuo de energia 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana. O fornecimento de energia deve ser considerado antes do desenvolvimento de um centro de dados. Os centros de dados são a infraestrutura fundamental para IA, computação em nuvem, comércio eletrônico, finanças digitais e muitas outras indústrias de alta tecnologia. O consumo de eletricidade desses centros representa um desafio significativo para o setor elétrico. O Dr. Ngo Duc Lam, ex-Diretor Adjunto do Instituto de Energia, acredita que o principal problema atual reside não apenas na crescente demanda por eletricidade, mas também na capacidade de mobilizar capital para o desenvolvimento de fontes de energia e redes de transmissão. O setor elétrico está sob imensa pressão em relação ao capital, enquanto a necessidade de investimento tanto em geração de energia quanto em linhas de transmissão aumenta constantemente. Portanto, depender exclusivamente dos recursos de empresas estatais dificultará o atendimento às necessidades de desenvolvimento. Segundo o Dr. Lam, ao desenvolver o Plano Geral de Desenvolvimento Energético 8 e suas revisões subsequentes, não previmos totalmente o aumento da demanda por data centers e inteligência artificial. Na realidade, houve um aumento repentino, e o Ministério da Indústria e Comércio, em seu relatório de revisão do Plano Geral de Desenvolvimento Energético 8, também alertou sobre essa questão. Os projetos de inteligência artificial estão impulsionando a necessidade de construir muitos data centers de grande escala para atender à demanda. "A estrutura de geração de energia também está passando por mudanças significativas, com o aumento da proporção de energia renovável. No entanto, a energia eólica e solar são inerentemente instáveis e dependentes das condições climáticas, portanto, quando surgem cargas especiais, como data centers – que exigem energia contínua 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana – é preciso considerar sistemas de energia de base, energia de reserva e armazenamento. Os data centers representam um desafio para o setor elétrico na garantia da segurança energética", alertou o Dr. Lam. artigo.texto: Stakeholders call for carbon trading framework reforms DAR ES SALAAM: CARBON trading stakeholders have called for reforms to carbon trading framework after Carbon Tanzania temporarily halted its YaedaEyasi Landscape Project due to shifting global market demands and rising compliance costs. The suspension comes as international buyers increasingly favour carbon credits certified under the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market’s (ICVCM) Core Carbon Principles (CCP), while existing domestic regulations make it costly for local projects to meet the new standards. Speaking to the Daily News recently, Carbon Tanzania Chief Executive Officer, Ms Sally Capper said the project had suffered a sharp decline in funding as buyers shifted away from traditional REDD+ forest protection credits. “The decision comes as the project faces a sharp decline in funding as a result of global demand that is prioritising Core Carbon Principles (CCPs)-labelled carbon credits, which entail high costs to upgrade projects to new methodologies and a prohibitive domestic regulatory framework,” Ms Capper said. She said the temporary suspension would allow stakeholders to address the challenges and identify solutions that would enable the project to transition to CCPlabelled standards and secure long-term funding. The Yaeda-Eyasi Landscape Project protects about 108,000 hectares of dryland forest in northern Tanzania, the ancestral homeland of the Hadza hunter-gatherers who have lived in the area for thousands of years. Implemented since 2013 through a partnership between Carbon Tanzania and Hadza and Datooga communities, the project works with 11 villages involving about 63,000 people across Manyara and Arusha regions. Ms Capper said the changing voluntary carbon market had significantly reduced demand for conventional REDD+ credits, with many buyers now preferring carbon removal projects over emission reduction initiatives. She said Tanzania also lacks some of the national datasets required under the new CCP methodologies, making it difficult for local project developers to transition their credits quickly to meet emerging global standards. According to her, the combination of changing market expectations and regulatory costs has disrupted revenues earned by communities participating in carbon projects. “Funds are actively being sought to bridge the gap until the project can upgrade,” she said. While reaffirming Carbon Tanzania’s commitment to its community partners, Ms Capper said the current framework places an unsustainable financial burden on project developers. “Our primary duty is to ensure they continue to receive the financial benefits of their stewardship. To do that, we need to bridge this funding gap and work alongside other stakeholders to build a regulatory framework in Tanzania that actually enables high-quality carbon projects to succeed,” she said. She said similar regulatory challenges had also forced Carbon Tanzania to pause development of another project covering the Tongwe and Masito forests in western Tanzania. The company is evaluating how that initiative can achieve long-term success for local district councils, surrounding communities and the company within the existing regulatory framework. Ms Capper said the experience highlighted the importance of transparent and supportive policies in unlocking both the economic and ecological value of Tanzania’s forest resources. “To make nature-based carbon projects viable in Tanzania over the long term, the national carbon trading regulatory framework needs to be reformed,” she said. She warned that without regulatory changes, high investment and compliance costs could threaten the viability of community-based carbon projects across the country. According to 2024 Uongozi Institute report, Carbon Trading in Tanzania, also calls for stronger regulatory and institutional frameworks, improved coordination across the sector and benchmarking Tanzania’s carbon trading system against more developed regional and international markets.

artigo.texto: The Baltimore Banner’s annual innovation conference returns for a second year with a program focused on the infrastructure supporting digital businesses and the research institutions helping develop new products and companies. BannerX will be Sept. 30, in Columbia, Maryland. The event launched last year to explore how organizations could navigate the intersection of AI and cybersecurity. This year, the conversation shifts to what it takes to build and sustain the foundation in this space through four main discussions: - Data center development - The risks of adopting AI - Collaboration in the life sciences - How tech intersects with economic policy The program also includes a conversation on Maryland’s innovation future, bringing technology, public policy, workforce development and economic strategy into one discussion. It will explore how those areas intersect and the role of partnerships across government, industry and the broader business community. Speakers leading the conversations represent a range of perspectives from academia, government and industry. They include W. Mason Emnet, senior vice president of public policy at Constellation; Jason Michael Perry, founder and chief AI officer at PerryLabs; and Monica Lopez, privacy officer at VHC Health and cofounder and CEO of Cognitive Insights for AI. Also slated to participate is Bezawit Sumner, chief information security officer and senior director of security and compliance at CRISP Shared Services; Mary Morris, director of innovation initiatives at the University of Maryland, Baltimore; and Bret Schreiber, senior vice president of life sciences and technology at Fulton Financial Corp. Together, the sessions aim to help answer questions like: “Who is prepared to use a new technology?” “What infrastructure does it require?” “Which organizations need to work together to put it into practice?” With the central discussions plus space for networking, the event creates a venue for conversation between the people and institutions involved in turning technological capability into everyday use. BannerX takes place Sept. 30, 2026, on the first floor of 10285 Lakefront at 10285 Little Patuxent Parkway in Columbia, MD. Doors open at 8:30 a.m., and the program runs from 9 to 11:30 a.m. Tickets are $45 and include the discussions, networking and breakfast. The full agenda and registration are available online.

artigo.texto: Data centers have become a hot-button issue for virtually every politician in the country as proposals for the hyperscale server warehouses continue to spark arguments amongst community members. President Donald Trump has repeatedly backed the idea of developing data centers, most notably writing late last month “the only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. (sic) should not want Data Centers (sic) is if they want to end up being backwards and poor.” That’s a position Amy Kremer, an ardent Trump supporter who helped organize the president’s rally in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 6, 2021, disagrees with. Lincoln was one of the latest stops on the AI Data Center Revolt bus tour organized by Kremer’s Humans First, “a conservative organization that is dedicated to ensuring American AI dominance delivers a better life for everyday people.” The tour started in Austin, Texas, on Sept. 12 and will travel through most of the country until it wraps up Oct. 5 in California. “I support the president. I have been one of his biggest supporters, I’m the founder of Women for Trump, the founder of Women for America First. I think he’s been an incredible president and he’s done amazing things for this country, and I’m grateful for that, but I just disagree with him on this,” Kremer told Illinois Times. “I hope that he hears from the American people when he’s out on the campaign trail and hopefully, he’ll moderate his position.” Kremer did not participate in the ensuing Jan. 6. insurrection on the Capitol and her organization issued a statement condemning the attack that took place after Trump told supporters: “We’re going to try and give them the kind of pride and boldness that they need to take back our country, so let’s walk down Pennsylvania Avenue.” More recently, Kremer was voted to be Georgia’s Republican National Committeewoman by the state’s Republican delegates – a title she still holds. “We were all elected. We aren’t just picked and plucked and put there, so we all have a constituency, and you pretty much have to be living under a rock to not see where the American people are on this (issue),” she said. “The technology is being shoved down our throats – nobody’s asked for it. The American people are not happy about it – nobody voted for it. It’s being shoved down our throats now with these data centers and the infrastructure that’s being built out across the country.” Still, Humans First is not an entirely anti-AI organization. The organization’s home website touts that “artificial intelligence is set to fundamentally change our lives… how we work, how we raise our children, and how a country is run.” Kremer’s organization argues there should be more local say in the development of artificial intelligence models and data center buildouts. She’s promoting a small-but-strong government approach where counties and cities integrate local protections – Humans First is against the idea of federal or state moratoriums, arguing they would tie the hands of local officials. “We’re not anti-data center, we’re not pro-data center,” Kremer said. “I’m saying the people in (those) communities should have a say in the process… (we’re) focused on putting guardrails and safety mechanisms in place to protect our children, our jobs, our land, our resources.” Local opposition Renee Sommer, a real estate broker in Logan County, visited the bus tour. She told IT she’s opposed to data centers, mostly citing environmental and wildlife concerns. “I do not want a data center in Latham, Illinois, and data centers are a new dividing point with people: they’re either for them or against them,” she said. “It’s too new of a field – the major data centers – everybody keeps comparing them to these small storage centers, it’s not the same.” AI models demand far more power than traditional cloud computing servers, which has led to a boom in constructing hyperscale data centers across the country. “I’ve said this to the county board many meetings – I don’t have children. I don’t have grandchildren. What happens to this Earth when I’m gone is somebody else’s problem, but it’s sad that I care about what’s going to happen to your children, your grandchildren, and your grandchildren’s children, and you don’t. “Logan County really does not have – and I hate to say this – but they do not have the (necessary) knowledge on that board, as most counties do not. They don’t have environmentalists that live in the county, they don’t have environmental engineers,” she said. Logan County Indivisible, a group of residents who have been opposing potential data center proposals near Latham, didn’t attend the bus tour. Rachel Stechman, founder of the group and vice chair of the Logan County Democratic Central Committee, told IT she didn’t feel comfortable participating in the bus tour because of Kremer’s involvement with the Jan. 6, 2021 rally in Washington, D.C.. However, she acknowledged that the bus tour is an example of how data center opposition is truly bipartisan, arguing people want to make sure they’re safe. “The vast majority of these municipalities that are having these data centers thrust upon them just aren’t aware of all of the different issues that will come up in the process of both building and operating the data centers,” Stechman said. It feels a “little bit like putting the cart before the horse, they don’t quite know what problems to anticipate (or what) to write those ordinances about. “I always just like to emphasize the enormity of this issue, that it’s not just in our little corner of the country. It’s all over,” she said. “We definitely do have a handful of board members who are actively working to properly protect the people. I’m sure that for some people, just proper regulation would be enough. The issue is just that our definition of proper and the board’s definition seems to be kind of different.”

artigo.texto: Timâs view We should probably talk less about data centers. That might sound like blasphemy, and also hypocritical, given how often I do exactly that. To be clear, the challenges have barely begun: What weâre seeing being built today is only a small fraction of the data center capacity in the pipeline. âIf thereâs a single narrative in the market that is most starkly divorced from the fundamentals weâre seeing on the ground, itâs that the demand for AI infrastructure and the energy that supports it is in some way fragile,â Connor Teskey, CEO of Brookfield Asset Management, told me this week. But if thereâs one thing I took away from New York Climate Week, itâs that the raging debate around AI infrastructure is just the tip of the iceberg of a much larger economy-wide struggle to cope with surging power demand. Between now and 2030, according to S&P Global, only 18% of new global power demand will come from data centers. The rest â air conditioning, onshore manufacturing, electrified buildings and vehicles â will also require an unprecedented and challenging power infrastructure buildout that barely got a mention in the dozens of conversations I had this week. We can already take a few lessons from the data center experience that will apply to the broader power rush, starting with that itâs a crucible for innovation. âLarge loads have been a catalyst to so much new innovation because weâve never had the opportunity to think about adding net new clean power at a big scale,â Veery Maxwell, founding partner of clean tech investment firm Galvanize, told me. But itâs clear that without more rapid policy reform and technology advances, the imperative of fast growth will lead to the adoption of solutions that are both unsustainable for the climate and economically inefficient, such as installing more behind-the-meter gas turbines. Power project developers and their customers â Big Tech or otherwise â also need to be much more transparent and accountable to the communities they build in to avoid backlashes and blockages that only make the problem harder and more expensive to solve. Even as policymakers and hyperscalers chip away at the narrow data center challenge, our current moment of AI infrastructure anxiety only proves how much we need to brace for many more difficult conversations ahead. Thank you so much to everyone who took time to meet me this week. Special shoutout to those of you who joined our happy hour last night, always my favorite evening of Climate Week, which this year brought together people working on critical mineral mining, commercial-scale solar, trade research, energy bonds, low-carbon fuels, Taiwanese drones, environmental lawsuits, and the âGrateful Dead of carbon creditsâ (although donât ask me to explain what that last one means). Special thanks to our excellent contributor ChloÃ© Farand, who always makes my life much easier. Weâre back to our regular programming next week. Notable - Oracle declared force majeure on a giant US data center under construction, showcasing the risks of the AI infrastructure buildout.

artigo.texto: A U.K. lab test detected only trace lithium in battery material provided by Finnish startup Donut Lab, and the company has cited the result as support for its argument that the much-discussed cell is not lithium-ion. Even so, the test left major questions unanswered — Donut Lab disassembled the sample before analysis, and, as Electrek reported on Sept. 23, no production vehicle used the battery. Here's what to know Intertek's lab in Wilton, U.K., reported 3.4 ppm lithium by weight and 632 ppm sodium in a small amount of material identified as the anode, cathode, and current collector, per Electrek. "We wanted to put this speculation to rest with an independent test demonstrating that it is neither a lithium-ion nor a sodium battery," Donut Lab CEO Marko Lehtimäki explained. Lithium-ion cells typically contain lithium at much higher levels. If the tested material truly came from a functioning Donut Lab cell, the result would seem to rule out the battery chemistry most commonly used in the market. Intertek did not attempt to determine the battery's complete chemistry and was asked only to measure lithium and sodium. The material also reached the lab in "tear down condition" from Donut Lab, so Intertek was not the party that opened a sealed cell. Electrek noted that the published report labeled the material only as "Pouchcell – Cell 1." It said nothing in the document clearly connected that sample to the Donut "V1.5" unit VTT used in energy-density testing. More background Better batteries can help cut EV charging time, extend driving range, strengthen backup power during blackouts and storms, and eventually lower costs for drivers, fleets, and cities transitioning away from fuel-burning vehicles. That promise helped Donut Lab attract significant attention at CES in January, when it said it had the "world's first solid state battery that is ready for use in OEM vehicle manufacturing." But the company's timeline has since come under greater scrutiny as independent testing has slowly emerged. Questions about Donut Lab's claims intensified in June, when Electrek reported that battery researcher Ziroth and more than 20 experts reviewed the voltage curve and swelling data from a Donut Lab cell sent to VTT. They said it behaved like a high-nickel lithium-ion battery with a graphite anode. VTT also measured 185.7 watt-hours per pound (409.3 watt-hours per kilogram) on a Donut cell cycled between 2.3 and 4.25 volts — numbers that fit familiar lithium-ion territory. What's being done? Companies including Toyota, Samsung SDI, Factorial, and QuantumScape have solid-state cells working in lab settings and prototype vehicles, even if large-scale production remains a difficult step. Lehtimäki admitted that the battery was "already in production," but also acknowledged that the 185.5 watt-hours per pound (409 Wh/kg) cell "is not even the cell that's going to be shipped to customers." Where can I learn more? Questions about Donut Lab's battery underscore a broader push to improve chemistry, safety, and real-world EV performance. These stories explore battery advances aimed at extending range and reducing reliance on conventional materials. • Researchers found lithium titanium phosphate could ease range limits that still worry EV buyers. • Engineers are testing long-range lithium-ion batteries with potential for EVs and airplanes. • At the University of Hong Kong, a high-temperature design could open new battery paths. artigo.texto: AI cloud company plans data center in Mayes County CHOUTEAU, Okla. (KOKH) — Cloud computing company Lambda plans to build a data center in Mayes County, a project the company said could generate $500 million in tax revenue over the next decade. The facility will be built in the industrial park’s southern section within the Chouteau-Mazie Public Schools tax boundary, according to Lambda and MidAmerica Industrial Park. Lambda said the project could create up to 1,000 construction jobs and 100 permanent jobs. The company did not announce a construction start date, completion date or total project cost. The company said its tax projection is based on current rates. “This project will bring an estimated $500 million in tax revenue to our county over the next decade,” Chouteau Mayor Brenda Cunningham said. Lambda said it will use closed-loop cooling technology to recycle water and reduce water use. The company also said it will pay its full electricity costs and fund infrastructure needed for the facility, rather than passing those costs to other Grand River Dam Authority customers. “Lambda will fund the upfront infrastructure costs required to serve the project, ensuring those expenses are not passed on to other GRDA customers,” Grand River Dam Authority CEO Dan Sullivan said. Cloverleaf Infrastructure was selected by GRDA and MidAmerica to prepare the site for Lambda’s development. Lambda and MidAmerica said they will continue meeting with local leaders and residents in the coming weeks.

artigo.texto: The hidden environmental cost of AI data centers September 4, 2026 Every question sent to AI models provides an instant reply that seems to appear out of nowhere, but answering queries requires physical infrastructure that consumes real energy, water and land. Somewhere around the world — maybe in Virginia, Sao Paulo or Hong Kong — a massive warehouse filled with fiber-optic cables and seemingly endless rows of humming servers is working to provide the processing power for the more than 2.5 billion questions ChatGPT alone fields daily. AI models, along with cloud storage, streaming, web hosting and social media, all have a very real physical footprint. If data centers were a country, their level of electricity use would make them the 11th largest electricity consumer in the world, according to researchers from the United Nations University. From energy to water to land, here's the real toll data centers take on the environment. An insatiable appetite for power Data centers are becoming some of the world's fastest-growing consumers of electricity. These warehouses of servers, routers and internet-connected devices run 24/7, while cooling systems operate continuously to keep the tech from overheating. In Frankfurt, Germany, the grid is currently so saturated that no new connections will be available until at least the 2030s. There, data centers consume about 41% of the city's electricity. In Dublin, it's double that. And data center electricity consumption is growing rapidly — it's expected to double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, around what Japan consumes annually, according to the International Energy Agency. How the AI boom could slow climate progress All that energy has to come from somewhere, increasing reliance on fossil fuels. One 2024 study found that more than half of the United States' data centers are powered by fossil fuels, emitting in excess of 105 million tons of CO2. Offsetting that would take more than 31,000 wind turbines running continuously for a year. The build-out is also keeping old coal plants alive. Utilities in the US have delayed the retirement of 15 coal-fired plants nationwide to meet surging demand, plants that together emitted nearly 65 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023 alone. And utilities are also constructing new gas-fired power plants, with more than 100 GW of additional facilities across the country already announced. That would lead to more carbon emissions than burning 111 million pounds (50.4 million kilograms) of coal. Of course, data centers can also be powered by renewable energy. Pairing a facility with on-site renewables can ease pressure on the local power supply, and any surplus energy can even be sold back to the grid, making it more stable. However, using green electricity for data centers means there is less available for electrifying transport or decarbonizing other emissions-heavy industries. Hidden water demand Many data centers consume millions of gallons of water to stay cool. Servers generate constant heat, and water is one of the most effective ways to absorb and carry that heat away through evaporation. A single large facility can use up to 5 million gallons a day, roughly the same as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. About 80% of the water withdrawn for cooling simply evaporates; the rest becomes wastewater that can overwhelm local treatment systems never designed to handle that volume. In northern Virginia, the almost 300 data centers clustered in one region of the US state supply about a third of the world's online traffic. There, in what is known as the world's data center capital, facilities collectively used nearly 2 billion gallons of water in 2023. There are several more efficient ways to cool data centers. These include immersion cooling, where devices are bathed in a coolant, and closed-loop cooling systems which recycle water and can reduce freshwater use by up to 70%. Data centers are making cities hotter Cooling a data center doesn't get rid of the heat, it just moves it outside. That can exacerbate the urban heat island effect, which is when cities experience higher temperatures than rural areas. Researchers in Phoenix, Arizona, found a single large data center can emit as much waste heat as tens or even hundreds of thousands of households, raising nearby land surface temperatures by up to 9 degrees Celsius (16 Fahrenheit) and air temperatures by up to 2 degrees Celsius. Those effects can be felt as far as half a kilometer away. Since cities are already 0.5–4 degrees Celsius warmer than their surroundings, these higher temperatures can increase heat stress risks for nearby residents and push up air conditioning demand, requiring still yet more energy. Not all of that heat goes to waste: a growing number of data centers are capturing and piping it into nearby homes and businesses. This process, called thermal energy networks, can reduce data center power demand by up to 30%. Coal, gas and diesel all contribute to dirty air Powering and running data centers pollutes the air on two fronts. First, coal and gas plants release toxic particulate matter, which can lead to respiratory disease, heart disease, asthma and more health conditions for nearby communities. On-site diesel generators, used as backup power when the grid fails, also release harmful air pollutants. These generators pump out 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than natural gas plants. One estimate found that when backup generators for all of Virginia's data centers were emitting at just 10% of their permitted level, they could contribute to 14,000 cases of asthma symptoms, more than a dozen deaths and up to $300 million in public health costs a year. Data centers take over large swaths of land Data center construction requires large plots of land to build on. artigo.texto: Segundo o InvestNews, análise da The Economist divulgada neste domingo (27) mostra que a indústria europeia vive crise concentrada, não generalizada. Montadoras e químicas perdem terreno, enquanto fabricantes de equipamentos para data centers e empresas de defesa ampliam atividades. A produção de veículos da União Europeia está 17% menor que antes da pandemia. A China, que já rendia lucros às montadoras europeias, agora lança carros mais rápido e com custos menores. Em 2025, a UE importou € 559,4 bilhões em mercadorias chinesas e exportou € 199,6 bilhões, com déficit de quase € 360 bilhões, segundo o Eurostat. Antes de subsídios, a eletricidade industrial na França e na Alemanha custa cerca do dobro da registrada nos EUA ou na China, conforme a Economist. Desde o começo de 2023, o emprego na manufatura da UE caiu cerca de 2%, para 28 milhões, e quatro quintos dessa perda vieram da Alemanha. No mesmo período, vagas para engenheiros e técnicos cresceram 7%. Empresas buscam novas receitas: Vestas e MTU Aero Engines vendem manutenção; Siemens comprou empresas de software; Solvay e K+S buscaram reduzir exposição à oscilação dos preços de energia. Componentes chineses podem baratear a produção europeia, e estudo do Banco Central Europeu associou essas importações ao avanço da produção. Para a análise, os problemas de algumas grandes companhias não decretam crise de todo o setor.

artigo.texto: The blue-collar AI job market is booming. Will data center backlash make it go bust? - AI is stimulating job creation in traditionally blue-collar professions. - Welders, plumbers, HVAC technicians, and electricians are all finding their skills in high demand for data center buildouts, though many of the construction jobs are temporary in nature. - Recent moves by states including New York and Texas to slow development, as well as local freezes across the U.S. in response to intense public backlash, could impact the labor market trend. When most people think of AI and jobs, the conversation often pivots to which occupations are most likely to be obliterated by its arrival. But, at least for some professions, the AI boom has been an employment one too. AI is creating jobs in a variety of trades that prop up the sprawling ecosystem that powers giants like Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, OpenAI, and others. The construction and maintaining of data centers and the entire AI ecosystem is requiring a new generation of HVAC technicians, construction workers, line workers, and pipefitters. "These are occupations that are becoming increasingly important to the AI economy," said Maria Flynn, president and CEO of national nonprofit Jobs for the Future. While data centers are the part that gets the publicity, they are only one piece of a much larger puzzle, requiring upgrades in transportation and modernization of the energy grid. "We are seeing major sources of demand that are converging at the same time," Flynn said. The skilled jobs often come with attractive pay. Flynn said an apprentice level technician can take home $40,000 to $60,000, with experienced electricians commanding north of $100,000. Nicole Bachaud, labor economist at online employment marketplace ZipRecruiter, is seeing salaries even higher for more specialized, high skill roles. Bachaud said that the mean minimum salary for data center jobs spiked by 125.1% year-over-year to nearly $208,000. "This is suggesting that highly specialized, top-tier engineering roles are pulling the overall average up drastically," Bachaud said. While many traditional blue-collar workers are seeing a boost, including truckers, the biggest blue collar beneficiaries, according to Bachaud's data, are welders and pipefitters. Postings for those jobs are up 164% year over year. While that could be partly the result of a small sample size as more data centers are built, even if each one only needs a few pipefitters, the demand for these roles will increase, she said. The construction demand is also uneven with some places getting in on it more than others. Houston and Birmingham have seen particularly robust growth. "Places with more land to expand and build, which are often places where building regulations make development easier, cheaper, and faster, will likely be where expansion continues, versus coastal hubs that have higher costs and more regulatory burdens," Bachaud said. That means an electrician or pipefitter in Birmingham will probably have more of a buyer's market than one in Boston. None of this surprises Justin Sinkovich, associate professor and associate director of the School of Business and Entrepreneurship at Columbia College Chicago. In his view, the usual AI jobs narrative of displacement is incomplete, with the data center counter-story as one example. While AI may automate some work, its deployment depends on the buildout of infrastructure, including not only data centers but also substations, cooling systems, water, and piping infrastructure, which AI cannot build. "Positive effects on the labor market are already visible, with an increased demand for cooling and HVAC engineers, industrial automation technicians, and traditional trade workers like construction workers and electricians. HVAC-engineering wages have risen, and many technical professionals entering data-center roles are seeing a pay premium," Sinkovich said. He pointed to Louisiana as a specific example, where both Amazon and Meta have massive projects. "Amazon committed $12 billion to a new data center with 540 new on-site jobs, including 1,700 electricians, technicians, and security personnel. Meta's Hyperion project in Louisiana is $27 billion," Sinkovich said. "These projects create demand for on-site workers and therefore cannot be offshored or conducted remotely, unlike manufacturing and software," he added. He also said there is a longer-term story of AI enabling more decentralized and dynamic energy systems. This not only improves energy efficiency but also creates additional work to build smart controls, battery systems, microgrids, and distributed energy infrastructure. Economic optimism vs. public skepticism Recent research from global real estate services firm Cushman & Wakefield indicates that every 100MW of new data center development creates nearly 1,300 jobs in the local economy, generating approximately $110 million in annual wages, $344 million in gross output, and $187 million in gross regional product. And many of these jobs aren't ones requiring a diploma. In fact, many of them are better suited to a path through trade school. But the optimistic shovels on the ground analysis don't match the national mood. Seventy percent of Americans oppose a data center being built in their local area, according to Gallup, and a New York Times/Siena poll conducted this month found roughly two-thirds opposed regardless of party — Democrats, independents and Republicans alike. Even where data centers are proceeding at a robust clip and creating the most jobs public opinion has turned against them. Fifty-seven percent of voters oppose one in their own community, according to a Texas Politics Project poll, enough that some experts see Democrats gaining ground in the Lone Star State. artigo.texto: Data centers may be the sleeper issue of the midterm elections. Fox News reported that Senate candidates are confronting growing voter anger over the electricity costs, water consumption, and sprawling developments associated with artificial intelligence. One recent Gallup survey found that 70 percent of Americans oppose the construction of new AI data centers in their own communities. Politicians are paying attention. Some are calling for moratoriums. Others are targeting tax incentives or demanding that projects generate their own power. The political temptation is obvious: When voters are worried about higher utility bills and rapid changes in their communities, blaming large technology companies is easier than explaining a complicated energy and infrastructure problem. ANXIETY GROWS OVER EMERGING ELECTION ISSUE, BUT GOP SAYS WASHINGTON ISN'T THE ANSWER The concerns are real. They should not be dismissed by industry, and they cannot be ignored by elected officials. No family should be forced to subsidize the grid upgrades required by one of the world’s wealthiest companies. Communities deserve honest answers about water use, noise, land, electricity demand, tax incentives, and who will pay for new infrastructure. But, legitimate concerns are quickly hardening into something far more dangerous: a political campaign against the physical infrastructure of American artificial intelligence. If that happens, we will repeat one of the most damaging patterns in modern American history. For decades, the United States surrendered factories, critical supply chains, mineral production, and industrial capacity to foreign competitors. Communities lost jobs, our national security became dependent on adversaries, and Washington eventually spent billions trying to rebuild industries that should never have left. THE AI REVOLUTION COULD BECOME A NATIONAL SECURITY DISASTER IF WE AREN'T CAREFUL We cannot make the same mistake with AI. Artificial intelligence does not exist somewhere in the cloud. It requires chips, servers, power plants, transmission lines, cooling systems, construction workers, electricians, pipefitters, engineers, and data centers. These facilities are not incidental to the AI economy. They are the factories of the next industrial age. AMERICA RUNS ON DATA. IF WE DON’T BUILD THE INFRASTRUCTURE, CHINA WILL China understands this. Beijing is not debating whether it should possess the energy and computing infrastructure necessary to dominate artificial intelligence. It is building. The International Energy Agency projects that data-center electricity consumption will increase substantially in both China and the United States through 2030. If America decides that data centers are too politically difficult to construct, the demand for AI will not disappear. The investment, jobs, technical expertise, and strategic advantage will simply move elsewhere. That would be a profound failure of American competitiveness. It would also create a serious political problem for Democrats. Data-center construction has become an important source of work for the building trades. The Associated Press recently reported that data centers account for at least 40 percent of the work hours performed by members of the Columbus-Central Ohio Building and Construction Trades Council and at least 50 percent for the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 26 in the Washington metropolitan area. WELDER TURNED LAWMAKER SEES A ‘NUCLEAR BOMB FOR WORK’ — AND A CHANCE TO HELP BLUE COLLAR AMERICANS Those are not theoretical jobs promised years from now. They are jobs for electricians, laborers, operating engineers, pipefitters, and other skilled workers today. Democrats cannot claim to represent organized labor while allowing progressive activists to shut down the projects employing union members. Republicans should resist a similar temptation. Conservatives have spent years arguing for reshoring, energy dominance, permitting reform, American manufacturing, and competition with China. Those commitments mean very little if they disappear when building the next American industry becomes locally controversial. The answer is not to wave every project through without conditions. It is to build responsibly and communicate honestly. Data-center developers should be expected to explain what they are building, how much electricity and water it will require, how they will protect residential ratepayers, and what the surrounding community will receive in return. Utilities and regulators should ensure that large customers pay the costs created by their demand. Projects should pursue closed-loop cooling, on-site generation, long-term power agreements, and other options that reduce pressure on local systems. TO BEAT CHINA IN AI, AMERICA MUST WORK WITH COMMUNITIES — NOT AROUND THEM Most importantly, America needs more energy. Data centers are exposing a problem that existed before the AI boom. Electricity demand from data centers has tripled over the past decade and could double or triple again by 2028. Electricity demand is rising after years of stagnant generation, premature plant retirements, congested transmission systems, and permitting processes that make major infrastructure nearly impossible to build on time. Stopping data centers will not modernize the grid. Building more reliable generation, accelerating transmission, preserving existing nuclear capacity, expanding natural gas infrastructure, and deploying advanced nuclear power will. Industry also needs to recognize that silence is no longer a strategy. As Sen. Jon Husted told Fox News, data-center companies have not done a good enough job explaining why they should be allowed to develop in communities. He is right. Americans hear about enormous power consumption, water use, and tax incentives. They need to hear, in plain language, what data centers make possible, which jobs they create, how they support national security, and why domestic computing capacity matters i

artigo.texto: - The companies plan battery projects in Spain and Slovakia with combined annual capacity of 37.5 GWh, alongside a cathode materials project in Morocco. - Gotion plans to invest about €1.598 billion, while Volkswagen's PowerCo plans to contribute about €1.62 billion. Gotion High-tech (SZSE: 002074) and Volkswagen Group plan to jointly invest about €3.22 billion ($3.67 billion) in battery and materials production projects in Europe and North Africa, deepening supply chain cooperation to serve Volkswagen's European market. The companies plan to establish 3 joint ventures through their subsidiaries in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco, Gotion said in a stock exchange filing on Monday. Gotion plans to invest about €1.6 billion in total, while Volkswagen's PowerCo plans to contribute about €1.62 billion, with funding to be provided in stages. The largest project, in Valencia, Spain, calls for an investment of about €2.26 billion to build annual lithium-ion battery production capacity of 29.1 GWh. Gotion plans to acquire a 49% stake in the existing PowerCo Spain through a capital increase. PowerCo will retain control with a 51% stake after the transaction. The project in Šurany, Slovakia, involves a planned investment of about €480 million for annual lithium-ion battery production capacity of 8.4 GWh. Gotion will hold 51% and PowerCo 49%. Cells produced by the 2 European projects will prioritize Volkswagen's demand in Europe. Specific purchase volumes and supply assurance arrangements remain subject to subsequent definitive agreements. The companies also plan to invest about €480 million in Kenitra, Morocco, to build a lithium iron phosphate cathode materials project with annual capacity of 100,000 metric tons, prioritizing supplies to the 2 battery joint ventures. Gotion will also control the Moroccan joint venture with a 51% stake, while PowerCo will hold the remaining 49%. The construction scope specified in the filing for all 3 projects excludes land and factory buildings. Each project is expected to take no more than 5 years to build, subject to actual construction progress. The cooperation will further strengthen the companies' equity and business ties. Volkswagen (China) Investment Co held a 24.28% stake in Gotion as of September 20, making it the battery maker's largest shareholder. Gotion said it will participate in the development of Volkswagen's key European cell production base, while PowerCo will take stakes in Gotion's battery and materials projects in Europe and Africa to jointly build a localized battery supply network for Europe. Gotion's board approved the proposal on September 28, but the companies have yet to sign the investment agreement. The transaction still requires shareholder approval and government clearances in China and overseas. The projects will increase capital expenditure in the near term, Gotion said, adding that financing, approvals and market changes could affect construction progress and expected returns. The investment plan comes as Gotion gains share in the global battery market. Its global EV battery installations totaled 34.0 GWh in the first 7 months of 2026, up 44.2% from a year earlier, according to South Korean market research firm SNE Research. Gotion High-tech ranked fifth globally during the period, with its market share rising to 4.7% from 3.9% a year earlier. ($1 = €0.8783)

artigo.texto: BYD says its new solid-state EV battery tech is nearly ready for the open road The Chinese company is one of several car makers expected to adopt solid-state batteries in the next few years. Switching from lithium-ion to solid-state batteries promises to extend the range and charging speeds of electric vehicles, and Chinese car maker BYD believes it's in a "leading position" to commercialize the technology. BYD's Executive Vice President Stella Li shared the claim in a recent interview with Carwow's Spanish outlet, alongside the news that BYD would release its first car with a solid-state battery in 2027. "Talking about solid-state batteries, BYD is in the leading position," Li said. "We're in the leading position for commercialization and technology. So to prove that, next year, we have one model that will be the first one with that technology." Li's comments further confirm plans shared by Sun Huajun, the Chief Technology Officer of BYD's battery subsidiary FinDreams, at a battery conference in February 2025. At the time, Sun said BYD would offer its first demonstration and installation of solid-state batteries in 2027 before the technology enters mass production around 2030, CarNewsChina reports. While that means people will be able to buy cars with the company's sulfide solid-state batteries, that doesn't mean its traditional lithium batteries will be phased out, BYD Chief Scientist Lian Yubo shared at the same conference. "Solid-state batteries will be mainly used in high-end models, empowering each other with lithium iron phosphate batteries, and used in vehicles of different levels," Lian said. In comparison to lithium-ion batteries, which move ions between positive and negative terminals through a liquid solution of dissolved lithium salts, solid-state batteries replace the liquid with solid electrolytes made from oxides, polymers or sulfides (the kind BYD is developing). Solid electrolytes give solid-state batteries higher energy density, which opens up the possibility of smaller, lighter batteries and a longer range on a single charge. Solid-state batteries are also theoretically safer because they're far less prone to catching fire and they're able to operate at extreme temperatures, an issue current lithium-ion batteries struggle with. The problem with using the battery technology as it exists now is cost, which is why BYD suggests you'll see its solid-state batteries on more expensive models first, like possibly a future version of its Denza Z. The company is one of several car makers planning to ship a vehicle with solid-state batteries in the next few years. For example, Toyota committed to offering cars with solid-state batteries by 2027 or 2028; Mercedes-Benz began testing a solid-state EQS model and shared that it would ship the technology before the end of the decade; and Stellantis began road testing a solid-state Dodge Charger in 2026. Earlier this year, Honda struck up a new partnership with QuantumScape to develop solid-state batteries it hopes will help it reach carbon neutrality by 2050. The potential for solid-state battery technology is exciting, but most car makers are only in the first leg of the race.

artigo.texto: Formas de reduzir as emissões e avançar rumo a um mercado de carbono em Phu Tho. TPO - À medida que as exigências de carbono se tornam cada vez mais interligadas com a produção, as cadeias de suprimentos e as exportações, a província de Phu Tho está intensificando os esforços para orientar as empresas no inventário de gases de efeito estufa, no desenvolvimento de planos de redução de emissões e na preparação para o mercado de carbono. Um repórter do jornal Tien Phong entrevistou o Sr. Nguyen Van Linh, chefe do Subdepartamento de Meio Ambiente e Mudanças Climáticas do Departamento Provincial de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente de Phu Tho, sobre este assunto. PV: Senhor, qual é o estado atual dos inventários de gases de efeito estufa em instalações e empresas na província de Phu Tho ? Senhor Nguyen Van Linh: De acordo com a Decisão nº 42/2026/QD-TTg, de 10 de agosto de 2026, a província de Phu Tho possui 177 estabelecimentos na lista que devem realizar o inventário de gases de efeito estufa, incluindo 82 estabelecimentos no setor de Indústria e Comércio, 93 estabelecimentos no setor de construção, 1 estabelecimento de transporte e 1 estabelecimento ambiental. De acordo com os resultados da avaliação de 2025, 84 instalações concluíram o inventário, representando 75,68% das instalações sujeitas à pesquisa; destas, 34 instalações concluíram o inventário e possuíam planos de redução de emissões, atingindo 30,63%. Esta é uma área relativamente nova para muitas empresas, portanto, aumentar a frequência de testes de emissões e desenvolver planos de redução de emissões são tarefas que precisam ser mais incentivadas no próximo período. PV: Com base na experiência de implementação, quais são os maiores desafios que as empresas enfrentam atualmente? Sr. Nguyen Van Linh: Uma dificuldade comum é que muitas empresas não compreendem totalmente suas responsabilidades ou os métodos para inventariar gases de efeito estufa. Coletar dados operacionais, identificar fontes de emissão e preparar relatórios exige conhecimento especializado, e nem todas as empresas têm o pessoal necessário para atender a esses requisitos. Você também pode gostar Portanto, para o relatório de inventário de gases de efeito estufa em nível de instalação de 2024, muitas empresas precisam contratar consultorias especializadas para realizar o processo com base nos dados fornecidos por elas mesmas. Essa é também uma das questões sobre as quais o órgão regulador precisa continuar orientando as empresas para garantir que o processo seja implementado de forma correta e eficiente. PV: De que forma a província de Phu Tho está apoiando as empresas no processo de inventário e redução de emissões? Sr. Nguyen Van Linh: No período anterior, o Comitê Popular Provincial e o Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente emitiram diversos documentos orientadores e incentivaram as empresas a implementar regulamentações sobre inventário, redução da emissão de gases de efeito estufa e adaptação às mudanças climáticas. A província também publicou o Plano nº 866/KH-UBND, datado de 28 de fevereiro de 2025, sobre a implementação de medidas para reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa, juntamente com muitos planos relacionados à redução de emissões na produção agrícola, à separação de resíduos na fonte e à adaptação às mudanças climáticas. O Departamento também coordena e envia funcionários e empresas para participar de cursos de capacitação sobre inventário de gases de efeito estufa, avaliação de danos climáticos, economia circular, compras públicas sustentáveis e produção e consumo sustentáveis. Quando as empresas precisam mudar de tecnologia, usar energia de forma eficiente ou adotar a produção sustentável, o Departamento as orienta nos procedimentos de acordo com as normas e as apoia na conexão com fontes de financiamento preferenciais do Fundo Provincial de Proteção Ambiental, caso tenham necessidade e atendam aos critérios de elegibilidade. PV: Que preparativos as empresas precisam fazer tendo em vista os requisitos de redução de emissões e a formação de um mercado de carbono, senhor? Você também pode gostar Sr. Nguyen Van Linh: As empresas precisam ser proativas desde o início, principalmente compreendendo as regulamentações, coletando dados completos e realizando inventários de gases de efeito estufa. A partir daí, elas podem identificar as principais fontes de emissão e desenvolver planos adequados de redução de emissões. Além disso, as empresas precisam se concentrar na conservação de energia, na inovação tecnológica, no uso eficiente de matérias-primas e na transição gradual para a produção sustentável. Este será um processo de longo prazo, que não só atenderá aos requisitos de gestão ambiental, mas também ajudará as empresas a se adaptarem às demandas de carbono cada vez mais rigorosas na cadeia de suprimentos e nos mercados de exportação. Do ponto de vista administrativo, a província continuará a divulgar e orientar as regulamentações sobre créditos de carbono e o mercado de carbono, além de orientar as empresas na execução dos procedimentos relacionados. Atualmente, o setor de mudanças climáticas conta com 7 procedimentos administrativos sob a autoridade do Presidente do Comitê Popular Provincial.

artigo.texto: NYE COUNTY (KTNV) — A pair of companies are suing Nye County over their ban on data center development. CDDC, LLC and 9 of a Kind, LLC own nearly 911 acres along Carpenter Canyon Road and Nevada State Route 160. For years they've sought to build the Manse Technology Center, also known as the MTC Project. Their attorneys suggest the Pahrump Regional Planning District essentially green lit the plan, causing the companies to heavily invest. But last month the Nye County Board of Commissioners voted to ban data centers in the Pahrump area and Water Basin 162. The companies believe the abrupt change is a violation of their State property rights. "Petitioners are entitled to develop their property under their common law property rights that existed long before the Pahrump Regional Planning Commission’s zoning designation of specific plan on the Petitioners property, which is a void zoning designation because it is vague, standardless, and encourages arbitrary enforcement," the lawsuit reads. Lawyers for the companies say they've followed all County zoning laws, even conforming to changes last made in 2023. Sean Dalesandro, developer of Manse Technology Campus, provided KTNV with this statement. "Manse Technology Campus proceeded with its data center project because Nye County’s zoning laws permitted it. Because our project complied with Nye County’s zoning, we made substantial investments toward the project and acted in lockstep with Nye County’s consistent positive guidance throughout the development process. Nye County then adopted Ordinance No. 631, disregarding our substantial investments in reliance on existing zoning, changing the rules after the fact and writing the change to reach backward. Earlier this month we filed a petition asking the court to review questions that should be of concern to everyone. We are asking the Court to confirm that when Nye County, adopted the ordinance it did not keep faith with firmly established principles, which mandate that an ordinance must be lawfully adopted, applied and uphold a principle that protects every landowner here: you should be able to rely on your property's zoning, the county's guidance, and the county's own process when you invest. If your zoning can be undone at any time, then property rights become property privilege and that should concern every property owner in Nye County. " We will continue to follow all new developments regarding Nye County data centers and any decisions that come associated with them.

artigo.texto: After completing its first 100 back-to-back charge-discharge cycles without faults or degradation, Qnetic has moved its 200-kilowatt-hour Pulsar energy storage prototype into low-speed testing. It's another sign the company believes flywheel storage can become a practical alternative to lithium-ion batteries. If the system keeps performing as expected, it could help address one of the biggest challenges tied to renewable energy: storing electricity cheaply, efficiently, and for long periods. Here's what to know According to Interesting Engineering, engineers are using this phase to verify how Pulsar's control and safety systems perform before spinning the machine at higher rotational speeds. Before reaching this stage, the prototype completed mechanical assembly in June and underwent structural and component tests meant to reduce technical risk ahead of full-speed operation. Instead of storing energy through chemical reactions, Qnetic's system holds it as motion. Solar or wind facilities generate electricity to accelerate a heavy rotor inside a frictionless vacuum chamber, and when demand increases, the system can convert that rotational energy back into power for the grid. Renewable generation is not constant. Solar panels stop producing at night, and wind output can rise or fall throughout the day, so storage helps make clean electricity available when people need it. Qnetic's motor surpassed 11,000 revolutions per minute and delivered 130 kilowatts of output at 97.3% efficiency, helping validate the system's power-conversion architecture. More background Interest in flywheel storage comes in part from the drawbacks of lithium-ion batteries. Although lithium-ion systems are widely used and can hold large amounts of energy, they are often expensive and tend to degrade as charge cycles accumulate. Because a flywheel stores energy mechanically rather than chemically, its core storage component does not undergo the same kind of wear as battery cells, which could allow it to operate for longer. For utilities and grid operators adding more renewable energy, that could be significant. A storage system that is both durable and efficient could support greater use of wind and solar while helping maintain grid stability without raising costs. What's being done? Rather than pushing Pulsar straight to full operating conditions, Qnetic is validating the system in stages. Michael Pratt, CEO of Qnetic, said the company is increasing operating demands step by step so engineers can confirm the data and solve problems before advancing further. Results from Pulsar testing are also being shared with the Electric Power Research Institute as part of the Readiness Informed by Shared Knowhow, Evaluation, and Data, or deRISKED, program. That kind of outside review could help utilities and customers assess the technology using measured performance rather than hype. If Qnetic's approach continues to hold up through higher-speed testing, it could strengthen the case for flywheels as a serious contender in grid storage. That would not replace lithium-ion batteries overnight, but it could give energy providers another option for storing renewable electricity in a way that is scalable and potentially more durable. "Our approach is to increase operating conditions methodically, validating the data at each stage and resolving issues before moving on," Pratt said in a press release. "That process fundamentally de-risks a system of this scale before full-speed testing and eventual customer deployment." Where can I learn more? Energy-storage technologies are advancing alongside flywheel systems like Pulsar. • Material scientists have unveiled a record-breaking storage device that could reshape clean energy systems. • Envision Energy said its grid battery system can deliver around 96% efficiency. • In Croatia, an automaker introduced an advanced battery system. • NASA engineers built a solid-state sulfur-selenium battery to push energy storage limits. • NASA has also created a battery that could power electric planes. artigo.texto: A aprovação, pelo Conselho Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Conema), de regras específicas para o licenciamento de data centers abre uma possibilidade concreta para o Rio Grande do Norte. O Estado avança na definição de critérios para avaliar projetos de um setor em expansão e dá aos investidores mais clareza sobre o caminho a percorrer. O próximo desafio é transformar essa condição em investimentos que gerem oportunidades para os potiguares. Os data centers fazem parte da infraestrutura por trás de serviços que usamos todos os dias, desde o armazenamento de arquivos e o funcionamento de sistemas pela internet, a chamada computação em nuvem, até as ferramentas de inteligência artificial. Dependem de energia, conectividade e equipes qualificadas. O Estado tem um ativo relevante nesse cenário. O RN em Foco 2027-2030, elaborado pela Fecomércio RN, registra 13,2 gigawatts de capacidade instalada de geração de energia e outros 8,9 gigawatts em projetos outorgados, ainda não construídos. O documento inclui expressamente esses centros de dados entre as atividades que essa expansão pode ajudar a atrair. A água exige atenção especial Para receber esses projetos, a capacidade de geração precisa vir acompanhada de infraestrutura adequada, previsibilidade para quem investe e responsabilidade com os recursos naturais. No Rio Grande do Norte, o uso da água exige atenção especial. A norma aprovada pelo Conema prevê estudos ambientais mais aprofundados para grandes projetos que utilizem sistemas abertos de refrigeração, associados a maior consumo de água. Assim, o licenciamento pode considerar as características e os impactos de cada empreendimento. A Fecomércio RN e outras entidades representativas do setor produtivo estiveram à frente das discussões, em articulação com o Governo do Estado. O diálogo permitiu examinar os aspectos técnicos e construir uma solução conjunta. No plano nacional, a recente criação do Redata soma-se a esse avanço. O regime federal de incentivos ao setor vincula seus benefícios a compromissos com energia de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, eficiência hídrica, pesquisa e desenvolvimento. Para competir por esses investimentos, o Rio Grande do Norte ainda precisará assegurar condições de conexão e fornecimento de energia para cada projeto. Também será necessário formar profissionais e aproximar empresas locais das demandas que surgirem, para que os efeitos desses empreendimentos alcancem outras atividades da economia potiguar.

artigo.texto: Vena Energy Wins 46.8 MW Battery Storage Contract in Japan Vena Energy's NRE Nakagawa 2 project in Nagano Prefecture has been selected in Japan's FY2025 auction for long-term decarbonised power sources. Vena Energy, the renewable energy arm of Vena Group and a provider of green energy solutions across the Asia-Pacific region, announced the selection of its NRE Nakagawa 2 Battery Storage project in Japan's FY2025 Long-Term Decarbonised Power Source Auction (LTDA), conducted by the Organisation for Cross-regional Coordination of Transmission Operators (OCCTO). The project, currently under development in Japan, was awarded a capacity of 46,828 kW, according to the company. This type of battery storage deployment reflects a broader trend of similar infrastructure being rolled out, such as the 210 MWh battery storage system installed in Nickelsdorf, Austria. An auction mechanism to support carbon neutrality Introduced in fiscal year 2023, the LTDA scheme is designed to support Japan's ambition to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050. The programme encourages investment in decarbonised power generation by providing long-term revenue certainty, thereby helping developers recover their development and capital costs, according to OCCTO. The NRE Nakagawa 2 project adds to the battery storage portfolio that Vena Energy is developing in Japan. It follows the Hikone Battery Storage project, which began commercial operations last year, according to the company. This new asset confirms Vena Energy's strategy in energy storage within the Japanese market. Company Vena Group: company profile A grid-connected site near Matsumoto The grid-connected battery storage system is located near Matsumoto City, in Nagano Prefecture. Raul Rienda, Head of Japan at Vena Energy, said that deploying battery storage systems is necessary to address the intermittency of renewable energy and enable more efficient use of electricity. According to Mr. Rienda, the project's selection in the FY2025 auction should help strengthen the reliability and resilience of Japan's power system. artigo.texto: Most digital services feel intangible to the people using them. The infrastructure that makes them possible is not. Every cloud application, artificial intelligence (AI) model, streaming platform, and online transaction depends on buildings filled with computing equipment, power systems, cooling infrastructure, networks, and increasingly dense hardware. That physical footprint is growing quickly. The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that electricity use by data centers will rise from about 485 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030, almost doubling in five years. Electricity demand from AI-focused data centers is expected to triple over the same period. By 2030, data centers could account for about 3% of global electricity demand. That raises a less comfortable question about data-center sustainability. Improving the efficiency of individual facilities matters, but it does not tell us whether those gains can keep pace with the amount of new computing infrastructure being added. The environmental pressure can also move from one part of the system to another. The growth problem is bigger than efficiency A more efficient server does not necessarily reduce total electricity use when thousands of additional servers are installed. The issue becomes harder to ignore as AI increases both the amount and density of computing. The IEA expects data-center electricity use to reach about 3% of global electricity demand by 2030, while AI-focused data centers are expected to grow considerably faster than the sector overall. MarkNtel Advisors‘ February 2026 research shows how quickly investment in the greener side of the sector is moving. Its Green Data Centers Market study projects the market to rise from $52.76 billion in 2026 to $235.4 billion by 2032, representing a 28.31% compound annual growth rate (CAGR). North America is identified as the largest regional market. That growth reflects genuine changes in the way operators build and run facilities. Renewable electricity, lower-energy systems, improved cooling and more efficient designs are all receiving greater attention. But there is another side to the same numbers. The market for greener data centers is expanding partly because the underlying data-center footprint is expanding. That makes the following questions important: - Total electricity demand: How much additional power will new capacity require? - Location: What are the grid and water conditions where the facility is being built? - Hardware intensity: How much equipment is needed to support the new capacity? - Replacement cycles: How long will that equipment remain in service? - Local resources: Can surrounding infrastructure absorb the additional demand? Efficiency remains necessary. It is simply harder to treat it as the whole answer when the amount of computing infrastructure is rising so quickly. Power is becoming a location constraint Electricity is becoming part of the siting decision, not just an operating cost. The IEA’s 2026 electricity outlook says data centers could account for about half of U.S. electricity-demand growth through 2030. In 2025 alone, data centers accounted for around 50% of total electricity-demand growth in the United States. A June 2026 assessment from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) estimates that data centers could account for 11.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption by 2030. Its modeled scenarios range from 9.5% to 15.3%. These figures do not mean every region will face the same level of pressure. They do show why access to electricity is becoming an important part of deciding where new computing capacity can be added. For a new facility, several power questions need to be answered: - Grid capacity: Can the local network take on a large new load? - Generation mix: What sources are actually supplying the electricity reaching the site? - Transmission: Can additional generation reach the data center without creating prolonged grid constraints? - Reliability: What backup and firm-power systems are needed to keep the facility operating around the clock? A data center can buy renewable electricity and still require new transmission capacity, substations, backup generation, or other grid investment. Where the facility is built also affects its environmental impact. The same technical design can place very different demands on the wider system depending on the local grid, available transmission capacity, and electricity mix. That is why the question is not only how efficiently a data center uses electricity. It is also whether the surrounding power system can accommodate the load. Where the sustainability trade-offs occur These pressures are connected. A measure that improves one area can have an effect somewhere else. Water shows this particularly well. Water makes the sustainability question local Global estimates are useful for showing the scale of data-center activity. They are less helpful when the question is whether a particular facility is appropriate for its location. A 2025 Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory study found that workload-level water use can vary by more than 10,000-fold. The study identified server efficiency, electricity-grid water consumption, server utilization, cooling system type, infrastructure efficiency, climate, inactive servers and hardware refresh cycles among the main factors behind the difference. That makes broad claims about “the water footprint of AI” difficult to assess without knowing how and where the computing is taking place. The practical questions are local: - What cooling system does the facility use? - What is the climate where it operates? - How water-intensive is the electricity supplying it? - How heavily are the servers being used? - What is the local availability of water, and what other users depend on it? Cooling technology matters, but it is only one part of the calculation. Electricity generation can carry an indirect water footprint, while climate affects how much heat

artigo.texto: Pro-data center party interrupted by protesters in D.C. A pro-data center party took place in Washington D.C. on Saturday night, as opposition to data center construction has intensified across the country. An invitation to the event on Partiful said: "In light of the bipartisan psychosis over AI data centers, it's about time that the people who haven't lost their minds get together and celebrate the glory of American compute." Videos posted on social media showed the party in full swing, complete with a DJ booth and dance floor. One X user wrote that the event had "a generative AI photo booth, AI themed cocktails." At one point, protesters appeared to crash the party. One female protester took to the stage and shouted to the crowd "thank you for using all the water" and "you're killing the world," as party-goers chanted "USA!" The protester was eventually seen being removed from the stage. As data center construction accelerates, the debate over how and where the facilities should be built is expected to remain a growing political and environmental issue. After the disruption, Adam Thierer from the R Street Institute took to the stage to say: "You know who doesn't believe in freedom, is the freaks who were just up here charging the stage," the Washington Sun reported. As demand for AI computing has boomed, data centers have become a growing source of tension over their enormous demands for power, water and land. Newsweek contacted Jonas Du and Young Voices via email on Monday, outside of regular working hours. The Party "Data After Dark: A Pro-Data Center Party" was held at the self-described "Bitcoin bar," PubKey in D.C. More than a thousand people had signed up to attend through the Partiful invitation, though it is not clear how many ultimately attended. Young Voices, Pirate Wires and The Compute Optimist were listed on a flyer as the organizations behind the party. The event was sponsored by several think tanks, technology advocacy groups and organizations promoting the expansion of computing infrastructure. The event featured themed cocktails with names inspired by the data center industry, one of the organizers wrote on X. These included the Loudoun County Iced Tea, a reference to the Virginia county at the heart of the region's "Data Center Alley," as well as the SMRtini and the Closed-loop Spritz. Who Were the Event Organizers? The event was organized by Ed Tarnowski, a technology policy fellow at the free-market R Street Institute who has launched the Substack publication The Compute Optimist; Jonas Du, a writer at technology and politics publication Pirate Wires; and Casey Given, the CEO of Young Voices, a nonprofit that trains and promotes young pro-liberty commentators. Tarnowski and Du appeared in a video filmed at the event, in which a reporter asked attendees why they loved data centers. "This is our industrial revolution," Tarnowski said. "AI is poised to deliver benefits that we couldn't imagine," he said, adding that technological progress was reliant on American "dominance of data centers." He also touted the "national security benefits" of data centers, particularly their importance to the U.S. in maintaining a technological edge over China. Du also appeared in the video, and said: "The only way we can get young people and everyday Americans feeling more optimistic about the economy and the future of the country and the American dream is by growing our economy and increasing our innovation rate. And data centers power AI, which is the number one thing driving that right now." "We should use common sense as to where we built them and how we build them, but no question we need to build more," he added. Along with the protesters who expressed their displeasure in person, the event also sparked backlash on social media. While one X user went so far as to say they wished the party would be set on fire with attendees inside, others expressed more temperate criticisms that hosting a glitzy D.C. cocktail party in support of data centers would not help ordinary Americans get on board. Data Center Debate Heats Up The U.S. is in the midst of a boom of data centers, which are large facilities that house the computer servers and other equipment needed to store and process vast amounts of digital information. There are at least 4,000 operational facilities nationwide and some 3,000 more planned or under construction. But the expansion has faced growing opposition over the facilities' demands for resources and their proximity to residential areas. A Gallup poll found that around 70 percent of Americans are opposed to data centers being built in their area. The issue has increasingly become a political flashpoint, as opposition to data centers has spread across party lines, even as the Trump administration promotes their expansion as essential to the U.S. race for AI dominance. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Ben Kelly and Cristina Diciu. Related Articles
