artigo.texto: What do school referendums and data centers have in common? They are both unpopular — but that doesn’t mean all of them are bad. That’s why I hope Hoosiers consider each proposal on its individual merits instead of automatically opposing them. There are key factors voters and residents should consider when weighing the pros and cons. Let’s Start With School Referendums Thirty-eight school districts in dozens of counties are asking voters this November to approve property tax referendums that would provide their schools with additional funding. Most of these proposals are for operational expenses, though several involve construction and public safety levies as well. This is a record number for a single election in Indiana, spurred in part by lawmakers’ recent limits on when school districts can take these requests to voters. The new law restricts referendum requests to once every two years, rather than the previous maximum of twice a year. Americans for Prosperity’s Indiana chapter launched a targeted digital advertising campaign urging voters in counties across Indiana to vote no on school property tax referendums. “Government spending accountability should come before tax increases, and we’re making sure voters have the facts they need before they go to the polls in November,” the group said. I believe this blanket approach is bad for Indiana. Each community has its own needs, and voters should consider those circumstances when casting their ballots. Here are a few things I think provide important context when considering a referendum: - Has the school district asked for a referendum before? A district may have already cut costs and could now need additional funding to accomplish its goals. - Does the referendum actually raise property taxes? Many of this year’s proposals simply renew an existing levy that is set to expire. That means homeowners may not see an increase — although they also would not see the decrease that would occur if the levy expired. In some cases, a district may have a bond payment obligation ending, and the referendum would simply take its place on the tax bill. - What will the money be used for? Paying for an extravagant new building is different from maintaining core course offerings or creating new programs for students. A public safety referendum, for example, could pay for school resource officers or security improvements designed to protect schools from outside threats. - Is the district responsible with its money? This is somewhat subjective, but voters should examine whether the district’s budget has grown at an unreasonable rate or whether administrative salaries appear excessive. If district leaders have demonstrated good stewardship of taxpayer dollars, that should also be taken into consideration. - What are the costs of saying no? In some communities, rejecting a referendum could lead to teaching positions or arts programs being eliminated — especially when an existing referendum is not renewed. In others, a defeat might simply preserve the status quo while preventing new programs or opportunities. Now, Let’s Talk About Data Centers Hoosiers have increasingly pushed back against hyperscale data center projects that consume significant amounts of electricity and water. Dozens of counties and communities have imposed temporary or permanent restrictions on these developments. Many state Republicans, however, support their growth, and President Donald Trump has argued that data centers are important to maintaining America’s position in the global artificial intelligence competition with China. So, here are a few things to consider if a data center is proposed near your community: - What benefits will flow to the community? These could include direct payments from the company, increased property tax revenue and new jobs. Employment is typically high during construction but generally falls once a facility becomes operational. I live in Lebanon, where Meta is spending millions of dollars on roads, infrastructure and community programs. - Are companies paying for the electric grid investments needed to operate the facility? This is important because one-time infrastructure upgrades should not simply fall on existing utility customers. Early in the data center boom, companies were not always paying those costs. After residents pushed back, lawmakers established requirements related to covering those expenses, including new generation and transmission infrastructure. In some cases, companies are paying the full cost. - What about water? Some communities have abundant water resources while others do not. If the water supply is sufficient, that can make a significant difference. But in communities such as Lebanon, where water must be brought in through an extended pipeline, a large data center may not be the right fit. Residents should also ask where wastewater will go and whether existing infrastructure can handle it. - Where will the data center be located? Many of these facilities are being built on productive farmland, which I see as a negative. Others are proposed near residential areas, where homeowners could be affected by noise, increased traffic and years of construction activity. Vacant industrial land — or property already zoned for business and industrial activity — seems like a better fit. Ultimately, I don’t believe either school referendums or data centers are inherently bad. Each proposal should be evaluated on its own circumstances, with all the relevant factors considered and local communities given a meaningful voice in the decision. The Indiana Capital Chronicle is an independent nonprofit news organization dedicated to giving Hoosiers a comprehensive look inside state government policy and elections. The site combines daily coverage with in- depth scrutiny, political awareness, and insightful commentary.

artigo.texto: Residents feel 'let down' by council as battery storage site approved Residents say they have been "let down" by their local council after a massive battery energy storage site was approved on appeal by Welsh government planning inspectors. Developers Innova have won a case to build a 400MW facility on a site near the village of Rhostyllen, Wrexham, which it said could power 900,000 homes. Campaigners claim Wrexham council officers failed to represent them properly at the inspectorate hearing. But the authority said it had presented as robust a case as it could and would now have to pay legal costs. Battery energy storage sites (BESS) are seen as an important part of reducing use of carbon by storing energy from renewables and releasing it to the grid when needed. Campaigners are concerned about the development's effects on agricultural land, biodiversity, the area's character and fire safety. "We were told by Wrexham planning department that they would represent us vocally and with evidence," said Alan Jones, chairman of Esclusham Community Group which has campaigned against the development. "We feel they didn't represent us at all. "Because we weren't represented, we have no case to take this to appeal so we're really disappointed." Developers appealed to inspectors at Planning and Environment Decisions Wales after Wrexham council failed to consider the application in the required time. The council's own planning committee then decided the local authority should oppose the plans at a hearing in July. Mark Andrew, from the local community council, said it had "hoped the local planning department would put a good argument in place". "The inspector said that no evidence was given against the case for the battery farm," he said. "It's angered so many people." Wrexham council said a senior officer was at the hearing and the authority had "presented as robust a case as it could explaining the reasons for the planning committee's decision". "The disappointment of the local community about the outcome of the appeal is understandable," it said. The council said it was now awaiting an invoice from the developers for costs after the inspector "concluded the council had acted unreasonably". Innova said it was pleased its appeal had been allowed and would "provide further updates to the local community as the project progresses towards construction".

artigo.texto: The New Economics of Enterprise AI AI costs stop being about tokens once it hits production — the real question is whether you own or just rent the economics. September 28, 2026 Sponsored by HPE Imagine your company just discovered electricity. At first only a few machines run on it, and nobody worries about efficiency — consumption is low and the value is obvious. But once electricity becomes infrastructure, every process depends on it, and the question changes from "can we use it?" to "how efficiently are we using it?" Enterprise AI is going through the same shift. What began as isolated chatbot and copilot experiments is becoming a foundational layer of the business, with models, agents, and data increasingly interconnected in production workloads. The important question stops being what a token or GPU-hour costs. It becomes how efficiently the AI environment converts paid capacity into useful business outcomes. That's the metric worth tracking: effective cost per useful outcome — the total platform, model, operations, and capacity cost required to complete work the business can actually use, whether a resolved request or a completed workflow. Three ways to run AI Utilization is central to this economics. Directing more work to paid-for capacity lowers effective unit cost; idle GPUs, fragmented workloads, and oversized models all raise the cost of every useful result. Enterprises generally choose among three models: A bespoke stack — procuring infrastructure and controls in-house. Flexible, but it creates a continuing burden, since teams must revalidate the environment as models and policies change. On-demand consumption — hyperscalers reduce the assembly burden and suit low or uncertain demand, but charges rise with every prompt or agent action. An integrated private AI platform — owned or dedicated capacity paired with a validated stack. The advantage isn't free inference; it's control over efficiency levers like scheduling, model selection, GPU partitioning, and cache management. The right model depends on the workload. APIs can be rational for experimentation or variable demand. As workloads become sustained and business-critical, enterprises need to weigh not just what they consume, but how efficiently they operate the system. Ownership is an operating discipline Buying a Formula 1 race car and parking it in your garage means owning one of the most sophisticated vehicles ever built — but ownership alone doesn't make you competitive; you still need drivers, mechanics, and track time to justify it. AI infrastructure works the same way. One of the biggest misconceptions in enterprise AI is that owning infrastructure automatically improves economics. Owning GPUs creates the opportunity for better economics, but only if the organization has sufficient demand and operational discipline to keep resources productive. The infrastructure that returns the best ROI isn't a reference architecture or a bespoke build-out — it's a fully integrated, qualified stack that lets teams route tasks to the least costly model that meets quality requirements and reuse context through techniques such as KV-cache management, reducing wasted capacity while maintaining responsiveness. Without these practices, committed infrastructure can become stranded capital. With them, rising demand improves economics as fixed costs are amortized across more useful work — increasingly important in agentic systems, where economics are shaped less by any single prompt than by the efficiency of the complete environment. From deployment to value HPE Private Cloud AI is a production-ready foundation combining infrastructure, software, models, tools, governance, and services, reducing the integration burden of operating private AI at scale. Its architecture lets teams manage scheduling, model selection, GPU partitioning, and cache management as operational levers, aligning capacity and service levels with each workload's requirements. It also includes a 90-day engagement with forward-deployed engineers who help customer teams deploy initial use cases and establish repeatable operating practices. In independent testing commissioned by HPE, an integrated platform serving multiple workloads at high utilization delivered a lower effective cost per token than repeatedly renting equivalent capacity. Actual results will vary based on workload mix and utilization. Measure what matters Token consumption remains useful, but it isn't a complete measure of AI economics. A fuller enterprise view tracks cost per business-relevant outcome, accelerator utilization, and model choice relative to task complexity. Enterprises already operating private AI should ask how mature their utilization is, and how workload volume will change over the next 12 to 18 months. Those earlier in the journey should build these practices in from the first deployment, so strategy anticipates growth before demand becomes a bottleneck. For low-volume, unpredictable demand, an API or hyperscaler may remain sensible. But as AI becomes a continuous production capability, enterprises have a growing incentive to control utilization, amortize fixed costs, and manage the environment as a long-term operating asset. The strategic question isn't whether enterprises will pay for AI — it's whether they will understand, and ultimately own, the economics behind it. For the past 15 years, his focus has been on bridging the gap between cutting-edge research and enterprise-scale deployment for Machine Learning and AI. His passion is turning the art of the possible into operational reality. David works at the intersection of innovation and reliability, helping organizations transform emerging technologies into production systems that deliver measurable busine

artigo.texto: I tested Belkin's 'semi-solid-state' battery — and it's the best iPhone portable charger I've ever used When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission. I'm a big fan of magnetic phone accessories, especially when it involves MagSafe-compatible wireless charging. Portable battery packs are great, but the reliance on cables is not something I will ever be happy about. Switching to wireless charging, and using magnets to keep everything in place, means that problem is eliminated — though it's not ideal that those batteries add a bunch of bulk and weight to your phone. Belkin's newest magnetic battery pack, UltraCharge Pro Slim Magnetic Power Bank with BoostSolid Cell, helps to eliminate that problem. The "Semi Solid State" battery design is significantly thinner and lighter than you might expect, which makes a surprising amount of difference for comfort. However, that also comes at the cost of overall capacity, which may or not be a dealbreaker. What the heck is a 'semi-solid-state' battery? You may be wondering what Semi-Solid-State actually means. The idea of solid-state batteries is nothing new, since those offer power without any of the chemical movements and reactions. According to Belkin, this "semi-solid" design utilizes a gel-like layer alongside a liquid electrolyte. The company hasn't gone into the specifics of how everything works, but the design enables a slimmer and more compact design, greater longevity and a much lower risk of overheating. That should help improve the overall safety of using these batteries, and considering the clampdown by airlines in recent months, that's definitely a good thing. Speaking of airlines, Belkin says that the $70 UltraCharge Pro Magnetic Power Bank has been built to comply with standard safety requirements, and the TSA's carry-on guidance. Though this doesn't necessarily mean that you are cleared to use this one in the air. Each airline has their own policies, and you need to be aware of them before you travel. The battery itself is Qi2 certified, offering up to 15W charging speeds on compatible phones. Wired USB-C charging is also available if you have a cable, with speeds up to 7.5W. The battery itself recharges at up to 22.5W. Naturally, being magnetic, it snaps onto the back of your phone — whether it has built-in magnets or you're using a special case. Materials-wise, you've got a battery that is a mix of metal and rubber, which is not exactly uncommon in magnetic batteries, though the actual size of the thing is arguably where its biggest strength lies. How does it compare to my existing magnetic power bank? The magnetic battery pack I use most of the time is UGreen's 10,000 mAh magnetic power pack. It's a fairly cheap option, which means it isn't officially certified as MagSafe or Qi2 — it's just a regular wireless charger with a MagSafe-compatible connection. That means it's slow, and it has a habit of getting pretty hot. UGreen's model is 0.79-inches thick, which is more than double Belkin's 0.35-inches. It's also heavier, weighing 7.9 ounces compared to 4.4 ounces for the Belkin. The UGreen battery is actually heavier and thicker than an iPhone 17 Pro (0.35-inches and 7.27 ounces), and only slightly lighter than the iPhone 17 Pro Max (8.33 ounces). The UltraCharge Pro Magnetic Power Bank is still going to add thickness and weight to your phone. However, it is a lot more comfortable and convenient to use compared to the bulky UGreen option I've been using. The downside is that it the Belkin has half the capacity of the UGreen. 10,000 mAh is enough to charge just about every phone at least once — and often more. 5,000 mAh doesn't go quite as far, but it's no small amount of power. It's enough to recharge a lot of phones in full, and enough to add a significant amount of power to others. Personally, while I like to overprepare and make sure I have more than enough energy to keep me going, I'll admit that 10,000 mAh is a bit overkill for most situations. So long as you have enough power to make it through the day, and get back to a home charger, then what does it matter how much of a reserve you have? In terms of charging and heat, I decided to test the two batteries on my iPhone 17 Pro Max starting at 47% charge. The Belkin battery restored 10%, bringing the total to 57% in that time, while the UGreen battery brought the charge to 54% — a 7% increase. It's not a huge amount of difference, but over the course of many hours that will add up. As for heat, the Belkin battery definitely felt warmer, but a quick check with a thermal camera saw the temperature peak at just under 95 degrees Fahrenheit. The UGreen battery didn't feel nearly as warm, but the thermal imaging revealed that a small part of the battery had risen to just shy of 97 degrees. That's not a huge difference, but you do have to remember that the UGreen charger is going much more slowly — and I did feel that heat start to add up over extended charging sessions. Wireless charging is always going to produce some heat if you don't have some sort of active cooling system. The Belkin UltraCharge does get warm, but it doesn't get too hot, which is quite nice. Bottom line I really like the Belkin UltraCharge Pro Magnetic Power Bank. Not specifically because it's a semi-solid-state battery, but because it manages to do all the things you need from a portable battery pack. It's slim and lightweight, with the magnetic connection making it incredibly easy to recharge your phone. Plus, the 15W Qi2 speeds mean it's fairly speedy as far as wireless charging goes. Admittedly, the 5,000 mAh capacity would be enough to make me hesitate on buying one for myself — especially with a $70 price tag. You can buy wired battery packs that offer four times the capacity for similar prices, if not less. artigo.texto: A blaze at the Moss Landing Power Plant in California has been linked to remediation work following the major battery energy storage system (BESS) fire at the site in January 2025. Firefighters from North Monterey County Fire District were dispatched to the facility on 18 September 2026, where they found smoke and flames coming from the north side of the site. As reported by the Santa Cruz Local, the site was evacuated of personnel with no injuries reported and a shelter-in-place warning was issued for surrounding areas as a precaution because of potential health risks associated with smoke and debris. The incident also affected traffic on the nearby Highway 1. Officials subsequently described the incident as a “flare-up” connected with clean-up operations following the January 2025 fire. The latest fire occurred in the Moss 300 building, which was extensively damaged during the original incident and experienced another fire in February 2025. Moss Landing’s Vistra battery storage facility comprises three buildings known as Moss 100, Moss 300, and Moss 350. Following the January 2025 incident, approximately 45,000 batteries reportedly remained intact and charged. Work has since been taking place to remove and de-energise them. At the time of this most recent incident, US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) officials said approximately 3,600 batteries remained to be removed from Moss 300, with some caught up in the latest incident. The incident was stabilised by 19 September, responsibility for continued monitoring was subsequently returned to facility personnel, and the shelter-in-place order was lifted. EPA on-scene coordinator Kazami Brockman said the remediation presented continuing challenges, saying, “this situation is complex”. Work crews have had to pause the clean up when encountering areas where removing batteries could create a risk of further flare-ups and officials have warned that additional incidents remain possible as work progresses. Katherine Hull, Federal On-Scene Coordinator for the EPA, said: “We’ve been doing everything that we absolutely can to prevent this from happening. Unfortunately, this did happen. So we just continue to monitor the batteries, and it’s a priority for us to get these batteries moved out of the building as quickly and as safely as we can.” Air monitoring during the incident did not record concerning concentrations of fine particles, while officials reported no detections of hydrogen fluoride as a result of the blaze. As reported by the Mercury News, Monterey County Supervisor Glenn Church said the latest incident again highlighted concerns surrounding the safety of battery energy storage installations. “It’s frustrating that this has continued to happen,” he said. “This fire is alarming for the community, bringing to the forefront once again that safety is paramount in every way we deal with battery energy storage systems.” He added: “While we need reliable and efficient battery energy storage systems, the key is that they really must be safe at all times whether while in operation or in a clean up.” Officials said the flare-up was not expected to alter the existing clean-up schedule, although unstable batteries remaining inside the damaged building mean further fires cannot be ruled out.

artigo.texto: Mercedes-Benz will test ProLogium’s latest Gen4 lithium ceramic battery cells as the German automaker evaluates next-generation battery technology for future electric vehicles. The companies have signed a joint testing agreement that gives Mercedes-Benz priority access to ProLogium’s Gen4 Superfluidized Inorganic Next-Generation Lithium Ceramic Battery cells. The cells will undergo electrical, thermal, and safety testing at Mercedes-Benz facilities and specialized external institutes. The program will assess whether the technology could eventually be integrated into future vehicle platforms. ProLogium says its Gen4 platform is designed to balance five areas: safety, performance, energy density, scalable manufacturing and cost. The technology combines a non-flammable inorganic electrolyte, ceramic separator and an active safety mechanism while targeting fast charging, high power output and low-temperature performance. Ceramic battery enters testing The agreement expands a partnership between Mercedes-Benz and ProLogium that dates to 2016. The automaker is also a strategic investor in the Taiwanese battery developer. The companies have previously worked on different lithium ceramic battery formats, including pouch and prismatic cells, as well as ProLogium’s Bi-Polar technology. Their collaboration has moved from early cell development and validation toward evaluating batteries for possible vehicle applications. “Over nearly a decade, our collaboration with Mercedes-Benz has evolved from early cell development and validation to testing our latest Gen4 technology for future vehicle applications,” said Vincent Yang, founder and CEO of ProLogium. More from Energy See All The Gen4 design follows ProLogium’s earlier hybrid-solid-state Gen3 technology. Its newer approach, introduced in 2025, is intended to combine characteristics associated with solid-state and liquid battery designs while addressing manufacturability and cost. Mercedes-Benz will now put those claims through its own testing process before determining whether the cells are suitable for automotive use. “By combining ProLogium’s pioneering solid-state battery approach with Mercedes-Benz’s deep battery development, testing and integration capabilities, we are taking the next step in exploring advanced battery technologies for future electric vehicles,” said Jörg Burzer, Mercedes-Benz Group’s chief technology officer for development and procurement. Gigafactories target larger scale ProLogium is also expanding production capacity as it moves the technology toward larger-scale automotive deployment. Its Taoke Gigafactory in Taiwan has completed GWh-scale manufacturing validation and currently supports C-sample production, demonstration vehicle programs and preparations for commercial production. The company is also building a gigafactory in Dunkirk, France. Its first phase is designed for 4 GWh of annual production capacity, expected to be progressively reached by 2030. The site is ultimately planned for a capacity of up to 44 GWh. The European plant is intended to replicate manufacturing processes developed in Taiwan and eventually supply enough cells to support EV platforms in Europe. ProLogium says it has delivered more than 2.4 million battery cells since commercializing its solid-state technology in 2013, including around 10,000 automotive battery samples.

artigo.texto: Portugal-headquartered Greenvolt Group has started construction of its 600 MW/2.4 GWh Siedlce battery energy storage system (BESS) in Poland through its utility-scale renewable energy business, Greenvolt Power. The project, expected to begin commercial operation by the end of 2027, will be Poland’s largest battery storage facility and one of Europe’s largest, it claims. BYD Energy Storage will supply the battery technology, with the project comprising 210 battery containers and 105 transformer containers equipped with power conversion systems. Siedlce is part of Greenvolt’s approximately 4.6 GW probability-weighted BESS pipeline, including around 2.4 GW in Poland. South Korean battery manufacturer LG Energy Solution has entered a strategic partnership with B2U Storage Solutions which is a US-based battery energy storage systems (BESS) manufacturer that works with repurposed EV batteries. Under the agreement, B2U will receive priority access to LG Energy Solution battery capacity and use its patented technologies to repurpose the batteries for grid-scale storage before recycling. The companies say their aim is to extend battery lifetimes and develop cost-competitive storage solutions for utilities, developers and large commercial users, including data centers. InoBat, a Slovakia-based BESS manufacturer and integrator is moving forward on its plans to list on the Nasdaq. The company along with Cartesian Growth Corporation II, a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC), recently filed a registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Their business combination agreement (BCA) values InoBat at $1.265 billion on a pre-money, pre-merger basis. Following completion, the combined company is expected to list on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol INBT. InoBat counts Volkswagen Group-backed Gotion High-Tech, mining giant Rio Tinto, and Indian battery maker Amara Raja Energy & Mobility Limited among its strategic shareholders and partners. Alongside the transaction, InoBat is expanding its European manufacturing footprint in Slovakia. At its Voderady site, the company is developing a BESS module, pack and container assembly facility with a targeted annual capacity of 5 GWh. Meanwhile, GIB EnergyX Slovakia, its gigafactory investment with Gotion in Šurany, is developing a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cell facility with an initial planned capacity of 20 GWh and targeted production start in 2027. The company is also advancing a sodium-ion battery roadmap in collaboration with Clarios and Altris. Decade Energy, a European developer of energy infrastructure for truck electrification, has signed a two-year supply framework agreement with Sungrow. The China-headquartered energy storage technology company will provide Decade Energy with up to 200 MWh of battery storage equipment in France. Decade Energy says this agreement is intended to support its growing French project pipeline. It will also enable the company to reduce complexity between projects and create a ‘repeatable’ delivery model across multiple sites. US-based SMT Energy has entered into an equity partnership with Climate Adaptive Infrastructure (CAI) for up to $268 million at the parent-company level. The investment, in addition to $32 million previously deployed by CAI into SMT assets, will support the development, construction and operation of battery storage projects across the US. SMT says the funding will enable it to develop and build energy infrastructure with an aggregate value significantly exceeding the equity investment. Its portfolio includes distributed-generation and utility-scale battery storage projects. Singapore-based renewable energy developer Vena Energy has secured a contract for its NRE Nakagawa 2 Battery Storage Project in Japan. The 46.8 MW grid-connected battery energy storage system (BESS), under development near Matsumoto City in Nagano Prefecture, was selected in Japan’s FY2025 Long-Term Decarbonised Power Source Auction (LTDA) conducted by the Organisation for Cross-regional Coordination of Transmission Operators (OCCTO). Vena Energy says the LTDA provides long-term revenue certainty to support investment in decarbonized power infrastructure. Nordic Solar, a Danish renewable energy company, has started commercial operation of a 20 MW/40 MWh BESS at its Moletai site in Lithuania. The battery is now integrated with the company’s existing 100 MW solar park, with hybrid trading now underway. The integration of solar generation and battery storage is expected to improve operational flexibility and enable the company to better utilize renewable power generation and market opportunities, stated Nordic Solar. The company switched on the 100 MW Moletai Solar Park in 2024 calling it the country’s largest back then (see Lithuania’s ‘Largest’ Solar Power Station Commissioned).

artigo.texto: During a recent trip to Sichuan Province in China, we got a chance to see BYD’s Flash Chargers up close. For those unfamiliar with the brand’s Flash Charging technology, these T-shaped structures provide EV charging at a rapid pace—around 9.7% charge per minute. According to BYD Philippines’ Adam Hu, these chargers are expected to arrive on our shores by 2027. The BYD Flash Chargers were first launched in China this year, with global rollouts expected for next year. The brand states that it can achieve charging times from 10% to 70% in only five minutes, and 10% to 97% in just nine minutes. During a live demonstration, the charging connector was plugged into a Denza Z9 GT, and while charging, a cup of pour-over coffee was being made on the side. The coffee was served in a cup just before the Z9’s battery topped off, achieving 97% from 33% in just seven minutes. What cars can use these chargers, you ask? Technically, anything with a CCS2 DC charging port can top up at these stations, but the Flash Charging feature is specific to cars with second-generation BYD Blade Batteries. In the Philippines, there are currently no cars equipped with the Blade Battery 2.0. However, the Denza Z9 GT and BYD Ti 7, which are both expected to come to the Philippines, are equipped with these batteries. The rest of the CCS2-equipped vehicles can charge at these stations but are limited to their maximum charging speed. OTHER STORIES YOU MIGHT HAVE MISSED: Fare hikes for jeepneys, buses, taxis, and TNVS take effect today Geely’s AI-powered EV charger will do sub-5min top-ups from 10% to 70% Even though most cars can’t take advantage of Flash Charging right now, it’s still a good thing that the infrastructure will be available. BYD and Denza’s future models will certainly feature Blade Battery 2.0 and later versions, so it shouldn’t be long before more consumers can use these ultra-fast chargers for their EVs.

artigo.texto: Os EUA estão apoiando pesquisas para um grande projeto de centro de dados de IA na cidade de Ho Chi Minh. A Agência de Comércio e Desenvolvimento dos Estados Unidos (USTDA) financiará um estudo de viabilidade para o Stavian Digital Park, um projeto de centro de dados de IA na cidade de Ho Chi Minh, destinado a atender grandes empresas de computação em nuvem e tecnologia. De acordo com um comunicado de imprensa datado de 23 de setembro, a USTDA assinou um acordo com a Stavian Hightech Infrastructure JSC, uma empresa de tecnologia pertencente ao Grupo Stavian, para apoiar um estudo de viabilidade para o projeto. O Stavian Digital Park é considerado um dos maiores centros de dados planejados no Sudeste Asiático. O projeto tem como alvo operadores de infraestrutura de IA e computação em nuvem de grande escala (hiperescala), incluindo empresas americanas. O centro de dados também foi projetado para ser aberto a provedores de serviços de telecomunicações que atendam a padrões de "confiabilidade". O estudo, conduzido pela Cushman & Wakefield, empresa sediada em Illinois (EUA), terá como foco o desenvolvimento de uma estrutura de aquisição, um modelo financeiro e um plano diretor para o campus. O estudo também incluirá elementos essenciais de infraestrutura, como fornecimento de energia, sistemas de refrigeração e conectividade de rede. Você também pode gostar Um ponto importante é que o projeto deverá introduzir critérios que exijam que os clientes utilizem dispositivos de segurança. De acordo com a USTDA, essa abordagem visa criar uma base para a arrecadação de fundos, além de abrir oportunidades para que empresas americanas forneçam tecnologia e soluções para o projeto. “O Vietnã está se tornando um polo de desenvolvimento de infraestrutura de dados e IA na região do Indo -Pacífico”, afirmou Thomas R. Hardy, Diretor Adjunto da USTDA. Segundo ele, o projeto contribuirá para atender às crescentes necessidades de infraestrutura digital do Vietnã e criará oportunidades para que empresas americanas forneçam tecnologia e conhecimento especializado para projetos semelhantes. Tony Dinh, presidente e CEO do Grupo Stavian, afirmou que o Parque Digital Stavian visa ajudar o Vietnã a atrair mais investimentos internacionais em tecnologia e a se tornar um polo regional de IA e computação em nuvem. O financiamento da USTDA ajudará a Cushman & Wakefield a elaborar um estudo de viabilidade com embasamento financeiro suficiente para apoiar decisões de investimento e captação de recursos. A USTDA não divulgou o investimento total, a capacidade energética ou a capacidade projetada de processamento de dados do Parque Digital Stavian em seu comunicado à imprensa. A agência afirmou que o projeto expandirá "significativamente" a capacidade de data centers do Vietnã, atendendo aos requisitos de infraestrutura dos sistemas de IA de próxima geração.

artigo.texto: WTO to Review EU's Carbon Border Mechanism Challenged by Russia The WTO's Dispute Settlement Body has decided to establish a panel to examine the European Union's carbon border mechanism, which Russia has been challenging since May 2025. The World Trade Organization's (WTO) Dispute Settlement Body decided on Friday, September 25, to establish a panel to examine the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) as well as the European Union's Emissions Trading System for CO2. The decision follows a renewed request from Russia as part of the trade dispute it opened against the EU. The case had already faced an initial block from Brussels before the panel was ultimately established. A Mechanism in Force Since January 2026 The proceedings concern the European scheme applied since January 1, 2026, to imports of certain carbon-intensive products. According to the WTO, Russia had formally requested, on July 10, 2026, the establishment of a panel, after having sought consultations with the European Union and its member states as early as May 12, 2025. CBAM, known as MACF in French, aims to align the carbon cost borne by certain importers with that paid by European producers covered by the EU's carbon market. Its initial scope covers steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, electricity and hydrogen. The European Commission publishes a CBAM certificate price based on auctions under the European Emissions Trading System. This price stood at â¬75.36/tCO2e for the first quarter of 2026, then at â¬75.28/tCO2e for the second quarter of 2026, according to data released by the Commission. Russia Invokes International Trade Rules Moscow contests the European mechanism, arguing it violates the principles of international trade. In the proceedings registered with the WTO, Russia targets both the CBAM regulatory package and what it describes as an export subsidy linked to the European Emissions Trading System. Russia's complaint cites several provisions of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) of 1994, as well as the Agreement on Import Licensing Procedures and the Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures. Russia also challenges the treatment of free allowances granted to certain European industries under the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), which has been in force since 2005. Brussels Limits Dialogue with Moscow The European Union had rejected, on May 22, 2025, Russia's request for consultations. Brussels had then argued that such talks "could not be fruitful and could not lead to a mutually satisfactory resolution of the matter," citing the "extraordinary circumstances" created by the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Following Russia's request on July 10, 2026, the EU had blocked an initial establishment of the panel, an option available upon the first presentation before the Dispute Settlement Body. In practice, WTO rules subsequently lead to acceptance of a second panel request. In a communication to the WTO, the European Union states it will engage with the panel but not directly with Russia. Brussels stated: "As long as the Russian Federation continues its war of aggression against Ukraine, it cannot expect to be able to invoke WTO rules to improve access for its exports to the European Union market."

artigo.texto: IESA Launches ‘BESS for C&I’ to Support 300 Consumers IESA has launched ‘BESS for C&I’ to address financing, policy, cost and awareness barriers as India’s C&I battery storage market expands. September 25, 2026. By News Bureau As India’s Commercial and Industrial (C&I) battery storage capacity surges from 40 MWh to 650 MWh, and is projected to reach nearly 4 GWh by FY 2027, the sector still faces major hurdles. High upfront costs, evolving regulations, limited financing options and gaps in user awareness continue to slow widespread adoption, even as demand accelerates. To close these gaps and support the next phase of market growth, the India Energy Storage Alliance (IESA) introduced the ‘BESS for C&I’ initiative in Mumbai. Through this initiative, IESA aims to empower 300 C&I consumers with storage solutions over the next three years. BESS for C&I will host monthly sessions from October 2026, bringing together industry, developers, and policymakers to discuss deployment, economics and best practices. Debmalya Sen, President of IESA, said, “The BESS for C&I platform is designed to address the unique challenges faced by commercial and industrial energy consumers as battery storage becomes essential for grid flexibility and business resilience. No single technology can meet all system needs; collaboration, knowledge-sharing and innovation across the value chain are critical to accelerating adoption and shaping India’s battery storage future.” This initiative creates a dedicated, free workgroup for commercial and industrial consumers. With battery storage now essential for India’s C&I sectors to manage rising power demand, control costs, and integrate renewables, IESA and industry leaders are calling for immediate policy action and targeted incentives to accelerate C&I battery storage adoption. Bharat Chhittarka, Director, Trex Energy, remarked, “To make India a global hub for battery manufacturing, we must expedite cell manufacturing and reduce dependence on imported raw materials, which currently account for 60-70 percent of battery costs. Battery energy storage is essential for managing time-of-day tariffs and accessing clean energy, especially as policies like Maharashtra’s TOD offer major savings. I recommend that all states create clear policies on TOD, energy arbitrage, and peak shaving, following Maharashtra’s example, to accelerate large-scale BESS adoption.” This community-driven platform will bring together industry stakeholders, policymakers, and energy users to share credible information, practical solutions, and best practices, empowering India’s C&I sector to unlock the full value of battery storage and accelerate the nation’s clean energy transition. Bimal Jindal, CEO, Energy Business, JBM Renewables, said, “To make India a global hub for battery manufacturing and supply chain, we must build a complete domestic ecosystem, including component-level manufacturing, securing lithium carbonate and cell production, and investing in R&D. The expansion of battery energy storage systems will be crucial for achieving net-zero goals, reducing long-term operating costs, and enabling the sale of green products internationally, despite initial cost challenges. The Government may consider increasing the mandated share of BESS deployment across relevant projects and reducing the GST on BESS from 18 percent to 5 percent, in line with solar panels." The group meets monthly to share policy updates, technology trends, and pricing insights, while offering exclusive access to B2B meetings, tech tours and masterclasses. Sushmita R. Ajwani, Head of Business Development (C&I), Aditya Birla Renewables, said, “For India to become a global leader in battery manufacturing, we must move beyond assembly and invest in internal cell manufacturing, backed by strong policy and financial support. Battery storage ensures reliable renewable supply, especially during peak demand. Although prices remain volatile, adoption will grow rapidly with clear regulatory guidelines and targeted incentives or rebates for BESS-backed renewable solutions.” Despite growth, battery storage faces project cost volatility, with utility-scale capex rising 15 percent in recent months. However, the right policy support and strong local supply chains will unlock the next phase of transformation. Inder Bhambra, COO-BESS and Chief Business Officer, India region, Envision Energy India, said, “To establish India as a global BESS manufacturing hub, we need to develop cell technologies and speed up assembly of DC containers locally, pack onwards. BESS enables an effective arbitrage against the rising peak tariffs and prepares the market for the upcoming new regulations, prescribing storage with every generation asset and mandating grid-forming features. The government must rationalise open access, removing transmission-related charges for charging of BESS, including the maximum demand charge, creating a supportive environment for large-scale deployment.” Through IESA Connect, IESA will take this conversation to cities and industrial clusters nationwide, so C&I consumers help shape policy, standards and safety, not just buy the technology. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: A Mombak concluiu a primeira etapa de captação de seu segundo fundo e prevê acesso a uma linha de R$ 200 milhões do Fundo Clima, enquanto prepara uma nova emissão de créditos até o fim de 2026 A Mombak deu um novo passo para financiar o reflorestamento de áreas degradadas na Amazônia. A startup brasileira concluiu a primeira etapa de captação de seu segundo fundo e anunciou um contrato plurianual para vender créditos de remoção de carbono à Salesforce. O fundo tem meta de US$ 150 milhões, valor que ainda não deve ser confundido com dinheiro integralmente captado. A empresa também prevê acesso a uma linha de crédito de R$ 200 milhões ligada ao Fundo Clima, conforme matéria publicada pela Reuters no dia 21 de setembro de 2026. O novo fundo busca ampliar o plantio em áreas degradadas da Amazônia Chamado Amazon Reforestation Fund II, o veículo pretende reunir recursos para novos projetos de restauração na Amazônia brasileira. Entretanto, a Mombak não divulgou à Reuters quanto recebeu nessa primeira etapa da captação. Por isso, US$ 150 milhões representam a meta do fundo, e não um montante já assegurado em sua totalidade. O financiamento previsto inclui acesso a R$ 200 milhões em crédito do Fundo Clima, operado pelo BNDES. Trata-se de uma linha de empréstimo, distinta dos aportes que o fundo busca junto a investidores. O Fundo Nacional sobre Mudança do Clima integra a estrutura brasileira de financiamento a projetos climáticos; no anúncio da Mombak, sua participação ajuda a compor os recursos disponíveis para a expansão. - Salinópolis, no Pará, recebeu 42,8 mil toneladas de sargaço em 2025, o maior volume estimado entre 51 registros de encalhe da alga na costa brasileira de 2010 a 2025, com efeito na pesca e no turismo, segundo estudo publicado em 2026 - Em 2000, mergulhador ajudou a filha em um projeto escolar e, 22 anos depois, iniciativa já havia possibilitado o replantio de mais de 200 mil corais - Mais de 200 pessoas foram à Praia de Iquipari e retiraram 2,6 toneladas de plásticos, microplásticos, isopor e madeira de área protegida pela Reserva Caruara, em São João da Barra - Mais de 80 mil geladeiras ficaram presas após falência, e 26 governos locais suspendem recolhimentos na Inglaterra e no País de Gales A empresa já tem uma operação anterior para mostrar. Seu primeiro fundo captou US$ 120 milhões de investidores que incluem um fundo da AXA, a CPP Investments e a Bain Capital. Com esses recursos, a Mombak financiou a restauração em 15 fazendas amazônicas e plantou quase 15 milhões de árvores nativas, segundo os números apresentados à Reuters. São resultados do primeiro fundo; a dimensão dos projetos que o segundo poderá financiar dependerá da captação e de sua execução. Reuters A Salesforce entra na lista de compradoras dos créditos florestais Além de buscar capital para plantar, a Mombak precisa encontrar compradores para os créditos gerados pelos projetos. Nesse ponto, anunciou um acordo plurianual com a Salesforce. A companhia de software se junta a clientes citados pela startup, como Google, Microsoft e McLaren Racing. A Reuters não informou o volume contratado pela Salesforce nem o valor da transação; portanto, o anúncio confirma a relação comercial, mas não permite calcular sua receita. O modelo da Mombak parte da recuperação de terras degradadas com espécies nativas. À medida que a vegetação cresce, as árvores retiram dióxido de carbono da atmosfera. Depois, a empresa precisa medir e verificar essa remoção para emitir créditos que possam ser vendidos. Plantar uma árvore não equivale, por si só, a emitir um crédito: a quantidade de carbono removida e as condições do projeto precisam ser demonstradas. A recuperação de ecossistemas também pode trazer benefícios ambientais que vão além do carbono, embora cada iniciativa exija avaliação própria. A Mombak realizou sua primeira emissão de créditos de remoção por reflorestamento em 2026. Agora, prevê uma segunda emissão, maior, de cerca de 80 mil toneladas de CO₂ até o fim do ano. Esse volume ainda é uma expectativa, não uma entrega concluída. Assim, os próximos meses mostrarão quanto do carbono projetado será efetivamente verificado e transformado em créditos. Mercado pode alcançar outras indústrias, mas a demanda ainda precisa se confirmar Empresas de tecnologia ajudaram a abrir mercado para a remoção de carbono. Segundo a Reuters, a expansão de centros de dados e da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial elevou a atenção dessas companhias às próprias emissões. Entretanto, a Mombak e o BNDES esperam que a demanda alcance também setores como petróleo, mineração e siderurgia. A diretora socioambiental do banco, Tereza Campello, afirmou que setores antes menos interessados passaram a procurar esse tipo de solução. Há outras rotas industriais para lidar com CO₂, entre elas projetos que dependem de captura e transporte do gás. Já os créditos da Mombak se apoiam no crescimento de florestas restauradas. Para compradores de qualquer setor, a decisão exige atenção à qualidade da medição e à permanência do carbono armazenado, além de esforços para reduzir as próprias emissões. O presidente da Mombak, Gabriel Silva, disse à Reuters que ganhos de produtividade e melhores técnicas de reflorestamento vêm reduzindo custos. Ainda assim, a ampliação do mercado permanece uma aposta. Os próximos resultados concretos serão o avanço da captação do fundo, a execução dos novos plantios e a emissão de créditos prevista para o fim de 2026.

artigo.texto: Why the rush to build data centers? Let’s ignore all the technology chatter for now. Forget the debates about the infrastructure demands of these massive computing sites. And we’ll also sidestep the big question marks about artificial intelligence – the key driver of data center demand. If you follow the money, however, you see a major force behind developers’ thirst to construct data centers: They’ve been one of the nation’s hottest real estate investments. That’s what my trusty spreadsheet found when looking at Nareit indexes tracking values of real estate investment trusts owning properties across 15 key categories. These benchmarks calculate price swings and dividends paid. The value of trusts that own data centers rose 33% so far in 2026, the second-best performance in the REIT industry, and more than double a 15% gain for all trust assets. What’s performing better in 2026? Trusts that own lodging and resort properties are up 37% on a strong year for tourism. No. 3 is healthcare properties, up 23% as an aging population needs more medical services. Remember, real estate sectors like data centers often heat up when there’s a shortage of specific assets. Big gains in value, plus perceptions of high demand, often get developers in a construction mood. Not just this year Note that the investment buzz for data centers isn’t just a 2026 story. Data center values are up 43% from the start of 2024 through August 2026, the industry’s third-best result, and nearly double the 23% gain for all assets. The gains were only topped by healthcare properties, up 96%, and regional malls, up 69%. Shopping hubs are enjoying a go-out-to-shop renaissance. Trailing the pack So, what properties will developers avoid? Well, look at which property trusts trail the pack. In 2026, the worst places to be are casinos, down 5% as in-person gambling wanes; telecommunications properties, down 2% as cell phone growth ebbs; and timberland, down 1% amid weak construction demand for lumber. Looking longer-term, back to 2024, the trust laggards have been timberland, down 25%; telecommunications, down 16%; and owning single-family rentals, down 4%, as the housing market weakens and regulatory concerns grow. artigo.texto: Policy Considerations for Orbital Data Centers Orbital data centers could complement terrestrial infrastructure by processing selected workloads in space, particularly where data is generated in orbit. Their value will depend on technical performance, life cycle economics, market demand, and a regulatory environment that does not hinder testing and deployment. KEY TAKEAWAYS Key Takeaways Contents Why Orbital Data Centers Are Gaining Relevance 3 Advantages of Orbital Computing. 3 Technical and Economic Challenges for Orbital Data Centers 4 Policy Challenges and Recommendations for Orbital Data Centers 6 Introduction Orbital data centers are specialized satellites that support computing functions by processing data in space.[1] This emerging technology is attracting growing attention amid both rising demand for computing capacity and advances in commercial space capabilities.[2] As the global space economy continues to grow and more digital services rely on space-based infrastructure, orbital computing may become useful for selected space-based workloads. Government assessments, technical research, and industry feasibility studies are currently examining whether selected computing functions could be performed in orbit for specialized applications, although significant engineering and economic questions remain.[3] Today’s orbital data center concepts should not be understood as near-term substitutes for terrestrial cloud infrastructure.[4] Data centers on Earth benefit from mature supply chains, easier repair and upgrade cycles, and lower operating complexity. Orbital systems, by contrast, must operate in a harsher environment that includes radiation exposure, thermal management challenges, communications constraints, and high deployment and replacement costs.[5] If orbital compute clears current technical and economic hurdles, then the central policy consideration is whether orbital systems can perform specialized computing functions well enough to justify their operational complexity rather than whether they can replace terrestrial hyperscale data centers. Orbital computing can reduce bandwidth demands and improve operational responsiveness, particularly where decisions must be made in orbit rather than on the ground. The strongest near-term opportunity for orbital computing lies in workloads that benefit from processing data where it is generated in space. These include Earth observation, remote sensing, and onboard spacecraft autonomy.[6] Over a longer time horizon, onboard or distributed computing could also become useful for certain lunar and cislunar missions, particularly where communications architecture or operational requirements favor local processing. In such settings, orbital computing may reduce bandwidth demands and improve operational responsiveness, particularly where decisions must be made in orbit rather than on the ground.[7] For that reason, orbital data centers are best treated as a complementary layer of digital infrastructure rather than a wholesale replacement for terrestrial systems.[8] Public policy should focus on ensuring that existing regulatory frameworks allow markets to identify and develop those applications for which orbital computing offers genuine comparative advantages, which could lead to orbital systems becoming a meaningful complement to the broader digital infrastructure ecosystem. Why Orbital Data Centers Are Gaining Relevance The simultaneous increase in demand for compute-intensive services alongside the improvement of commercial space capabilities is generating interest in orbital data centers. The Government Accountability Office’s (GAO’s) April 2026 “Science & Tech Spotlight” describes space-based data centers as “satellites that would house data processing and storage systems for AI and other computing needs,” potentially reducing the land, electricity, and water required by terrestrial facilities.[9] This framing, in the context of resistance to expanding terrestrial data center infrastructure, helps explain why the concept is now receiving policy attention, even though the underlying technology remains in an early stage.[10] Orbital data centers may eventually complement terrestrial infrastructure in specialized use cases. Private-sector research has reinforced that interest. Google's Project Suncatcher is an exploratory initiative that examines the feasibility of scaling machine-learning compute in space using solar-powered satellite constellations, special processors, and free-space optical communications links.[11] Thales Alenia Space’s ASCEND project likewise presents space-based data centers as a feasibility question, indicating that orbital computing has become the subject of structured technical and commercial investigation.[12] The broader relevance is that orbital computing may become a useful layer of digital infrastructure for specific workloads before it becomes competitive with terrestrial cloud infrastructure.[13] A space-based architecture that is appropriate for one mission class may still be uneconomical for general-purpose computing, particularly where latency, maintenance, replacement, and scale economies continue to favor Earth-based facilities. Therefore, the current evidence supports measured attention rather than exaggerated expectations. Orbital data centers may eventually complement terrestrial infrastructure in specialized use cases, but their near-term significance will depend on whether the technical and economic constraints can be managed at acceptable costs. The role for policymakers is to create a regulatory environment that minimizes unnecessary barriers to testing and deploying this new technology. The true value of orbital data centers will be easier to assess once these regulatory barriers are reduced. artigo.texto: The people of northern Virginia have been living with data centers for many years. The area is home to the world’s largest concentration of data centers. In a survey we conducted, we found northern Virginians support development restrictions that could make data centers more transparent and accountable to the public. But they care about some types of regulations more than others. As public concerns about data centers’ electricity demand and effects on the environmental and surrounding communities have grown around the nation, organized opposition to their construction is also on the rise – not only around the country but also at the epicenter of data centers. In northern Virginia, public protest and legal action led developers to withdraw a proposal for an 2,100-acre campus for as many as 37 data centers in Prince William County in early July 2026. A week later, county officials cited that opposition when rejecting a proposal that would have rezoned another 2,000-acre area elsewhere in the county to allow more data centers. Our research explored Virginians’ views on living near and among data centers, identifying what they think about their experiences and how they want to shape future data center development projects that might come to their communities. In the fall of 2025, we surveyed 1,004 residents of northern Virginia and the Richmond metropolitan area – homes of the two largest data center clusters in Virginia. What we asked Rather than asking whether they supported or opposed specific policies, we presented survey respondents with pairs of policy combinations that combined different policy measures to regulate data centers and asked them which combinations they preferred. Those measures included locations of the centers, placement of power lines, electricity rates, environmental effects, reporting of energy and water usage and requirements for public review before approval. For instance, a respondent might choose between two combinations. One combination might include power lines being placed underground and data centers being allowed near homes and parks, but environmental impact assessments not being required. The other combination might include above-ground power lines, restrictions on data centers near homes and parks, and a required environmental impact assessment before approval. Each respondent compared five pairs of combinations. Because the policy measures were varied across combinations, the same option appeared for different respondents alongside many combinations of other policies. This allowed us to statistically separate the influence of each individual option from the rest of the combination. In effect, we could see whether including a particular policy measure made people more or less likely to choose a combination, while averaging across the many combinations of other policies respondents saw. In this way, even though respondents evaluated complete policy combinations rather than individual measures in isolation, we could determine the independent influence of each policy option on their choices. Visible and immediate impacts matter Our analysis shows that residents most strongly supported policies addressing visible, immediate and tangible results, including requiring new electricity transmission lines to be built underground and restrictions on building data centers near homes, schools and parks. They also strongly support regular reporting of energy and water use. Our findings also underscore the importance that residents place on having a voice before data center projects are approved. Public participation is ranked second among the six policy provisions in shaping residents’ preferences. For many years, many jurisdictions in Virginia have allowed developers to build data centers without public review, so long as the buildings meet existing zoning requirements. The public has often found itself asking questions only after major decisions have been made. For instance, in July 2024, residents of Fairfax County’s Bren Mar neighborhood raised concerns about a proposed 466,000-square-foot data center, only to find that local zoning laws allowed the developer to build it without a public hearing or much review or oversight. In early 2025, Loudoun County, nicknamed “Data Center Alley,” ended automatic zoning approval for new data centers and required public hearings before local officials decided on the proposals. By contrast, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency under the Trump administration has moved to reduce requirements for public hearings for air-pollution permits from data center projects. Complex issues need clearer explanations Our research found less public support for policy provisions governing more complex issues related to data centers. In particular, respondents were ambivalent about whether data centers should be charged higher electricity rates than other customers. Infrastructure costs incurred to support data centers can ultimately pass down to other customers. According to a Bloomberg analysis, wholesale electricity prices near data centers more than tripled between 2020 and 2025. As for retail price, in August 2026, Reuters reported that rapid data center growth in Virginia has forced local power company Dominion Energy to rely more on costly wholesale power, contributing to a proposed rate adjustment that could raise a typical residential bill by about $20 per month. We believe that members of the public can come to informed decisions about complex issues. But before they can do so, they may need help from technical experts like those who work for local and state governments to clearly communicate what’s involved and the trade-offs at stake. Growth and oversight can coexist Given their support for regulations on data centers, it’s tempting to assume that the respondents to our survey simply don’t want data centers in their communities. artigo.texto: Advait Battery Ecosystem, a subsidiary of Advait Energy Transitions, signed a Master Supply Agreement with energy storage manufacturer HiTHIUM for the supply of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells. Under the agreement, HiTHIUM will supply its 314 Ah LFP battery cells to support Advait’s upcoming battery energy storage system (BESS) assembly plant in India. 1 GWh Cell Supply to Support BESS Production Advait plans to procure up to 1 GWh of battery cells from HiTHIUM over the next 12 months. The supply arrangement will support the company as it moves towards commercial production and scales its domestic BESS assembly capabilities. Advait is developing a BESS assembly facility with an annual capacity of 2.5 GWh. The company plans to build capabilities across battery module and pack assembly as it expands its presence in India’s energy storage market. Securing a reliable battery cell supply is therefore an important part of Advait’s manufacturing strategy and will help establish a sourcing base for its initial production phase. 314 Ah LFP Cells for Energy Storage Systems The 314 Ah prismatic LFP cells will serve as the core energy storage component for BESS units assembled at Advait’s facility. LFP chemistry is widely used in stationary energy storage applications because of its combination of cycle life and thermal stability. Consequently, the cells are suited to applications requiring reliable and durable energy storage. Supporting India’s Battery Storage Supply Chain Advait’s planned 2.5 GWh facility forms part of its broader expansion into battery energy storage systems. The company is developing domestic assembly capabilities as demand for energy storage infrastructure increases alongside renewable power generation and grid modernisation. The company’s manufacturing strategy will integrate imported battery cells into locally assembled battery modules and packs. Over time, this approach could help strengthen domestic capabilities across the BESS value chain. HiTHIUM Expands Presence in India’s BESS Market For HiTHIUM, the agreement establishes a supply relationship with an Indian BESS manufacturer and expands the deployment of its 314 Ah LFP cell technology in India. Meanwhile, Advait will gain a defined cell supply base as it moves towards higher-volume commercial production. The planned offtake of up to 1 GWh over 12 months represents a significant portion of the facility’s 2.5 GWh annual assembly capacity, although actual utilisation will depend on production schedules and customer demand. Building Domestic BESS Manufacturing Capabilities The partnership will support Advait’s efforts to develop an integrated battery assembly ecosystem in India. By securing battery cells and combining them with domestic module and pack assembly capabilities, the company aims to establish a foundation for commercial BESS production. As India continues to expand renewable energy and modernise its power grid, battery energy storage systems are expected to play an increasingly important role in balancing electricity supply and demand. As reported by manufacturingtodayindia.com, Advait’s planned facility and its agreement with HiTHIUM position the company to participate in this growing energy storage market.

artigo.texto: India commercial and industrial (C&I) battery energy storage capacity is growing rapidly, reaching around 650 MWh from 40 MWh previously. The capacity is projected to reach nearly 4 GWh by FY27. However, high upfront costs, evolving regulations, limited financing options and low user awareness continue to pose challenges to large-scale BESS adoption. To address these challenges and accelerate battery storage adoption in the C&I sector, the India Energy Storage Alliance (IESA) has launched the ‘BESS for C&I’ initiative at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai. The initiative aims to help 300 C&I consumers adopt energy storage solutions over the next three years. Under ‘BESS for C&I’, monthly sessions will be held from October 2026, bringing together industry players, BESS developers and policymakers to discuss storage deployment, costs, business models and best practices. Debmalya Sen, President, IESA, said the platform has been designed to address the specific challenges faced by C&I energy consumers. He noted that battery storage is becoming increasingly important for grid flexibility and business resilience, while collaboration, knowledge-sharing and innovation will be critical to accelerating adoption. The initiative will operate as a dedicated and free workgroup for C&I consumers. As electricity demand rises, battery storage can help businesses manage energy costs and integrate renewable energy more effectively. IESA and industry leaders have called for policy measures and targeted incentives to accelerate C&I BESS deployment. Bharat Chhittarka, Director, Trex Energy, said India needs to accelerate cell manufacturing and reduce dependence on imported raw materials to become a global battery manufacturing hub. According to him, imported raw materials currently account for around 60-70% of battery costs. He recommended clear state-level policies on Time-of-Day (TOD) tariffs, energy arbitrage and peak shaving. Bimal Jindal, CEO, Energy Business, JBM Renewables, said India needs to strengthen its battery manufacturing and supply chain ecosystem through component manufacturing, lithium carbonate and cell production, as well as investment in R&D. He also suggested that the government consider reducing GST on BESS from 18% to 5% and increasing the mandated share of BESS deployment in relevant projects. Sushmita R. Ajwani, Head of Business Development (C&I), Aditya Birla Renewables, said India needs to move beyond battery assembly and focus on domestic cell manufacturing supported by strong policy and financial measures. She added that clear regulatory guidelines and targeted incentives could accelerate BESS adoption. Inder Bhambra, COO-BESS and Chief Business Officer, India region, Envision Energy India, said India needs to develop cell technologies and promote local assembly of DC containers to establish itself as a global BESS manufacturing hub. He also called for more supportive open-access regulations, including the removal of transmission-related charges and maximum demand charges for BESS charging. Despite the growth in the sector, volatility in battery storage project costs remains a challenge. Utility-scale BESS capital expenditure has increased by around 15% in recent months. IESA said that appropriate policy support and stronger domestic supply chains can help drive the next phase of C&I battery storage growth. Through its IESA Connect platform, IESA plans to take the initiative to cities and industrial clusters across India. The objective is to enable C&I consumers to actively participate in shaping policies, standards and safety frameworks, rather than simply remain buyers of BESS technology.

artigo.texto: Perto de R$ 3,5 milhões em crédito de carbono já foram liberados a pecuaristas brasileiros em uma área de 950 hectares, antes mesmo de os créditos serem gerados e vendidos. A conta está na reportagem que deu ao jornalista Ariosto Mesquita o segundo lugar na categoria Sustentabilidade do IFAJ Star Prize 2026, prêmio da Federação Internacional de Jornalistas Agrícolas entregue no sábado (19), em Osijek, na Croácia. O trabalho premiado é “De utopia à realidade: dinheiro do crédito de carbono já remunera pecuaristas brasileiros”, publicado pela Revista Feed & Food, de Sorocaba (SP). Mesquita assina o texto e as fotos. É a segunda premiação internacional seguida do jornalista com uma reportagem sobre sustentabilidade na bovinocultura de corte, a criação de gado para carne. Os R$ 3,5 milhões e os 950 hectares estão na página de abertura da reportagem. Dividido pela área, o valor dá cerca de R$ 3,7 mil por hectare. A mesma página projeta novos projetos em mais 35 mil hectares nos biomas Cerrado e Amazônia até o fim de 2027, o que equivale a 37 vezes a área já contratada. O dinheiro chega antes de o crédito existir A apuração levou o jornalista a Porangatu, em Goiás, onde o produtor Rodrigo Barros de Azevedo recebeu US$ 62 mil poucas semanas depois de assinar um contrato de crédito de carbono. Pela cotação usada na reportagem, o valor equivale a aproximadamente R$ 360 mil. Em São Valério do Tocantins, nas fazendas Rio Verde, Bacabal e Spinelli, Mesquita encontrou o produtor Erivan Spinelli, que já havia recebido US$ 150 mil, cerca de R$ 870 mil, como antecipação de um projeto cujo crédito de carbono total foi estimado em US$ 451 mil. O adiantamento corresponde a um terço do que o projeto deve render ao produtor. As duas conversões citadas na reportagem indicam dólar em torno de R$ 5,80. Quem for comparar os valores hoje precisa refazer a conta pela cotação do dia. Quem antecipou o dinheiro é uma startup do Vale do Silício, nos Estados Unidos, que decidiu pagar antes por arranjos silvipastoris, sistemas em que árvores dividem a mesma área com o pasto e o gado. A reportagem também ouviu técnicos, representantes do setor e integrantes da empresa. O elo com Mato Grosso do Sul está na premiação anterior A reportagem vencedora deste ano não passa por Mato Grosso do Sul. O estado aparece no trabalho anterior do jornalista, “Crédito de carbono chega à pecuária”, publicado pela Revista DBO e premiado em 2025 em Nairóbi, no Quênia, também com o segundo lugar. Naquele texto, um dos primeiros contratos de crédito de carbono da pecuária brasileira era o da Fazenda Saltinho, em Camapuã. Segundo a reportagem, a propriedade assinou contrato com previsão de receber cerca de US$ 270 mil, perto de R$ 1,45 milhão na cotação citada, com pagamento projetado para 2029. A diferença entre os dois trabalhos está no prazo. Em Camapuã, o produtor espera quatro anos pelo dinheiro. Em Goiás e no Tocantins, ele entrou em semanas. Um brasileiro levou o título de jornalista do ano Julio Cezar Huber, do Espírito Santo, ficou em primeiro lugar na categoria Cultura Rural com a reportagem “Caparaó: um território que transforma quem vive e quem visita”, publicada pela Revista Negócio Rural. O trabalho contribuiu para que ele recebesse também o título de Journalist of the Year, jornalista do ano, dividido com a australiana Pip Courtney. Huber ficou ainda em segundo lugar na categoria Digital Media com “Regenerar é semear o amanhã”. Os brasileiros participaram do prêmio por meio da Rede Brasil de Jornalistas Agro, a Rede Agrojor. O que o IFAJ Star Prize premia O prêmio reúne trabalhos jornalísticos produzidos em diferentes países sobre agricultura, pecuária, desenvolvimento rural e temas ligados ao setor. A categoria Sustentabilidade desta edição foi coordenada pelo jornalista australiano Kerry Staight. O certificado enviado à redação traz as assinaturas de Steve Werblow, presidente da federação, e de Adrian Bell, secretário-geral.
