artigo.texto: CHARLOTTESVILLE, VA (CVILLE RIGHT NOW) – With community concerns about data centers rising, the Orange Town Council this week released a letter affirming it was not “engaging in any discussions with any data center developers or companies” and it scheduled an upcoming informational forum on the topic. “There’s just been a good deal of misinformation that has gotten out into the public,” Orange Mayor Harrison Cluff told Cville Right Now. “And we’re just trying to clarify exactly what has gone on and get the truth out.” According to the letter, signed by four of the town’s five council members, including Cluff, Orange is not involved in talks with any data center developers or companies, is not currently reviewing any data center applications, and is not actively recruiting data centers to the town. The letter also said the council isn’t considering annexing any property from Orange County and that it’s not “aware of any conversations between data center developers or companies and any private property owners within the town boundary or in the town environs.” For his part, Cluff said he wants more information, and for the town to hear more about the topic, before making any decisions on whether attracting a data center to Orange would be beneficial or harmful. “My position is the same as it would be for any other business that would want to perhaps look at locating in our town: to give it a full look, full due diligence,” Cluff said. “Go through public hearing processes, special use permits if necessary, get their input, and once we’ve fully got their input, make a determination based on that. I just want to have an honest conversation about it.” During council’s most recent meeting, Cluff said he read a statement regarding the data center situation that said, “there has been no activity in the town of Orange regarding data centers since December of last year, other than discussion between town staff related to policy, and in the search for qualified speakers.” Cluff said earlier this year the town changed its zoning ordinances to make it more difficult to build a data center in Orange and that the council clearly defined a “more modern definition of a data center.” The Council had planned to begin crafting policies and regulations regarding data centers but opted to table that discussion “to seek out expert guidance on both sides of the issue.” To that end, Orange has scheduled an Oct. 5 work session to serve as a public information session on the topic. Bill Donohue, who spent 45 years working in manufacturing, defense and consulting before retiring earlier this year and who is the Vice Chair of the Orange County Virginia Republican Committee, is scheduled to give an informational presentation that Cluff said will present the “pros and cons” of data centers. But Councilman Jason Cashell – the lone council member not to sign Wednesday’s letter to the public – told Cville Right Now he had “concerns” with the letter when he first saw it Wednesday and wanted some things clarified before signing. “And next thing you know, it was put out there,” said Cashell, an outspoken opponent of data centers who is not on the ballot for re-election when his term runs out at the end of this year. “I’m like, ‘Guys, we need to take our time on this thing.’ It’s important to get this right because if you don’t get it right, then what you risk is the opposite effect, where you’re trying to calm the people, you’re trying to convey transparency. If you get this wrong in rushing it, then something comes out that’s obviously contrary to what you’re saying, this is gonna look even worse.” Chief among Cashell’s concerns about the letter was the fact that it did not lay out any specific time period, while Cluff’s public statement included a reference to December of last year. “It was so broad that it really left the town open for speculation and for future mistrust,” Cashell said. “I wanted to pump the brakes, to take our time. At our last town council meeting, the mayor told everybody that had gathered, ‘Hey, listen. Since December, we have not had any conversations with data centers.’ But the letter doesn’t say, ‘Since December.’ It just says, ‘In general.’ In fact, it says categorically, that we have not engaged in any discussions with data center developers or companies. I’ve got a real concern there because it’s inconsistent with what I’ve seen.” Cashell said he’s felt “left out” of data center discussions because, “I made my position clear very early on that I was opposed to data centers within the small 2000 acre town of Orange. Your average data center needs 50 acres. We only have two plots that are even big enough to even have one. One’s under conservation easement, and one is a residential area.” Cashell said he’s skeptical of what smaller data centers, sometimes labeled boutique data centers, would do to Orange. “Historically, that tactic has been used by data center companies to at least crack the door into the possibility of data centers,” he said. “If you allow a small one in, does that set precedent for a bigger one? Not only that, but even a small one is going to require power transmission. It’s going to require generators. It’s going to put off noise. It’s going to put off pollution. It going to put off lighting. And then, even after all of that, are you really getting that much of tax revenue from a small kind of boutique data center? You just start calculating, I don’t know if that’s really worth it.” Of course, that’s part of the reason Cluff is hoping the public turns out for the Oct. 5 presentation, to get information to answer some of those questions. Wednesday’s letter also said, “speculation and rumor mongering are harmful to public discourse and the fabric of our community. artigo.texto: China’s EV industry is pushing charging technology into territory that remains largely out of reach for passenger cars in the US. Geely’s latest battery technology is the newest example, promising charging speeds that could dramatically reduce one of the biggest frustrations associated with electric vehicles: waiting to recharge. Credits: Ars Technica Geely Unveils 2.2 MW EV Charging Technology Geely has introduced a new battery system capable of charging at up to 2.2 megawatts, with the company claiming it can recharge from 10% to 70% in just 4.5 minutes. A more substantial 10% to 98% charge takes 8 minutes and 40 seconds, according to Geely. If the technology performs as claimed in real-world conditions, charging an EV could begin to resemble the experience of refuelling a conventional petrol or diesel vehicle. The battery uses AI-powered predictive thermal management to control temperatures during high-speed charging. Geely says the pack maintains an average temperature of around 55°C, while its peak temperature during charging reaches approximately 65°C. The company has also addressed concerns over battery degradation caused by repeated ultra-fast charging. AI Could Help Extend Battery Life According to Geely, its charging system uses AI-controlled micro pulses of current to reactivate lithium ions that accumulate at the negative electrodes during repeated fast charging. The automaker claims this approach can extend battery life by 20%. The battery pack has reportedly been tested in vehicles including the Zeekr 001 and Lynk & Co 10, suggesting that the technology is moving beyond the laboratory stage. The development reflects a broader trend among Chinese EV manufacturers, which are competing aggressively to reduce charging times while adding software and connected features to their vehicles. Instead of treating charging speed as a secondary specification, companies are increasingly making it a central part of the EV ownership experience. Geely Takes on BYD and CATL Geely’s figures are impressive, but the company is not alone in the race for faster charging. BYD introduced a battery system earlier this year capable of charging from 10% to 70% in around five minutes, while a 10% to 97% charge takes approximately nine minutes. CATL has reported even faster figures. Its latest LFP battery can reportedly charge from 10% to 80% in 3 minutes and 44 seconds, while reaching 98% from 10% takes 6 minutes and 27 seconds. That puts China’s leading battery manufacturers in an increasingly intense competition over charging speeds, with incremental improvements potentially becoming a major differentiator between EV models. For consumers, the significance is straightforward: if charging times continue falling toward single-digit minutes, range anxiety could increasingly be replaced by concerns about charger availability rather than the time required to use one. US Charging Infrastructure Still Trails Megawatt Levels The difference becomes particularly noticeable when comparing the charging infrastructure available in China and the US. Most Tesla Superchargers in the US currently top out at 250 kW, while newer high-power systems from other networks have pushed that figure higher. Electrify America offers chargers rated at up to 350 kW, IONNA has introduced machines capable of 400 kW, and ChargePoint has a 600 kW charger. Those figures remain well below Geely’s claimed 2.2 MW charging capability. The gap is not only about charging stations. Passenger EVs sold in the US also generally cannot accept power at the levels being targeted by China’s latest battery technology. American EVs Are Also Limited by Battery Hardware Hyundai and Kia’s popular 800-volt EVs, including the Ioniq 5 and EV6, can accept roughly 240 kW of DC fast-charging power. Porsche’s Taycan supports charging of up to around 320 kW. The newest generation of 800-volt German EVs is beginning to close that gap, with models such as the BMW iX3 and Porsche Cayenne arriving with 400 kW charging capabilities. However, even those systems remain significantly below the megawatt-level charging being developed in China. There is an important distinction, though: the highest charging speeds depend on more than the battery. Vehicles need compatible charging hardware, connectors, thermal systems and electrical infrastructure capable of safely delivering enormous amounts of power. Credits: The Economic Times Megawatt Charging Is Still Mostly for Heavy-Duty EVs In the US, megawatt charging remains primarily associated with heavy-duty electric vehicles such as buses and electric trucks. ChargePoint has indicated that two of its 600 kW charging units could potentially be combined through a common DC bus to deliver 1.2 MW through a single port. The company has also pointed to the Megawatt Charging System, or MCS, as a solution designed to handle the much larger power requirements of heavy-duty vehicles. For passenger cars, however, the technology remains considerably less mature. Geely’s announcement therefore highlights a widening technology race around one of the EV industry’s most important challenges. Chinese manufacturers are not simply increasing battery capacity; they are attempting to make the charging process dramatically faster. If these systems can achieve their claimed performance without compromising safety, cost or long-term battery durability, the traditional advantage of petrol vehicles—quick refuelling—could become considerably less significant.

artigo.texto: Vivo V80 launches with 7200mAh battery and 144Hz display Vivo is set to expand its mid-range smartphone portfolio with the launch of the V80 on October 6, 2026, introducing significant upgrades in battery capacity and display performance. Next-Generation Battery and Display Technology Vivo is set to expand its mid-range smartphone portfolio with the launch of the V80 on October 6, 2026, introducing significant upgrades in battery capacity and display performance. The most notable enhancement is the inclusion of a massive 7,200mAh battery, a substantial increase from the 6,500mAh cell found in its predecessor, the V70. This 11 percent boost in capacity is engineered to deliver extended usage times, addressing one of the primary demands of modern smartphone users who require reliable all-day performance without frequent recharging. Complementing the large battery is a 90W fast-charging capability, which Vivo claims can replenish 50 percent of the battery in just 30 minutes under laboratory conditions. This rapid charging technology mitigates the inconvenience of a large battery, ensuring that users can quickly top up their devices during short breaks. The physical dimensions of the phone have been carefully managed despite the larger battery; the V80 measures 7.69mm in thickness and weighs 203g, representing only a marginal increase over the V70. The visual experience is driven by a 6.59-inch AMOLED display with a 1.5K resolution of 2750 x 1260 pixels. The most significant display upgrade is the increase in the maximum refresh rate from 120Hz to 144Hz, providing smoother scrolling and more responsive interactions in supported applications. This high refresh rate is particularly beneficial for mobile gaming and navigating complex user interfaces, positioning the V80 as a compelling option for multimedia consumption and interactive entertainment. Advanced Camera System and Imaging Capabilities Vivo continues its partnership with ZEISS to deliver a sophisticated rear camera system on the V80. The primary setup features a 50MP main sensor with optical image stabilization, ensuring sharp and stable footage even in challenging lighting conditions. This is paired with a dedicated 50MP telephoto lens that offers 3x optical zoom and its own stabilization system, allowing users to capture detailed portraits and distant subjects without the quality degradation typically associated with digital cropping. The camera array is completed by an 8MP ultrawide lens, providing versatility for landscape and group photography. While Vivo advertises digital zoom capabilities up to 100x, the practical utility of the system lies in its high-resolution optical lenses. The front-facing camera is equally robust, featuring a 50MP autofocus sensor that ensures high-quality selfies and clear video calls, a critical feature for social media engagement and remote communication. Video recording capabilities include 4K resolution at 60 frames per second, alongside a Cinematic Video mode that applies movie-style color grading and depth-of-field effects. The integration of AI-powered lighting effects and tools for converting live photo elements into stickers adds a layer of creative flexibility, appealing to content creators and casual users alike. These software enhancements leverage the powerful hardware to provide a comprehensive imaging suite that competes favorably with higher-tier devices. Processing Power and Market Positioning Under the hood, the Vivo V80 retains the Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 processor, the same chipset that powered the V70. While this means there is no generational leap in raw processing power, the Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 remains a highly capable mid-range chipset, offering excellent thermal efficiency and sufficient performance for everyday tasks and demanding mobile games. The decision to retain the processor allows Vivo to optimize the software experience and maintain a competitive price point. The V80 is positioned to compete in a highly contested segment of the Kenyan smartphone market, where consumers are increasingly demanding premium features at accessible prices. The combination of a massive battery, high-refresh-rate display, and versatile camera system addresses the core needs of the target demographic. Competitors in this space, including offerings from Tecno and Infinix, will need to match these specifications to remain relevant. As the October 6 launch approaches, industry observers will be watching the pricing strategy and local availability of the V80. The success of the device will depend not only on its hardware specifications but also on Vivo's ability to provide robust after-sales support and software updates. For consumers seeking a balanced device that prioritizes battery life and imaging without compromising on display quality, the Vivo V80 presents a formidable option in the evolving mid-range landscape. artigo.texto: O mercado de IPOs de empresas de data centers enfrenta juros mais altos e maior exigência dos investidores, que priorizam companhias com demanda contratada, energia garantida e clientes diversificados. Apesar do cenário, a DayOne mantém planos de abrir capital em novembro e pode buscar até US$ 5 bilhões, com avaliação próxima de US$ 20 bilhões. A empresa opera na Ásia-Pacífico e na Europa. O movimento contrasta com o adiamento do IPO da SB Energy e uma disputa envolvendo Oracle e Blue Owl. Investidores também demonstram preocupação com projetos dependentes de poucos clientes e elevados investimentos iniciais. A Autoridade Portuária de Santos aprovou acordo com o Centronave para encerrar disputa sobre tarifas de acesso aquaviário. Com o entendimento, a APS deverá receber cerca de R$ 416,9 milhões após homologação judicial. A controvérsia começou em 2022, quando armadores e operadores questionaram a cobrança integral das tarifas, alegando que investimentos previstos não haviam sido realizados. Durante o processo, os valores permaneceram depositados judicialmente. Cinco candidatos à Presidência defendem o início da reforma tributária em janeiro de 2027, segundo levantamento da Roit. Lula apoia o modelo aprovado, enquanto Renan Santos, Augusto Cury, Romeu Zema e Ronaldo Caiado propõem ajustes sem mudar o calendário. Flávio Bolsonaro é apontado como o candidato que faz a crítica mais estrutural. Durante a campanha, chegou a defender a suspensão por um ano, mas depois passou a falar em corrigir distorções e abreviar a transição prevista no sistema. O equilíbrio entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro nas pesquisas tem levado investidores a buscar proteção. Analistas citam títulos públicos e CDBs, além de ações de serviços públicos e commodities, como alternativas diante da volatilidade. Na renda variável, bancos projetam desempenhos diferentes conforme o resultado das urnas. O Citi aponta empresas que poderiam se beneficiar em cada cenário, enquanto o BTG afirma que investidores estão se preparando para uma eleição acirrada. A agricultura brasileira alcançou R$ 927,2 bilhões em valor de produção em 2025, alta nominal de 18,4% sobre o ano anterior. O montante é o maior registrado desde pelo menos a criação do Plano Real, em 1994. A produção de cereais, leguminosas e oleaginosas chegou a 345,4 milhões de toneladas, avanço de 18,2% ante 2024. No ano anterior, a atividade havia sido prejudicada por condições climáticas associadas ao El Niño. O dólar voltou a ganhar força diante de outras moedas após indicadores robustos nos EUA. O rendimento do Treasury de 10 anos retornou a 5%, maior nível desde 2007, em meio à maior exigência de retorno dos investidores de acordo com a CNN. Entre os fatores estão a criação de 162 mil vagas de emprego, ante expectativa de cerca de 60 mil, a menor demanda em leilão de títulos e o petróleo a US$ 105. Dados de atividade também reforçaram a perspectiva de juros elevados por mais tempo.

artigo.texto: A California AI company that signed the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge, and vows to protect Oklahoma ratepayers from paying for the power used at the facility announced Sunday plans to build a new data center at MidAmerica Industrial Park (MidAmerica) near Chouteau in Mayes County, Oklahoma. Lambda Inc., the Superintelligence Cloud, based in San Jose, California said it is also working to design the project to be a more flexible grid customer with the ability to shift or reduce certain computing loads during periods of peak demand. The company is expected to pay an estimated $500 million in taxes over the next 10 years based on current rates, and the project is expected to create up to 1,000 construction jobs and up to 100 permanent positions. In compliance with Oklahoma’s Data Center Customer Ratepayer Protection Act, Lambda said it will take full responsibility for the resources and infrastructure needed to operate the facility, including paying 100 percent of its energy costs. The company added that it will also manage local resources responsibly by minimizing water use through closed-loop cooling technology and optimizing energy efficiency. “Lambda is committed to being a good neighbor and long-term partner with the town of Chouteau and Mayes County,” said Stephen Balaban, Co-Founder and Chief Technology Officer at Lambda. “We’ve been meeting with local leaders to understand their priorities and help shape our long-term investments in the community. We’re going to keep listening, keep showing up, and let our work here speak for itself.” “When developed responsibly, data centers can create lasting economic opportunities and investments in the communities where they operate,” said Michel Combes, Chief Executive Officer of Lambda. “Our responsibility is to ensure that this project delivers value to Mayes County while respecting the community’s resources, infrastructure, and priorities. We are committed to meeting that responsibility at every stage of the project.” Lambda’s Commitments - Ratepayer Protection: Lambda will protect local ratepayers by paying for all electricity the facility uses and ensuring the project meets Oklahoma’s requirements under the state’s ratepayer protection laws. The company has also signed the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge, and is working to design the project to be a more flexible grid customer with the ability to shift or reduce certain computing loads during periods of peak demand. - Water Stewardship: The facility will implement closed-loop cooling technology that dramatically reduces water use compared with traditional data center cooling. - Siting Away from Residents: The project is being built at the existing MidAmerica Industrial Park with infrastructure designed to minimize impacts on surrounding residential areas. “Oklahoma is leading the nation in building the modern economy, bringing major investments to our state and creating opportunities that will benefit our people for generations to come,” said Governor Kevin Stitt. “Lambda has committed to taking responsibility for the energy costs associated with its facility, ensuring those costs are not passed along to residential customers while generating hundreds of millions in tax revenue and economic growth right here in Oklahoma. These are commitments that reflect the kind of responsible investment we want to see in Oklahoma.” “Major investments like this demonstrate the opportunity we have to continue growing Oklahoma’s economy and attracting innovative companies to our state,” said Oklahoma Department of Commerce CEO John Budd. “Lambda’s decision to build here is a vote of confidence in Oklahoma’s workforce, infrastructure and business-friendly environment. We look forward to supporting this project and the new opportunities it will create for Oklahomans, while continuing to build an economy that can compete for investment and high-quality jobs for years to come.” “Lambda’s decision to build in Mayes County represents a transformative commitment to economic development in our community,” said Chouteau Mayor Brenda Cunningham. “This project will bring an estimated $500 million in tax revenue to our county over the next decade, which will go toward supporting our schools, public services and local priorities. This is the kind of partnership we want in our community.” “This is a significant investment in Mayes County and an important opportunity for our community,” said Steve Grossman, Mayes County Commissioner. “Beyond the economic activity it will bring, this project will strengthen our local tax base and create new resources that can support schools, infrastructure and other community priorities for years to come. We’re pleased to welcome Lambda to Mayes County and look forward to working with them as the project moves forward.” The new data center will be located in the south section of the industrial park and will sit within the Chouteau-Mazie Public School District tax boundary. “This investment will have a lasting impact on Chouteau-Mazie District Schools and the students we serve,” said Josh Gwartney, Chouteau-Mazie Public School Superintendent. “The tax revenue will support our schools and allow us to invest in better facilities, competitive teacher salaries, advanced programs and more career and technical education opportunities. artigo.texto: A Rússia leva o "imposto sobre carbono" da UE à OMC, e muitas economias aderem. O Órgão de Solução de Controvérsias (OSC) da Organização Mundial do Comércio (OMC) aprovou o pedido da Federação Russa para estabelecer um painel de avaliação com o objetivo de analisar a legalidade do Mecanismo de Ajuste de Carbono na Fronteira (CBAM) e do sistema de comércio de emissões da União Europeia (UE). Este é o segundo pedido da Rússia, depois de a UE ter rejeitado o primeiro pedido na sua reunião de julho de 2026. Segundo o argumento de Moscou, o pacote de políticas CBAM da UE cria sérias barreiras comerciais para bens importados para o mercado europeu. Ao mesmo tempo, a Rússia alega que a alocação de cotas de emissão pela UE a certas empresas nacionais no âmbito do Sistema de Comércio de Emissões (SCE) constitui "subsídios à exportação", aumentando injustamente a competitividade dos produtos europeus. Em resposta a essa medida, representantes da UE criticaram, em 25 de setembro, o uso do direito internacional pela Rússia para exigir acesso ao mercado da UE em meio ao conflito em curso na Ucrânia . No entanto, a UE reafirmou sua participação no processo para demonstrar seu compromisso com o sistema multilateral de comércio, expressando confiança de que tanto o CBAM quanto o ETS estão em plena conformidade com as normas da OMC. Devido à importância e ao caráter inédito do caso para o comércio global, diversos países se registraram para participar como terceiros, a fim de monitorar e apresentar seus pontos de vista. Essa lista inclui os EUA, a China, a Índia, o Reino Unido, o Japão, a Coreia do Sul, o Brasil, a Argentina, a Arábia Saudita, a Indonésia, a Malásia, Singapura e vários outros. A participação como terceiros permite que esses países acompanhem de perto os argumentos jurídicos da Rússia e da UE, e apresentem suas próprias opiniões sobre o impacto do imposto de carbono na fronteira sem precisar entrar diretamente com uma ação judicial. O CBAM (Imposto sobre o Carbono na Fronteira) é atualmente uma grande preocupação para muitos países que exportam bens com alta emissão de carbono, como aço, alumínio, cimento e fertilizantes, para a UE. Embora o painel de juízes já tenha sido formado, espera-se que o processo de resolução de disputas dure meses, até mesmo anos. Dependendo do resultado, o caso também corre o risco de ser "congelado" na fase de apelação. Isso ocorre porque o Órgão de Apelação, a mais alta instância judicial da OMC, está inativo desde o final de 2019 devido aos repetidos vetos dos EUA à nomeação de novos juízes. Na sessão de 25 de setembro, o representante da Colômbia (em nome de 130 países membros) propôs, pela centésima vez, a retomada do processo de seleção de juízes, mas a proposta foi novamente rejeitada pelos EUA. artigo.texto: Os bombardeios russos deste domingo (27) atingiram em cheio a espinha dorsal das telecomunicações ucranianas: a sede da Kyivstar, maior operadora de telefonia móvel do país, e data centers de concorrentes e provedores de internet foram alvos de ataques na região de Kiev. Segundo a Reuters, a Kyivstar informou à agência Interfax Ucrânia que sua sede na capital foi atingida, sem registro de vítimas. Horas antes, o Ministério da Defesa da Rússia havia declarado ter destruído um data center pertencente à Vodafone Ucrânia, segunda maior operadora celular do país. A companhia não respondeu aos pedidos de comentário. O presidente Volodymyr Zelenskiy afirmou que um data center em Kiev foi bombardeado duas vezes na manhã deste domingo, deixando dois menores e um adulto feridos. Na semana anterior, ataques a data centers de provedores de internet ucranianos já haviam interrompido o serviço para cerca de 100 mil residências em Kiev e na região vizinha, conforme o Ministério Digital da Ucrânia. O ministro das Relações Exteriores, Andrii Sybiha, escreveu no X que Moscou tem como alvo os principais data centers do país para interromper o fluxo de informações, e que alertas rápidos sobre ameaças de mísseis e drones são essenciais porque salvam vidas.

artigo.texto: GENEVA, Sept 26 — The World Trade Organisation (WTO) is to examine a Russian complaint alleging that the European Union’s carbon border levy and its emissions trading system violate international trade rules, reported German news agency dpa. Russia submitted a second request for a WTO dispute panel to determine whether the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and an alleged export subsidy under its Emissions Trading System (ETS) are consistent with the bloc’s WTO commitments. The EU had blocked Russia’s first request for a panel in July. Under WTO rules, however, a panel is automatically established following a second request. Russia argues that CBAM creates significant trade barriers for goods imported into the EU. The mechanism is designed to ensure that certain imports face carbon costs comparable to those imposed on products manufactured within the bloc, with the aim of preventing companies from shifting carbon-intensive production abroad. Moscow also argues that the EU’s allocation of emissions allowances to certain companies under the ETS amounts to an export subsidy intended to make European industries more competitive. The EU said it was extraordinary that Russia, which it said continues to “wage its war of aggression against Ukraine,” was seeking to invoke international law to improve access for its exports to the European market. It said it would participate in the proceedings to reaffirm its support for the rules-based multilateral trading system rather than to legitimize Russia’s actions. The EU also expressed confidence that both CBAM and the ETS comply with WTO rules.

artigo.texto: 247 – A Weg ampliou o projeto de sua nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), em construção em Itajaí, Santa Catarina, e elevou o investimento previsto para R$ 330 milhões. A unidade terá capacidade anual projetada de 4 GWh, contará com maior nível de automação industrial e deverá iniciar as operações no segundo semestre de 2027. O projeto havia sido anunciado em fevereiro, mas passou por uma revisão para incorporar novas soluções de automação e medidas destinadas a aumentar a eficiência da produção. Com a atualização, a companhia pretende ampliar a capacidade produtiva inicialmente planejada para a fábrica catarinense. O investimento de R$ 330 milhões será direcionado ao empreendimento dedicado aos chamados BESS, sigla em inglês para sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias. A tecnologia permite armazenar eletricidade em períodos de maior disponibilidade e disponibilizá-la posteriormente, quando houver necessidade no sistema elétrico. Esse tipo de solução ganha relevância especialmente com a expansão de fontes renováveis de geração intermitente. Segundo a Weg, os sistemas BESS podem contribuir para a integração de fontes como energia solar e eólica. Como a produção dessas fontes varia de acordo com condições naturais, o armazenamento possibilita reter parte da energia gerada e utilizá-la em outros momentos, favorecendo a estabilidade e a eficiência da rede elétrica. A ampliação do empreendimento em Itajaí também ocorre em meio à expectativa da companhia com o avanço do mercado brasileiro de armazenamento de energia. A Weg mencionou a previsão de realização do primeiro Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade de Armazenamento Nacional, programado para dezembro de 2026. A companhia relaciona a perspectiva do leilão à expansão da demanda por soluções capazes de armazenar energia em larga escala. artigo.texto: NineDot Energy cuts ribbon on Bronx energy storage site Community battery storage developer NineDot Energy has energized its new 20 MW battery storage site in The Bronx’s Hunts Point neighborhood. Now fully operational, the new installation will deliver nearly 20 MW of power to the Hunts Point community, NineDot officials say. That energy is enough to power about 20,000 homes during peak grid hours, bringing “significant benefits” to the community, which the company says has been suffering from environmental injustice. “We’re honored to bring this battery storage site to the Hunts Point community,” says Adam Cohen, NineDot’s co-founder and CTO. “Hunts Point has historically been overburdened by high-emitting fossil fuels, and this battery storage facility marks an inflection point in improving the local environment and grid reliability.” NineDot estimates that about 10,000 diesel trucks travel through the borough on a daily basis, adding to the environmental struggles The Bronx has faced in recent decades. The firm says that in 2023, the Hunts Point to Mott Haven area recorded asthma-related emergency room incidents at 2-3 times New York City’s average. Providing for the Big Apple Energy storage is an integral asset to New York City and its energy future, say officials from NineDot. The practice is crucial, not only in retiring more traditional power plants, but in providing resiliency to a grid that strains heavily during peak summer hours. The company adds that during New York’s extreme heat wave in early July 2026, its fleet of community battery systems helped reduce stress on the grid. “Battery energy storage is an important tool for modernizing New York’s electric grid and making it more resilient to extreme weather and high-stress conditions,” says David Sandbank, SVP of the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA). “This Hunts Point project demonstrates how the right policies, partners and programs can deliver benefits for communities throughout New York City and beyond.” As of September 2026, NineDot Energy is on track to meet its goal of having 400 MW of battery storage either in operation, under construction, of in development by the end of the year. The firm currently boasts a set of eleven projects operating at six different locations and totaling 39 MW across Staten Island and The Bronx. This makes it the largest operating battery fleet inside Con Edison’s New York City territory, and the firm adds it has 60 additional projects in development.

artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Lambda planeja novo data center no MidAmerica Industrial Park de Oklahoma Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Lambda anunciou planos em 27 de setembro de 2026 para construir um novo data center no MidAmerica Industrial Park, no condado de Mayes, Oklahoma, um projeto que a empresa disse que deve pagar cerca de $500 million em impostos nos próximos 10 anos, com base nas tarifas atuais. Receita Fiscal Projetada e Empregos Espera‑se que o projeto crie até 1.000 empregos de construção e até 100 cargos permanentes, de acordo com o anúncio da empresa. A instalação ficará localizada na seção sul do parque industrial e estará dentro da zona fiscal do Chouteau-Mazie Public School District. A prefeita de Chouteau, Brenda Cunningham, disse que o projeto traria uma receita fiscal estimada em $500 million para o condado ao longo da próxima década, financiamento que, segundo ela, seria destinado ao apoio de escolas, serviços públicos e prioridades locais. O comissário do condado de Mayes, Steve Grossman, afirmou que o investimento fortaleceria a base tributária local e criaria novos recursos para apoiar escolas, infraestrutura e outras prioridades da comunidade. O superintendente da Chouteau-Mazie Public School, Josh Gwartney, declarou que a receita permitiria ao distrito investir em instalações melhores, salários competitivos para professores, programas avançados e mais oportunidades de educação profissional e técnica. Proteção dos Consumidores de Energia e Compromissos de Recursos A Lambda afirmou que, em conformidade com a Oklahoma’s Data Center Customer Ratepayer Protection Act, assumirá total responsabilidade pelos recursos e infraestrutura necessários para operar a instalação, incluindo o pagamento de 100 % dos custos de energia. A empresa disse que está projetando o projeto para ser um cliente de rede mais flexível, com a capacidade de deslocar ou reduzir determinadas cargas de computação durante períodos de pico de demanda. A instalação utilizará tecnologia de refrigeração de circuito fechado, que a Lambda afirmou reduzir drasticamente o consumo de água em comparação com a refrigeração tradicional de data centers, e a empresa disse que otimizará a eficiência energética. O projeto está sendo construído no parque industrial existente, com infraestrutura projetada para minimizar impactos nas áreas residenciais circundantes. O governador Kevin Stitt afirmou que os compromissos refletem o tipo de investimento responsável que ele deseja ver em Oklahoma. “A Lambda se comprometeu a assumir a responsabilidade pelos custos de energia associados à sua instalação, garantindo que esses custos não sejam repassados aos consumidores residenciais, ao mesmo tempo em que gera centenas de milhões em receita fiscal e crescimento econômico aqui em Oklahoma”, disse Stitt. O CEO do Departamento de Comércio de Oklahoma, John Budd, chamou a decisão da Lambda de construir no estado de um voto de confiança na força de trabalho, na infraestrutura e no ambiente favorável aos negócios de Oklahoma. O CEO da Grand River Dam Authority, Dan Sullivan, declarou que a Lambda financiará os custos iniciais de infraestrutura necessários para atender ao projeto, garantindo que essas despesas não sejam repassadas a outros clientes da GRDA. Sullivan afirmou que a concessionária criou um processo de planejamento focado e abrangente ao avaliar projetos potenciais dessa magnitude e fez os investimentos necessários na última década para estar preparada para projetos dessa escala. O projeto segue o anúncio de 14 de setembro de 2026 da Lambda, que havia assinado o White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge. Naquela declaração, a empresa afirmou que apoia políticas de proteção dos consumidores que exigem que os desenvolvedores de data centers paguem pela energia que suas instalações utilizam, e que apoia a expansão da capacidade de geração, o fortalecimento da rede elétrica, a manutenção de um serviço confiável e a proteção dos consumidores à medida que a demanda por infraestrutura de IA cresce. Processo de Seleção e Próximas Etapas A MidAmerica selecionou a Lambda dentre uma variedade de parceiros potenciais com base na abordagem da empresa ao desenvolvimento responsável e aos padrões de construção. David Stewart, CEO e membro do Board of Trustees do MidAmerica Industrial Park, afirmou que a MidAmerica e a GRDA adotaram uma abordagem deliberada para encontrar o parceiro certo. “Por meio do que chamamos de reverse RFP, começamos com os pontos fortes deste local e procuramos um desenvolvedor cujos planos entregariam valor duradouro à região”, disse Stewart. Ele afirmou que, à medida que a construção avançar, o projeto deverá criar aproximadamente 1.000 empregos e gerar oportunidades para fornecedores, empreiteiros e fornecedores locais. A Cloverleaf Infrastructure foi selecionada pela GRDA e pela MidAmerica para preparar o local no condado de Mayes para o desenvolvimento pela Lambda. Aaron Bilyeu, chief development officer da Cloverleaf, afirmou que o trabalho será orientado pelo Cloverleaf Standard, que ele descreveu como o compromisso da empresa de desenvolver infraestrutura crítica de forma responsável, transparente e em parceria com as comunidades que atende. O cofundador da Lambda e Chief Technology Officer, Stephen Balaban, disse que a empresa tem se reunido com líderes locais em Chouteau e no condado de Mayes para entender suas prioridades e ajudar a moldar seus investimentos de longo prazo na comunidade. O CEO da Lambda, Michel Combes, afirmou que a responsabilidade da empresa é garantir que o projeto entregue valor ao condado de Mayes, respeitando os recursos, a infraestrutura e as prioridades da comunidade. Lambda e MidAmerica disseram que, nas próximas semanas, continuarão se reunindo com líderes locais e residentes para ouvir e coletar sugestões que orientem o investimento na comunidade, e que mais informações sobre o cronograma do projeto e seu impacto econômico esperado serão compartilhada

artigo.texto: Fox ESS has unveiled Power Beast, its new commercial and industrial energy storage system, at the company’s first large-scale APAC product launch. Held in Wenzhou, China, on 21 September 2026, the Fox ESS New Product Launch Event welcomed more than 200 customers from around the world. The open-air event marked a significant step in Fox ESS’s expansion into advanced commercial and industrial (C&I) battery energy storage. Power Beast combines the 125 kW H3 Plus hybrid inverter with Fox ESS’s high-voltage CQ series batteries. The CQ20 is described as the industry’s first modular C&I energy storage system with a fully integrated hybrid inverter. This integrated design allows businesses and installers to deploy a flexible, all-in-one commercial energy storage solution. Michael Zhu, CEO of Fox ESS, said: “Today, we are not only launching a product, we are demonstrating our capability as an integrated energy storage provider. Power Beast reflects our commitment to global clients by delivering higher efficiency, lighter weight, and smarter energy management.” Fox ESS puts Power Beast installation to the test The Power Beast launch went beyond a traditional product presentation. Lyren Liu, CCO of Fox ESS, shared insights into market growth and his perspective on battery storage. He then revealed a Cybertruck loaded with CQ batteries from behind a black curtain on stage. An installation team was invited to assemble a complete system live, with a timer displayed on the main screen. The team assembled battery packs comprising: - eight modules of CQ20; - 12 modules of CQ7; and - 12 modules of CQ6. Together, the system provided 316 kWh of energy storage capacity. The completed battery system was then connected to charging piles, a diesel generator, and a motor. Fox ESS completed the entire live demonstration in under 30 minutes. Power Beast offers scalable C&I battery storage Power Beast has been designed around modular expansion, allowing system capacity to grow alongside a business’s energy requirements. With one H3 Plus hybrid inverter, Power Beast can support capacities ranging from 28 kWh to nearly 1,000 kWh. The system supports several installation environments, including rooftop, outdoor, and indoor applications. For larger projects, multiple Power Beast systems can operate in parallel. In grid-connected mode, the system supports up to 100 units in parallel, providing total capacity of up to 96 MWh. In off-grid mode, Power Beast supports up to 30 units in parallel, reaching a total capacity of 28.8 MWh. Modular design simplifies commercial battery installation Fox ESS has also focused on reducing installation complexity. Power Beast’s modular architecture is designed to improve deployment efficiency and accommodate challenging or irregular installation environments. According to Fox ESS, the system’s design can reduce total installation time by 90 per cent. This modular approach gives installers greater flexibility when configuring commercial energy storage systems across different sites. Lighter C&I battery storage with integrated energy management Power Beast has been designed to integrate with multiple energy sources and loads. The CQ20 series batteries achieve a unit energy weight of 7 kg per kWh. This helps reduce the system’s physical footprint while maintaining energy output. Fox ESS has also incorporated a five-layer, end-to-end safety approach. This covers: - cell-level protection; - electrical design; - structural design; - active detection; and - emergency response. The system connects with FoxCloud 2.0, Fox ESS’s proprietary smart energy management platform. FoxCloud 2.0 provides real-time monitoring and visibility of energy flows, alongside detailed performance analysis. The platform also supports scheduling across up to 96 time slots, providing centralised smart energy management for Power Beast installations. Fox ESS introduces AI energy management agent Maimai Alongside Power Beast, Fox ESS introduced its AI agent, Maimai. Maimai provides product, installation, and usage information through natural dialogue. Using large-model conversational capabilities, the AI agent can interpret user requirements and provide relevant information at any time. Maimai can also generate optimised energy strategies using historical energy consumption patterns and real-time dynamic electricity prices. The technology adds another layer of intelligent energy management to Fox ESS’s growing commercial energy storage ecosystem. Michael Zhu said Fox ESS remains focused on creating products that deliver measurable value for customers. “We believe a great product speaks louder than marketing. That is why we aim to make our products the best kind of promotion, by delivering real value every single day,” Michael Zhu said. With scalable storage from 28 kWh through to multi-megawatt-hour deployments, Power Beast expands Fox ESS’s offering for businesses seeking flexible commercial battery storage. The combination of the H3 Plus hybrid inverter, CQ series batteries, FoxCloud 2.0, and Maimai also brings hardware, monitoring, and intelligent energy management into one C&I energy storage ecosystem.

artigo.texto: BYD, Batteries, and the Architecture of Dependence Dateline, Canberra, Austrlia I have just arrived in Canberra for the October 1 seminar hosted by the Sir Richard Williams Foundation. So no place better to start than by focusing on one of the themes in my latest book with Kenneth Maxwell on China’s informal empire. BYD is not simply a car company that got good. It is the clearest automotive expression yet of what I have called, with Kenneth Maxwell, the “Architecture of Dependency”: a strategy that pursues vertical integration of an entire value chain — from mineral extraction through midstream processing to the logistics that move finished goods to market — rather than conventional market access. In The Australian, Brazilian, and Chinese Dynamic, we traced this architecture through lithium refining, rare-earth processing, and port infrastructure such as Chancay. The global automobile is now a fourth front in the same campaign. BYD’s pricing is not merely competitive; it is engineered to convert every vehicle sold abroad into a node in a Chinese-controlled battery and software supply chain. A car buyer in São Paulo, Bangkok, or Budapest who chooses a BYD is not just choosing a product. They are choosing a dependency relationship whose terms were set upstream, in cell chemistry and mineral processing capacity that China already dominates. Toyota’s solid-state battery program in progress for launch projected within the next five years is the most credible industrial counter to this dynamic now on the table, not because it beats BYD on price, but because it proposes an entirely different chemistry, supply chain, and manufacturing geography. This article examines both halves of that contest: how BYD builds dependence, and Toyota’s bet to break it. BYD’s Global Expansion Strategy: Asymmetrical Market Penetration BYD’s rise has been startling in its speed. In April 2026 alone the company exported 135,098 vehicles worldwide, every one fully electric or plug-in hybrid, a figure that by some analyst estimates exceeded Tesla’s global monthly deliveries for the same month. SNE Research put BYD’s non-China deliveries at roughly 497,000 units in the first half of 2026, up 81 percent year on year, placing it third worldwide behind Volkswagen and Tesla in overseas volume. BYD’s own target is 1.6 million overseas sales in 2026, backed by new or expanding plants in Hungary, Brazil, Thailand, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Turkey, with Spain under consideration. The strategy behind these numbers is not a frontal assault on the most fortified Western markets. It is what one industry analysis calls “asymmetrical market penetration”: BYD largely avoided the politically hardened U.S. market where tariffs and political resistance keep it effectively locked out and instead targeted the Global South and secondary Western markets where legacy automakers had grown complacent. Thailand became a regional hub and template for ASEAN expansion; Brazil, Hungary, and Turkey became manufacturing footholds that double as tariff workarounds and in June 2026 Canada cut its tariff on Chinese EVs from 100 percent to 6.1 percent as part of a broader energy and climate partnership with Beijing, opening a new North American corridor. What makes this expansion durable rather than opportunistic is BYD’s unparalleled vertical integration. Unlike Western automakers, which depend heavily on third-party suppliers for battery cells, semiconductors, and software, BYD manufactures nearly everything in-house, an inheritance from its origins as a battery maker before it built a single car. That integration is precisely why the company can build factories concurrently across continents while still undercutting incumbents on price: it is not buying components at a margin, it is capturing the margin at every stage of the chain. Chinese EV factories capable of producing more than 200,000 vehicles a year have sprung up in Indonesia, Thailand, Pakistan, Turkey, Hungary, and Brazil, offering vehicles that are, on average, around 20 percent cheaper than their Western counterparts even before subsidies are considered. Domestically, this expansion is not evidence of strength alone. BYD’s first-quarter 2026 net profit fell 55 percent, its worst showing in three years, as a brutal domestic price war and thinning subsidies compressed sector-wide margins to an average of 3.2 percent. Exports abroad, where BYD can command significantly higher average selling prices, have become less a growth option than a financial necessity which only sharpens the incentive to keep undercutting Western rivals in every market it can reach. The Battery Dependency Mechanism BYD began life as a battery manufacturer, and that lineage is the key to understanding its strategy. Its battery subsidiary, FinDreams, is one of the largest EV battery producers on earth, second only to CATL, and together the two Chinese firms anchor a domestic battery-cell industry that supplies the overwhelming majority of the world’s electric and plug-in-hybrid vehicles. This is where the automotive story connects directly to the argument Kenneth Maxwell and I made in The Australian, Brazilian, and Chinese Dynamic. China today controls 57 percent of global lithium refining and 85 percent of global rare-earth processing, even though Australia alone produces 45 percent of the world’s raw lithium. A nation can extract the resource from its own soil and remain, in our phrase, a “feeder economy” so long as it lacks the midstream processing capacity to break the refining monopoly. The battery pack under a BYD Seal or a Dolphin is that same architecture, miniaturized and rolling on four wheels: raw lithium, cobalt, and rare-earth inputs processed almost entirely within Chinese-controlled facilities, assembled into cells by Chinese battery makers, and sold into foreign markets as a finished vehicle whose entire value chain, mine to midstream to cell to car, never leaves Beijing’s sphere of control. artigo.texto: Pennsylvania’s legislators return to the capitol Monday following a 10-week recess, with several unresolved issues awaiting action, including the future of skill games, regulation of data centers, rising utility costs and restrictions on cell phone use in schools. Skill Games Following a Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruling in June that determined skill games are slot machines, the legislature was given 120 days to establish a law to keep the industry alive. Advocates for skill games have encouraged Pennsylvanians to call their representatives to ask them to support bills that would regulate the machines. HB2213 and SB1079 are bipartisan measures. Rep. Danilo Burgos (D-197) is prime sponsor of the house bill. “This is about job security for community members across Pennsylvania,” he said. “And helping keep doors open at VA clubs, at VFWs, and a slew of other community groups that benefit.” Republican Sen. Gene Yaw (R-23) is prime sponsor of the Senate bill. “It’s going to be a tremendous hit to a significant number of Pennsylvanians if we don’t address it,” Yaw said. “I can’t remember anything that I have been involved in in the Senate that would affect so many people negatively in one instant happening.” The Senate only has six session days to address it before the deadline, but Yaw says lawmakers could reach an agreement. Last week, Rep. Brad Roae (R-6) proposed legislation to extend the deadline by six months. The House unanimously passed the bill in June, and Fiedler is hopeful for a Senate vote soon. Cell phone ban in schools There are two bills that would ban cell phone use in schools waiting to be voted on. HB1814 passed the house in June, while SB1014 was passed in the Senate in February. Polls show the majority of Pennsylvania voters support leaving cell phones out of the classroom. Shapiro called on the General Assembly to pass legislation during his February budget address, but a ban did not end up in the approved budget. “Students need to spend less time focused on their phones and more time focused on learning, on talking to their friends face to face, and on developing the critical skills they’ll need later in life,” he said. “I know there are bills in both chambers to do this — come together and send a bill to my desk.”

artigo.texto: Protests against data centers have exploded across the US, with communities revolting against a multitude of proven damaging effects on energy prices, clean air and water – and the devastation of tens of thousands of acres of agricultural land. Recent headlines in national publications report that farmers and rural communities are rejecting multimillion-dollar bids from institutional investors and tech companies to buy their farmland to build data centers. A farmer in Kentucky rejected $33 million for her farmland; another in Pennsylvania turned down a $15 million offer; and one farmer in Wisconsin even reportedly refused a whopping $70+ million bid. Land has become the next big asset class for investors, especially billionaires and private equity firms, to hide and protect their wealth. It is seen as a safe, low-risk way to park money to hedge against inflation – at the expense of farmers and local communities alike. These investors aren’t just seeking out farmland to build data centers. Just like they’re targeting housing, investment firms are buying up land and renting it back to farmers for a hefty profit. The 2024 Tenure, Ownership, and Transition of Agricultural Land (TOTAL) Survey, released this March, shows that 87% of the more than 2 million landowners renting out farmland are non-operators – that is, they are not actively farming, and the majority of these landowners never have. While these landlords raked in more than $34 billion in rent combined, the total value of farmland held for rent is $1.7 trillion – up 47% since 2014. We are watching in real time the emergence of a long-term, non-farming rural landlord class. While the TOTAL survey provides a useful indicator of farmland ownership trends, it doesn’t give us the full picture. Farmland ownership has never been effectively tracked in the US with regularity, and what limited data exists is difficult to find. The data we do have shows that investment in farmland has risen dramatically over the past two decades. Companies like AcreTrader, Farmland Partners, and others that allow individuals to invest in farmland have become increasingly popular. The most alarming growth has come from institutional investors, like pension funds, private equity firms, and wealth management groups. The value of farmland held by institutional investors has more than doubled over the past three years up to $16.6 billion dollars by 2024, an eightfold rise since 2008. Based on publicly available data alone, the largest corporate owners of US farmland control more than 2 million acres. But why are farmers selling their land in the first place? The hard truth is that farming just isn’t working as a viable livelihood anymore, and hasn’t for years. In just five years from 2017-2022, we lost 159,000 US family farms. The Farm Crisis didn’t go away in the 1980s – it’s just become quieter and less visible to most. Chronic low and volatile prices across sectors, coupled with a handful of multinational corporations tightening their iron grip over global agriculture, have pushed farmers to the brink of existence. With farm debt at an all-time high, selling the farm for the best offer possible is often the only feasible way to escape dire financial straits. And when the farm is for sale, companies with billions in assets are primed to outbid new and beginning farmers seeking land to start their own businesses. The best opportunity we have to protect farmland comes from strong federal policies that safeguard land for multiple generations of working farms and ensure farmers make a living wage. Right now, the Farmland for Farmers Act is one of the boldest pieces of federal legislation to combat this worrying trend. Modeled after anti-corporate farming laws in Midwestern states, the bill would stop large corporate entities from being able to purchase farmland only to let it lie fallow in the hopes that its value will skyrocket over time, or to rent it back to farmers at a premium price. With policies like it, coupled with a Farm Bill that allows farmers to pay their bills and sustainably grow their businesses, farmers might stand a chance. It’s long overdue for policy solutions championed by federal representatives not afraid to stand up against deep pocketed special interests. We need Congress to enact policies like the Farmland for Farmers Act that fight back against the profiteering on the backs of farmers, communities, and our natural resources. The first step in protecting farmland means supporting the next generation of farmers to enter the business with confidence and without having to compete with billionaires. We need to ensure that farmers now and in the future actually have the land they need to feed us all. Tim Gibbons is the Executive Director of the National Family Farm Coalition, a national coalition representing 30 grassroots farm, ranch, and fishing organizations in Washington, DC. A life-long Missourian, Tim has spent decades organizing family farmers, ranchers, and rural residents in support of fair, healthy and thriving rural economies, fair markets, and clean water and air. Dena Hoff represents the Northern Plains Resource Council on the NFFC Board. Since 1979, she’s raised sheep, cattle, alfalfa, corn, and edible dry beans, among other crops, on her farm in Glendive, Montana. She is an active member of and advocate for her rural community.

artigo.texto: O Grupo FonNet criou a AIKS, uma empresa independente especializada em inteligência artificial e observabilidade para redes, data centers e ambientes corporativos. A nova companhia nasce como spin-off da FonNet Networks e terá atuação voltada ao desenvolvimento de software e à oferta de serviços gerenciados para operadoras de telecomunicações, provedores de internet, data centers e empresas. CONTEÚDO RELACIONADO – Ipiranga troca monitoramento por observabilidade e reduz em 75% tempo de resposta no KMV A proposta da AIKS é atuar sobre um dos desafios enfrentados por operações de infraestrutura: a dispersão de métricas, logs, alertas e demais informações operacionais em diferentes ferramentas e equipes. Segundo a empresa, essa fragmentação dificulta a identificação das relações de dependência entre sistemas e pode aumentar o tempo necessário para determinar a origem de incidentes. A plataforma combina recursos de inteligência artificial e observabilidade para coletar, organizar e correlacionar eventos operacionais em tempo real. Os dados de processos e infraestrutura são reunidos em uma camada de observabilidade que busca oferecer uma visão integrada do ambiente e mais contexto para a tomada de decisão pelas equipes de operação. A AIKS também pretende apoiar a identificação das causas de falhas, a avaliação dos impactos e a priorização dos incidentes. A estratégia prevê a integração com as ferramentas já utilizadas pelos clientes, sem a necessidade de substituição imediata da infraestrutura existente. De acordo com a empresa, a abordagem permite que as soluções sejam implementadas de forma gradual e adaptadas às características de cada operação, com o objetivo de reduzir retrabalho e melhorar o tempo de resposta das equipes. Experiência em redes e infraestrutura A nova empresa aproveita a experiência acumulada pela FonNet Networks em 17 anos de atuação. Segundo o grupo, sua trajetória inclui projetos realizados para cerca de 800 empresas, entre operadoras de telecomunicações, ISPs, data centers e organizações do mercado corporativo no Brasil e em outros países da região. A FonNet também mantém parcerias com empresas globais de tecnologia. Entre elas está a Precision Optical Technologies, fabricante com a qual mantém uma relação comercial há quase duas décadas e da qual é distribuidora exclusiva. Estrutura executiva Arthur Filgueira, CEO da FonNet Networks, assumiu também a presidência da AIKS. Emerson Sampaio será CTO e cofundador da nova companhia. A estrutura reúne profissionais das áreas de engenharia, arquitetura de TIC, desenvolvimento de software, segurança cibernética, suporte e negócios. “A quantidade de ferramentas e dados disponíveis nas empresas aumentou, mas isso nem sempre se traduziu em maior capacidade de decisão. A AIKS vem para conectar essas informações, preservar os investimentos já realizados e ajudar as equipes a evoluir a operação de forma gradual e mensurável”, afirma Filgueira. CSDC Finance, subsidiária indireta integral da CleanSpark, concluiu a oferta em 25 de setembro de 2026 sob um contrato de compra datado de 18 de setembro de 2026 entre a empresa, CSRE Properties Sandersville, LLC, e Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC como representante dos compradores iniciais, de acordo com o Formulário 8-K arquivado na Securities and Exchange Commission no mesmo dia. O registro indica que o valor principal agregado das notas vendidas foi de $2,276.0 million, emitidas a um preço igual a 98.500% do principal, e que as notas foram vendidas para revenda a pessoas que se acredita razoavelmente serem compradores institucionais qualificados sob a Regra 144A e, fora dos Estados Unidos, a pessoas não americanas sob o Regulamento S. As notas não foram registradas sob o Securities Act de 1933 e não podem ser oferecidas ou vendidas nos Estados Unidos sem registro ou uma isenção aplicável de registro. Termos da Escritura Em 25 de setembro de 2026, CSDC Finance, CSRE Properties Sandersville e CSDC Holdings I, LLC, a controladora direta da CSDC Finance, celebraram uma escritura que rege as notas com a U.S. Bank Trust Company, National Association, como fiduciária e agente de garantia. As notas são obrigações seniores garantidas da CSDC Finance, com juros de 7,875% ao ano, pagáveis semestralmente em atraso em 1º de abril e 1º de outubro de cada ano, a partir de 1º de abril de 2027. Elas vencem em 1º de outubro de 2031, salvo se forem resgatadas ou recompradas anteriormente de acordo com seus termos. O principal será amortizado semestralmente em cada 1º de abril e 1º de outubro após a Data de Início Final, conforme definido na escritura, em um valor necessário para atingir a Razão de Cobertura de Serviço da Dívida do Projeto Alvo, também definida na escritura. Em ou após 1º de outubro de 2028, o emissor pode resgatar as notas a seu critério, integralmente a qualquer momento ou parcialmente de tempos em tempos, pelos preços de resgate estabelecidos na escritura. Antes dessa data, pode resgatar as notas a um preço igual a 100% do principal mais um prêmio de compensação e juros acumulados e não pagos. A escritura limita a capacidade do emissor e da subsidiária garantidora de, entre outras coisas, contrair ou garantir dívidas adicionais; pagar dividendos ou distribuições, ou resgatar ou recomprar ações e fazer outros pagamentos restritos; realizar certos investimentos; criar ou contrair gravames; concluir determinadas vendas de ativos; celebrar transações de venda e arrendamento; manter ativos ou conduzir operações não relacionadas à operação da Instalação de Sandersville; envolver-se em determinadas transações com afiliadas; e fundir, consolidar ou transferir ou vender a totalidade ou a maior parte de seus ativos. Essas cláusulas estão sujeitas a várias qualificações e exceções importantes. A escritura também prevê eventos de inadimplência habituais. Pacote de Garantia e Segurança As notas são totalmente e incondicionalmente garantidas pela CSRE Properties Sandersville, LLC, subsidiária direta integral do emissor, de acordo com o anúncio de precificação da empresa. As notas e a garantia associada são asseguradas por gravames de primeira prioridade sobre praticamente todos os ativos do emissor e da CSRE Properties, exceto certos bens excluídos, e sobre todas as participações acionárias do emissor detidas pela CSDC Holdings I, LLC, uma sociedade de responsabilidade limitada de Delaware. O 8-K também afirma que a CleanSpark fornecerá uma garantia de conclusão habitual para a Instalação de Sandersville, sob a qual financiará o emissor conforme necessário para garantir a conclusão pontual da instalação caso os recursos das notas e fundos disponíveis, incluindo as contribuições de capital anteriores da CleanSpark relacionadas à instalação, sejam insuficientes. artigo.texto: The Chicago-based battery technology startup Pure Lithium is building its case around a simpler idea: remove some of the materials that make today’s batteries heavy, complex and deeply tied to overseas supply chains, then rethink how lithium reaches the cell in the first place. The race to build the next generation of batteries has produced no shortage of ambitious ideas. Solid-state cells, silicon anodes and new cathode chemistries have all been pitched as possible answers to the limitations of today’s lithium-ion technology. Pure Lithium is taking another route. The company describes itself as a vertically integrated lithium metal vanadium, or LVO, battery technology business. At the centre of its approach is its Brine to Battery™ electrodeposition technology, designed to turn unconventional sources of lithium into a battery-ready electrode without first going through the conventional compound-production route. The company says that process can create an electrode in a single day. That manufacturing philosophy is important to understanding Pure Lithium. Rather than treating lithium extraction, processing and battery manufacturing as disconnected stages, the company is trying to bring them much closer together. And at the battery level, its ambitions go beyond changing where lithium comes from. Pure Lithium is also working on lithium-metal cells that eliminate graphite from the anode. The technology highlighted in recent testing pairs a lithium-metal anode with lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, chemistry. Pure Lithium says this configuration removes the need for graphite as well as nickel, manganese and cobalt, materials that feature prominently in conventional battery supply chains. That matters because graphite remains one of the less visible dependencies in the battery industry. More than 90% of the world’s graphite processing takes place in China. In a conventional lithium-ion battery, graphite acts primarily as a host material for lithium ions during charging and discharging. Pure Lithium’s approach is to remove that host altogether and use lithium metal directly, opening additional room inside the cell for energy-storing material. For Chief Executive Emilie Bodoin, eliminating graphite is central to the company’s performance argument. “It’s half the weight and double the energy density of the battery that we’re all using today,” Bodoin said in an interview cited by InsideEVs. Those claims are still being tested against the realities of commercial production, but Pure Lithium has recently put forward a striking laboratory result. The company said one of its lithium-metal cells reached 9,315 charge-discharge cycles, with testing conducted at a 1C charge and discharge rate. That means the cell was repeatedly charged over one hour and discharged over another hour. Pure Lithium said the result was unprecedented for a lithium-metal battery tested under equivalent conditions. The test was not uninterrupted. Pure Lithium paused testing around the 6,000-cycle point while moving its headquarters from Boston to Chicago, leaving the cell at room temperature for roughly four months. When testing resumed, the company reported that the cell continued to show strong capacity retention. It also disclosed that some of the earlier fluctuations in the test were linked to a lack of temperature control and multiple power failures in its Boston laboratory. A previous test in January 2025 had shown that a Pure Lithium cell had maintained over 80% of its charge capacity after 2,200 cycles at the same 1C rate. It should be noted that the company has also claimed its Gen 1 battery to have 300 Wh/kg energy density, with its Gen 2 model projected to achieve 425 Wh/kg. However, the energy density of the particular cell used for testing 9,315 cycles was not provided. That distinction is important. Long cycle life in a laboratory cell is not the same thing as a commercially produced automotive battery, and Pure Lithium has not yet reached mass production. The company is currently building a pilot line in Chicago and is looking for partners to help commercialise the technology. Bodoin has said Pure Lithium is in discussions with more than 40 companies about scaling its approach. The way Pure Lithium manufactures its lithium-metal anode is another part of the story. Its battery is graphite-free, but not anode-free. Instead, lithium metal is deposited directly onto a copper current collector through electrodeposition until the required thickness is reached. In effect, the anode is formed as part of the manufacturing process rather than being produced through the conventional graphite-based route. Bodoin has described that electrodeposition step as a way of making the lithium anode in a single manufacturing stage. For Pure Lithium, that manufacturing method connects back to the bigger idea behind Brine to Battery™: shorten the distance between raw lithium and a usable battery component. It is an approach that could become increasingly relevant as battery companies rethink both chemistry and supply chains. Pure Lithium is not alone in pursuing lithium-metal technology. Factorial, Solid Power and QuantumScape are also developing graphite-free lithium-metal batteries, although their technical routes differ. Factorial and QuantumScape have focused on solid-state or semi-solid-state electrolytes, while Solid Power has been developing technologies around a sulfide solid electrolyte. Pure Lithium, by contrast, uses a liquid electrolyte and is placing particular emphasis on how its lithium-metal anode is produced. That difference may ultimately prove as important as the chemistry itself. The battery industry is not simply looking for a cell that stores more energy. Companies are also trying to reduce manufacturing complexity, lower material dependence and create supply chains that can operate closer to where batteries will eventually be produced. artigo.texto: Virginia rejoins carbon market as utilities seek $13 monthly charge after allowance prices surge - Virginia has rejoined the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, leading to a sharp increase in the price of carbon allowances that utilities must pay, potentially impacting electricity bills and state climate programs. Virginia's return to the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative has come with a sharp jump in the price utilities pay for carbon allowances, a change that could affect electricity bills and how the state funds climate and energy programs in the years ahead. Here's what to know Virginia has rejoined the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, or RGGI, an agreement among 11 states designed to cut carbon pollution from power plants. The state was part of RGGI from 2020 to 2023, before Gov. Glenn Youngkin withdrew it, citing high costs for little payoff, reported The Virginian-Pilot. In the first auction since Virginia's return, allowances sold for $37.65 each, more than double the $14.88 price from the last auction before the state left. That auction generated $259 million for Virginia, according to The Virginian-Pilot. "I think the people who designed this 15, 20 years ago knew the price was going to go up," said Steve Haner, senior fellow for energy and the environment at the Thomas Jefferson Institute for Public Policy, in an interview with the Pilot. More background Under RGGI, power producers must buy an allowance for every metric ton of carbon pollution they emit, and utilities like Dominion Energy can pass that cost on to customers. William Shobe, director emeritus of the University of Virginia's Center for Economic & Policy Studies, said prices have climbed roughly 14% a year since 2012 and are likely to keep rising as allowance caps shrink through 2033. Dominion is now asking state regulators to add a $13 monthly charge to a typical customer's bill to cover its allowance costs, up from about $4.40 a month before Virginia left RGGI. What's being done? Virginia has changed how it splits RGGI revenue. Before, half went to low-income energy efficiency programs and 45% to flood preparedness. Now, 45% is set aside for customer rebates, with the rest split between flood resiliency and low-income programs. Some environmental advocates worry the smaller flood-fund share could slow projects in Hampton Roads. Not every customer stands to benefit equally. Industrial and large retail users won't get rebates, which Haner said could push those companies to raise prices elsewhere to cover their higher utility costs. "Businesses just pass along their costs to the extent they can," Haner said. "Kroger's not going to get a rebate, Walmart's not going to get a rebate. Your small doctor's office might, but the hospital's not." Where can I learn more? Virginia's return to RGGI is part of a larger conversation about how state energy policy shapes power prices and cleaner electricity. • Virginia became the first state to take a solar-buying program statewide, cutting system costs. • Connecticut and Virginia moved to speed home solar as advocates pushed for cheaper power. • Across the U.S., energy storage installations kept rising as utilities prepared for demand. • In California, an unorthodox power market drove lower bills while clean generation expanded. artigo.texto: Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) is facing growing scrutiny over the financing of its AI infrastructure after about $18 billion of loans tied to its Project Jupiter data center in New Mexico were quoted at 89 to 91 cents on the dollar, according to the Financial Times, as reported by Reuters. The project is part of Oracle's AI infrastructure expansion with OpenAI, but local opposition over water and air-quality concerns and a regulatory setback involving a proposed natural-gas pipeline have raised questions about its development. Banks have also struggled to distribute the debt to other investors as concerns about Oracle's leverage have increased. Reuters noted that S&P downgraded Oracle in July to one notch above junk. Photo from Oracle website Oracle's AI Backlog Could Provide a Cushion for Rising Financing Needs The debt pressure is occurring alongside exceptionally strong demand for Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL)'s cloud infrastructure. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, cloud revenue rose 62% to $11.6 billion, while cloud infrastructure revenue increased 121% to $7.4 billion. Oracle's remaining performance obligations also reached $664 billion, up $209 billion year over year, providing substantial contracted demand to support continued infrastructure investment. The financing model is also becoming less dependent on Oracle funding every dollar itself. Oracle said $75 billion of its large AI contracts involved customers prepaying for GPUs or supplying the GPUs themselves, substantially reducing the capital it needs to raise for AI data centers. Oracle raised $43 billion of debt and $5 billion of equity in fiscal 2026, while expecting about $40 billion of additional debt and equity financing in fiscal 2027. If customer-backed contracts continue expanding, the revenue generated from infrastructure could increasingly offset the financing burden. Rising Infrastructure Costs Could Test Oracle's AI Investment Strategy The immediate concern is that Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) is committing capital faster than its infrastructure generates cash. Capital expenditures jumped to $55.7 billion in fiscal 2026 from $21.2 billion a year earlier, producing negative free cash flow of $23.7 billion. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027 alone, capital expenditures reached $28.5 billion, and Oracle expects fiscal 2027 spending to exceed the prior year. The balance sheet leaves less room for execution problems. As of August 31, Oracle had $125.3 billion of notes payable and other borrowings, compared with $37.1 billion of cash and marketable securities. It also had $34.6 billion of recognized operating lease liabilities and another $288 billion of additional data-center lease commitments expected to begin between fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2029.
