artigo.texto: City of Hopkinsville to host public hearing over data center zoning What This Story Is About - Hopkinsville Community and Development Services is holding a public hearing to gather community feedback on proposed zoning amendments governing data centers. Why It Matters - The proposed changes will establish legal definitions, operational guidelines, and designated zoning districts for future data center developments, directly influencing local land use, infrastructure demand, and commercial growth. What Happens Next - Following the public hearing at Hopkinsville Community College, CDS will review public feedback and formulate recommendations before the proposed ordinance heads to the Hopkinsville City Council for final review and approval. For Context - Municipalities across Kentucky and the region are increasingly updating their zoning ordinances to manage the rapid rise of data center facilities, addressing potential impacts on electric grids, water systems, noise levels, and property boundaries. HOPKINSVILLE, Ky. (WBKO) - The City of Hopkinsville has announced Community and Development Services will hold a public hearing Monday evening to gather public input on proposed zoning regulations for commercial data centers. The hearing is scheduled for 6 p.m. in the Lecture Hall of the Hopkinsville Community College Auditorium Building, 720 North Drive. The proposed amendment to the Hopkinsville Zoning Ordinance outlines how data centers are defined locally, establishes siting and operational standards, and determines which zoning districts would permit such facilities. Residents and business owners are invited to attend and provide feedback before officials advance the amendment to local governing bodies for formal consideration. Copyright 2026 WBKO. artigo.texto: O Gabinete do Governo emitiu o documento nº 498/TB-VPCP, datado de 25 de setembro de 2026, anunciando as conclusões do Vice-Primeiro-Ministro Pham Gia Tuc na reunião de revisão do projeto de Resolução Governamental que promulga o Plano de implementação da Resolução nº 05-NQ/DU, datada de 12 de junho de 2026, do Comitê do Partido Governamental, sobre a aplicação de mecanismos e políticas para implementar o Projeto de construção de um centro de dados para gerenciamento, monitoramento, tratamento de violações e operação de tráfego no período de 2026 a 2030, com uma visão para 2050. O comunicado declarava: Para acelerar o processo de transformação digital na garantia da ordem e segurança do trânsito, em 20 de março de 2026, o Primeiro-Ministro emitiu a Decisão nº 456/QD-TTg aprovando o Projeto de construção de um Centro de Dados para gerenciar, monitorar, lidar com infrações e operar o trânsito no período de 2026 a 2030, com uma visão para 2050 (o Projeto). Estas são tarefas importantes e urgentes que precisam ser implementadas rapidamente para contribuir com a modernização antecipada do monitoramento e gerenciamento de tráfego. Portanto, em 12 de junho de 2026, o Comitê do Partido do Governo emitiu a Resolução nº 05-NQ/DU, que determina a implementação de diversas soluções para a execução do Projeto. Ao longo do último período, o Ministério da Segurança Pública assumiu a liderança proativa e coordenou com ministérios, setores, localidades e unidades o desenvolvimento do plano do Governo para implementar a Resolução 05-NQ/DU; e coordenou com o Gabinete do Governo a implementação dos procedimentos de reporte ao Governo, em conformidade com o regulamento interno do Governo. Para agilizar a publicação do Plano de Governo, o Vice-Primeiro-Ministro Pham Gia Tuc solicitou ao Ministério da Segurança Pública que coordenasse com o Gabinete do Governo a revisão e finalização da minuta da Resolução Governamental, e que a apresentasse ao Primeiro-Ministro para publicação antes de 28 de setembro de 2026. Durante a implementação do Projeto, o Ministério da Segurança Pública é o órgão permanente responsável, coordenando-se com ministérios, agências e localidades para definir cada item de trabalho, cada unidade responsável pela implementação e atribuir claramente cada tarefa a uma unidade específica, com a coordenação das agências relevantes; cada agência deve implementar proativamente as tarefas de acordo com a urgência do Projeto. Ministérios, setores e localidades devem implementar as tarefas do Projeto, garantindo o pleno cumprimento dos procedimentos e regulamentos legais para cada projeto de investimento, assegurando a qualidade, a sincronização e interconexão dos sistemas, a segurança, a eficiência e evitando a duplicação de tarefas; e prevenindo o desperdício e a corrupção. artigo.texto: Amazon Taps Prysmian and Rio Tinto for Low-Carbon Data Center Cables. What Does it Mean for Investors? Prysmian is finding another way into the data-center buildout, and this time the story isn't about fiber. The Italian cable maker has partnered with Rio Tinto (NYSE:RIO) to supply electrical cables made with low-carbon aluminum for an Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) data center in Ohio. The cables will use aluminum produced with ELYSIS inert-anode technology, which Prysmian says eliminates direct greenhouse-gas emissions from the aluminum-smelting process and releases pure oxygen instead. For Prysmian investors, the project's significance lies in the fact that the technology Prysmian and Rio Tinto were developing earlier this year is now being put to use in a data-center project for Amazon. Bull Case The Amazon project gives Prysmian's work with ELYSIS something it didn't have when the company announced its expanded collaboration with Rio Tinto in March, which is a specific data-center application. Prysmian says this will be the first known use of aluminum produced through inert-anode smelting in a data center, and the cables will be manufactured at its Sedalia, Missouri facility. The project didn't emerge from a new supplier relationship either, as Prysmian and Rio Tinto (NYSE:RIO) signed a five-year supply agreement in 2023 for low-carbon aluminum produced using renewable hydropower from Rio Tinto's Canadian operations. They later strengthened the relationship through a joint development agreement before announcing their work with ELYSIS-produced aluminum in March 2026. Data centers were already part of the thinking at that point, as Prysmian said in March that its customers, particularly those in the data-center sector, shared similar sustainability commitments, while Rio Tinto specifically identified the rapidly expanding data-center sector as an area where lower-carbon aluminum could support decarbonization efforts. Amazon has now provided a concrete example, with AWS Vice President of Data Center Engineering Joern Tinnemeyer linking the Ohio initiative to Amazon's target of reaching net-zero carbon emissions across its operations by 2040. The project also fits with targets Prysmian has set for its own business. The company is targeting Net Zero by 2035 and has said it wants sustainability-linked solutions to account for 55% of revenue by 2028. Bear Case There is an obvious reason not to get carried away with the announcement, as Prysmian has not provided a contract value or expected revenue contribution of the Amazon project. Without a contract value, volume figure, or expected revenue contribution, there is no basis for arguing that the Ohio data center will materially change Prysmian's financial performance.

artigo.texto: Marshall County approves six-month moratorium on data center applications The Marshall County Board of Supervisors unanimously passed a six-month pause on new data center applications to allow time for drafting regulations. The Marshall County Board of Supervisors has unanimously approved a six-month moratorium on applications for new data centers, artificial intelligence computing facilities, data mining facilities and cryptocurrency mining operations. The resolution was passed during Wednesday's meeting. The county zoning commission will now draft rules and regulations that data centers must follow if they want to build in the county. That list of regulations is expected to be ready by spring of next year. Multiple other cities and counties across our state have temporary pauses in place, including Ames, Marshalltown, Boone County and Madison County.

artigo.texto: BYD Teases Rolls-Royce Rival with Brand’s 1st Solid-State Battery BYD has shown the first official pictures of its next Yangwang flagship sedan. Its imposing shape and rear-hinged doors invite comparisons with the Rolls-Royce Phantom. But the most exciting possibility is hidden beneath the camouflage: this could be the first BYD fitted with a solid-state battery. Executive Vice President Stella Li has said a vehicle using the technology will arrive in 2027, but she has not named it or announced when production will begin. A low-volume luxury car is a plausible starting point for a battery that is still expensive to make. Why the Battery Could Be the Bigger Reveal Most EV batteries use a liquid electrolyte to move lithium ions between their electrodes. A fully solid-state battery uses a solid electrolyte instead. The technology could allow a smaller, lighter pack to store more energy, giving an EV more range without adding battery weight. Replacing flammable liquid could also improve safety. Those benefits are promising, but they are not guaranteed in every battery. Engineers still have to solve problems with internal contact, durability and lithium growth that can damage a cell. BYD has released no battery capacity, range or charging figures for the Yangwang sedan. One teaser image shows the car beside a BYD Flash Charging station. That has added to the speculation, although it is not evidence of a solid-state pack. BYD already offers Flash Charging with its conventional Blade Battery 2.0. Where the Solid-State Race Stands NIO already offers a 150 kWh battery for its premium EVs, making it a useful example of how advanced batteries can reach customers first in expensive cars. There is an important distinction: supplier WeLion describes NIO’s pack as semi-solid-state. It still contains some liquid electrolyte, so it is not the same as a fully solid-state battery. Other manufacturers are working toward the next step. Mercedes-Benz has road-tested a solid-state battery in an EQS, while BMW has tested all-solid-state cells in an i7. Toyota is developing the technology and aims to introduce EVs using it in 2027–28. BYD plans to put its own technology in a vehicle in 2027, though it has yet to identify that car. What We Know About the Yangwang Sedan The camouflaged car has a long, upright body, rear-hinged coach doors and a roof-mounted lidar sensor. Yangwang has not shown the interior or announced its final name, specifications, price or launch date. The doors will turn heads. Confirmation of a solid-state battery would be the development to watch: it would put BYD’s next-generation technology in a car people can see and, eventually, drive. Follow the PakWheels Blog for the sedan’s confirmed specifications and the latest EV battery developments.

artigo.texto: ebm-papst Hungary is investing approximately €570,000 (about $670,000) to expand the photovoltaic and energy storage infrastructure at its Vecsés site in Hungary. The project will add 100 kW of photovoltaic capacity and a battery storage system with a total capacity of 1,572 kWh. The battery system consists of six blocks weighing around 2.5 tonnes (approximately 5,500 lb) each. When fully charged, the storage system can support continued production for an additional three to four hours during a power outage. It will also enable the company to store more self-generated electricity and reduce exposure to electricity price fluctuations. The site currently covers an average of around 25% of its annual electricity needs with an existing 800 kW photovoltaic system. Following the expansion and installation of the battery storage system, the self-sufficiency rate is expected to reach around 45%. The project will also enable an additional 400 MWh of electricity to be generated and used on site annually. According to the company, the investment is expected to pay for itself in under 3.5 years. The installed infrastructure also provides the potential for future expansion into a scalable energy storage array. “The new battery system is a key component in making our site energy-efficient and future-proof. It reduces our dependence on external factors while strengthening our commitment to sustainability,” said Sándor Egri, Head of the Facility and Maintenance Department.

Christina Henriksen and her own Cisco’s Calor Z held their lead from start to finish in the Intermediate Division, finishing their weekend on a 38.1. Waylon Roberts and FVF Top Gun LLC’s FVF Top Gun moved up to second place after a quick trip around the cross country. The combination finished on a 54.7. Karl Slezak was one of only two to produce a double-clear round, moving up to win the division by 6.8 points on a 30.7 aboard Elizabeth Leete’s HSH Marshall. Slezak also finished in second place on Elizabeth Leete’s Herald De La Rose. The combination finished on a 37.5. Allison Springer and Nancy Winter’s Herald De La Rose also finished on a 37.5, with Slezak finishing just ahead of her on the tie-break. Stable View sponsors, GGT Footing and The Sharer Dale Team, enjoyed their course-side gazebos with their clients and friends. The four-star saw plenty of shifting in the leaderboard as well. artigo.texto: Ar-condicionado do carro elétrico gasta bateria? Veja o impacto Sistema de climatização de alta tensão deixa de focar apenas no conforto da cabine e passa a gerenciar a temperatura de componentes vitais do veículo O avanço acelerado dos veículos eletrificados no mercado brasileiro começou a transformar a arquitetura dos sistemas de climatização nos carros. No primeiro semestre de 2026, o país registrou o emplacamento de 215.023 veículos leves híbridos e elétricos, uma expansão de 125% em relação às 95.493 unidades vendidas no mesmo período de 2025, segundo dados da Associação Brasileira do Veículo Elétrico (ABVE). Com o aumento da frota em circulação, o ar-condicionado ganha novas atribuições técnicas. Nos modelos eletrificados, o sistema vai além da ambientação térmica escolhida pelos ocupantes e passa a atuar diretamente no gerenciamento da temperatura de funcionamento da bateria de tração, da eletrônica de potência e do motor elétrico. Compressores de alta tensão e eficiência energética A principal mudança estrutural em relação aos carros convencionais está no acionamento do compressor. Enquanto nos veículos a combustão o componente depende da rotação do motor via correias, nos híbridos e elétricos são adotados compressores elétricos movidos por circuitos de alta tensão. A arquitetura permite que a climatização opere independentemente do motor a combustão estar ligado ou desligado. "Nos veículos eletrificados, a climatização passa a ter uma função mais ampla. O sistema não está relacionado apenas ao conforto dos passageiros, mas também ao controle da temperatura de componentes importantes para o funcionamento e a eficiência do veículo", explica André Eduardo Oliveira, diretor da Mastercool Brasil. Nos modelos 100% elétricos, como o compressor consome a energia armazenada na bateria principal, a eficiência do sistema reflete diretamente na autonomia do automóvel. Para reduzir o impacto no alcance do veículo, as montadoras têm incorporado soluções como bombas de calor, climatização por zonas e o pré-condicionamento da cabine enquanto o carro ainda está conectado ao carregador. Segurança e novos protocolos para oficinas A transição tecnológica impõe ainda mais desafios para a rede de manutenção e reparação. A presença de circuitos de alta voltagem, combinada à exigência de lubrificantes e fluidos de arrefecimento com especificações dielétricas rígidas, exige que os técnicos utilizem novos equipamentos de proteção individual (EPIs) e sigam rotinas específicas de desenergização para diagnósticos e consertos. As transformações na cadeia de Aquecimento, Ventilação, Ar-Condicionado e Refrigeração (AVAC-R) e os impactos da eletrificação no setor automotivo serão debatidos durante a Febrava RIO, entre 6 e 8 de outubro. "A eletrificação está mudando sistemas que já fazem parte da rotina dos veículos e trazendo novas exigências para a indústria e para os profissionais", afirma Tatiana Rassini, gerente-geral do evento. "A convivência entre diferentes gerações tecnológicas amplia a necessidade de capacitação contínua para acompanhar a evolução desse mercado."

artigo.texto: Ontario EV shopper weighs Bolt or BYD Dolphin, then gets warning: 'A tin can with a battery' Buying an affordable EV is supposed to be a practical decision with objective pros and cons. But for one shopper in Canada, the calculation got complicated as they decided whether to buy a Chevrolet Bolt or wait for BYD's widely discussed Dolphin. Here's what to know The question came from an Ontario buyer turning to the r/BoltEV subreddit to decide whether to purchase a Bolt LT or hold off for BYD's compact EV. In a Reddit thread, the original poster wrote: "Currently deciding between a Bolt LT at 41k all in (incl taxes) and waiting for the BYD Dolphin." They asked owners what tipped them toward the Chevy and what to consider before deciding. Many of the replies favored the Bolt for a simple reason. It already has a foothold, as demonstrated by a vibrant Reddit community. Commenters repeatedly returned to the comfort of existing dealers, easier access to parts, and a service network buyers can count on instead of one that may take time to develop. The discussion also touched on materials and day-to-day livability. "The Bolt interior is nicer and will age better than the Dolphin," one commenter wrote. Another pointed out that some Dolphin versions sold abroad have smaller battery packs than the Bolt. One commenter was particularly harsh on the model. "Chinese cars sound nice on paper but in my experience with the BYD Dolphin it's a tin can with a battery, the Bolt feels more solid all around and way more reliable," they wrote. More background Affordable EVs remain one of the biggest sticking points for shoppers hoping to cut gas costs without paying luxury-car prices. The Bolt has long drawn attention as a relatively accessible all-electric hatchback, while the BYD Dolphin has built a reputation in other markets as a budget-friendly compact EV. EVs can lower ownership costs in meaningful ways. Home charging is often much cheaper per mile than paying for gasoline, and drivers also avoid oil changes. Still, those savings matter only if the vehicle is reliable and easy to service. In the thread, concern about after-sale support kept resurfacing. Buyers worried that a thinner Canadian presence could mean harder warranty claims, slower parts sourcing, or long drives for repairs, particularly outside the largest cities. What can be done? Comparing total ownership costs rather than focusing only on sticker price means looking at taxes, insurance, charging costs, expected winter range, battery warranty, and the distance to the nearest qualified service center. Ontario weather changes the calculation too. One commenter urged buyers to "be VERY aware of the Bolt LT trim." The commenter added, "Imagine not having heated seats and steering wheel in Ontario, Canada. Hard pass." How a driver expects to charge the car can matter just as much. Someone who plugs in at home every night may not care as much about weaker fast-charging performance, while a buyer who depends on public chargers or plans frequent longer trips may put far more emphasis on charging speed and network support. Some commenters were jealous of the original poster's predicament. "I wish I even had the opportunity to add BYD Dolphin to something I was considering," an envious commenter shared. Where can I learn more? The affordable EV market is one that is still evolving and facing perceived hurdles from some consumers. • In the U.K., BYD pushed cheap compact EVs closer to mainstream-car territory. • Persistent doubts about price and carbon still cloud EV decisions for first-time buyers. • A Nissan Leaf owner described the unexpected reality of owning an EV amid lingering myths. artigo.texto: “A fraction of proposed data centers will get built. Utilities are wising up.” That was the headline on a May 2025 Utility Dive article that explored the conundrum speculative data center requests pose for U.S. electric utilities. More than a year later, it’s unclear how much has changed. Community opposition has emerged as a major barrier to data center development, with other challenges including construction labor shortages, long lead times for critical electrical equipment, limited power availability in key markets and uncertainty around consumer demand for artificial intelligence tools. More than $170 billion in AI data center capacity has been “blocked, withdrawn, or stalled” by community opposition since January 2024, the energy advisory company Relae, formerly Carbon Direct, said in June. That’s a sizable chunk of the roughly $581 billion Goldman Sachs expects the big tech companies known as hyperscalers to spend in the U.S. on AI infrastructure, including data center construction, this year. Yet market analysts see no sign that the AI-driven construction boom will disappear anytime soon, despite challenges. Goldman Sachs said in May it sees U.S. data center power demand more than doubling from its 2025 levels to reach 66 GW in 2027. Only about half of data center capacity scheduled for the next one to two years is expected to come online on time amid delays and cancellations, it said. The Electric Power Research Institute, a research nonprofit, said in February that data centers will represent 9% to 17% of U.S. electricity demand in 2030 and up to 20% by 2035. Questions persist around the scale, timing and location of new data center load. If anything, the uncertainty is growing amid public backlash to data centers that is fueling state-led efforts to impose stricter rules on data center development, up to and including moratoriums on new facilities in some places. Firmer answers would benefit not only the utility planners and regulators ensuring that the electric grid is neither over- nor under-built, but also the millions of other customers who could bear the consequences of a disorderly buildout, industry experts say. Texas hits the brakes on large loads as states assert control Many utilities and their regulators have turned to large-load tariffs to try and weed out speculative load by requiring minimum contract durations, minimum billing demand and collateral requirements, upfront payments for impact studies, exit fees and specific ramp schedules. Some states have also introduced incentives for developers that bring their own capacity, agree to be flexible in their energy use or commit to state clean energy or economic development goals. The question of just how much data center capacity is going to come online, and when, is particularly urgent in Texas, which has paused new data center interconnections pending an audit of its 474-GW queue. That’s more than five times the Texas grid’s recent all-time peak demand record of a little over 90 GW set this summer. Few experts expect all that load to materialize. Pablo Vegas, president and CEO of the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, is among the skeptics. “We believe this forecast to be higher than expected future load growth,” Vegas said in an April statement, citing uncertainty around protocols for identifying, verifying and incorporating large load demand into long-range planning. Vegas said ERCOT would work with the Public Utilities Commission of Texas to adjust its forecasting methodology. Thomas Gleeson, the PUCT’s chairman, was more blunt in an appearance on the Energy Capital podcast in June. “The projections are extremely high, and what we know is that a lot of that load will not actually come here. A lot of it is speculative,” Gleeson said in comments made before the interconnection pause. The sheer number of large-load interconnection requests compounds the state’s challenge. Texas’s load growth — not only from large computing and industrial loads, but also garden-variety residential and commercial demand — is leading to congestion in load pockets that previously had capacity to spare, Gleeson said. That creates unwelcome uncertainty for large-load customers eager to put steel in the ground. “That has been the problem we have been trying to solve for the past eight or so months — that when [a customer has] an interconnection agreement and they are ready to move forward, they know that the capacity will be there to serve them so they can make proper business decisions,” Gleeson said. Texas has developed “gating” conditions to discourage speculative interconnection requests, balance load and capacity and “make sure that no one is harmed by these large loads,” Gleeson said. Last summer, Gov. Greg Abbott, R, signed Senate Bill 6, a sweeping measure requiring prospective large-load customers to demonstrate site control, substantially cover necessary grid upgrades, disclose duplicative interconnection requests elsewhere in Texas and accept curtailment during firm load shed events, among other provisions. On June 18, the PUCT adopted a cluster study framework for prospective loads larger than 75 MW that officials said would streamline a “lengthy and repetitive” sequential study process as ERCOT stakeholders work to develop a comprehensive transmission planning framework later this year. ERCOT said at the time that it expected to publish a final transmission plan for the first study cluster, known as “Batch Zero,” in late 2027. Gleeson said on the podcast that the cluster study and transmission planning frameworks will mitigate uncertainty for large loads, grid operators and generation owners across Texas. Together, they assure loads that “once they interconnect, they will get the electricity they need to fully energize,” and they assure other stakeholders that “all the loads coming here are real and will stay,” he said. artigo.texto: Data Centers and Carbon Capture: A Dangerous Alliance Published Sep 25, 2026 Carbon capture and storage is an expensive failure. So why is Big Tech teaming up with Big Oil to add it to data center projects? Communities across the country are fighting against the pollution, water demands, climate emissions, and higher energy bills driven by data centers. Many are successfully grinding data center projects to a halt. In response, Big Tech is teaming up with the fossil fuel industry to promote carbon capture and storage (CCS) as a way to paint themselves as “clean.” This self-serving corporate greenwash opens additional lines of profit and harms at the expense of frontline communities, giving anyone fighting one of these industries a reason to fight both. It’s a match made in hell. Combining data centers and CCS won’t save the climate or make projects less harmful. It’ll only mean less water, dirtier air, higher electricity bills, and more money for Big Oil. Both the carbon capture industry and Big Tech have expanded rapidly in recent years by threatening local democracy and forcing projects on communities. Both industries have claimed they’re helping us fight climate change, while in reality propelling us further into climate chaos. Two Industries, Two Problems, One Big Carbon Capture Scam AI data centers are incredibly energy-hungry; by 2028, they may command as much electricity as 55 million households. Already, 40% of data center energy comes from dirty gas. The AI boom is already driving the construction of new gas-fired power plants and keeping old power plants on life support. This is creating a real credibility issue for the tech industry’s unenforceable climate and environmental pledges. The fossil fuel industry has a different problem. They need new customers to justify massive new pipelines, new power plants, and fracking. CCS is the bridge between these two destructive industries. It’s providing Big Tech a new fig leaf and the fossil fuel industry a massive new customer base. Given this, it’s no surprise that Google will join the oil and gas industry at a major CCS conference in Houston. Last year, the tech giant announced that it’s helping move forward a first-of-its-kind project combining CCS and data centers. What is surprising is that Google chose a CCS project by agribusiness giant Archer-Daniels-Midland that leaked and threatened nearby drinking water, prompting a notice of violation from the Environmental Protection Agency. Following this disaster, members of Congress and over 150 groups from around the country called for a halt to all carbon dioxide injection wells. Exxon is not shy about this partnership with Big Tech, either. It claims AI data centers could account for 20% of the CCS market by 2050. Exxon is also touting its partnership with NextEra Energy on a massive 1.2GW plant in the Gulf — where Exxon is working to aggressively build out CCS infrastructure — to serve data centers. In New Mexico, regulators are working to fast-track carbon capture injection well approvals at the same time the tech industry is planning a 500-mile data center pipeline to transport gas to power Oracle’s Project Jupiter and other data centers stretching from Arizona to Texas. All while Oracle is touting a million-dollar investment into carbon capture research, no doubt to provide some cover for Jupiter’s projected 10 million tons of annual climate pollution. Tacking on Data Centers to CCS’s Long History of Failure While these promises are big on hype, CCS projects routinely fail to deliver on climate promises. They’re also facing significant financial headwinds, despite massive public subsidies. For years, the fossil fuel industry has falsely presented CCS as a “climate solution.” It purports to pull carbon dioxide from smokestacks or the air and inject it deep underground to lower carbon emissions. At first blush, the idea may sound plausible. What the fossil fuel industry doesn’t mention is that adding carbon capture to gas and coal plants increases emissions and costs. And it conveniently fails to mention that over 90% of all carbon dioxide captured in the U.S. is used to pump more oil. Now, data centers are starting to be built in oil fields, which will help the CCS and tech industries get around one of their major roadblocks: local opposition. Moreover, this arrangement will allow data centers to share in the profits from federal CCS subsidies, which could cost taxpayers hundreds of billions of dollars. Ultimately, carbon capture has done nothing for the climate. It’s only given license to Big Oil to continue burning fossil fuels. And that’s exactly what carbon capture will do for data centers. Tell Congress: End carbon capture subsidies! Data Centers + Carbon Capture Worsen Our Water Crisis Even without a massive data center and CCS expansion, communities across the country are struggling to protect existing water supplies. Forty-four states faced at least a moderate drought as of June 30 of this year. In the West, Lake Mead and Lake Powell, which collectively supply 40 million people with water, are facing unprecedented droughts. Now, enter data centers, which need massive amounts of water. By 2028, data centers may require as much water as 18.5 million households just for cooling the super-hot computers inside. But that’s just the tip of the iceberg. Because the vast majority of data centers run on fossil fuels, the water needed for energy generation makes up 71% of data centers’ water footprint. CCS projects increase the water usage at power plants by as much as 55%, which would compound the excessive water demands for data centers. CCS is also threatening the quality of our precious water supplies. Right now, the industry is pushing Congress to weaken protections for underground drinking water. artigo.texto: Oracle’s Collapse–$200 Billion In Data Center Shut Downs Oracle's Project Jupiter is just one casualty in a growing wave of blocked and delayed data center construction that threatens to destabilize the entire AI infrastructure boom, and the warning signs point far beyond one struggling company. This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them. Oracle (NYSE: ORCL | ORCL Price Prediction) is in trouble. Its Project Jupiter in New Mexico has been delayed, in part, by local resistance. It has begun to take legal action to stop payments to suppliers. According to Bloomberg, “Oracle Corp. is moving to shield itself from racking up expenses on a massive data center being built in New Mexico, adding a fresh wrinkle to a project beset by opposition and regulatory setbacks.” It is just the tip of the iceberg. Depending on who is counting, the data centers being blocked by local groups and politicians have a combined value of between $64 billion and $200 billion. Most recently, WSLS put the figure at $130 billion, but that is for construction blocked earlier this year. Earlier this week, Gizmodo put the figure at $200 billion. The Information says 500 data centers have been delayed this year. Oracle is a small player in the data center world, at least compared to the megacaps like Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) and the massive private companies led by OpenAI and Anthropic. Wall St. worries it lacks the balance sheet to handle major delays. And that may be true for much of the industry, eventually. Depending on who is counting, again, data center investments could reach $10 trillion in the next three years. That is more than double Germany’s annual GDP. Economists believe that most of US GDP growth over the same period will be AI-related. That may be revenue for the biggest AI players. It will also be the costs of data center buildouts. Nervousness already exists about whether data center building debt is risky. As Apollo recently told CNBC regarding credit default swaps, “Corporate debt issued by the giant cloud computing players powering the artificial intelligence boom is getting riskier.” There are two risks. One is that AI will not create explosive revenue growth. That means some data center capacity will go unused and not create revenue to pay for the infrastructure. The other is delays for data centers already designed and partially paid for. Oracle has been the AI warning signal. As worries about its future have risen and balance sheet risk across the industry has spread, Oracle’s stock is down 55% in the last year. Contrast that with Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), whose stock is flat over the same period. If there is real trouble in the AI world, Oracle’s stock will reset much further down. It has already proven that it is a downside risk warning signal. Project Jupiter may only be the start. Contact [email protected] for any questions or corrections.

artigo.texto: O governo federal segue em tensão quanto à regulamentação do Redata, programa para o desenvolvimento do setor de data centers no Brasil, que espera atrair investimentos da ordem de R$ 500 bilhões. A Fazenda, responsável pelo desenho do programa, tem pressionado para que o presidente Lula sancione o decreto regulamentador do Redata sem incluir o gás natural como fonte energética incentivada, mantendo assim a ênfase em fontes renováveis. A expectativa da pasta é que o decreto seja assinado na segunda (28/9). A possibilidade de incluir o gás natural no programa surgiu a partir de uma emenda de redação aprovada no Congresso Nacional durante a tramitação do projeto. Essa alteração abriu brecha para a entrada do gás natural como fonte complementar. O texto original do Redata priorizava energias renováveis e “limpas”, este último termo foi substituído por “de baixa emissão”. A disputa coloca em lados opostos o Ministério de Minas e Energia, publicamente favorável ao uso do gás natural no programa, e a Fazenda, contrária à inclusão. Na sexta-feira (25/9) à tarde, representantes do setor privado de gás natural se reuniram com interlocutores do Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços (MDIC) e para tentar destravar as conversas, que permanecem bloqueadas na Fazenda. Fontes que participaram da reunião afirmaram à agência eixos que, sem o gás natural no decreto, o Redata cria uma espécie de reserva de mercado para as energias renováveis, o que pode trazer desafios para projetos de data centers no Sul e Sudeste do país. Esses projetos poderiam demandar maiores investimentos em linhas de transmissão para trazer energia do Nordeste e acarretar encargos que recairiam sobre o consumidor final de energia. Disseram ainda que não houve abertura da Fazenda para diálogo com o setor. Uma das fontes citou com estranheza o fato da pasta “querer fazer política energética”. O fantasma da adicionalidade Dentro do governo, há ainda outra questão polêmica que ganhou força, que é a exigência de adicionalidade energética no decreto, que implica que os projetos beneficiados pelo Redata precisem contratar energia nova. É uma ideia que sempre reaparece. Da última vez surgiu na Medida Provisória 1304/2025, tornando obrigatória a contratação de energia gerada exclusivamente de usinas novas no modelo de autoprodução. Mas antes disso, esteve na MP 1307/2025, que tratava das Zonas de Processamento de Exportação, depois de ter sido discutida e rejeitada na legislação de hidrogênio de baixo carbono, por ser visto como um entrave à expansão do setor. Durante ato em Santa Catarina, na semana passada, o presidente Lula ressaltou que o Brasil tem enorme potencial para se tornar um polo de data centers, justamente por sua abundância de energia renovável. Ele reforçou, porém, que as empresas que vierem a se instalar no país terão que investir na construção de suas próprias usinas renováveis para abastecer seus centros. “Não vamos deixar que a energia produzida vá somente para o data center, quem quiser vir pra cá terá que investir na construção em energia renovável”, afirmou Lula.

artigo.texto: Advait Energy Signs Cell Supply Deal With HiTHIUM; Shares Fall 1.79% Authored By HDFC SKY | Published at: Sep 28, 2026 03:07 PM IST Advait Energy Transitions signs a 1 GWh cell supply agreement with HiTHIUM for its planned 2.5 GWh BESS assembly facility, while shares fall 1.79%. Open Free Demat Account Open Free Demat Account Mumbai, September 28: Advait Energy Transitions has entered into a Master Supply Agreement with HiTHIUM for the purchase of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells, covering cell supply of up to 1 GWh over the next year. Advait Energy Signs 1 GWh Battery Cell Supply Agreement According to the company’s exchange filing, the agreement was executed on September 18, 2026, with HiTHIUM, a global energy storage manufacturer and BloombergNEF Tier 1 supplier. Under the arrangement, HiTHIUM will supply 314 Ah LFP prismatic battery cells to Advait Battery Ecosystems Private Limited. The agreement is structured to support cell offtake of up to 1 GWh over the next year. The supply will be used for Advait’s upcoming cell-to-container Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) assembly facility. The arrangement is linked to Advait’s planned 2.5 GWh annual-capacity BESS assembly facility, which is being developed for utility-scale, commercial and industrial energy storage as well as renewable energy integration applications. Stock Market Snapshot The Advait Energy share price stood at ₹1,871.80 as of 2:28:37 PM IST on September 28, 2026, down ₹34.20 or 1.79% from the previous close. The stock traded lower during the session, while the company disclosed its battery cell supply arrangement with HiTHIUM. The announcement comes as Advait continues to build out its domestic BESS manufacturing and supply-chain capabilities. HiTHIUM Deal Supports Advait’s BESS Manufacturing Plans The company said the cell supply arrangement is intended to support the planned scale-up of its domestic BESS assembly operations. Advait’s facility is being developed with capabilities spanning cell sourcing, module and pack assembly, container integration and system commissioning. The company said the HiTHIUM agreement will provide a structured supply framework as the facility moves towards commercial production. The upcoming assembly capacity is aimed at applications across utility-scale energy storage, commercial and industrial users, and renewable energy integration. HiTHIUM will supply 314 Ah LFP prismatic cells under the agreement. The company is described in the release as a BloombergNEF Tier 1 global energy storage manufacturer supplying battery cells and energy storage systems across international markets. Advait Energy Expands Domestic Energy Storage Business Advait Energy Transitions is developing an integrated energy storage platform around its planned BESS manufacturing capabilities. The company is also building capabilities across battery module and pack assembly, container integration and related system commissioning. Its broader energy transition portfolio includes power transmission infrastructure, renewable energy, green hydrogen, electrolyser manufacturing, fuel cell manufacturing and clean energy EPC activities. About Advait Energy Transitions Advait Energy Transitions Limited, formerly known as Advait Infratech Limited, is an energy transition and infrastructure company based in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. The company operates across power transmission, renewable energy, BESS and other clean energy technologies. Its business portfolio includes battery energy storage manufacturing, green hydrogen projects, electrolyser manufacturing, fuel cells and clean energy infrastructure solutions. Conclusion The 1 GWh supply agreement with HiTHIUM gives Advait a defined cell supply framework for the next stage of its BESS manufacturing plans. The arrangement supports the company’s broader objective of developing domestic energy storage capabilities around its planned 2.5 GWh annual-capacity facility. The Advait Energy share price stood at ₹1,871.80 as of 2:28:37 PM IST on September 28, 2026, down ₹34.20 or 1.79% from the previous close. artigo.texto: The rapid expansion of data centers has become one of the most tangible expressions of the artificial intelligence revolution. But debate about their environmental, economic and social impact threatens their future development. And rightly so. Every cloud service and AI application depends on massive physical infrastructure that takes up land, consumes energy, uses water and requires ever-increasing investment. International experience suggests that as the data center industry scales up, tensions emerge. In Ireland, data centers accounted for 21% of the country’s electricity consumption in 2023 and could reach 32% this year. In the U.S., their share of demand is expected to triple from 4% in 2023 to a projected 12% by 2028. No surprise, then, that this is a source of growing political and public concern. A Gallup poll found that 71% of Americans oppose data center construction in their local community. Researchers at Cambridge University have identified what they call a “data heat island effect,” whereby large facilities can raise temperatures in surrounding areas. And a recent study by researchers from Yale and the University of Chicago found that the development of a new data center is associated with an increase in nearby housing prices. The question isn’t whether data centers are needed — they are — but how they are developed. What type of data centers do we need? And who will govern their expansion? Economic experience teaches a simple lesson: that proactive regulation is more effective than reactive intervention. And it’s certainly much better than no intervention at all. Having clear rules from the start makes it possible to separate responsible projects from unsustainable ones, align private incentives with public interests and ensure that investment and growth go hand in hand with protecting critical resources and communities. International experience is, again, instructive. Ireland tightened its rules only after data centers became a major source of pressure on the electricity grid. In the US, the state of New York has adopted a temporary moratorium, and a growing number of projects have faced delays or cancellation as local resistance intensified. The lesson could not be plainer: Failing to plan and regulate up front ends up being costlier and less effective. Spain is still a long way from facing that kind of pressure. And yet, our healthy economy and renewable capacity has sparked huge investor interest in building data centers. Current estimates of electricity demand for computing power run as high as 4 gigawatts by 2030, but requests and permits granted for this type of facility exceed that target several times over. We are approaching a tipping point, and we must act to stay ahead. In August, my government launched a public consultation on a new regulatory framework designed to do exactly that. The proposal starts from a straightforward principle: Access to the electricity grid is a scarce strategic asset and should not be held up by projects that lack credibility, viability or a meaningful contribution to the economy and society. Our proposal introduces energy- and water-efficiency standards. Data centers will have to disclose key performance indicators, letting us assess and compare their resource use and discourage waste. Any increase in electricity demand must also be accompanied by additional renewable capacity. The framework includes requirements to make sure that a significant portion of data center consumption is supported by newly built clean-energy projects. The regulation recognizes, too, that data centers are a strategic asset. In a world where Europe still relies heavily on non-European digital capabilities, the framework combines safeguards on how data is controlled — and how the infrastructure is managed — with incentives designed to expand Europe’s technology sector and strengthen the continent’s sovereignty. Our objective must be to trade in bytes, not in watts. The challenge is making sure the infrastructure expands in line with the capacity of the power system, that valuable energy resources are directed toward useful projects and that this all makes Europe less dependent technologically. The goal is not to slow down growth or constrain innovation. Quite the opposite: It is to ensure that they remain economically sustainable, and environmentally and socially fair. Countries that understand this will be the ones best positioned to lead the next phase of the digital economy. Pedro Sanchez is the prime minister of Spain. He wrote this for Bloomberg Opinion.

artigo.texto: Sodium-ion batteries have long promised a cheaper, safer alternative to the lithium-ion cells that power everything from phones to electric cars, but a new comprehensive review argues that artificial intelligence may finally be the key to unlocking their full potential. Writing in Discover Industrial Chemistry and Materials, Zhong Hu of South Dakota State University surveys how machine learning, generative AI and autonomous laboratories are transforming the discovery of cathodes, anodes and electrolytes for sodium-ion systems, replacing decades of slow, intuition-driven trial and error with data-driven, predictive design. The stakes are enormous: sodium is the Earth’s sixth most abundant element at roughly 2.6 percent of its crust, and unlike lithium, it allows manufacturers to use inexpensive aluminum current collectors on both electrodes, eliminating the costly copper foils required in lithium cells. The commercial case for sodium-ion technology is strengthening rapidly. Recent industrial breakthroughs between 2025 and the present have seen announced manufacturing capacities exceed hundreds of gigawatt-hours, with particularly aggressive deployment in China. Commercial electric-vehicle packs now achieve energy densities above 170 watt-hours per kilogram, while the technology’s inherent safety, thermal stability and strong low-temperature performance make it ideal for grid-scale energy storage, where cost per kilowatt-hour matters more than compact size. High-power sodium chemistries are also attracting interest for drones, portable electronics and robotic platforms that demand rapid charging at low cost. Yet sodium-ion batteries face stubborn material-level bottlenecks rooted in the element’s physics. The sodium ion is significantly larger than its lithium counterpart, with an ionic radius of 1.02 angstroms compared with 0.76 angstroms, leading to sluggish diffusion kinetics and substantial structural strain during repeated charging cycles. Layered oxide cathodes can undergo phase transitions and transition-metal migration that cause voltage fade, while hard carbon anodes suffer from low initial Coulombic efficiency and unstable interface formation. Alloy-type anodes based on tin, antimony and phosphorus promise theoretical capacities exceeding 1000 milliampere-hours per gram, but swell by more than 300 percent during sodiation, pulverizing particles and draining capacity. At high charging rates, non-uniform sodium deposition, dendrite growth and electrolyte decomposition compound these durability problems. The review identifies four critical knowledge gaps that have kept traditional research methods from closing the performance gap with lithium. First, the solid electrolyte interphase, the protective film that forms on the anode, remains a molecular black box in sodium systems because sodium-based interphase components dissolve far more readily than their lithium analogues, driving continuous electrolyte consumption. Second, predicting high-voltage degradation and phase transitions with density functional theory calculations is computationally prohibitive. Third, high-quality standardized datasets for sodium materials lag dramatically behind the lithium literature. Fourth, many machine learning models function as inscrutable black boxes, offering predictions without the physical insight researchers need to understand structure-property relationships. To overcome these obstacles, Hu argues, researchers are deploying an increasingly sophisticated AI toolbox. Graph neural networks represent crystal structures directly as atomic graphs, learning relationships between connectivity and properties without manual feature engineering, and have proven especially powerful for predicting formation energies, phase stability and electrode voltages in layered oxides. Deep neural networks serve as fast surrogate models for electrochemical performance metrics, while generative models such as generative adversarial networks, variational autoencoders and diffusion models can propose entirely new crystal structures that exist in no database. Inverse design flips the traditional workflow on its head: instead of making a material and measuring its properties, researchers specify desired performance targets and let the algorithm identify candidates likely to meet them. Each cathode family demands a different AI strategy. For layered transition-metal oxides, machine learning models trained on density functional theory data distinguish P2 from O3 structures using descriptors like sodium concentration and mixing entropy, and AI-guided screening has identified phase-stable iron-nickel-manganese-titanium high-entropy oxides with improved cycling retention and air stability. Polyanionic cathodes of the sodium superionic conductor type benefit from active-learning frameworks that slash computational costs while exploring thousands of compositions, with generative models coupled to quantum simulations finding candidates with volume changes below 4 percent. Prussian blue analogues, whose modular open frameworks are plagued by vacancy defects and structural water, are ideally suited to variational autoencoders and Gaussian process regression that optimize composition and suppress degradation mechanisms. On the anode side, machine learning is equally transformative. Ensemble methods such as XGBoost and random forests trained on biomass-derived datasets now predict reversible capacity and initial Coulombic efficiency from synthesis parameters, revealing how carbonization temperature tunes porosity and graphitic ordering in hard carbon. For alloy anodes, crystal-structure search algorithms combined with machine-learning-accelerated annealing identify thermodynamically stable sodium-alloy phases, while high-entropy alloy concepts redistribute sodiation-induced stress. Anode-free designs, in which sodium plates directly onto a bare current collector for maximum energy density, rely on AI to engineer artificial interphases

artigo.texto: NANTICOKE — Newport Twp. residents gathered Sunday at West Side Park in Nanticoke to begin rallying against a developer who seeks to build 15 data centers in the township. The meeting, organized through a Facebook event, served as a preliminary step to gather interested residents and supporters and voice their opposition to the project. The packed field house was standing room only that spilled out into the park. Brenda Grabowski, who helped organize the meeting and started the Facebook event, said she did so after going to the previous commissioners’ meeting looking for answers and receiving none. “I don’t know a lot about data centers; I’m learning myself now. But I want to know what’s going to happen in my backyard,” said Grabowski. Fern Leard, who is running to capture a seat in the state House 120th District, spoke at the meeting, telling residents, “This is where it starts.” Leard, who is not running to represent Newport Twp., said she showed up and spoke to show support. “The fact that you guys organized this so quickly is amazing,” said Leard. “It just showcases how when communities come together and work together we can get it done.” Newport commissioners were asked about a rumored data center coming to the township at a meeting earlier this month. In response, Township Manager Joe Hillian issued a prepared statement that left residents with more questions than answers. Hillian said a developer seeks to build three gas generation facilities and 15 closed-loop data centers — seven in the mixed-use zone and eight in the industrial zone. The township’s zoning ordinance, drafted earlier this year, allows data centers by right in mixed-use zoning districts and permits them in industrial districts. Derek Sutcliffe, who has been fighting data center development in Lackawanna County, urged residents to think about how these facilities will be powered and what that will do to their community. “You are not defeated,” Sutcliffe told residents. “Where you are in your process is the beginning. If you think you’re going to lose, you’re going to lose. Don’t think that. You can beat this.” The next Newport Twp. commissioners meeting is scheduled for 6 p.m. on Oct. 5.

artigo.texto: A proposed battery storage project in Hadley, Massachusetts, is nearing approval after a consultant concluded it should remain within state noise limits. Here's what to know According to the Daily Hampshire Gazette, board members were told at a Sept. 15 continued hearing that the proposed 5-megawatt battery energy storage system would meet the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection's noise policy. With the proposed mitigation in place, sound from the facility would stay below 34 A-weighted decibels at the property boundary, Marc C. Wallace, a vice president at Tech Environmental Inc. in Chelmsford, said. Wallace noted that the noise reduction kit would cut sound by 20 decibels and keep that level from extending beyond the lot lines, even during the quietest overnight conditions. Planned for a nearly 5-acre former gravel pit, the stand-alone system would use five energy storage containers and related equipment. Peter Forte, vice president of ZP Battery Devco, said the project would also include inverters, converters, and a gravel access road, and would connect to three-phase lines along Breckenridge Road, the Daily Hampshire Gazette reported. Grid-scale batteries can store electricity when it is plentiful and discharge it later when demand rises. In New England, that can help shift less-needed midday power into the more in-demand evening peak, potentially easing pressure on the grid during periods of heavy use and extreme weather. More background The project has already taken a long road to reach this stage. The Gazette reported that Hadley's Planning Board rejected the plans in 2024, halting the development and setting up a legal dispute over whether the town could block it. That denial led the developers to sue in Hampshire Superior Court, after which the board resumed reviewing a proposal nearly identical to the one it had rejected. A central issue in the dispute was the Dover Amendment, a Massachusetts law that can limit local zoning restrictions on certain land uses tied to public health, safety, and environmental goals. Local officials were weighing whether nearby residents would face an unreasonable burden from the battery system. Although insect sounds created substantial background noise during the study, the consultant said the project would still meet the state standard under the quietest overnight conditions. What's being done? The developer is relying on a noise reduction kit to address the Planning Board's biggest concern. If the board accepts that analysis, the project could move much closer to final approval. Forte said the project must comply with the state's noise policy at all times and that residents can bring complaints to the building commissioner. The system will be monitored remotely 24 hours a day. Board members closed the public hearing, so no further comment will be accepted, and indicated a review by the town attorney and a vote on conditions would take place Oct. 6 or 20. Where can I learn more? Battery storage proposals across the country face similar local scrutiny, even as some continue to win approvals. They cover neighborhood concerns, permitting fights, and major approvals and financing. • In Massachusetts, regulators approved a battery site near seniors' homes after neighbors won 100 conditions. • In Pike County, Indiana, regulators approved a massive energy storage system near a power plant. • In Arizona, developers financed the state's largest battery storage project as the state's market surged. artigo.texto: On September 10, 2026, Reuters reported that Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) plans to expand its global data center capacity to more than 38 gigawatts by 2032, more than tripling its current roughly 12-gigawatt footprint, according to Bloomberg News reporting that cited people familiar with the plans. Only about 2 gigawatts of Microsoft's current capacity is dedicated to AI-specific chips, a share the company expects to grow to roughly one-third of the much larger 38-gigawatt total by 2032, though Microsoft has not confirmed the target in any public filing or statement. Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) already has strong cloud demand to support a major expansion of its data center footprint. Azure and other cloud services revenue increased 43% year over year in fiscal Q4. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $59.3 billion for the quarter and $214.4 billion for fiscal 2026. Microsoft also said capacity constraints have limited its ability to satisfy some demand, so expanding from roughly 12 gigawatts toward the reported 38-gigawatt target could allow the company to capture cloud and AI business that its existing infrastructure cannot currently support. Microsoft's massive contracted backlog gives management substantial revenue visibility as it adds new computing capacity. Commercial remaining performance obligations increased 84% year over year to $678 billion, while Microsoft expects to recognize roughly 30% of that amount as revenue during the next 12 months. The large backlog gives Microsoft a significant pool of committed business that can help support the economics of its aggressive infrastructure expansion as new capacity comes online. Microsoft has already shown that it can add capacity quickly while securing long-term power for its expanding data center network. The company added another gigawatt of capacity in fiscal Q4 and remains on track to roughly double its overall capacity within two years. Microsoft has also signed a 20-year agreement with Constellation Energy linked to the restart of the 835-megawatt Three Mile Island Unit 1. It gives the firm another long-term electricity source as AI workloads drive sharply higher power requirements. Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT)'s data center expansion requires enormous capital commitments that could continue weighing on free cash flow. Microsoft expects more than $50 billion of capital expenditures in fiscal Q1 2027 and about $175 billion during calendar 2026 under its broader capex definition, which includes finance leases. Microsoft reported roughly $145 billion of capital expenditures in fiscal 2026, while cash additions to property and equipment totaled about $116 billion. Power availability and growing political resistance could make a 38-gigawatt network harder to build on schedule. Texas temporarily halted approvals for new data center grid connections as officials reviewed the industry's electricity and water demands. New York imposed a moratorium on large new data centers amid concerns about electricity costs. Microsoft needs to secure enormous amounts of power, land and regulatory approval across multiple jurisdictions as it more than triples its reported footprint. The 38-gigawatt figure remains a reported internal roadmap rather than formal Microsoft guidance. It adds uncertainty to the long-term investment case. Bloomberg reported the target through people familiar with Microsoft's plans. Reuters said Microsoft did not immediately comment on the figure. Multi-year construction timelines, changing customer demand and improvements in computing efficiency could alter how much physical capacity Microsoft ultimately needs. So investors should treat the 2032 target as a planning framework rather than a guaranteed outcome. Hedge Fund Sentiment Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT)'s hedge fund count slipped to 273 in the second quarter from 282 in the first, even as position value rose to $66.51 billion from $63.58 billion, according to Insider Monkey's database. Alphabet, which announced its own major data center expansion in Finland the same week, saw stronger conviction, with holders climbing to 275 from 265 and position value jumping to $93.74 billion from $72.41 billion. Conclusion Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT)'s reported plan to expand data center capacity from roughly 12 gigawatts to 38 gigawatts by 2032 shows the extraordinary demand that Azure and AI services continue to make. Azure's 43% growth, Microsoft's $678 billion commercial backlog and management's progress toward doubling capacity within two years give the company strong commercial support for further infrastructure investment. However, Microsoft must commit enormous amounts of capital, secure enough electricity, and navigate growing regulatory resistance to execute the roadmap. Investors should watch whether new capacity drives enough cloud revenue and cash flow to make attractive returns on the hundreds of billions of dollars Microsoft is committed to AI infrastructure. While we acknowledge the potential of MSFT as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. Presented at Energy Storage Canada Conference: The Storage Advantage, the annual awards celebrate leadership, innovation, research and achievement across Canada's energy storage industry. This year's recipients reflect the breadth of work underway to strengthen electricity systems, introduce new technologies and applications, improve grid reliability and support the continued growth of energy storage across the country. Energy Storage Canada's awards program is technology agnostic and recognizes accomplishments from across the sector, including generators, developers, utilities, regulators, researchers, manufacturers and technology and service providers. The recognized project leveraged AI-driven platforms to coordinate stationary energy storage and electric vehicles as a single, grid-aware flexible resource, including one of Canada's first AI-driven, multi-manufacturer electric vehicle demand-response events. Mohamad Shamelstein demonstrated how energy storage assets supporting large data centres can provide services to the broader electricity system without compromising essential IT infrastructure. Landmark Application of Energy Storage Award: AlumaPower Corporation This award recognizes a new energy storage technology or an innovative application of an existing technology. AlumaPower was honoured for its off-grid microgrid demonstration using solid recycled aluminum, which demonstrated a pathway beyond the traditional single-use model of aluminum-air energy storage. Energy Storage Milestone Award: NextStar Energy This award recognizes a company or organization for achieving a significant milestone in energy storage development, with a clear path toward realizing its broader benefits. Energy Storage Trailblazer Award, In Memoriam: Jim Fonger This award recognizes an individual selected by ESC's Board of Directors who demonstrated exceptional leadership and contributed to the development of energy storage above and beyond the promotion of their organization. artigo.texto: Samsung SDI's (006400.KS) lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for energy storage systems (ESS) have passed a global fire safety test. The company said on Sept. 28 that its integrated ESS product, the SBB 2.0, met all evaluation criteria in a large-scale fire test conducted by UL Solutions, a global safety certification body. The SBB 2.0 is the first Samsung SDI energy storage solution to use LFP batteries. It will be produced at StarPlus Energy (SPE), the company's joint venture with Stellantis in Indiana. The test involved deliberately igniting a fire inside an SBB 2.0 container and checking whether the flames spread to adjacent containers. No fire spread occurred, and there was no gas venting, explosion or overheating. Samsung SDI attributed the result to the structural advantages of its prismatic batteries and to technology built up over many years. In July, the company also passed a large-scale fire test and won certification for an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) unit equipped with nickel-cobalt-manganese batteries. "Prismatic cells use a rigid aluminum can structure that withstands heat, impact and pressure, and they allow various safety devices to be added, which makes them superior to batteries in other form factors," a Samsung SDI official said.

artigo.texto: OCP, Envision power up first phase of BESS at Morocco mining site OCP Green Energy, a subsidiary of Morocco’s OCP Group, signed a contract in 2025 with Chinese technology supplier Envision Energy to supply and commission a storage system based on LFP (lithium iron phosphate) technology. OCP Green Energy, the OCP Group subsidiary dedicated to generating and storing electricity from renewable sources, has installed its first BESS (Phase I) at the Benguerir mining site in Morocco. This comes just a few months after Phase I of OCP Green Energy’s solar PV program entered service, with a total capacity of 202 MWp across the solar plants at Benguerir (67 MWp), Foum Tizi (30 MWp) and Oulad Farès in Khouribga (105 MWp), OCP said in a press release. OCP Green Energy signed a contract in 2025 with Chinese technology supplier Envision Energy to supply and commission a storage system based on LFP (lithium iron phosphate) technology. With a capacity of 25 MW / 125 MWh, equivalent to five hours of storage, the system is coupled with the existing solar plant at the Benguerir mining site. This investment of close to 170 million dirhams (approximately USD 17.5 million) covered the acquisition of BESS equipment and batteries, together with the full scope of integration works, including civil and electrical engineering, as well as studies and project management, OCP said. The project also benefits from USD 20 million in financing from the Clean Technology Fund (CTF), a program led by the African Development Bank. “As we announced last year when our first solar PV projects were commissioned, storage is the natural extension of our energy strategy,” Omar Kadir, General Manager of OCP Green Energy, said. “It allows us to reconcile the variable output of renewable energy with the continuous needs of our industrial platforms, while strengthening the reliability of our energy supply.” Envision Energy said that it provided the full storage system and led the commissioning work, integrating the BESS with the site's solar generation, grid conditions and industrial load profile. “The successful energisation of Morocco’s first large-scale battery storage project demonstrates the reliability, flexibility and cost-effectiveness of integrated renewable-plus-storage solutions in industrial applications,” said John Lee, General Manager of Envision Energy for the Middle East and Africa, according to a press release issued by Envision.

artigo.texto: The rapid expansion of data centers has become one of the most tangible expressions of the artificial intelligence revolution. But debate about their environmental, economic and social impact threatens their future development. And rightly so. Every cloud service and AI application depends on massive physical infrastructure that takes up land, consumes energy, uses water and requires ever-increasing investment. International experience suggests that as the data center industry scales up, tensions emerge. In Ireland, data centers accounted for 21% of the country’s electricity consumption in 2023 and could reach 32% this year. In the U.S., their share of demand is expected to triple from 4% in 2023 to a projected 12% by 2028. No surprise, then, that this is a source of growing political and public concern. A Gallup poll found that 71% of Americans oppose data center construction in their local community. Researchers at Cambridge University have identified what they call a “data heat island effect,” whereby large facilities can raise temperatures in surrounding areas. And a recent study by researchers from Yale and the University of Chicago found that the development of a new data center is associated with an increase in nearby housing prices. The question isn’t whether data centers are needed — they are — but how they are developed. What type of data centers do we need? And who will govern their expansion? Economic experience teaches a simple lesson: that proactive regulation is more effective than reactive intervention. And it’s certainly much better than no intervention at all. Having clear rules from the start makes it possible to separate responsible projects from unsustainable ones, align private incentives with public interests and ensure that investment and growth go hand in hand with protecting critical resources and communities. International experience is, again, instructive. Ireland tightened its rules only after data centers became a major source of pressure on the electricity grid. In the US, the state of New York has adopted a temporary moratorium, and a growing number of projects have faced delays or cancellation as local resistance intensified. The lesson could not be plainer: Failing to plan and regulate up front ends up being costlier and less effective. Spain is still a long way from facing that kind of pressure. And yet, our healthy economy and renewable capacity has sparked huge investor interest in building data centers. Current estimates of electricity demand for computing power run as high as 4 gigawatts by 2030, but requests and permits granted for this type of facility exceed that target several times over. We are approaching a tipping point, and we must act to stay ahead. In August, my government launched a public consultation on a new regulatory framework designed to do exactly that. The proposal starts from a straightforward principle: Access to the electricity grid is a scarce strategic asset and should not be held up by projects that lack credibility, viability or a meaningful contribution to the economy and society. Our proposal introduces energy- and water-efficiency standards. Data centers will have to disclose key performance indicators, letting us assess and compare their resource use and discourage waste. Any increase in electricity demand must also be accompanied by additional renewable capacity. The framework includes requirements to make sure that a significant portion of data center consumption is supported by newly built clean-energy projects. The regulation recognizes, too, that data centers are a strategic asset. In a world where Europe still relies heavily on non-European digital capabilities, the framework combines safeguards on how data is controlled — and how the infrastructure is managed — with incentives designed to expand Europe’s technology sector and strengthen the continent’s sovereignty. Our objective must be to trade in bytes, not in watts. The challenge is making sure the infrastructure expands in line with the capacity of the power system, that valuable energy resources are directed toward useful projects and that this all makes Europe less dependent technologically. The goal is not to slow down growth or constrain innovation. Quite the opposite: It is to ensure that they remain economically sustainable, and environmentally and socially fair. Countries that understand this will be the ones best positioned to lead the next phase of the digital economy. Pedro Sanchez is the prime minister of Spain. He wrote this for Bloomberg Opinion.

artigo.texto: A corrida pela supremacia da inteligência artificial está prestes a abandonar a superfície do planeta. A Google está prestes a enviar o primeiro centro de dados experimental para o espaço já no dia 1 de Outubro, marcando o passo inicial do ambicioso Projeto Suncatcher. Este lançamento será feito a bordo de um foguetão Falcon 9, cimentando uma fase de testes depois de a Google e SpaceX terem criado uma aliança para construir data centers no espaço. O objectivo principal passa por validar a viabilidade de colocar infraestruturas de alto desempenho fora do nosso planeta. O satélite de testes, baptizado MVP, tem aproximadamente o tamanho de um frigorífico e foi desenvolvido em parceria com a Planet Labs. No seu interior, a máquina esconde quatro aceleradores TPU desenhados especificamente pela gigante tecnológica para treinar modelos complexos. Estes componentes são alimentados por painéis solares capazes de gerar cerca de um kilowatt de energia. Trata-se de uma capacidade modesta, suficiente apenas para ligar um microondas doméstico, mas que serve de prova de conceito para um futuro onde a luz solar não filtrada poderá sustentar operações de maior dimensão, segundo o site Ars Technica. Os desafios da computação no cosmos Transferir o processamento de dados para o vácuo espacial resolve vários problemas terrestres, como o consumo excessivo de água e a sobrecarga das redes eléctricas. No entanto, o ambiente orbital traz obstáculos formidáveis. O lixo espacial ameaça colidir a altas velocidades com os equipamentos, enquanto a radiação cósmica pode destruir a electrónica sensível. O arrefecimento constitui talvez a barreira mais imediata. Actualmente, os engenheiros limitam o funcionamento dos chips a períodos de apenas 15 minutos, após os quais os sistemas têm de ser desligados para dissipar o calor acumulado. Apesar destas adversidades técnicas, os planos da empresa a longo prazo são colossais. A estratégia passa por lançar mais dois satélites no próximo ano, escalando posteriormente para uma constelação de 80 unidades interligadas por lasers de alta velocidade. Enquanto a Europa perde terreno para os EUA na corrida global aos centros de dados tradicionais, as empresas norte-americanas começam já a disputar o domínio da infra-estrutura espacial. A Google estima que, em meados da década de 2030, os investimentos em instalações orbitais igualem os montantes aplicados em solo firme. Este primeiro protótipo deverá permanecer em órbita durante um período máximo de seis anos antes de reentrar na atmosfera e arder por completo. A manutenção humana nestas condições é impossível, o que obriga a uma fiabilidade extrema dos componentes. Embora os executivos da marca admitam que uma rede totalmente operacional ainda demore mais de uma década a concretizar-se, este lançamento inaugural prova que a ficção científica está a transformar-se rapidamente em engenharia real.

artigo.texto: B2U Storage Solutions and LG Energy Solution Partner to Repurpose Batteries B2U Storage Solutions and LG Energy Solution announce a strategic partnership giving B2U priority access to the South Korean firm's batteries to develop large-scale stationary storage solutions in the United States. B2U Storage Solutions and LG Energy Solution have announced a strategic partnership aimed at developing battery energy storage system (BESS) solutions across the United States. The agreement gives B2U Storage Solutions priority access to LG Energy Solution's battery capacity and allows both companies to jointly explore business opportunities in this market. The partners plan to use B2U Storage Solutions' patented repurposing technologies to give LG Energy Solution batteries a second life in grid-scale storage applications. Extending battery life before recycling The joint initiative aims to extend batteries' service life through repurposing, keeping them in operation longer while deferring the costs and environmental impacts associated with recycling. Once integrated into BESS systems, these batteries could continue generating value for several years, according to both companies. "This partnership advances our strategy to extend the value of our batteries beyond their original applications," said Seung Tak Joo, leader of the Energy as a Service (EaaS) business department at LG Energy Solution. "By repurposing batteries for grid-scale energy storage, we can lengthen their useful life and create new growth opportunities that deliver long-term economic returns." Company LG Energy Solution: company profile Targeting data centers and grid operators The partnership intends to make BESS more accessible by offering cost-competitive storage solutions to utilities, energy storage developers, and large commercial energy users, including data centers. Both companies are working to expand energy storage infrastructure and strengthen the stability of the U.S. electrical grid by leveraging repurposed batteries, with the ambition of delivering storage capacity measured in gigawatt-hours. "We are committed to driving down the cost of energy storage by unlocking the inherent value of repurposed batteries. The alliance unites proven technology with a reliable supply of batteries, making energy storage more cost-effective and bankable," said Freeman Hall, founder and chief executive officer of B2U Storage Solutions. A response to mounting pressure on the U.S. grid The announcement comes as rising electricity demand and the growing integration of intermittent renewable energy sources place increasing pressure on the U.S. electrical grid.
