artigo.texto: Trinity Airways (091810) will work with NH Investment & Securities to prepare for the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). Trinity Airways said on the 28th that it signed a memorandum of understanding on CORSIA and emissions trading with NH Investment & Securities on the 21st at Sono Trinity Commons in Seoul's Gangseo District. It is the first such agreement between a Korean airline and a financial firm in the areas of CORSIA and emissions trading. The two companies plan to cooperate on exchanging information and building a joint response system for CORSIA and the domestic greenhouse gas emissions market and related policies, jointly pursuing emissions credit projects, and carrying out activities to develop the carbon market. As a first step toward meeting its CORSIA offset obligations, Trinity Airways purchased 20,000 tons of CORSIA-eligible carbon credits and signed a contract to retire them, becoming the first Korean airline to do so. The company plans to buy additional eligible credits by the end of this year, gradually securing more than 10% of the volume it must offset by January 2028. "Through this partnership with NH Investment & Securities, we have laid the groundwork to secure emissions credits at home and abroad on a stable basis and to respond systematically to carbon regulations," said Seo Dong-bin, head of management support at Trinity Airways. "We will strengthen our capabilities in sourcing and managing credits and build an efficient response system from a medium- to long-term perspective."

artigo.texto: Hanoi (VNA) – Hanoi is establishing an inter-agency mechanism to coordinate greenhouse gas inventories, emissions reduction and participation in the carbon market, with departments assigned specific tasks in emissions data, carbon-credit projects, financial management, technology, and benefit-sharing mechanisms. Under a decision of the municipal People’s Committee on establishing an inter-agency working group, departments and agencies are responsible for identifying facilities subject to greenhouse gas inventories, developing emissions-reduction plans and studying projects capable of generating carbon credits. These are considered key steps towards the city’s participation in the carbon market. The Department of Agriculture and Environment is responsible for compiling greenhouse gas emissions inventory data in the city, serving the development of national climate change reports and implementation of the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) and Net Zero 2050 targets. It will also update the list of facilities subject to inventories and consolidate results of inventory inspections and emissions-reduction plans for 2026-2030. The department will study and propose a list of emissions-reduction and potential carbon-credit projects in areas including waste treatment and methane recovery, wastewater, low-emission agriculture, forestry and urban greenery, wetlands and circular agricultural economy. This is a group of sectors capable of generating quantifiable emissions reductions, providing a basis for developing carbon credits. From energy, industry to transport and construction The municipal Department of Industry and Trade will manage data on energy consumption, production, energy efficiency and emissions intensity, and review facilities subject to inventories, allowance allocation and participation in the carbon market pilot. It will also guide businesses in developing emissions baselines in energy saving, rooftop solar power, clean electricity, waste-heat recovery, fuel switching and technological innovation, while identifying potential carbon-credit projects. Meanwhile, the municipal Department of Construction will manage emissions related to construction, buildings, urban infrastructure, housing and transport. It will develop emissions data on construction materials, buildings, lighting, air conditioning, water supply and drainage, demolition and construction waste, as well as vehicles, fuels and passenger and freight transport, and electric vehicles. The department will quantify emissions reductions from switching buses and taxis to clean energy, developing urban railways, restricting high-emission vehicles and promoting public transport. It will also review potential carbon-credit sources from energy savings in buildings, replacement of cooling equipment, smart lighting, gas recovery at wastewater treatment facilities and the use of low-emission materials. Finance and technology emerge as two critical links The municipal Department of Finance is also tasked with handling financial issues related to allowances and carbon credits, including revenues from credit transfers and budgets for purchasing allowances and credits, and accounting for assets and property rights arising from carbon credits. It will also study approval procedures for credit generating projects using public assets, the State budget and city resources, while clarifying credit ownership, partner selection and principles for sharing revenues and benefits from credits generated from public land, forests, greenery, water surfaces, public works, State data and infrastructure managed by State-owned enterprises or public service units. Meanwhile, the municipal Department of Science and Technology will provide the technological foundation, covering standards, measurement, innovation, digital transformation, and data infrastructure. It will coordinate the development of digital platforms and online databases on greenhouse gases and carbon credits, while researching sensor-based emissions monitoring and advanced calculation technologies. Notably, the healthcare sector has also been included in the emissions reduction and the carbon credit development mechanism. The municipal Department of Health will review hospitals, healthcare and pharmaceutical facilities with significant energy use, refrigerant consumption, waste, wastewater or greenhouse gas emissions, and develop emissions reduction plans while promoting energy efficiency, green procurement and green healthcare facilities. It will also identify programmes and projects with carbon-credit potential, clarifying funding sources, assets used, ownership of emissions reduction results, credit rights and benefit-sharing mechanisms. The division of responsibilities will establish links among emissions data, measurement, reporting and verification, finance, ownership and data infrastructure, laying the foundation for Hanoi to gradually develop its carbon market ecosystem./.

artigo.texto: Hobart residents opposing the Amazon Web Services data center project are pursuing a legal strategy to hopefully hit the reset button on the city’s site plan approval process. The plaintiff’s petition, filed in Lake Superior Court, seeks injunctive relief over procedural matters involving the city’s plat and zoning approval process. However, the lawsuit experienced another delay when one of the plaintiff’s attorneys was unable to make a September 22 court appearance due to personal reasons, according to Hobart resident Barbara Koteles. Koteles is one of the plaintiffs in the case and a resident of the Eagle Creek subdivision, which is located directly across the street for the data center along 61st Avenue. An attorney conference is scheduled for Sept. 30. Koteles is joined in the complaint by fellow Hobart residents Joe Conn, Angelita Soriano and Albina Venegas-Roman. The complaint, filed against the Hobart Plan Commission and the Hobart Common Council, seeks a preliminary injunction to nullify a fill permit allowing mass grading on the property, according to court documents. Earlier this year, Hobart Plan Commission voted to treat the project’s site plan application as an application for a fill permit, the court filing states. Furthermore, “the Plan Commission voted (without findings of fact) to approve the morphed fill permit for mass construction grading activities in preparation for the project …”. The plaintiffs are challenging the fill permit solely on legal grounds, contending that the Plan Commission had no power to authorize it because it failed to provide all of the information required for a such an application nor did it produce the required findings of fact required for issuance of the permit. In series of court filings over the past several months, including motions by the city to dismiss the case, the matter reached a possible ruling on September 22. But as the case has dragged out in court, the city of Hobart has allowed grading and fill work on the 723-acre site to proceed. The Plan Commission granted the data center preliminary plat approval at a highly-charged five-hour meeting in May, but tabled final plat approval at its September 4 meeting. Final plat approval concerns two separate parcels of land. One area is 555-acre parcel, located south of 61st, east of Colorado Street and north of 69th Avenue, known as Hobart Tech Park and is owned by Amazon Web Services. The other parcel, described as the Ewen Farm property, encompasses 168 acres and is located southeast of 61st and Arizona Street. That parcel will be leased by Amazon Web Services from the current owner Meanwhile, the plaintiffs are hopeful that their legal strategy can turn back the clock and re-start the plat approval process, as well as reexamine the site plan altogether. By seeking to invalidate the fill permit, which concerns only grading of the land, the plaintiffs hope they can win new concessions, such as air and truck traffic monitoring, if not permanently halt the project. Koteles said that a judge’s order to re-start the planning process could trigger a review of the community benefits agreement signed between Amazon and the city of Hobart. She also hoped the city would develop a comprehensive ordinance governing data center development and operations. “The ordinances the city has passed, such as the one involving noise, have been done rather piecemeal,” Koteles said. She added that there has not been so much work done on the site yet, primarily grading of the land, over which the project could not be reasonably halted without a detrimental financial impact to either Amazon or the city. The plaintiffs also contend in the court filing that the data center development is negatively impacting their property values (within Eagle Creek), and will do so in the future. The city argues in court documents that the plaintiffs have failed to meet the requirements for a preliminary injunction. “I wish it (the data center) was just half the size and farther away from residents,” Koteles said. “I’ve been saying that from day one, and if that were the case it wouldn’t even be an issue.” Soriano said she is concerned about air quality in the neighborhood from the ongoing site work. “We have asked the city to measure particulate matter and monitor the air quality to make sure that all the dust blowing around is not harmful to residents,” she said, adding that she received a portable air purifier and gift cards for car washes from Amazon. The city is already spending direct payments from Amazon, having granted tax abatement on the development. Hobart Mayor Josh Huddelston explained that the city negotiated a plan for direct payments, thus granting Amazon a 35-year tax abatement on personal property (equipment on site) and a 10-year abatement on real property (buildings). The city has already received $47 million, with another $10 million arriving in September, according to Huddleston. He expects a $45 million payment in-hand by the end of 2026, with a $43 million coming in 2027. The city will receive approximately $40 million in both 2028 and 2029 and approximately $52 million in 2030 when the project is expected to be completed. Then, Hobart will receive approximately $52 million per year over the next 35 years. The data center will have 26 buildings spread out across the two sites, with six buildings at the 61st Avenue location and 20 at the Colorado Street location. Amazon is planning 170 emergency backup diesel generators at the location on 61st, and 612 emergency backup generators along Colorado, enabling a combined power capacity of 2,119 megawatts. Attempts to reach Hobart City Attorney Heather McCarthy by phone at the city’s Law Department on Thursday and Friday for comment were unsuccessful. Jim Masters is a freelance reporter for the Post-Tribune.

artigo.texto: Brasil amplia infraestrutura de inteligência artificial enquanto gigantes da tecnologia aceleram construção de data centers pelo mundo Por Sandro Felix Publicado em 27/09/26 às 07:24 A corrida pela inteligência artificial está transformando a infraestrutura digital global, com investimentos bilionários em data centers, chips especializados e energia elétrica. No Brasil, novos projetos buscam ampliar a capacidade de processamento e reduzir a dependência de estruturas instaladas no exterior, enquanto Estados Unidos, China e países europeus disputam espaço na expansão dessa tecnologia. A mudança vai muito além dos chatbots. Para treinar e operar modelos avançados de IA, empresas precisam de instalações capazes de abrigar milhares de processadores, sistemas de refrigeração e redes de alta velocidade. Quanto maior a demanda por serviços como ChatGPT, Gemini e Copilot, maior a necessidade de infraestrutura para sustentar essas operações. O Brasil participa desse movimento com projetos concentrados principalmente nas regiões Sudeste, Sul e Nordeste. A disponibilidade de energia renovável, a conectividade internacional e a possibilidade de atender empresas locais estão entre os fatores que atraem investimentos. Brasil já ultrapassa 1 GW de infraestrutura de data centers O mercado brasileiro atingiu 1 gigawatt (GW) de capacidade de TI comissionada no primeiro trimestre de 2026, segundo dados da datacenterHawk divulgados pela Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC). O indicador considera a capacidade de equipamentos de tecnologia já comissionada e não deve ser confundido com a potência total anunciada para empreendimentos ainda em construção. Outro levantamento, realizado pela consultoria JLL e divulgado pela Exame em 16 de setembro, apontou 706 megawatts (MW) de capacidade instalada no primeiro semestre, com previsão de entrega de mais 134 MW até dezembro. As diferenças entre os números refletem metodologias e recortes distintos de acompanhamento do setor. O crescimento ocorre em um mercado que já concentra aproximadamente 48% da capacidade instalada de data centers da América Latina, conforme relatório publicado pelo GRI Institute em julho. Entretanto, nem toda essa infraestrutura é dedicada à inteligência artificial. Parte dos equipamentos atende serviços tradicionais de nuvem, armazenamento, aplicações corporativas e plataformas digitais. Ceará receberá data center do TikTok com investimento superior a R$ 200 bilhões Um dos maiores empreendimentos anunciados no país está no Complexo Industrial e Portuário do Pecém, no Ceará. O TikTok confirmou um investimento estimado em mais de R$ 200 bilhões para instalar seu primeiro data center na América Latina, com início da operação previsto para 2027. O projeto envolve a Omnia, operadora de data centers do grupo Pátria Investimentos, e a Casa dos Ventos, responsável pela parceria energética. Do investimento anunciado, R$ 108 bilhões estão previstos para equipamentos de alta tecnologia até 2035, enquanto o restante contempla expansões e atualizações ao longo dos anos seguintes. A primeira etapa prevê aproximadamente 200 MW de capacidade de TI e demanda energética próxima de 300 MW. A expansão poderá levar o complexo a uma potência de até 900 MW, conforme informações divulgadas sobre o empreendimento. A empresa afirma que a instalação utilizará energia renovável proveniente de novos parques eólicos dedicados ao projeto. O sistema de refrigeração terá circuito fechado, com recirculação de água e resfriamento por ar. Embora a instalação represente uma expansão expressiva da infraestrutura digital brasileira, não se trata de uma confirmação de que toda sua capacidade será destinada ao treinamento de modelos de IA. O complexo foi anunciado para atender operações do TikTok. Rio Grande do Sul e Rio de Janeiro apostam em grandes complexos de IA No Rio Grande do Sul, a Scala Data Centers desenvolve o projeto Scala AI City, em Eldorado do Sul, na Região Metropolitana de Porto Alegre. A primeira fase prevê investimento de R$ 3 bilhões e capacidade de 54 MW, com infraestrutura voltada ao processamento de inteligência artificial. O empreendimento foi concebido para permitir ampliações conforme a demanda e a viabilidade das próximas etapas. Em maio de 2026, o projeto avançava na elaboração do plano de negócios e na preparação para o licenciamento, segundo informações divulgadas pela GaúchaZH. A proposta de longo prazo contempla a formação de uma cidade de data centers, mas as dimensões futuras dependem da concretização das expansões planejadas. O Rio de Janeiro também participa dessa disputa com o Rio AI City, da Elea Data Centers, que combina infraestrutura existente com planos de ampliação voltados à computação de alto desempenho. Em São Paulo, a concentração de clientes corporativos e de infraestrutura de conectividade continua atraindo operadores. A Scala mantém operações e projetos em Barueri, Campinas e Jundiaí, enquanto a Tecto, do grupo V.tal, anunciou um empreendimento de 200 MW em Santana de Parnaíba. Estados Unidos concentram megaprojetos de IA Fora do Brasil, os Estados Unidos continuam no centro da expansão das instalações destinadas aos modelos mais avançados de inteligência artificial. O projeto Stargate, liderado pela OpenAI em parceria com outras empresas, tem como objetivo desenvolver uma ampla rede de infraestrutura computacional no país. Em abril de 2026, a OpenAI informou que havia superado o marco de 10 GW de capacidade de infraestrutura assegurada, inicialmente estabelecido para 2029. Segundo a companhia, mais de 3 GW foram adicionados nos 90 dias anteriores ao anúncio. O número representa compromissos de capacidade e não significa que toda essa potência já esteja em funcionamento. Entre os locais associados à expansão estão Abilene, no Texas, e outros campi norte-americanos desenvolvidos por diferentes operadores. artigo.texto: O comunicado declarava: Para acelerar o processo de transformação digital na garantia da ordem e segurança do trânsito, em 20 de março de 2026, o Primeiro-Ministro emitiu a Decisão nº 456/QD-TTg aprovando o Projeto de construção de um Centro de Dados para gerenciar, monitorar, lidar com infrações e operar o trânsito no período de 2026 a 2030, com uma visão para 2050 (o Projeto). Finalizar o Plano de Implementação do Projeto do Centro de Dados de Tráfego antes de 28 de setembro. (Inspeção) - O Gabinete do Governo emitiu o documento nº 498/TB-VPCP, datado de 25 de setembro de 2026, anunciando as conclusões do Vice-Primeiro-Ministro Pham Gia Tuc na reunião de revisão do Projeto de Resolução do Governo que promulga o Plano de implementação da Resolução nº 05-NQ/DU, datada de 12 de junho de 2026, do Comitê do Partido do Governo, sobre a aplicação de mecanismos e políticas para implementar o Projeto de construção de um centro de dados para gerenciamento, monitoramento, tratamento de violações e operação de tráfego no período de 2026 a 2030, com uma visão para 2050. Estas são tarefas importantes e urgentes que precisam ser implementadas rapidamente para contribuir com a modernização antecipada do monitoramento e gerenciamento de tráfego. Portanto, em 12 de junho de 2026, o Comitê do Partido do Governo emitiu a Resolução nº 05-NQ/DU, que determina a implementação de diversas soluções para a execução do Projeto. Ao longo do último período, o Ministério da Segurança Pública assumiu a liderança proativa e coordenou com ministérios, setores, localidades e unidades o desenvolvimento do plano do Governo para implementar a Resolução 05-NQ/DU; e coordenou com o Gabinete do Governo a implementação dos procedimentos de reporte ao Governo, em conformidade com o regulamento interno do Governo. Implementação das tarefas do Projeto de Garantia da Qualidade e Interconexão Síncrona Para agilizar a publicação do Plano de Governo, o Vice-Primeiro-Ministro Pham Gia Tuc solicitou ao Ministério da Segurança Pública que coordenasse com o Gabinete do Governo a revisão e finalização da minuta da Resolução Governamental, e que a apresentasse ao Primeiro-Ministro para publicação antes de 28 de setembro de 2026. Durante a implementação do Projeto, o Ministério da Segurança Pública é o órgão permanente responsável, coordenando-se com ministérios, agências e localidades para definir cada item de trabalho, cada unidade responsável pela implementação e atribuir claramente cada tarefa a uma unidade específica, com a coordenação das agências relevantes; cada agência deve implementar proativamente as tarefas de acordo com a urgência do Projeto. Ministérios, setores e localidades devem implementar as tarefas do Projeto, garantindo o pleno cumprimento dos procedimentos e regulamentos legais para cada projeto de investimento, assegurando a qualidade, a sincronização e interconexão dos sistemas, a segurança, a eficiência e evitando a duplicação de tarefas; e prevenindo o desperdício e a corrupção. artigo.texto: O relatório ‘The AI Datacenter Study – Part 1: The Global Build-out Race’, desta consultora, conclui que a capacidade global instalada de data centers deve quadruplicar, passando de 88 , em 2025, para até 340 GW em 2035. O estudo, que analisa a evolução da capacidade dos data centers, a procura de energia, a actividade de investimento e conta com entrevistas a 70 decisores europeus, prevê que as cargas de trabalho de IA nos data centers aumentem dos actuais 20 para quase 60% até 2035. Por outro lado, estima que a quota da Europa na capacidade global instalada de data centers diminua de aproximadamente 13 para cerca de 10% até 2030. Pedro Galhardas, managing partner da Roland Berger Portugal, explica à businessIT que esta redução «é, acima de tudo, um sinal de perda de competitividade numa economia cada vez mais impulsionada pela inteligência artificial». Segundo o responsável, «a capacidade computacional está a tornar-se um activo estratégico e as regiões que lideram o investimento em infraestrutura digital vão estar mais bem posicionadas para captar inovação, talento e crescimento económico». Sobre o impacto para as empresas europeias, Pedro Galhardas salienta que «poderá traduzir-se numa maior dependência de infraestruturas externas e numa menor capacidade de acompanhar o ritmo de desenvolvimento de soluções de IA. Mais do que uma questão tecnológica, trata-se de uma questão de soberania digital e de capacidade para capturar os benefícios económicos da próxima vaga de transformação digital». Portugal pode ser excepção, mas … O managing partner destaca que Portugal se encontra numa posição «particularmente interessante dentro do panorama europeu» e esclarece que o País «combina uma localização geográfica estratégica, uma forte aposta em energias renováveis e projectos de grande dimensão, como Sines, identificado no estudo como um dos mais relevantes actualmente em desenvolvimento na Europa». No entanto, deixa um alerta: «Os desafios identificados pelo estudo são igualmente relevantes para Portugal. O acesso à rede eléctrica, os processos de licenciamento e a disponibilidade energética serão factores decisivos para determinar a capacidade do País em converter o interesse dos investidores em projectos concretizados. A oportunidade existe, mas dependerá da rapidez com que estes obstáculos forem ultrapassados». Assim, realça algumas medidas que devem ser adoptadas a nível europeu e nacional, para colmatar as lacunas existentes e que não passam apenas por «incentivos financeiros». É por isso que identifica que «as prioridades devem passar por acelerar o desenvolvimento da infraestrutura energética, simplificar os processos de licenciamento e criar um enquadramento regulatório mais previsível e favorável ao investimento». Isto porque, «num contexto em que a inteligência artificial será um dos principais motores de crescimento económico, a capacidade de construir infraestrutura digital de forma rápida e eficiente será um factor determinante para a competitividade europeia».

artigo.texto: Many gather to discuss proposed Newport Township data centers NANTICOKE — A standing-room crowd filled the hall at West Side Park Sunday as Newport Township residents gathered to learn more about proposed data center development and hear from activists, residents, and others who have been following similar projects across Northeast Pennsylvania. The roughly hourlong community meeting came less than two weeks after residents learned that zoning permits had been issued for 15 data centers and three natural gas generation facilities proposed in Newport Township. For Jennifer Lobb, a Newport Township resident and one of the meeting’s organizers, the goal Sunday was less about providing residents with all the answers and more about making sure they knew questions remained to be asked. “We’re just here to let people know about what’s going on, to encourage them to get involved with our local government, to attend the commissioners meetings, to let them know how they feel, and to bring the power back to the people who have to live with these decisions,” Lobb said in an interview before the meeting. Lobb said residents began organizing after learning about the scope of the proposed development earlier this month. “A lot of us woke up in the morning to a newspaper article about 15 data centers and three new gas power plants that were permitted for our township,” she said. Sunday’s turnout suggested the issue has gotten residents’ attention. Chairs filled the hall, while others stood along the perimeter as speakers discussed potential effects of large-scale data center development, including water and electricity use, noise, pollution, emergency response, and changes to surrounding communities. Much of the meeting also focused on encouraging residents to attend the Newport Township commissioners meeting Oct. 5 and press township officials for additional information. Luzerne County resident Nate Eachus, who said he has spent about a year attending municipal meetings throughout the region and researching environmental issues associated with data center development, urged residents to ask detailed questions about water, wastewater, diesel fuel, and power generation. “Everybody needs to show up at this October 5 meeting,” Eachus told the crowd. “Ask good, hard questions.” Eachus pointed to data center development elsewhere in Luzerne County as examples residents could study as they consider what may come to Newport Township. Jeremy Benscoter, a candidate for the Pennsylvania House’s 117th District who described himself as having a background in information technology, told residents the scale and demands of newer hyperscale data centers distinguish them from traditional facilities used to host websites and other internet services. Benscoter focused much of his remarks on the complexity of regulating the facilities, particularly when it comes to water use, electricity demand, and municipal zoning. “We have to basically decide, as a community, what you think is the best option for you,” Benscoter said. He also encouraged residents to consider effects beyond Newport Township, arguing that the rapid development of data centers throughout the region could have implications for the electrical grid and other infrastructure shared across municipal boundaries. Fern Leard, a candidate for the state House’s 120th District, focused on community organization and emergency preparedness, telling residents that first responders could require additional equipment and training to respond to emergencies at large data center facilities. “What I see in this room is people taking the time to listen to one another,” Leard said. She encouraged residents to continue attending municipal meetings and participating in the public process. Paul Shiptuski, who said he has lived in Newport Township’s Lee section for 42 years, spoke about changes his neighborhood has already experienced from nearby industrial activity. Shiptuski said residents contend with truck traffic, dust, noise, and blasting associated with a quarry near his home. He questioned what additional development could mean for residents who rely on wells and value the area’s rural surroundings. “How does that benefit us in the long run?” Shiptuski asked. Other speakers brought perspectives from neighboring communities. Derek Sutcliffe, a Moosic resident involved in opposition to a proposed data center development in Archbald, discussed the substantial electrical infrastructure required by hyperscale facilities and encouraged Newport Township residents to scrutinize how proposed facilities would be powered. Dr. Gere Reisinger, who spoke as a representative of the Seneca Nation and local Native American historian, emphasized the cultural and environmental importance of the Susquehanna River and Wyoming Valley. Lauren McCurdy, a candidate for the Pennsylvania House’s 119th District who attended Sunday’s meeting, said she sees the issue as one that extends beyond individual municipal boundaries. McCurdy, who did not address the crowd, said in an interview that she is concerned about the potential long-term environmental effects of rapid data center development throughout Northeast Pennsylvania. “We have an obligation to protect our communities from interests that are not coming here to improve the quality of life for people in Northeastern Pennsylvania,” McCurdy said. For Lobb, Sunday’s meeting was a starting point. She said residents have not yet formed a formal organization but came together quickly after learning about the permits and are encouraging neighbors to educate themselves and become involved. “They just really need to stay informed,” Lobb said. Residents were repeatedly encouraged Sunday to attend the next Newport Township commissioners meeting, scheduled for 6 p.m. Oct. 5 in the Nanticoke Area High School auditorium. artigo.texto: Kuehne+Nagel and battery manufacturer CATL have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to cooperate on battery logistics, transport electrification and emissions reduction. The partnership will initially focus on practical projects in Europe and Asia. These include the electrification of CATL’s transport flows in Europe and a battery-swapping pilot for heavy-duty trucks in China, which is expected to launch in 2026. Partnership targets battery and road logistics Under the agreement, Kuehne+Nagel and CATL will also explore cooperation in battery recycling and aftersales support, as well as energy storage and charging solutions for logistics facilities. The companies said these initiatives will support efforts to reduce Scope 3 emissions across their logistics and transportation value chains. “Battery-electric vehicles are essential to decarbonising road freight,” said Søren Schmidt, Executive Vice President Road Logistics at Kuehne+Nagel. “Accelerating the transition requires solutions that are both high-performing and operationally viable.” Schmidt added that combining CATL’s battery expertise with Kuehne+Nagel’s logistics capabilities could support projects aimed at reducing emissions from both the company’s operations and those of its customers. Heavy-duty battery swapping pilot planned in China One of the first projects will involve a battery-swapping pilot for heavy-duty trucks in China using technology provided by Qiji. The two companies will also work on electrifying CATL transport flows in Europe, although no details have been provided on the number of vehicles or routes involved. The partnership comes as demand for batteries used in electric trucks continues to increase. According to the companies, demand for electric truck batteries rose by more than 75% in 2024, while global battery manufacturing capacity continues to expand. “As global leaders in our respective industries, CATL and Kuehne+Nagel share a commitment to accelerating the energy transition and achieving a net-zero emissions future,” said Akin Li, Executive President of CATL Overseas Business. The companies did not disclose any investment value or timeframe for expanding the cooperation beyond the initial projects.

artigo.texto: Could abandoned mines house Pa.’s unwanted data centers? As opposition to data centers grows, researchers eye the state’s thousands of acres of polluted mine lands as potential solutions. This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here. Almost nobody wants a data center for a neighbor. Residents fear noise and air pollution, excessive energy and water use and the loss of open land. In Pennsylvania, a hot spot for new data centers, researchers see an opportunity to solve some of these issues by taking advantage of a much older environmental hazard: abandoned coal mines. Pennsylvania has the most abandoned coal mines in the country, totaling around 5,586 sites across the state. The state reports it would take roughly $5 billion to reclaim these polluted and sometimes dangerous areas, which have contaminated thousands of miles of waterways and are linked to underground fires, subsidence and sinkholes. At the same time, local opposition to data centers is growing. Building data centers on abandoned mine lands would provide an alternative to destroying farmlands or local forests, instead making use of already unwanted acreage. Underground mine pools could cool data centers without relying on outside water sources. And companies could help shoulder cleanup costs of existing contamination. The idea is appealing enough that federal researchers investigated it in 2023, concluding that abandoned mine lands offer “land, power infrastructure, and mine water cooling” to data center developers, particularly in a place like Pennsylvania. “If the data centers can demonstrate that they can clean up, treat the acid water and help restore their local environment, the local people are more likely to accept such development proposals,” says Zhongyang He, a researcher in Penn State’s Department of Energy and Mineral Engineering who’s been examining possible data center development on abandoned mine lands in the state. His research suggests that it’s a proposition worth pursuing—at least compared to building data centers in people’s non-polluted backyards. But could it actually work at scale? Or would Pennsylvania end up replacing one intractable environmental problem with another? An Opportunity for Reuse There’s already some proof of concept in western Pennsylvania, where a former mine has housed a data center since 2013. The site of an old limestone mine, Iron Mountain’s West Pennsylvania data center in Boyers sits 220 feet below ground, a 330,000-square-foot facility on a 315-acre campus that doesn’t bring in any outside water. Instead, the data center cools through a closed-loop system that relies on the 53-degree water in a 100-acre, underground lake (not a mine pool, but a comparable concept). “We are using what the miners had left behind,” said Iron Mountain’s senior director of energy and sustainability, Chris Pennington. Boreholes, dug in mines to reach deep water or minerals, provide infrastructure for internet access, and data center clients appreciate the security of storing their information deep underground. Though the facility regularly recycles its lake water, Iron Mountain brings in some refrigeration to supplement the system. Former coal mine sites in Western Pennsylvania slated to become data centers include the former Robena Mine in Greene County, which members of the county’s Planning Commission voted in favor of late last year and would use water from a nearby river that it would convert into steam. Another proposed data center at the former Consol coal mine in Washington County, owned by natural gas company CNX Resources, would use nearby natural gas reserves and “remediated mine gas,” per the Pittsburgh Business Times. There’s precedent outside of Pennsylvania, too. In West Virginia, Energy DELTA Lab’s 450-acre Data Center Ridge boasts access to almost “10 billion gallons of underground water” for cooling at a former mine site. In Italy, an active dolomite mine is home to a data center located 328 feet underground, cooled by the surrounding rock and chilly air. Typically in the 40s or low 50s degrees Fahrenheit, mine pool temperatures are theoretically low enough to cool data centers. Mechanical cooling accounts for around 40 percent of an average data center’s energy consumption, and medium-sized data centers can consume around 100 million gallons of water per year. Penn State researcher He and his colleagues found that of the 5,586 abandoned mine sites they analyzed in Pennsylvania, 160 had mine pools large enough to accommodate data centers (there are currently at least 100 data centers proposed in Pennsylvania). He’s research team landed on other advantages in addition to natural cooling, like “legacy infrastructure,” he said. That could include proximity to roads and the electricity grid, which can be repurposed for data centers. Transmission lines powered large equipment at former mines, and some of that infrastructure remains. “That does not mean that … the line transmission capacity is enough for data centers,” He said, but it does mean relevant permits could be in place. Both Penn State and the Eastern Pennsylvania Coalition for Abandoned Mine Reclamation have assessed a former mine in northeastern Pennsylvania called Morea as a possible data center site. It harbors an estimated 7 billion gallons of underground water via a nearby creek that was routed underground when the mine was active. It still has an electric transmission line, “sufficient for utility-scale solar or a large industrial facility, and expensive and slow to replicate,” per the coalition’s report. That report also acknowledges the ongoing economic burdens carried by communities that once produced coal. In Mahanoy Township, home to the Morea site, the coalition notes a 20.3 percent poverty rate (compared to 11.6 percent statewide)—a commonality across former Pennsylvania mining

artigo.texto: O relatório Flexera State of the Cloud 2026 indica que 73% das organizações operam com um modelo de Nuvem Híbrida (essa taxa sobe para 78% em empresas com mais de 5.000 funcionários). Notavelmente, a taxa de migração de cargas de trabalho e dados da Nuvem Pública para outros ambientes também aumentou 2% em comparação com o ano anterior. Essa mudança reflete uma tendência real: as empresas estão cada vez mais posicionando suas cargas de trabalho de forma proativa onde alcançam a máxima eficiência operacional. Isso não significa que as empresas estejam "abandonando a nuvem". Pelo contrário, os gastos com a nuvem continuam a crescer. A realidade é que, quanto mais disseminada for a adoção da nuvem, mais clara ficará para as empresas a compreensão de quais cargas de trabalho podem aproveitar o ambiente da nuvem e quais exigem uma arquitetura especializada. Essa necessidade de diferenciação clara redefiniu o papel do Data Center na arquitetura híbrida. Quando uma arquitetura simplesmente não consegue "se adequar" a todas as cargas de trabalho. Uma aplicação digital que exige escalabilidade rápida para atender às demandas de tráfego certamente terá requisitos de infraestrutura diferentes de um sistema central que necessita de estabilidade 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana. Da mesma forma, uma carga de trabalho de análise de dados pode exigir poder computacional flexível, enquanto um sistema de segurança demanda hardware dedicado, arquitetura de armazenamento ou uma arquitetura independente de rede. Este é o grande diferencial da Nuvem Híbrida: liberar as empresas da pressão de ter que "amontoar" todas as cargas de trabalho em um único ambiente. Embora as nuvens públicas ofereçam um vasto ecossistema de serviços com recursos de alocação instantânea, para componentes que exigem um nível mais profundo de personalização, as empresas ainda precisam de "espaço" para projetar proativamente sua infraestrutura de acordo com suas necessidades. É essa lacuna que os data centers preenchem na arquitetura híbrida. Em vez de ser apenas um "local de hospedagem" para servidores, um data center (DC) é uma plataforma de lançamento para que as empresas implementem sua própria infraestrutura: desde computação e armazenamento até redes e segurança. As empresas podem ajustar a configuração para cada carga de trabalho principal, aproveitando ao máximo o poder da nuvem para os demais componentes. Em outras palavras, as soluções híbridas ampliam as opções, enquanto os data centers ajudam as empresas a manter o controle sobre essa personalização. Quanto mais nos aprofundamos na computação em nuvem, mais importante se torna o papel dos centros de dados. No entanto, uma infraestrutura perfeitamente "sob medida" não tem significado algum se se transformar em um oásis isolado. As aplicações em nuvem ainda precisam extrair dados de bancos de dados localizados em infraestrutura privada. O sistema central deve sincronizar-se continuamente com as plataformas digitais na nuvem. E, à medida que o negócio se expande, a arquitetura atual precisa ser flexível o suficiente para se conectar com outras nuvens, plataformas ou parceiros. É aqui que entra em jogo o segundo papel do Data Center: a infraestrutura dedicada não só precisa estar operacional, como também precisa estabelecer uma "via expressa" perfeita que a conecte à parte da Nuvem da arquitetura híbrida. O estudo de caso da Equinix e do Credit Saison no Japão é um exemplo claro. Essa instituição financeira migrou aproximadamente 80% de seus sistemas para a nuvem. Com o aumento do uso da nuvem, o Credit Saison precisava resolver o problema de conectar seus sistemas internos aos serviços em nuvem. Por meio da infraestrutura de data center da Equinix e da solução de interconexão direta, a largura de banda do Credit Saison para a AWS saltou de 10 Mbps para 10 Gbps. Ainda mais impressionante, o tempo para ativar uma nova conexão foi reduzido de vários meses para apenas 3 dias úteis. Esta história oferece uma nova perspectiva: o fato de 80% dos sistemas serem baseados em nuvem não significa que os data centers estejam se tornando infraestrutura "obsoleta". Pelo contrário, o uso em larga escala da nuvem gerou uma nova tarefa para os data centers: garantir que a infraestrutura privada e a nuvem se comuniquem na velocidade desejada pelos negócios. Portanto, à medida que a presença da nuvem se expande, a questão central não é mais "Qual é o volume de trabalho da empresa em seu data center?". Uma pergunta mais prática deveria ser: "A partir desse data center, qual o alcance da arquitetura híbrida da empresa em termos de conectividade e escalabilidade?". De "Estação de Armazenamento" a "Camada de Suporte" para a Nuvem Essa mudança não diminui o valor de padrões tradicionais como fornecimento de energia, capacidade, segurança ou disponibilidade do data center. No entanto, a arquitetura híbrida impõe uma camada adicional de requisitos. As empresas precisam conhecer o grau máximo de personalização de sua própria infraestrutura; como conectar essa parte à nuvem; e a adaptabilidade do sistema atual quando uma nova carga de trabalho ou plataforma é adicionada. Isso é especialmente crucial à medida que a arquitetura de TI se torna cada vez mais complexa. O relatório da Flexera para 2026 aponta para um crescimento contínuo do modelo de Nuvem Híbrida, com um crescimento de 2% em Multicloud; simultaneamente, fluxos de migração e repatriação para a Nuvem ocorrem de forma concomitante. A infraestrutura corporativa agora é um ecossistema multiambiente adaptado a necessidades específicas, em vez de uma jornada com um único destino: a Nuvem. Dentro desse ecossistema, o Data Center surge como uma poderosa camada de infraestrutura de suporte. Ele fornece espaço para a personalização de ativos que exigem controle profundo, além de servir como um hub central que conecta sistemas internos com o poder ilimitado da Nuvem. artigo.texto: A single photo of the BYD Great Seagull at a Flash Charging station has changed the outlook for affordable electric cars. The image points to a big jump in charging speed and tech for city drivers. One photo has changed the story for budget electric cars in China. The BYD Great Seagull, once thought too basic for the brand’s top Blade 2 battery, has now been seen parked at a Flash Charging station—BYD’s own megacharger. No camouflage. No staged press event. Just a real car, out in the open. This is the first hard sign that BYD might bring ultra-fast charging to the city car class. The image, posted by Liang Xiao Ping on Weibo and reported by CarNewsChina, shows the new Seagull set up for what looks like an official photo shoot. Carmakers don’t do this unless the car can actually use the charger behind it. The message is simple: BYD is getting ready to show off the Great Seagull’s ability to use Flash Charging. This could change what buyers expect from entry-level EVs. Reuters has reported that BYD already has megawatt-class Flash Charging systems and Blade batteries that can charge from 10% to 97% in just nine minutes. This tech is real, not just a rumor. But BYD is keeping the details close. There’s no official word on the system voltage or the top charging power. The MIIT homologation lists two LFP batteries—30 kWh and 39.2 kWh—both made by FinDreams. They offer CLTC ranges of 320 and 420 kilometers. The LFP label doesn’t say if these are first or second generation Blade batteries. Chinese sources, as cited by CarNewsChina, say Flash Charging will likely be for higher trims, probably the bigger battery. That fits BYD’s pattern with other models. The numbers matter. If the Great Seagull gets the Blade 2 battery, the specs are eye-catching. BYD says it can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes, and 10% to 97% in nine minutes—even at minus 30 degrees Celsius. For the 39.2 kWh battery, that’s about 23.5 kWh in five minutes. The average power is 282 kW, with peaks over 300 kW. For comparison, the Dolphin Surf charges at under 90 kW. The Geely E2 averages 60 kW between 10% and 80%, taking about 30 minutes for a similar charge. The Great Seagull could do it in five. That’s a sixth of the time. It could add 200 kilometers of range in five minutes. Still, the 1,500 kW figure often linked to Flash Charging is about the charger, not the car. The real test is whether the Seagull’s system runs at 400 or 800 volts. Higher voltage means less current for the same power, but it costs more. It needs better electronics and cooling. Most CCS2 chargers in Europe max out at about 500 amps. So, the Seagull’s real charging speed will depend on both its voltage and the chargers it plugs into. Price is still unknown. The current Seagull sells in China for 69,900 to 85,900 yuan (about 9,200 to 11,300 euros before taxes and homologation). The new model is bigger and better equipped, so it will cost more. If BYD can offer Flash Charging below 100,000 yuan (around 13,100 euros), it would be a first for the brand at this price. Until now, the cheapest BYDs—Seagull, Dolphin, Yuan UP—haven’t had Blade 2, even though half the lineup already uses it. Earlier reports said the Seagull and Dolphin wouldn’t get Blade 2 until 2027. This new photo hints at a much earlier launch. Market pressure is building. In August, BYD sold 10,103 Seagulls in China. The rival Geely Xingyuan (sold in Spain as the Geely E2) sold 39,651 units. Geely is ahead in size, seats, and sales. BYD’s best move is to jump ahead in charging speed, not fight on price. The Great Seagull’s place in the lineup is still unclear. It was first announced as a model between the Seagull and Dolphin. Later, BYD’s Zhang Zhuo called it the “second generation Seagull.” The company hasn’t said if it will replace the current Seagull or sit above it. The new car is 4,205 mm long—42.5 cm longer than the old Seagull and just 6.5 cm shorter than the Dolphin. It has a single 95 kW front motor and a top speed of 150 km/h. The design brings trident-shaped headlights, a lower window line, and a simple interior with all info on a central floating screen. For buyers in Europe, things get tricky. The 3.78-meter Seagull is sold as the Dolphin Surf, stretched to 3.99 meters with bigger bumpers. BYD just launched five-seat versions of the current body in Spain, starting at 24,490 euros for the Boost trim. The fifth seat came through rehomologation, not a new model. This shows BYD plans to keep the current Dolphin Surf in Europe for now, especially after sales dropped due to the missing fifth seat. But in China, the Seagull was refreshed in May and replaced just four months later. Europe could see the new model sooner than expected, but there are no confirmed dates yet. BYD’s charging plans are just as bold. The company has promised 300 Flash Charging stations in Spain, open to any car with a CCS2 plug and priced under 0.50 euros per kWh. The first station is already running in Leganés. There, a Denza Z9 GT charged from 10% to 97% in under nine minutes. But only the Denza, which starts at 115,000 euros, can use this speed in Spain. No BYD sold in Spain has the Blade 2 battery yet. The brand says it will take about 24 months before these models arrive. For now, the stations mostly serve cars limited to 150 kW. A small city car that can add 200 kilometers in five minutes would change everything for urban drivers without home charging. As Chinese brands put pressure on Spain’s electric car market, with recent analysis showing the shift, BYD’s push to bring ultra-fast charging to the masses could force the whole segment to adapt. If the Great Seagull launches with Flash Charging before the end of 2026, BYD will have moved faster than anyone expected. It would set a new standard for what city drivers can get from an affordable EV. The next few months will show if this photo is the start of something big or just a clever tease. The stakes for city EVs have never been higher.

artigo.texto: Marisa Wanzeller, da Agência iNFRA O setor de gás natural entrou em alerta com a possível publicação de decreto na segunda-feira (28) para a regulamentação do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter) sem a inclusão do insumo como fonte de suprimento energético. Segundo interlocutores do governo, a Fazenda está articulando a edição do normativo com o entendimento de que o gás não atende à exigência de “baixa emissão de carbono”. Do outro lado, agentes do setor se apoiam no MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia), que já fez a defesa pública da inclusão da molécula na lista de fontes para atendimento dos data centers. A pasta estaria tentando segurar a publicação do decreto e ganhar tempo para que o insumo seja contemplado, disseram fontes da Esplanada. Defesa do gás Marcelo Mendonça, diretor executivo da Abegás (Associação Brasileira das Empresas Distribuidoras de Gás Canalizado), disse à Agência iNFRA que os “rumores” de que o gás não será contemplado no Redata preocupam. “Existe uma falta de sintonia nesse discurso entre os ministérios, têm chegado informações equivocadas em relação ao tratamento do gás natural”, aponta. O executivo diz que o insumo não irá substituir ou concorrer com as fontes renováveis, mas tem como objetivo garantir a segurança para que os empreendimentos funcionem sem interrupções. “É uma característica das renováveis, a intermitência”, comenta ele, sobre a característica da energia solar, por exemplo, de interromper a geração quando o sol se põe, e da eólica, que varia conforme o vento. Outro executivo do setor entende que o presidente Lula “está sendo mal assessorado” sobre o tema. Ele se refere a falas recentes do candidato à reeleição sobre os investidores de data center no Brasil precisarem “investir na construção em energia renovável”. A manifestação de Lula durante a campanha eleitoral repete o conceito de “adicionalidade energética”, regra em que há a exigência de que novos grandes consumidores comprem energia apenas de usinas recém-construídas ou novas, excluindo empreendimentos já existentes. “Falar em adicionalidade em um momento que você tem o nível de curtailment [cortes de geração renovável] que tem no mercado brasileiro, você vai aumentar o curtailment”, considera o agente. “É óbvio que se o empreendedor está entrando com uma carga muito grande, é natural que ele venha a precisar de novos projetos para poder atender aquela carga nova. Você não deveria atrelar uma regra de adicionalidade para a eficiência do sistema, deveria deixar o player que vai desenvolver o data center buscar as melhores alternativas de energia que ele virá a ter”, defende. Redata O projeto de lei que criou o Redata foi aprovado em 1º de setembro no plenário do Senado, após acordo entre o presidente da Casa, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), e o governo. Ele estava parado desde a aprovação na Câmara dos Deputados, em fevereiro deste ano. Os senadores abriram caminho para a inclusão do gás natural entre as fontes de suprimento dos empreendimentos que quiserem se enquadrar no programa. Uma emenda de autoria do senador Laércio Oliveira (PP-SE) alterou a exigência de “fontes limpas ou renováveis”, como estava no texto inicial, por “fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão”. Agora, caberá ao governo, durante a regulamentação, detalhar quais fontes se enquadram no texto da lei e sob quais condições. Durante a sanção da Lei, em 16 de setembro, o secretário-executivo do Ministério da Fazenda, Rogério Ceron, disse que o decreto inicial deveria manter o texto de forma genérica, deixando a lista de insumos para uma portaria interministerial a ser publicada posteriormente. Ele admitiu que não havia consenso entre os ministérios sobre o tema. No entanto, fontes alertam para a possibilidade do decreto já constar as fontes de energia.

artigo.texto: Google está levando seus data centers de IA para o espaço; mas por quê? Por Marcelo Fischer | O Google quer levar parte de sua infraestrutura de inteligência artificial (IA) para o espaço. A empresa prepara para 1º de outubro o lançamento de um satélite experimental capaz de processar consultas simples do Gemini em órbita, primeiro teste prático do Project Suncatcher, iniciativa que estuda a criação de data centers formados por frotas de satélites alimentados por energia solar. O projeto ainda está muito longe de substituir estruturas terrestres. O satélite, batizado de MVP, terá capacidade equivalente à de apenas um servidor de data center e servirá principalmente para descobrir se os chips de IA do Google conseguem funcionar por longos períodos no ambiente espacial. A aposta ajuda a entender um dos maiores problemas da corrida atual pela IA: como aumentar a capacidade computacional sem esbarrar nos limites de energia, espaço físico e infraestrutura disponíveis na Terra. Por que colocar um data center no espaço? A principal resposta está na energia. Data centers de IA precisam de grandes quantidades de eletricidade para alimentar os milhares de chips usados no treinamento e na execução dos modelos. Segundo o New York Times, a ideia que deu origem ao Project Suncatcher surgiu justamente após uma discussão sobre o crescimento acelerado da demanda energética dos sistemas de IA. Em órbita baixa da Terra, satélites podem receber luz solar quase continuamente. O Google afirma que isso permite gerar até oito vezes mais energia solar do que seria possível na superfície terrestre, reduzindo uma das limitações para ampliar a infraestrutura de computação. A proposta é que, no futuro, dezenas de satélites trabalhem juntos como partes de um grande data center. Eles seriam conectados entre si para dividir cargas de processamento de IA, enquanto painéis solares forneceriam energia diretamente no espaço. O Google já desenha uma possível frota com mais de 80 satélites operando em formação. A empresa também conversa com projetistas sobre um satélite específico para essa finalidade que poderia ter o comprimento de um campo de futebol. Primeiro "data center espacial" será pequeno Por enquanto, chamar o equipamento que será lançado em outubro de data center exige algumas ressalvas. O MVP leva quatro TPUs (Tensor Processing Units), chips desenvolvidos pelo próprio Google para tarefas de inteligência artificial. Juntos, eles oferecem poder computacional comparável ao de um servidor convencional dentro de um data center. Seus painéis solares fornecerão cerca de 1 kW de energia, aproximadamente o consumo de um secador de cabelo, segundo a reportagem. Isso será suficiente para executar consultas curtas do Gemini e avaliar como o hardware se comporta fora da Terra. O satélite deve permanecer operacional durante aproximadamente um ano, embora possa continuar em órbita por até seis anos antes de reentrar na atmosfera. A principal dificuldade técnica está no resfriamento. Chips de IA geram muito calor quando fazem cálculos, mas os ventiladores usados em data centers tradicionais não funcionam no vácuo. Para contornar o problema, o Google desenvolveu um sistema com camadas de materiais condutores, incluindo alumínio e cobre, que transferem o calor dos chips para um radiador voltado ao espaço. Mesmo assim, atualmente as TPUs conseguem operar por aproximadamente 15 minutos antes de precisarem ser desligadas para esfriar. Radiação também pode atrapalhar os chips Outra ameaça vem da radiação espacial. Desde fevereiro de 2025, o Google testa seus chips em laboratório usando doses de radiação equivalentes a cerca de cinco anos de exposição no espaço. A preocupação envolve os chamados bit flips, erros nos quais a radiação pode alterar um valor binário armazenado pelo chip, transformando um zero em um ou vice-versa. Os primeiros resultados foram considerados promissores. Segundo o NYT, reiniciar os chips normalmente conseguiu corrigir os erros observados durante os testes. Mesmo assim, colocar dezenas ou centenas de máquinas em órbita traz problemas adicionais. Manutenção, comunicação entre os equipamentos e principalmente o custo dos lançamentos continuam entre os obstáculos. O Google estima que data centers orbitais poderiam atingir custos semelhantes aos terrestres por volta da metade da década de 2030, desde que o preço dos lançamentos de satélites continue diminuindo. Veja mais no Canaltech: O que falta para o Google construir um novo data center no Brasil?

artigo.texto: Securing the energy storage surge This article is authored by Arun Goyal, former CERC member and senior advisor, MSL, and Jaisal Sarma, public policy professional, MSL. India’s ambitious commitment to establish 500 GW of non-fossil electricity capacity by 2030 marks one of the most dramatic clean energy expansions. Achieving this goal, however, hinges on an operational reality: solar and wind power are inherently variable, requiring massive utility-scale energy storage capacity to keep the electric grid balanced, stable, resilient, and reliable. The Central Electricity Authority’s National Generation Adequacy Plan estimates that India will need the energy storage installed capacity of 174 GW/888 GWh including Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) of 80 GW/321 GWh by the year 2035-36 to effectively manage this clean power transition. Yet, as the nation accelerates its energy transition, it faces a new and complex strategic vulnerability. Clean energy technology is no longer simply an environmental and economic transaction; it is fundamentally a global contest for critical raw materials. Without secure, cost-effective access to key battery inputs, such as lithium, graphite, cobalt, and nickel, India’s energy storage deployment remains deeply exposed to global price volatility, unilateral export restrictions, and geopolitical disruption across international supply corridors. To build energy sovereignty in an increasingly fractured global order, India cannot rely on conventional market imports alone. It must instead execute a thoughtful, dual-track strategy that pairs strategic international technology alliances with a robust domestic circular economy. Across the globe, clean energy supply chains are re-aligning along geopolitical lines as major economies seek to de-risk their manufacturing hubs and secure raw material inputs. Multilateral frameworks like the US-led Pax Silica initiative, designed to build resilient supply chains across semiconductors, critical minerals, and advanced technologies, alongside the Minerals Security Partnership, reflect a historic shift towards friend-shoring. For India, active participation in these technological coalitions offers vital strategic advantages. It provides access to international co-investment mechanisms for overseas mineral processing, technology sharing for next-generation battery chemistries like sodium-ion and helps diversify raw material inputs away from single-country concentrations. However, foreign alliances, no matter how well-negotiated, are an incomplete shield against supply chain volatility. Diplomatic access to minerals extracted or refined abroad does not fully eliminate risks of long maritime shipping routes, foreign exchange volatility, or international refining bottlenecks during global crises. To turn global partnerships into lasting national resilience, India requires a strong domestic anchor. Through the National Critical Mineral Mission, supported by a ₹16,300 crore central outlay up to 2030-31, the Indian government has formally elevated secondary mineral recovery to a cornerstone of national economic policy. The mission’s dedicated ₹1,500 crore incentive scheme for critical mineral recycling explicitly targets the extraction of battery-grade minerals from e-waste, manufacturing scrap, and end-of-life electric vehicles. This strategy complements domestic exploration by focusing on urban mining that converts domestic waste into high-value strategic mineral reserves. From an economic perspective, establishing a closed-loop domestic recycling ecosystem fundamentally improves the financial viability of clean energy infrastructure over its entire operational lifecycle. Processing secondary battery scrap inside India creates an immediate buffer against wild fluctuations in global critical mineral spot prices, thereby stabilizing long-term power purchase agreements and lowering the overall lifetime cost of storage systems. At the same time, implementing clear Extended Producer Responsibility guidelines ensures that valuable battery materials remain within the domestic industrial ecosystem rather than moving overseas as unprocessed scrap. A predictable stream of recycled secondary feedstocks lowers raw material costs for domestic cell manufacturers, creating a self-sustaining feedback loop that supports long-term industrial competitiveness. By recovering these critical inputs locally, India can expand its energy storage capacity while significantly reducing the net capital outlay required for fresh critical mineral imports. Translating this strategic blueprint into an operational reality requires pragmatic policy execution, cluster-based industrial infrastructure, and aligned fiscal structures. Foremost among these is updating tax policy to support new clean technologies. Lowering the GST on standalone energy storage systems and specialised recycling machinery to a uniform 5% can immediately lower upfront capital barriers and attract private investment. Simultaneously, regulatory bodies can establish clear, standardised quality and safety benchmarks for battery state-of-health diagnostics, enabling second-life electric vehicle batteries to be safely repurposed for stationary grid storage applications. Furthermore, public procurement agencies and energy developers should modernize their evaluation frameworks to assess storage projects based on full lifecycle economic value, factoring in secondary material recovery and recycling buybacks, rather than relying strictly on initial capital expenditure. Ultimately, India’s clean energy sovereign future cannot be built on import dependencies or uncoordinated execution. International technology blocs like Pax Silica open vital doors to global capital and advanced research, but internal administrative execution will decide whether India achieves true energy independence. artigo.texto: - Mercedes will test the safety credentials of ProLogium’s solid-state batteries. - The fourth-generation tech includes a non-flammable inorganic electrolyte. - ProLogium is planning a large solid-state battery plant in Dunkirk, France. For more than a decade, Mercedes-Benz has worked with Taiwanese energy company ProLogium to help bring advanced solid-state battery technology to the auto industry. The two firms have now strengthened their partnership, meaning Mercedes will get priority access to test the firm’s fourth-generation cells, which could help to reshape the automotive industry. Solid-state batteries have long been viewed as the holy grail of battery tech. By replacing the liquid electrolytes of traditional lithium-ion batteries with non-flammable solid materials, these batteries offer higher energy density, support faster charging, are safer, and last longer. Read: Geely’s New Solid-State Battery Lasts 621,000 Miles And Starts Pilot Testing Next Year Mercedes-Benz, much like BYD, Toyota, Nissan, Honda, VW, Stellantis, Chery, and others, is actively developing and testing these batteries for its next generation of EVs. Some may be ready to hit the market within the next 12 months. Through its deal with ProLogium, Mercedes-Benz will perform electrical, thermal, and safety testing on the company’s Gen4 lithium ceramic battery cells at its facilities and at third-party testing institutes. These batteries use ceramic separator technology and have a non-flammable inorganic electrolyte, which is said to enable not only fast charging but also high power output. “At Mercedes-Benz, we are committed to shaping the future of electric mobility through technological leadership and innovation,” Mercedes-Benz Group AG member of the Board of Management, Jörg Burzer, said. “Our long-standing partnership with ProLogium is a strong example of how we bring the best expertise together to advance next-generation battery technologies. By combining ProLogium’s pioneering solid-state battery approach with Mercedes-Benz’s deep battery development, testing and integration capabilities, we are taking the next step in exploring advanced battery technologies for future electric vehicles.” Solid-State Battery Production Is Coming To Europe ProLogium already operates a large battery factory in Taiwan and is planning a site in Dunkirk, France, with a capacity of up to 44 GWh. It says this factory will allow it to provide cells to customers across the continent, including Mercedes. The German brand has another important solid-state battery partner. In addition to working alongside ProLogium, Mercedes-Benz is also testing lithium-metal battery cells from American company Factorial Energy. Last year, a Mercedes-Benz EQS equipped with one of Factorial’s solid-state battery packs was driven 748.8 miles (1,205 km) on a single charge. It could have been driven even further, as Mercedes says the EQS finished the test with an estimated range of 85 miles (137 km) left.

artigo.texto: How Data Center Growth Is Reshaping Facility Design Rapid demand, AI workloads and power constraints are pushing developers into new markets while changing how data centers are designed and operated. September 28, 2026 By Jeff Wardon, Jr., Assistant Editor Key Takeaways: - Data center demand is pushing developers beyond traditional markets as they seek available power, land, connectivity and workforce capacity in emerging locations. - AI workloads are increasing power density and driving greater adoption of liquid cooling, adaptive reuse and other approaches to meet growing capacity needs. - Rapid growth is accelerating changes in data center mechanical and electrical design as operators seek new ways to overcome power and capacity constraints. North American data center demand reached 25 gigawatts (GW) of absorption in the first half of 2026, while vacancy has fallen to 1 percent or below, according to JLL’s North America Data Center Report Midyear 2026. However, this rapid growth isn’t due to AI alone. Society continues to create and consume more data, with data creation growing at roughly 23 to 25 percent annually, says Sean Farney, vice president of data center strategy at JLL. The bigger picture is that data center development is basically responding to the increasing demand for and dependence on digital services. “This is similar to what happened 100 years ago or so with the introduction of electricity,” Farney says. “Once people saw the benefits of electricity, they wanted to have electrical devices and they consumed more electricity. So, we’re dealing with a very similar kind of societal force. The industry is positioned well to take advantage of this new paradigm and the way we operate as humans.” Changes in site selection The ongoing shortage of land and power in traditional data center markets is changing how developers select sites. Historically, development was clustered around major metropolitan or telecommunications hubs such as Chicago, Dallas, Atlanta, Washington, New York and Los Angeles. Farney describes this as a shift towards what he calls a “de-marketization” of data center site selection. “So, it’s forced this new, what I call this new de-marketization of data center site selection,” Farney says. “It used to be there were things like markets, a real estate topic. Now the data center developers are simply going to where they can get to revenue fastest.” Factors influencing site selection now include power availability, fiber and network connectivity, land, taxes and regulations and workforce availability. New areas for data centers are being considered as well, including West Texas, Ohio, Louisiana, Indiana and Wisconsin. Moreover, developers are becoming more willing to solve individual site constraints rather than limiting development to established markets. However, this geographic shift poses a second issue: What happens when major infrastructure projects enter communities that haven’t traditionally hosted them? “When a data center comes into town, a whole bunch of jobs are created,” Farney says. “I built a data center in suburban Chicago years ago, and I kept 600 union electricians busy for more than nine months working triple shifts. That supported a lot of families, putting a lot of meals on tables.” Similarly, he points to large multi-gigawatt developments in West Texas as examples where entire towns are being employed for development projects. “JLL hired more than a couple of 100 people to staff a large project in Abilene over the last few years,” Farney says. “We work with local trades, local colleges and so on, to find, train and hire folks.” AI and changing data center requirements While AI is the fastest-growing segment, Farney cautions against treating it as the only source of growth. Traditional cloud-service-provider data centers continue to be built as well. AI facilities can operate at 50+ kilowatts (kW) per cabinet, he says. They also require much higher power density, and liquid cooling is becoming increasingly important for those environments. Farney adds that liquid cooling can be about 40 percent more efficient than moving air around in a closed-loop system. The bigger idea is that the basis of design for data centers is changing rapidly, as mechanical and electrical technologies have evolved significantly in just the past few years. Additionally, enterprises are reconsidering older on-premises data centers that had previously been emptied in favor of cloud computing. Some of these facilities may be retrofitted to support higher-density AI workloads. “It generally saves money over the long term for the enterprises,” Farney says. “It’s an adaptive reuse project. It’s not going out and trying to build a new data center. You don’t have to compete with the big guys. So that’s a great solution to some of this low vacancy that we’re seeing across the US.” Another consistent constraint is utility power availability. Developers are increasingly exploring their own power generation, including natural-gas generation, rather than waiting on traditional utility connections. This further illustrates how the industry is adapting its infrastructure strategy to keep pace with demand. Overall, the industry has historically been relatively conservative about mechanical and electrical systems because reliability is paramount, says Farney. However, pressure to bring capacity online is accelerating the adoption of cutting-edge technologies. “I really like to emphasize the massive change in data center basis of design,” Farney says. “We’ve experienced more change in the last three years from a tech perspective, the mechanical and electrical tech that runs data centers than we saw in the prior 20 years. I see all kinds of fascinating new technologies as part of this creative destruction as we move faster.” Jeff Wardon, Jr., is the assistant editor for the facilities market. artigo.texto: Novo BYD Dolphin Mini fica maior e é flagrado sem camuflagem na China Entre as principais mudanças está o crescimento da carroceria, que aproxima o novo Dolphin Mini de modelos como o Geely EX2, seu principal rival em vários mercados O BYD Dolphin Mini está prestes a ganhar uma nova geração e o modelo ficará bem maior. Depois de aparecer em registros do Ministério da Indústria e Tecnologia da Informação da China (MIIT), o hatch foi flagrado novamente, desta vez sem camuflagem, durante gravações de ações comerciais da BYD. As imagens foram divulgadas pelo perfil brasileiro Elétricos da China e mostram detalhes do carro que ainda não haviam sido vistos com tanta clareza. Entre as principais mudanças está o crescimento da carroceria, que aproxima o novo Dolphin Mini de modelos como o Geely EX2, seu principal rival em mercados como China e Brasil. Apesar de manter o nome Mini, o novo hatch terá dimensões significativamente maiores que as da geração atual. Segundo os dados divulgados para o novo modelo, o hatch terá 4,20 metros de comprimento, 1,81 m de largura, 1,57 m de altura e 2,65 m de entre-eixos. Na comparação com o Dolphin Mini atual, o crescimento chega a 42,5 cm no comprimento, 9,5 cm na largura e 15 cm na distância entre os eixos. O modelo ficou maior, inclusive, do que o irmão Dolphin GS. Na dianteira, o novo Dolphin Mini adota elementos semelhantes aos encontrados nos modelos mais recentes da família Ocean. Os faróis são mais finos e ficam posicionados nas extremidades da carroceria, enquanto o para-choque ganhou formas mais marcadas. O exemplar utilizado nas gravações chama atenção ainda pela presença de um sensor LiDAR instalado sobre o teto. O equipamento aparece nas configurações mais sofisticadas do modelo destinadas ao mercado chinês. Novo modelo deve conviver com o atual A mudança de posicionamento não significa necessariamente o fim imediato do Dolphin Mini atual. A estratégia da BYD é fazer com que as duas gerações possam conviver por um período, ocupando faixas diferentes. O modelo atual permaneceria como uma alternativa mais acessível, enquanto a nova geração teria dimensões e características para enfrentar diretamente a nova geração de compactos elétricos chineses. Entre os concorrentes que entram nessa disputa estão o Geely EX2, o GAC Aion UT, MG4 Urban, entre outros modelos. Por enquanto, ainda não há uma data confirmada para a chegada do carro no Brasil, mas essa nova geração só deve vir para cá entre 2027 ou até 2028.

artigo.texto: The submerged battery was the next-generation cell Geely unveiled that day, and it completed charging in just eight minutes. Geely introduced its "Xiandun Golden Battery," which can charge from 10% to 70% in four minutes and 30 seconds and from 10% to 97% in eight minutes and 40 seconds. Built on 2.2-megawatt charging infrastructure and a battery that supports high-rate charging, it is the fastest charging technology Geely has readied for mass production. Speaking on stage, Geely CEO Gan Jia Yue said, "The faster the charging, the greater the concerns about safety," adding, "Through AI-driven innovation, Geely has secured charging safety, timeliness and convenience all at once." Geely also put artificial intelligence front and center to ensure stability and safety during ultrahigh-output charging. The company unveiled "Xingrui PowerMind," a smart energy AI model developed jointly with Chinese AI firm StepFun. The system uses algorithms to predict battery temperature up to 30 seconds in advance and adjusts charging output in real time accordingly. It is designed to keep the average battery temperature below 55 degrees Celsius and cap the peak temperature at 65 degrees. A liquid cooling system manages heat across the charging station's energy storage system, charger, cable, charging port and battery pack, reducing heat concentration in specific areas during high-output charging. "Through AI innovation, we manage the battery while charging, meeting users' demand for both fast charging and long battery life," Gan said. Geely's new ultrafast charging technology is a counterattack against BYD, its rival in vehicles, and CATL, its battery supplier. BYD has invested heavily in ultrafast charging technology and megawatt-class charging networks to ease range anxiety and long charging times, long seen as the biggest bottlenecks to mass adoption of electric vehicles. Early this year it unveiled a second-generation Blade battery that can charge from 10% to 97% in nine minutes. CATL also entered the technology race early this year with its third-generation Shenxing battery, which supports ultrafast charging in about six minutes. According to local media tallies, batteries from Geely's battery unit Ji Yao Tong Xing accounted for 28.50% of the batteries installed in Geely vehicles from January to July this year, up from 18.46% in 2024. Still, CATL's share remained at 63.21% over the same period, leaving supply chain diversification in its early stages. Behind Chinese automakers' intense focus on battery and charging technology lies weak domestic demand and deteriorating profitability. As price-cutting competition dragged on, profits in China's auto industry fell about 20% year over year in the January-July period. To cut costs and strengthen their bargaining position, automakers are reducing reliance on the dominant CATL and accelerating in-house battery development and supply chain diversification. CATL posted a net profit of 43.28 billion yuan in the first half of this year, more than double the combined 21.05 billion yuan net profit of 15 major listed Chinese automakers over the same period. Chinese tech outlet 36Kr said, "As profits continue to concentrate among battery makers, automakers face growing pressure to secure core technology and control over costs."
