artigo.texto: Tennessee Governor candidates weigh in on data centers, AI and energy demands CHATTANOOGA — WTVC reached out to candidates in Tennessee’s gubernatorial race from the Democratic, Republican and independent fields for their positions on data centers and the growing use of artificial intelligence in the state. Candidates were asked about data center development, electricity and water usage, local government regulations, the recent developments in Bradley County and what guardrails they would support if elected. So far we've heard back from Dr. Robert C. Vick (Independent), Misam Abidi (Independent) and Lauren Pinkston (Independent). We are still awaiting responses from other candidates. Once we have those, they will be added to this story. - What is your candidate's general feeling towards both data centers and AI adoption in Tennessee? Dr. Robert C. Vick: General feeling towards data centers/AI adoption- I think data centers should be a local decision within each county. Concerning AI, we do need to look at guardrails to protect our children, privacy concerns, and employees while balancing the need for economic innovation. We want AI to honor human dignity, not exploit it. Misam Abidi: I strongly support Tennessee becoming a leader in artificial intelligence—but leadership means shaping the future, not simply surrendering our resources to it. AI should expand human capability, not replace human purpose. It can strengthen medicine, education, agriculture, manufacturing, emergency response, scientific research, small businesses, and government services. But its benefits must reach ordinary Tennesseans rather than being concentrated among a small number of corporations. I would pursue a Tennessee Community Compute Network: a balanced system combining responsibly located large facilities, regional facilities, and voluntary smaller computing nodes installed in businesses, schools, farms, community buildings, and eventually participating homes. Emerging distributed-computing models, including technology being developed by companies such as SPAN using NVIDIA computing infrastructure, demonstrate that computing capacity does not always have to be concentrated inside enormous campuses. Properly designed smaller systems could help support AI computing while giving participating Tennesseans access to compensation, lower utility costs, battery backup, improved internet connectivity, or a share of the economic value being created. These technologies are still developing, but Tennessee should help test the future rather than waiting for someone else to define it. State-supervised pilot programs could establish strict safety, cybersecurity, privacy, electrical, and consumer-protection standards while determining how distributed computing can benefit both residents and technology companies. Our AI infrastructure should resemble a healthy forest—not a plantation. Large and small systems should coexist, reinforce one another, and make the entire state more resilient. Lauren Pinkston: I was the first major candidate in the governor's race calling for a statewide moratorium on new data center construction until the Legislature enacts real siting standards covering water use, distance from schools and public institutions, and mandatory community input. When a data center was proposed next to the Nashville Zoo, I signed the petition opposing it. Tennessee needs rules in place before the next site is chosen, not damage control after the fact. - How do you feel about the number of data centers currently operating in the state? Do they feel this number is too high? Too low? Or ideal? Dr. Robert C. Vick: Current number of data centers- Its the question of economic innovation vs the impact of infrastructure. As I've traveled to all 95 counties in Tennessee, I hear concerns about data centers but I never heard first hand impact from citizens. Hopefully in the coming days I will get the opportunity to visit a data center. Misam Abidi: I do not believe there is a magic number that is automatically too high or too low. Different trackers also count data centers differently. The real question is not simply how many facilities Tennessee has. It is whether each project strengthens or weakens the community in which it is placed. One data center is too many if it raises household electric bills, threatens drinking water, overwhelms the grid, damages nearby schools or neighborhoods, and leaves residents with little lasting benefit. More facilities may be appropriate when they bring their own energy capacity, protect natural resources, create meaningful employment, strengthen infrastructure, and share their prosperity with the surrounding community. Before approving additional large projects, Tennessee should develop a statewide carrying-capacity map examining electrical supply, transmission capacity, water availability, drought risk, existing industrial and brownfield sites, proximity to homes and schools, roads, noise, emergency services, and workforce readiness. I would support neither a blanket statewide moratorium nor blank checks for developers. Every proposal should be judged by what the land, the grid, the water, and the community can responsibly sustain. Lauren Pinkston: Tennessee has had data centers for many years, but citizens are rightfully pushing back because the state has not coordinated with local governments to protect local resources. Private citizens should never be the ones paying for the infrastructure that a private company demands. Uttar Pradesh's push to build a battery and electric vehicle production base received a fresh boost with the launch of a INR 700-crore battery manufacturing project in Aligarh, a senior state government official said on Wednesday. The project by Maxvolt Energy Industries Ltd is expected to strengthen the state's EV and energy-storage manufacturing ecosystem and create 1,500-2,000 direct jobs and 7,500-10,000 indirect employment opportunities, according to a statement. Alok Kumar, Additional Chief Secretary, Infrastructure and Industrial Development and NRI Department, said projects of this scale were important for creating an industrial ecosystem around battery and EV manufacturing in the state, noting that the state's Electric Vehicle Manufacturing and Mobility Policy had been framed to attract exactly this kind of investment. He said what followed a plant of this size, from component suppliers to skilled employment, was what turned a single factory into an industrial cluster. Kumar also highlighted the pace of industrialisation in the state, saying a record 4,500 units were made functional during 2025-26, a milestone he said reflected the state doing more in one year than it used to accomplish in an entire decade. The Bhoomi Pujan of the Maxvolt Energy facility was held in Aligarh in the presence of Kumar and company representatives. The plant, spread over nearly six acres, is planned to have an annual manufacturing capacity of 10 GWh in two phases. Together with the company's operational facility at Duhai, the planned capacity is expected to reach 12.5 GWh annually. The Aligarh facility will manufacture batteries for electric mobility, energy storage and other applications, including batteries for two-, three- and four-wheelers, according to the statement, and is also expected to have dedicated production lines for original equipment manufacturers. The project is estimated to have an annual turnover potential of more than INR 6,800 crore at full capacity, with the government saying its wider impact could extend to component suppliers, logistics, engineering and other parts of the supply chain. The Aligarh project adds to Uttar Pradesh's growing cluster of battery and electric vehicle manufacturing facilities, as the state continues to position itself as a hub for EV-linked industrial investment under its dedicated mobility policy. The scale of indirect employment projected for the project, several times larger than the direct jobs figure, reflects the broader industrial ecosystem effect state officials expect such large manufacturing investments to generate, spanning component suppliers, logistics providers and ancillary services in the surrounding industrial belt. artigo.texto: B2U Storage Solutions has announced the start of commercial operations at its Bexar Martinez battery energy storage system (BESS) project in Texas. The facility will provide 28 MWh of grid services to the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT). Located near San Antonio and within the CPS Energy service territory, the project uses exclusively repurposed electric vehicle (EV) batteries, demonstrating the deployment of second-life battery technology at utility scale. B2U’s Texas Portfolio Exceeds 50 MWh Bexar Martinez is the second BESS project in Texas developed and equipped by B2U using its patented battery storage cabinets containing repurposed EV batteries. The company said its approach extends the useful life of EV batteries beyond their initial automotive applications, while reducing battery waste and lowering the cost of grid-scale energy storage. With the Bexar Martinez project now operational, B2U’s total portfolio providing grid services to ERCOT has surpassed 50 MWh. Across Texas and California, the company is managing more than 5,000 repurposed EV batteries and operates approximately 100 MWh of energy storage capacity across solar-paired and standalone configurations. Freeman Hall, CEO of B2U Storage Solutions, said the Bexar Martinez project demonstrates the ability of second-life batteries to provide grid services at scale while extending the useful life of battery resources. Additional ERCOT Capacity Planned The project is located in one of the fastest-growing regions of the ERCOT market and is intended to support grid reliability amid rising electricity demand. B2U expects to deploy an additional 50+ MWh of energy storage capacity in ERCOT over the next six months. The company said its second-life battery projects can provide a lower-cost storage option while contributing to grid reliability. Project Receives Financing and ITC Benefits B2U said the Bexar Martinez project and its other operating sites qualify for the domestic content bonus under the Investment Tax Credit (ITC). The projects have also received third-party financing and have been acquired by B2U Infrastructure Partners, supporting the commercial and financial viability of the second-life battery storage model. The commercial operation of Bexar Martinez marks another deployment of repurposed EV batteries for grid-scale energy storage as the U.S. energy storage market expands to address increasing electricity demand and grid flexibility requirements. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no WEG amplia fábrica de baterias em Santa Catarina e dobra produção anual com aporte 18% maior antes de leilão em dezembro Publicado 25/09/2026 • 10:35 | Atualizado há 29 minutos KEY POINTS Divulgação / WEG Planta da WEG em Itajaí, Santa Catarina A WEG vai dobrar a capacidade de produção anual da fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS, na sigla em inglês) que constrói em Itajaí, em Santa Catarina. Com a ampliação, a unidade passa a ter capacidade de 4 gigawatts-hora (GWh) por ano, ante os 2 GWh previstos no anúncio original, informou a companhia em comunicado ao mercado. Para isso, o investimento total estimado sobe de R$ 280 milhões para R$ 330 milhões, alta de cerca de 18%. O início das operações segue previsto para o segundo semestre de 2027. Na comunicação aos acionistas, a WEG relaciona a ampliação à proximidade do primeiro Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade de Armazenamento Nacional, marcado para dezembro. A companhia também cita a demanda por equipamentos ligados à transição energética. O projeto atualizado, de acordo com a empresa, incorpora mais automação e ganhos de eficiência industrial, o que permite aumentar a capacidade produtiva sem mudar o cronograma. A WEG não detalhou no comunicado a origem dos recursos adicionais. A fábrica foi anunciada em 4 de fevereiro, com financiamento de R$ 280 milhões do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES), por meio do programa BNDES Mais Inovação. Na época, a capacidade de 2 GWh por ano equivalia a cerca de 400 sistemas de 5 megawatts-hora (MWh) cada. Pelo projeto divulgado em fevereiro, a unidade terá linhas de montagem automatizadas e semiautomatizadas, robôs móveis para a logística interna, laboratório de testes e subestação elétrica própria. A previsão inicial era de cerca de 90 empregos diretos. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC O leilão citado pela WEG foi criado por portaria do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) publicada em 1º de junho de 2026. O texto estabeleceu dois certames de baterias, que serão realizados ao mesmo tempo em dezembro. Na disputa de Armazenamento Nacional, os projetos precisam usar sistemas nacionalizados, conforme as regras de credenciamento do BNDES. Já o outro leilão aceita equipamentos importados. Nos dois casos, os acordos terão duração de 15 anos, com início do fornecimento em 1º de agosto de 2028. Cada projeto precisa oferecer potência mínima de 30 megawatts (MW), com capacidade de descarga de pelo menos quatro horas. Os empreendedores vencedores recebem uma receita fixa anual, paga em 12 parcelas mensais e ajustada pelo desempenho operacional dos sistemas. Os sistemas de armazenamento em baterias guardam energia nos momentos de maior disponibilidade e a liberam quando necessário, segundo a WEG. Com isso, ajudam a integrar à rede as fontes solar e eólica, que dependem das condições do tempo. artigo.texto: A handful of north Macomb County residents opposed to data centers in their communities voiced their concerns to county commissioners, and asked them to pass a moratorium on centers and help local communities fight them. “We need you guys to step into the fight. I need my commissioners to step into the fray,” said Tarra Samander, who owns a farm near I-94 and 26 Mile Road in Lenox Township and said she and her husband rejected an offer of $500,000 from a data-center developer as a 10% deposit to purchase their property. Residents spoke Thursday during the public-participation agenda item at the full county Board of Commissioners meeting in the Administration Building in Mount Clemens. Commissioner MIchael Howard of Warren said during commissioner comments that while the county can’t help them with a moratorium they can provide some expertise and assistance through county planners. “The county has very, very, very limited zoning and land authority” under state law,” Howard said. “This is truly a local municipality issue as well as a state issue.” There are currently three potential AI data center developments in the county in Lenox, and Washington and Richmond townships. Lenox is closest to development at this time. Also speaking was Arianna Welsh, who resides in Bruce Township but owns property in Lenox and Richmond, and runs a business in New Haven. Welsh asked commissioners to “expand and better coordinate technical assistance available to our 27 local communities when evaluating major and emerging developments.” “There is urgency to this request,” Welsh told the board. “Industry is not waiting for local governments to catch up. Communities are being approached now with increasingly large and complex projects.” The projects involve rezonings, master plan updates, development agreements, infrastructure commitments, environmental impacts, road-capacity considerations and tax implications on properties for “hundreds of acres” and “hundreds or millions or even billions of dollars,” Welsh said. “The window to obtain specialized expertise can become very short,” she said. “The county does not need to make decisions for communities, but it can give them better tools, though, to help themselves.” The assistance could be provided through the county planning department, Welsh said. Commissioner Phil Kraft of Chesterfield Township, located adjacent to Lenox, said he sent a letter many months ago to Lenox officials asking them to work with New Haven on a moratorium on data centers together but that didn’t happen.” “I think it would’ve been in our communities’ best interests for them to work together,” Kraft said at the meeting. “I have a lot of the same concerns that you do.” Lenox passed a 4-month moratorium last February that expired without renewal after attorney James R. Andary, representing a company called Lenox & Chesterfield Economic Development Alliance, a data-center developer, threatened a lawsuit in May. It was registered by Paul Reschke. “Our Client has expended substantial time, capital and professional resources to develop a large-scaled, phased technology infrastructure complex .. a proposed Data Center Campus would be generally located on the I-94 Development District,” Andary wrote In a May 4 letter to the township obtained by The Macomb Daily. “Under Michigan Law, Lenox Township cannot use zoning laws or a moratorium to ban or block either temporarily or permanently, a lawful land development use. I must emphasize the Campus and the Data Center is a lawful development use of the property that is owned or controlled by my Client. “We have been authorized to pursue legal action to not only seek injunctive relief, but also substantial economic damages from Lenox Township if the moratorium is extended.” According to another letter in May, the company again threatened a lawsuit if the township delayed efforts to draft the I-94 Development District ordinance, which has been subject of a first reading but was sent back by the township Board of Trustees to the township Planning Commission for more work. A web site has been created in support of the project, touting the benefits that would come to the area. State anti-data center forms Companies’ efforts to build data centers in Michigan spawned the creation of the Economic Development Responsibility Alliance of Michigan, which is helping local communities fight the centers and tracking close to three-dozen projects in the state, including in Lenox and Washington. “We’re pretty much across the board opposed to AI data centers,” said Marjorie Steele, executive director of the EDRA. “Based on what we are seeing … it’s become increasingly clear at this point that the purpose of these data centers is not the stated purpose they’re being marketed for. The reason that these data centers need such computing power and why they need such exponentially greater processing power than the standard internet and cloud-computering centers that we’ve had for decades is they’re trying to build a surveillance state.” Steele also pointed to the recent increased use of license-plate readers and AI software for surveillance. “We believe that local communities and local township can and should use any and all reasonable, legal means at their disposal to protect themselves, and that includes zoning and regulation,” she said. The organization says AI or “hyperscale” data cents consume large amount of water and energy; create only a minimal number of jobs post-construction; increase the risk of water contamination and “well depletion”; increase the number and level of power outages in the surrounding area; are “susceptible to toxic fires”; and receiving funds from the state and federal government. Of 34 potential sites in Michigan, the EDRA says it is “fighting” 13 projects, “winning” 12 and “won but vigilant” at nine sites, including Washington Township, where the developer withdrew the project last May. artigo.texto: BYD has released the first official images of its upcoming Yangwang flagship sedan, revealing a large luxury car with rear-hinged doors that have drawn comparisons with the Rolls-Royce Phantom. However, the more significant development could be underneath the body. The sedan is being considered as a possible candidate for BYD’s first vehicle equipped with a solid-state battery. Solid-State Battery Could Be the Bigger Story BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li has previously said that a vehicle using the company’s solid-state battery technology will arrive in 2027, although she has not identified the model or confirmed when production will begin. A luxury vehicle produced in relatively small numbers could provide a possible starting point for the technology while production remains expensive. Most current EV batteries use a liquid electrolyte to transport lithium ions between electrodes. Fully solid-state batteries replace that liquid with a solid electrolyte. The technology could potentially allow manufacturers to build smaller and lighter battery packs with higher energy density. It could also reduce some safety concerns associated with flammable liquid electrolytes. However, solid-state batteries still face engineering challenges, including maintaining internal contact, durability and lithium growth that can damage cells. BYD has not announced the sedan’s battery capacity, driving range or charging specifications. Flash Charging Adds to the Speculation One teaser image shows the Yangwang sedan alongside a BYD Flash Charging station. This has added to speculation about the vehicle’s battery technology, although the image does not confirm that the sedan will use a solid-state battery. BYD already offers Flash Charging technology with its conventional Blade Battery 2.0, meaning the presence of the charging station alone does not establish a connection with solid-state batteries. Solid-State Technology Is Moving Toward Production Several automakers are developing or testing solid-state battery technology. NIO already offers a 150kWh battery in some of its premium EVs, although battery supplier WeLion describes the pack as semi-solid-state because it still contains some liquid electrolyte. It therefore differs from a fully solid-state battery. Mercedes-Benz has road-tested solid-state battery technology in an EQS, while BMW has tested all-solid-state cells in an i7. Toyota is also developing the technology and aims to introduce EVs using solid-state batteries in 2027–28. BYD has separately said it plans to put its own solid-state battery technology into a vehicle in 2027, but has not identified the model. What We Know About the Yangwang Sedan The camouflaged sedan features a long and upright body, rear-hinged coach doors and a roof-mounted lidar sensor. Yangwang has not yet revealed the interior or confirmed the vehicle’s final name, specifications, price or launch date. The distinctive doors are likely to attract attention, but confirmation of a solid-state battery would make the sedan particularly significant for BYD’s next generation of EV technology. artigo.texto: On September 12, 2026, CNBC reported that General Motors Company (NYSE:GM) is in the early stages of developing next-generation battery cells that it says can reduce U.S. dependence on China, days after Ford Motor Company (NYSE:F) faced Trump administration criticism over its own Chinese battery-technology ties. GM has partnered with Denver-based startup Peak Energy to develop sodium-ion battery cells for stationary energy storage systems, using domestically available materials like sodium from soda ash instead of lithium and other inputs China dominates. GM vice president of battery and sustainability Kurt Kelty told CNBC the company is “developing a supply chain such that, two years from now, three years from now, it will be domestic.” Don’t Miss: Ford (F) Answers Washington’s China Criticism with a $1 Billion Kentucky Bet Bull Case General Motors Company (NYSE:GM) could strengthen its domestic battery position by developing U.S.-based technology rather than relying heavily on Chinese intellectual property. GM vice president of battery and sustainability Kurt Kelty said the company wants to establish a domestic battery supply chain within the next two to three years. Its work with Peak Energy focuses on sodium-ion technology developed for stationary energy storage. GM says sodium-ion cells can operate across a wider temperature range and endure more cycles than incumbent chemistries. It gives the strategy a potential technical advantage alongside its supply-chain benefits. Ford Motor Company (NYSE:F) already has a more immediate path to U.S. battery production despite the political controversy surrounding its CATL relationship. Ford owns and controls its Marshall, Michigan battery plant and employs the American workforce there while licensing battery technology from CATL. Access to established technology could help Ford scale domestic battery manufacturing faster than companies that still need to develop and commercialize new chemistries. Ford retains operational control of the U.S. facility. Both GM and Ford could strengthen their competitive positions if they successfully localize more of their battery supply chains in the United States. Washington is scrutinizing dependence on Chinese automotive technology and materials. China still dominates several critical battery supply chains. GM is pursuing more domestic technology development, while Ford is bringing licensed battery technology into a U.S.-owned plant. Successful execution could give both automakers greater supply security and more control over strategically important battery production. Look Into: GM and Ford Take their Century-Old Rivalry to the Battlefield and the Power Grid Bear Case General Motors Company (NYSE:GM) still faces a long commercialization timeline, and its current sodium-ion program does not directly solve its near-term EV battery challenges. Kelty said GM needs another two to three years to establish the domestic supply chain it envisions, while GM designed its Peak Energy sodium-ion cells primarily for grid-scale stationary storage rather than electric vehicles. GM must still prove that its broader domestic battery investments can eventually improve EV costs, margins, and supply-chain independence. Ford Motor Company (NYSE:F) faces much greater immediate political risk because its U.S. battery strategy still depends on licensed technology from China’s CATL. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Republican lawmakers have criticized Ford’s CATL relationship and other ties with Chinese companies, even though Ford owns and operates the Michigan plant itself. Additional restrictions on Chinese automotive technology could force Ford to modify its battery strategy, increase costs, or find alternative technology if political pressure intensifies. Both automakers still face a difficult and expensive path toward genuine battery independence from China. China controls large portions of global refining and battery-material processing, including about 98% of LFP cathode materials, so domestic cell production alone cannot eliminate supply-chain exposure. GM must commercialize new technologies at competitive costs, while Ford must manage political risk around licensed Chinese technology. Both companies ultimately need their localization strategies to lower costs and protect margins rather than simply shift where they assemble batteries. Hedge Fund Sentiment General Motors Company (NYSE:GM)’ hedge fund count fell to 75 in the second quarter from 77 in the first, with position value dropping to $4.87 billion from $6.08 billion, according to Insider Monkey’s database. Ford Motor Company (NYSE:F), the rival GM is implicitly contrasting itself against, held steady at 50 hedge fund holders, with position value slipping to $1.02 billion from $1.12 billion. Conclusion General Motors Company (NYSE:GM) and Ford Motor Company (NYSE:F) are pursuing two distinct approaches to the same strategic challenge. GM is emphasizing domestic technology development and building expertise in sodium-ion batteries. Ford is using established CATL technology inside a battery plant that it owns and operates in Michigan. GM’s approach could reduce long-term political and technological dependence on China, while Ford’s approach could give it a faster route to large-scale U.S. battery production. Nonetheless, GM still faces a lengthy development timeline, Ford faces significant political scrutiny, and both companies remain exposed to Chinese-dominated battery-material supply chains. Investors should watch whether each automaker can turn its respective strategy into competitive battery costs, stronger margins, and greater supply security. artigo.texto: Publicidade 25 Set (Reuters) – A operadora de centrais de processamento de dados DayOne segue em frente com seus planos de abrir capital já em novembro, segundo três fontes a par do assunto, mesmo com o aumento dos juros e os contratempos em outras áreas do ecossistema ameaçando reduzir a janela de oportunidade para as empresas acessarem o mercado de IPOs. A empresa sediada em Cingapura desenvolve e opera centrais de processamento de dados para clientes de computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial. A companhia planeja tornar público seu pedido de registro junto à Comissão de Valores Mobiliários dos Estados Unidos (SEC) em meados de outubro e abrir o capital em novembro, disseram as fontes. A DayOne se recusou a comentar. É preciso entender se IA está se tornando grande demais para falir, diz membro do Fed Presidente fez referência à necessidade de resgates públicos de grandes instituições financeiras durante a crise financeira de 2007 a 2009 IA na saúde: Anthropic e OpenEvidence levam diagnóstico onde falta até luz A nova iniciativa trata-se de uma versão especializada disponível gratuitamente para profissionais de saúde em dezenas de países de baixa e média rendas As intenções de IPO da DayOne surgem após dois contratempos para operadoras de data centers nesta semana: o adiamento do IPO da SB Energy e notícias de uma disputa envolvendo Oracle e Blue Owl, que pode atrasar um grande projeto de centrais de processamento de dados no estado norte-americano do Novo México. O contraste destaca como o mercado de infraestrutura de IA está amadurecendo. Empresas com clientes diversificados e maior visibilidade da demanda ainda podem atrair interesse, enquanto projetos que dependem fortemente de um único cliente de IA ou exigem grandes quantias de capital inicial enfrentam um cobranças maiores dos investidores. “A linha divisória está em saber se a demanda já foi contratada e está em operação, ou se é apenas planejada”, disse Ke Yan, chefe de pesquisa da Shenton Research, empresa de pesquisa de investimentos com sede em Cingapura. Com a energia sendo agora a principal restrição ao setor, os investidores preferem operadoras com fornecimento de eletricidade garantido, uma grande parcela da capacidade contratada já em operação ou em fase de conclusão e contratos “take-or-pay” de longo prazo, disse ele. Continua depois da publicidade As exigências dos investidores estão se intensificando à medida que um número crescente de empresas se encaminha para os mercados de capitais, com desenvolvedores e operadores de data centers, incluindo Switch, Vantage Data Centers e CyrusOne, explorando IPOs. Oferta mais diversificada A diversificação geográfica da DayOne e o fato de possuir data centers em operação, e não apenas em desenvolvimento, ajudaram a diferenciá-la de alguns concorrentes aos olhos dos investidores, disse uma das fontes. A empresa, apoiada por investidores como Coatue e Hillhouse, levantou US$4,5 bilhões em uma rodada de financiamento série C encerrada em junho. Ela poderia buscar levantar até US$5 bilhões na oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO), com uma avaliação de cerca de US$20 bilhões, segundo reportagem da Reuters. Continua depois da publicidade A companhia garantiu cerca de 2,1 gigawatts de reservas de capacidade e opera na Ásia-Pacífico e Europa, incluindo Malásia, Hong Kong, Japão, Finlândia e Espanha. Enquanto isso, a SB Energy, apoiada pela SoftBank, adiou os planos de divulgar formalmente seu IPO nesta semana, enquanto trabalha para esclarecer questões adicionais da SEC. Também há preocupações dos investidores quanto à avaliação que a empresa busca e à sua dependência da OpenAI como principal cliente, segundo uma das três fontes familiarizadas com o assunto e outra fonte. A SB Energy busca ser avaliada em cerca de US$60 bilhões, acrescentou uma delas. A SB Energy se recusou a comentar. Houve várias negociações entre SoftBank, SB Energy, OpenAI e Nvidia, fornecedora de chips da OpenAI, nos últimos meses. Continua depois da publicidade A Nvidia concordou em fornecer uma garantia de até US$105 bilhões para ajudar a OpenAI a alugar o data center no estado norte-americano de Ohio que está sendo desenvolvido pela SB Energy, além de investir US$1,5 bilhão na SB Energy. A SoftBank, que apoia a OpenAI, está recebendo pedidos de investidores para uma operação de dívida no valor de US$10 bilhões, denominada em dólares, para ajudar a financiar seus investimentos na OpenAI. A empresa já havia obtido um empréstimo garantido pela participação na OpenAI. Investidores mais exigentes O custo do financiamento da expansão da IA está sob maior pressão. Taxas de juros mais altas tornam mais caro financiar instalações cujos retornos podem levar anos para se concretizar, enquanto os investidores exigem maior visibilidade sobre os clientes e os fluxos de caixa que sustentarão esses investimentos. Continua depois da publicidade Para desenvolvedores que dependem de dívida, a receita contratada de clientes com boa capacidade de crédito é crucial para o pagamento dessa dívida, já que eles financiam instalações caras preparadas para IA, incluindo racks de alta densidade e sistemas de resfriamento líquido, disse Neil Bear-Hetherington, diretor de mercados de capitais de data centers para a Ásia-Pacífico da CBRE. Para os desenvolvedores de data centers, isso torna a identidade e a solidez financeira de seus clientes cada vez mais importantes para os investidores que avaliam projetos que podem exigir bilhões de dólares em investimento inicial. Para empresas que se preparam para abrir capital, um mercado de IPO menos tolerante e um maior escrutínio sobre a infraestrutura de IA criam um incentivo para agir rapidamente enquanto a demanda dos investidores ainda existe.

artigo.texto: Energy Storage Sector Buzz: Owner Returns, Market Saturation, and Northvolt Asset Deal Energy Storage News has published its latest roundup of industry commentary drawn from user-posted analysis across the energy storage sector, according to the outlet. The publication noted that the current edition mixes recent posts with some items that would otherwise have appeared in the prior week's installment, making parts of the collection older than usual. Jordan D, founder and chief executive of energy trading infrastructure consultancy A115, offered a perspective on how risk and reward are distributed between parties that own battery energy storage system projects in Europe and those that trade them. He argued that recent developments have left project owners and developers facing difficult conditions while the trading segment experiences strong growth. Romania has become an increasingly active market for grid-scale storage, a trend Energy Storage News addressed in a separate roundup covering four projects moving forward. Daniel Pintilie, founder and lead advisor at Solarcap Investments, which serves as a battery storage mergers and acquisitions broker in Romania, wrote about the pace at which capacity is being connected and what that trajectory implies for project investors. In Australia, Sheng Fang, who works on global strategy at electric vehicle infrastructure firm StarCharge, wrote that the market has matured to the point where simply developing and selling projects is no longer a workable business model. He said the venture-capital-style returns that previously resulted from securing land, approvals, and a connection offer have disappeared. Angie Z, director of strategic partnerships at supplier Gooree, examined why two battery storage systems with nearly identical data sheets can still produce very different return on investment timelines. Her post attracted substantial commentary. Michael Barnard, chief strategist at consultancy TFIE Strategy, discussed why Energy Vault's first large-scale commercial project using gravity-based energy storage technology remains unproven despite having been online for several years. Academic and battery storage industry figure Jan Rosenow wrote that thermal energy storage has arrived, pointing to 51 large-scale projects in operation worldwide. On the mergers and acquisitions front, critical materials firm Refinyx and investor Qarlbo Energy have jointly acquired the recycling assets of failed lithium-ion battery manufacturer Northvolt, a story that originated with Bloomberg and was confirmed when one of the companies involved commented on the reporter's post. Most of the remainder of Northvolt has already been acquired by US startup Lyten. Aurora Energy Research analyst Gabriela Pena Balderrama discussed the implications of proposed grid fee reforms by transmission system operator Fingrid for those building battery storage projects in Finland. Munir Khan, a quality and production specialist at lithium-ion solution manufacturer Robust Energy Solutions, wrote that the reason flow batteries have not spread widely lies in the balance of plant rather than in performance. The roundup also noted that the publication regularly covers battery startups that showed significant promise but ultimately failed to turn lab-proven technology into commercially viable products, with scientific advisor Nigel Taylor and colleagues examining that pattern. - 1. artigo.texto: Nova unidade da WEG em Itajaí (SC) terá capacidade de 4 GWh por ano e deve iniciar operações no segundo semestre de 2027, mirando o avanço do mercado de armazenamento de energia no Brasil A WEG (BOV:WEGE3) ampliou o projeto de sua nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), em construção em Itajaí (SC). Com a revisão, o investimento total estimado passou para R$ 330 milhões, enquanto a capacidade produtiva prevista subiu para 4 gigawatts-hora (GWh) por ano. O movimento reforça a aposta da WEG no mercado de armazenamento de energia e ocorre em um momento de expansão da demanda por soluções ligadas à transição energética. A companhia prevê iniciar as operações da unidade no segundo semestre de 2027, colocando a nova capacidade em operação antes de uma etapa importante de desenvolvimento do mercado brasileiro de baterias. Quando anunciou a fábrica, em fevereiro, a WEG estimava uma capacidade de até 2 GWh anuais e mencionava financiamento de R$ 280 milhões. A atualização, portanto, representa uma duplicação da capacidade inicialmente projetada e eleva o investimento previsto em R$ 50 milhões. A ampliação também acontece em meio à preparação do Brasil para o primeiro leilão destinado à contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias. O governo programou os certames para dezembro, incluindo uma disputa específica para projetos que atendam requisitos de conteúdo local. Os sistemas BESS são utilizados para armazenar eletricidade e disponibilizá-la posteriormente, contribuindo para aumentar a flexibilidade do sistema elétrico. A tecnologia ganha relevância com o crescimento da geração solar e eólica, fontes cuja produção varia de acordo com as condições climáticas. A WEG já vinha preparando sua estrutura para participar das oportunidades relacionadas ao novo mercado. Em julho, o vice-presidente Administrativo e Financeiro da companhia, André Rodrigues, afirmou que a empresa estava se estruturando para atender à demanda esperada pelo leilão. Naquele momento, a WEG tinha cerca de 1 GWh de capacidade produtiva em baterias, considerando aplicações de mobilidade elétrica e sistemas estacionários. O primeiro leilão brasileiro de armazenamento está previsto para dezembro de 2026 e deverá contratar sistemas BESS para o Sistema Interligado Nacional. As regras definidas pelo governo contemplam uma disputa com exigência de conteúdo local e outra aberta à participação de projetos que cumpram os requisitos estabelecidos. Nesse cenário, a expansão da capacidade industrial da WEG pode ampliar sua exposição a uma nova frente de negócios, embora a efetiva captura dessa demanda dependa da participação da companhia nos projetos e dos contratos que eventualmente sejam conquistados. O movimento também se conecta à estratégia mais ampla de investimentos da WEG. No segundo trimestre de 2026, a empresa destinou R$ 794,9 milhões à modernização e expansão de capacidade produtiva, máquinas, equipamentos e licenças de softwares. Até o momento, o anúncio sobre a ampliação da fábrica, conforme as informações disponíveis para esta notícia, não traz declaração adicional de representante da companhia sobre o novo valor de investimento e a capacidade revisada. Como a notícia está sendo publicada antes da abertura do pregão desta sexta-feira (25/09), a referência de mercado é o fechamento da sessão anterior. As ações WEG encerraram a quinta-feira (24/09) a R$ 50,74, sem variação no fechamento informado pela ADVFN. Assim, ainda não é possível comparar o preço atual com a abertura, máxima e mínima do pregão de sexta-feira (25/09). Com o mercado ainda fechado, o anúncio da expansão da fábrica de baterias poderá entrar no radar dos investidores na abertura, especialmente pela combinação entre o aumento da capacidade produtiva e a proximidade do primeiro leilão brasileiro de armazenamento de energia. A reação efetiva, porém, dependerá das negociações ao longo do pregão. A WEG é uma fabricante brasileira de equipamentos elétricos e soluções para automação, energia, eletrificação e sistemas industriais, com atuação no Brasil e no exterior. A companhia também vem ampliando sua presença em soluções relacionadas à transição energética, incluindo sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias. A empresa mantém ainda negócios em motores elétricos, transformadores, automação, geração e transmissão de energia e outras soluções industriais. QUER SABER COMO GANHAR MAIS? artigo.texto: Sterling does not have a code or ordinance allowing or forbidding data centers or battery energy storage systems from locating within the city limits. “We can’t simply say no,” Tim Zollinger, Sterling city attorney, told the Sterling Plan Commission at its Thursday meeting. That meeting was the first one following the City Council’s unanimous vote at its Sept. 7 meeting to impose a 180-day application moratorium on processing and approving applications for data centers and battery energy storage systems. “We don’t have any code that says you can have either of those entities in the city,” said Dustin Wolff, city planner. Wolff said the city has been receiving requests from battery energy storage system companies but has not received any requests from data center developers wanting to locate within city limits. Why the city needs codes and ordinances to set out rules and regulations for data centers and BESS, and why the City Council cannot issue an overall ban on those specific facilities, was one of the main topics of discussion for the commission. “We need to have those rules because, as a non-home-rule municipality, the City of Sterling does not have the authority to completely ban what is a lawful business. Within the state of Illinois right now, a data center is a lawful business. We can’t simply ban something permanently. We can have a moratorium but we cannot permanently ban something,” Zollinger said. “I just don’t understand why, if you don’t want it in your community, why you can’t deny, say, ‘You can’t come here,’” one of the audience members said during a public comment period in the meeting. The state of Illinois, based on court decisions from the 1970s and 1980s, does not allow communities to ban specific businesses or industries. Those court cases stemmed from the adult entertainment industry. “Years ago, communities wanted to get rid of all types of adult entertainment. Those businesses went to court and said you can’t completely zone us out of the town. We are a lawful business permitted by state law, you can’t say we can’t be anywhere in your community,” Zollinger said. When courts ruled in favor of those businesses, communities turned to zoning and regulation to control what businesses and industries could locate within their city limits. “Those cases developed and the courts said, ‘Correct, if you are a lawful business permitted to operate, the city can zone it, the city can adopt rules to regulate it but you can’t completely ban it,’” Zollinger said. At a ribbon cutting in Monee on Thursday, Gov. J.B. Pritzker said he does not have the authority to impose a statewide moratorium on data centers on his own. Pritzker said he hopes that the state legislature will take up the POWER (Protecting Our Water, Energy and Ratepayers) Act during the legislative veto session after the November elections. The POWER Act was introduced in the spring session as Senate Bill 4016 and House Bill 5513. The bill requires data centers to pay for their own infrastructure connection costs, source clean energy for their electric service, and imposes water use guidelines. The bill stalled before the May 31 legislative deadline. On June 1, Pritzker ordered the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity to halt tax incentives for data centers, effective July 1, 2026. Unless the state takes further action to limit or ban data centers and BESS facilities, communities like Sterling will have to address data centers and BESS facilities through their own ordinances and zoning codes specifically addressing those businesses. “The goal here is to say where is the balance that the community is comfortable with, we know we can’t say no. So where do you balance that with if you want to come here, if you want to be in Sterling, these are the rules you have to play with. You have to play by these rules to locate here. It’s going to be this setback, it’s going to be this fire rating, suppression system, it’s going to be this zoning district, it’s going to be this noise level or lower. You adopt the rules that you are comfortable with and balancing that with still permitting a form of that business operating if they want to play by those rules,” Zollinger said. If the city cannot develop an ordinance and rules within the 180-day moratorium, that moratorium can be extended, but it cannot be extended indefinitely. In answer to a question from the audience, Zollinger said a company could sue the city for delaying its decision via repeated or indefinite moratoriums on an application to locate a BESS facility or data center. “I would rather that the council and the city be proactive in saying we want to make sure we can address this. Better to be proactive and address it than be reactive,” Zollinger said. The Plan Commission will next meet at 6:30 p.m. Thursday, Oct. 22.

Kyivstar told Interfax Ukraine news agency that its head office in Kyiv had been hit, but there were no casualties. Russia's Defense Ministry also said on Sunday it hit a data center belonging to Vodafone Ukraine, the country's second-largest cell network provider. Vodafone Ukraine did not respond to a request for comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Russia struck a data center in Kyiv twice on Sunday morning, wounding two children and an adult. Moscow has also hit data centers belonging to Ukrainian internet providers over the past week, causing service outages to about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the surrounding region, according to Ukraine's Digital Ministry. "Russia has targeted major Ukrainian data centers, seeking to disrupt the flow of information. Rapid alerts about missile and drone threats are essential — they save lives," Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X on Wednesday. artigo.texto: A Rede Agroflorestal do Vale do Paraíba realiza em 26 de setembro, das 14h às 18h, em Pindamonhangaba, um seminário para cobrar debate público sobre o centro de processamento de dados de R$ 5 bilhões anunciado para o município pelo prefeito Ricardo Piorino (PL) e pela Riverhook Village 18. O ponto sensível é material. O projeto promete ocupar mais de 500 mil metros quadrados, mas a empresa aparece em cadastros públicos com capital social de R$ 100 mil, valor equivalente a 0,002% do investimento anunciado. A companhia foi constituída em novembro de 2025, cinco meses antes do anúncio. O encontro, chamado “A nuvem tem endereço: data centers e a defesa das águas e da vida no Vale do Paraíba”, será realizado no Sindicato dos Metalúrgicos de Pindamonhangaba, Moreira César e Roseira. A entrada é gratuita, com inscrição prévia, e a programação inclui participantes de São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Ceará e Rio Grande do Sul. Promessa bilionária exige prova pública A Prefeitura de Pindamonhangaba divulgou em abril que a cidade receberia um dos maiores centros de processamento de dados do Brasil, instalado na Via Estrutural. O anúncio foi feito em 28 de abril com Piorino, o sócio-fundador da Riverhook, Fabio Gordon, e o secretário municipal de Desenvolvimento Econômico, Marcelo Martuscelli. Pela apresentação oficial, o investimento começa em R$ 5 bilhões e pode chegar a R$ 10 bilhões em fases seguintes, com obras previstas para outubro de 2026, operação em junho de 2028, mais de mil vagas durante a construção e cerca de 150 empregos diretos depois que o centro entrar em funcionamento. A diferença entre a promessa de R$ 5 bilhões e o capital social registrado não prova, por si só, incapacidade financeira da empresa. Projetos de infraestrutura podem ser financiados por fundos, bancos, parceiros e estruturas societárias que não aparecem no capital inicial de uma limitada. Essa ressalva não elimina a pergunta central. Antes de o poder público tratar o empreendimento como desenvolvimento contratado, Pindamonhangaba precisa saber quem financia, quem opera, quais garantias foram apresentadas e quais obrigações ficarão para o município se a obra avançar. Água, energia e território entram na conta A Rede Agroflorestal afirma que ainda não foi apresentado publicamente um estudo capaz de medir os efeitos do projeto sobre abastecimento de água, rede elétrica, ruído, ocupação territorial e comunidades próximas. O sindicato informou que o debate também tratará de possível escassez hídrica, aumento nas contas de luz, quedas de energia e baixa geração de empregos permanentes. A própria Prefeitura reconheceu em 2026 problemas de abastecimento no município e registrou 2025 como o ano mais seco em 11 anos, com 803 milímetros de chuva acumulada, segundo balanço da Defesa Civil municipal. A chegada de uma infraestrutura intensiva em energia e refrigeração entra, portanto, em uma cidade que já discute segurança hídrica. O projeto divulgado para Pindamonhangaba prevê carga energética inicial de 150 megawatts, com possibilidade de expansão para 300 megawatts, além de mais de 150 empregos diretos após o início da operação. A escala da potência ajuda a explicar por que o seminário desloca a discussão do marketing tecnológico para a infraestrutura real que sustenta a chamada nuvem. O precedente do Ceará pesa no debate O caso de Caucaia, no Ceará, deve aparecer como alerta. Em 10 de setembro de 2026, o Ministério Público Federal e a Defensoria Pública da União ajuizaram ação civil pública para impedir que o Data Center Pecém inicie operação antes de consulta ao povo indígena Anacé e da elaboração de Estudo de Impacto Ambiental e Relatório de Impacto Ambiental. A ação aponta que o empreendimento cearense, conhecido como centro de dados do TikTok, prevê cerca de 70 hectares, duas edificações principais, 120 geradores a diesel, subestação elétrica, captação de água subterrânea e impactos potenciais sobre água, sistema elétrico, ruído e comunidades. Reportagens sobre o processo registraram que a previsão de consumo diário de água saltou de 19,7 mil litros na licença prévia para 144 mil litros na licença de instalação. A diferença mostra por que a transparência precisa vir antes da licença, e não depois que a obra já virou fato consumado. Incentivo federal não substitui controle local O debate ocorre poucos dias depois da sanção da Lei 15.504, de 15 de setembro de 2026, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, o Redata. O instituto também cobra regras para consumo de água, ocupação territorial e distância mínima de comunidades e áreas residenciais. artigo.texto: ERS Energy Sdn Bhd has surpassed 1.5 GWh of cumulative utility-scale Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity across Southeast Asia, with the company securing the majority of its portfolio over the past 12 months. The milestone includes a 520 MWh BESS project for ACEN in Zambales, Philippines, which ERS Energy described as a landmark project. The company has also secured two utility-scale projects under Malaysia’s inaugural Battery Energy Storage Programme (MyBeST), with the projects having a combined capacity of 800 MWh. ERS Energy said the latest project wins build on its expansion across strategic markets in Southeast Asia. The company combines project structuring, financing frameworks and energy storage system integration capabilities as part of its utility-scale BESS business. The company has expanded from its earlier focus as a solar engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning (EPCC) specialist into utility-scale energy storage development and system integration. Its growing BESS portfolio is aimed at supporting grid stability and addressing the intermittency associated with renewable energy generation. Jonathan Kan, Managing Director of ERS Energy, said the company’s 1.5 GWh milestone reflects its execution capabilities and the confidence of its partners, lenders and regional grid operators. ERS Energy said renewable energy expansion across Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam and Australia is increasing the need for grid flexibility and energy storage. The company’s BESS portfolio is intended to provide grid services and support the deployment of renewable energy across the region. The company said it works with technology partners and financial institutions to support utility-scale storage projects from design and project financing through to grid synchronisation. artigo.texto: Vena Energy has announced that its NRE Nakagawa 2 Battery Storage Project, with an awarded capacity of 46.828 MW, has been selected under Japan’s FY2025 Long-Term Decarbonised Power Source Auction (LTDA) conducted by the Organisation for Cross-regional Coordination of Transmission Operators (OCCTO). The battery storage project is currently under development in Japan and is designed as a grid-connected battery energy storage system (BESS) near Matsumoto City in Nagano Prefecture. The LTDA scheme was introduced in fiscal year 2023 to support Japan’s target of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. The programme provides long-term revenue certainty for selected decarbonised power projects, supporting investment and helping developers recover development and capital costs. The selection of the NRE Nakagawa 2 project expands Vena Energy’s battery storage portfolio in Japan. It follows the commencement of commercial operations at the company’s Hikone Battery Storage Project in 2025. According to Vena Energy, battery storage deployment is expected to play a role in managing the intermittency of renewable generation and improving the efficient utilisation of electricity as Japan increases its reliance on decarbonised power sources. Raul Rienda, Head of Japan at Vena Energy, said the selection of the project under the FY2025 LTDA would support efforts to strengthen the reliability and resilience of Japan’s power system. Vena Energy said it will continue to engage with local communities and consider environmental factors as it advances the NRE Nakagawa 2 project. The company is developing the project as part of its broader focus on battery storage and renewable energy infrastructure in Japan, supporting the country’s long-term decarbonisation objectives. O presidente ucraniano, Volodymyr Zelenskiy, afirmou que a Rússia atacou um data center em Kiev duas vezes na manhã deste domingo, ferindo duas crianças e um adulto. Moscou também atingiu data centers pertencentes a provedores de internet ucranianos na semana passada, causando interrupções no serviço para cerca de 100 mil residências em Kiev e na região circundante, de acordo com o Ministério Digital da Ucrânia. artigo.texto: FORT MCMURRAY — As Fort McMurray-Lac La Biche MLA and Alberta Energy and Minerals Minister Brian Jean returns from an international carbon capture summit in London, the federal government is exploring a new framework that could give Canadian companies greater access to international carbon markets. Environment, Climate Change and Nature Minister Julie Dabrusin announced Wednesday Ottawa is examining how Canada could trade internationally transferred mitigation outcomes, or ITMOs, under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The system could allow Canadian companies to participate in international carbon markets by generating or trading emissions reductions and removals, including through carbon removal technologies and nature-based solutions. The announcement comes as Jean returns from the 2026 Carbon Capture Global Summit, where he promoted Alberta’s carbon capture, utilization and storage sector to international government, industry, finance and technology representatives. “Alberta is the global leader in CCUS,” Jean said in a statement ahead of the trip. “I’m proud to represent a province dedicated to responsible energy development.” Jean said broader deployment of carbon capture will depend on collaboration among governments, researchers and industry. Ottawa says an ITMO framework could help attract investment into projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions while creating opportunities for Canadian technology and expertise. “The trading of ITMOs under the Paris Agreement can unlock greater global climate action by making it easier to transfer emission reductions and removals between countries,” Dabrusin said. “This is about turning our natural advantages and homegrown climate innovation into investment, good jobs, and new export opportunities.” Under Article 6, countries can co-operate in meeting national climate targets, including through international carbon markets. The federal government says any credits traded as ITMOs would have to meet requirements designed to ensure emissions reductions or removals are additional, verified and not counted by both the exporting and importing country. Ottawa says it will consult provinces and territories, Indigenous organizations and other partners as it develops a possible Canadian approach. Jean’s London trip also included meetings with European and industry stakeholders as Alberta seeks to attract investment, expand energy market access and promote its carbon capture sector.

artigo.texto: BYD says a long-awaited upgrade to electric vehicle batteries is finally getting close to real-world use. The world's largest EV maker is preparing to take solid-state technology out of the lab and put it into vehicles people can actually drive. BYD's Solid-State Battery For EV Is Nearly Ready BYD's executive vice president Stella Li said the company sits in the leading position in the solid-state battery race, with plans to introduce its first EV powered by the new technology in 2027. The company has been researching solid-state batteries since 2013, and by 2023 it had shown that mass production was feasible. Testing of prototype cells rated at 20 and 60 ampere-hours followed throughout 2024, laying the groundwork for the move from lab proof to commercial manufacturing. The batteries rely on sulfide-based electrolytes, which offer higher conductivity and better safety than the liquid setups found in most EVs today. BYD's battery business, FinDreams, aims to begin producing them in limited batches in 2027 before ramping up toward mass production by 2030 (via CarNewsChina). BYD Solid-State EV Battery For Open Roads The first vehicles to get the technology will likely come from BYD's premium brands, including Denza, Yangwang, and Fangchengbao, before it trickles down to higher volume models. According to Engadget, the first two years are expected to serve as a demonstration phase with limited production. Early estimates suggest cars using these batteries could reach roughly 800 kilometers, or nearly 500 miles, on a single charge, with some observers speculating the range could eventually pass 1,000 kilometers. Reports point to energy density targets of up to 400 watt-hours per kilogram, compared with roughly 160 to 180 for BYD's current lithium iron phosphate batteries and around 300 for the best nickel manganese cobalt cells. Charging times as short as 12 minutes have also been mentioned in early projections. Other Brands Have Been Working on the Tech BYD is not alone in chasing the technology. Chery has said its prototypes reach 400 watt-hours per kilogram and aims to push that to 500, while Toyota, Honda, and Mercedes Benz are also developing their own solid-state solutions. Even so, BYD executives describe the company as out in front, and its CTO has said scaled production could eventually bring solid-state costs down to parity with conventional liquid electrolyte batteries. BYD expects the technology to reach more affordable models between 2030 and 2032 as production costs come down. The company also does not see its Blade batteries, built on lithium iron phosphate, disappearing anytime soon, with its chief scientist projecting they will stay important for budget-friendly EVs for the next 15 to 20 years. Why Are Solid-State Batteries a Big Deal? Most EVs today run on lithium-ion batteries, where charged particles called ions move through a liquid medium. Solid-state batteries swap that liquid for a solid layer, which improves safety because EV batteries are known for catching fire, and the flammable liquid inside conventional cells is often part of the problem. A solid electrolyte offers better thermal stability, lowering the risk of fires and leaks. Solid-state cells also pack more energy into the same space, which means longer range and more compact battery packs. Sulfide electrolytes in particular are described as longer-lasting and more stable than liquid options, giving the batteries a more durable life and faster charging. The technology is difficult to build, since ions move through liquids more easily than solids and gaps between solid layers can raise electrical resistance.

artigo.texto: Omaha residents talk data center regulations amid rapid AI expansion OMAHA, Neb. (WOWT) - As a new CNN poll finds nearly nine in 10 Americans fear AI surpassing human intelligence, the debate over regulating the industry is hitting home in Nebraska. At a meeting led by the Nebraska Sierra Club, advocates focused on the benefits and drawbacks of AI, calling for regulations to ensure long-term sustainability and harm reduction when it comes to data center growth. The organization acknowledged data centers help supply modern digital expansion, but said the accelerating demand for them is driving a spike in both their size and number. Ken Winston, chapter director of the Nebraska Sierra Club, said more electrical use is increasing rates for residents near data centers. He said the centers can also put a strain on the water supply and cause noise and light pollution. While data centers are not going anywhere, Winston said, they need regulation — and pausing data center builds can buy communities time. “A moratorium shouldn’t be just, oh my goodness, what are we going to do now? And we go and hide our heads in the sand, and wait a year, and then all of a sudden, the issue is in front of the county board and the planning commission,” Winston said. “They need to use this time to develop some regs, some standards to protect themselves.” Winston added that developers should have to disclose projected electrical demand, water usage, and greenhouse gas emissions before projects are approved. He also emphasized the importance of having community benefit agreements, where companies that build data centers are required to provide ongoing, agreed-upon resources to the communities that surround them. Google has built several data centers in Nebraska. The company said it has three projects in the works to steward local water and recharge groundwater. -- Watch breaking news unfold on our livestream. artigo.texto: Handwritten on pieces of cut-up poster paper, Amy Wright made her case that members of her city council have allegedly voted on issues they had a financial stake in and violated open meetings laws along the way. Tensions are ratcheting up in Carroll County, where two different data center developers are planning hyperscale projects in the rural community of 11,000 people. One project in particular, pitched by Louisville-based Poe Companies and PowerHouse Data Centers, has drawn the ire of local residents after the project went public a year after Carrollton city officials signed land deals with the company. Now, community members, including Wright, are filing ethics complaints saying several members of the city council who voted to move forward with that secret land deal should have abstained from the vote because they or an immediate family member works for Louisville Gas & Electric and Kentucky Utilities, which stands to profit from the energy-intensive data center. KPR obtained financial disclosures filed by each city council member via open records request — they are sparse, but at least two members noted LG&E-KU as a source of income for themselves or their spouse. Multiple Kentucky communities have been divided over hyperscale data center concerns, with opponents accusing officials of not keeping the community’s best interests in mind. Poe and PowerHouse are building a center in Louisville, where anti-data center activists have filed numerous complaints, including with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Office of Civil Rights. In Mercer County, activists uncovered emails showing an LG&E-KU employee in public office pushing other officials to support a controversial data center project. Proponents of data centers argue they would pay huge dividends to local governments through taxes to fund better schools, roads and more. The Carroll County Ethics Commission heard one set of complaints on Sept. 17 — several anti-data center activists and representatives of council members accused of violating the ethics code attended the hearing. After coming out of a lengthy closed discussion, Ethics Commission member Zach Spencer addressed the room of waiting community members. The commission voted to table the complaint over the financial conflicts, but moved forward with another complaint, and Spencer said they would open a formal investigation into “the alleged misconduct [and] required disclosure of withheld records.” “I want to air this out. I don’t want to keep coming back in for more and more complaints,” Spencer said. “I want everything. I want it out in the open.” Community concerns to be aired out Two days before the county ethics commissions met, the Carrollton City Council was scheduled to start the process of opting-out of those very ethics rules and “create its own ethics commission.” According to multiple people present at that public meeting, Mayor Robb Adams decided not to move forward with the reading and did not explain why it was on the agenda. Anastasia Coots, who lives in Carrollton and has previously clashed with Adams during her stint on the city’s Planning and Zoning Board, said she believes the council has violated multiple state and local ethics laws. “This is so much bigger than just a data center,” Coots said. “All of those people that voted and the mayor and the Carrollton Utilities Commission are beholden to the actual city to do anything in the best financial interest of the city, so when they went into executive session and signed an [agreement] with Poe, it actually only benefited Poe.” She has submitted complaints to various law enforcement agencies, including the commonwealth attorney’s office. She and Wright allege that multiple members of the Carrollton City Council have conflicts with LG&E-KU — they say one is a current employee, one is retired with a KU pension, and another has a son working with KU. Another council member’s husband got a job with the company after voting in favor of the land deal. Kentucky Public Radio asked for comment from the council’s lawyer, each council member allegedly tied to KU, but did not receive a response in time for publication. In a statement to KPR, LG&E-KU spokesperson Drew Gardner said the company has not reviewed the complaint. He said the company “has an obligation” to serve businesses seeking to locate in the area and have established procedures for doing so. “This project is no exception, and a connection to LG&E and KU gives no one special standing in that process,” Gardner said. “Because the review is ongoing, we won’t speculate about the allegations.” The Carroll County code of ethics specifically calls on officers with a prohibited financial interest to submit the “precise nature and value of the interest, in writing.” The code says that officers are prohibited from participating in public duties that present a “substantial conflict” to the business interests of themselves or “any immediate family member.” “The officer or employee shall refrain from taking any action with respect to the matter that is the subject of the disclosure,” the ethics code reads. As Wright showed me her handwritten complaints in the Carrollton Public Library, she explained that she isn’t trying to wage war against the city council, but she also doesn’t want this data center coming to her community. She said she’s glad the ethics commission is taking her complaints seriously and is interested in a “fair and impartial review.” “I'm glad that they're willing to just take a step back, look at all of the facts together, and make a determination on it,” Wright said. The ethics commission’s chair recused himself from the committee hearing — he too is a retired employee of KU. Spencer, who took his place to lead the meeting, read a lengthy open records request he was making to the city. It’s the start of the group's investigation into how the council came to enter a contract with Poe to sell hundreds of acres of land, near residential proper

artigo.texto: The next generation of data centers is changing more than how much electricity utilities must supply. It is also changing the speed, concentration and uncertainty of load growth. This demand is arriving amid transmission constraints, lengthy interconnection timelines and competition for grid capacity. Artificial intelligence is creating large, power-dense loads while also giving utilities tools to automate studies, analyze data and plan faster. That dual role was central to Siemens Grid Software’s webinar, Planning the grid at the speed of AI: From interconnection queues to grid readiness, featuring experts from Siemens, NVIDIA and Dominion Energy. Utilities need more infrastructure, but also smarter, faster and more collaborative planning. AI factories are changing the scale of demand Traditional data centers hosted enterprise applications and delivered computing and storage services. AI factories create value through model training and inference. As AI advances toward reasoning models and physical AI systems, its computing and electricity requirements are rising dramatically According to NVIDIA’s webinar remarks, traditional data center racks typically consume 15 to 25 kilowatts. Current AI infrastructure can require approximately 230 kilowatts per rack, while future systems could approach one megawatt per rack. For utilities, this is not incremental growth. Large loads may cluster geographically and seek service much faster than generation, transmission and distribution infrastructure can be planned, permitted and built. The grid is part of the AI technology stack As NVIDIA observed during the webinar, energy has become part of the AI technology stack. AI cannot operate without reliable electricity, making power availability a strategic factor in where AI infrastructure is developed. Utilities, regulators, system operators, developers, technology providers and customers must coordinate earlier on project certainty, ramp schedules, location, reliability and potential load flexibility. Dominion Energy’s Northern Virginia experience reinforced that integrating large loads is not solely a utility challenge. Stakeholders must align timelines and assumptions early. Planning must account for uncertainty Deterministic forecasts alone become less effective when planners face many possible futures. An AI facility may be delayed, resized, relocated, or phased. Its load profile may change as technology evolves, while renewable output, electrification, distributed resources and transmission constraints add variables. Utilities should complement deterministic studies with scenario-based and probabilistic planning. Key considerations include project probability and timing, load ramp rates, hourly and seasonal demand, generation and transmission availability, storage performance, flexible-load participation, behind-the-meter resources and permitting timelines. The goal is not to predict one future perfectly, but to identify decisions that remain sound across many futures. Flexibility could change the equation Some AI workloads may be more flexible than commonly assumed. Certain training processes could be shifted, throttled, or scheduled for different times or locations, although inference and other time-sensitive applications may have strict availability requirements. Even partial flexibility could reduce stress during constrained periods, improve use of existing assets and potentially defer selected investments. Options include workload scheduling, demand response, battery storage and phased energization. Utilities cannot assume flexibility. They need dependable information about which workloads can move, response speed, duration and operational limits. Behind-the-meter generation may accelerate projects, but it raises fuel, permitting, reliability, market and economic questions. AI can help utilities plan for AI Planning teams are evaluating more interconnection requests, operating conditions and investment scenarios, often without equivalent growth in engineering resources. Automation and AI-enabled workflows can expand analytical capacity by handling repeatable tasks, supporting data analysis and helping planners focus on higher-value engineering decisions. Faster simulation, improved data integration and interoperable platforms can shorten study cycles and create a consistent view of assumptions and results. Combined with probabilistic methods, AI can expand scenario analysis without compromising engineering rigor. The objective is not to replace engineers, but to give them the speed, scale and information to plan across more possible futures. Preparing for the AI factory era Utilities must preserve reliability, safety and affordability while becoming more agile and growth-oriented. Physical reinforcement will remain necessary, but building alone is not enough. Utilities must also use existing capacity more effectively, improve data quality, automate repeatable work and evaluate uncertainty systematically. AI factories make the urgency visible, but the implications extend beyond data centers. Electrification, renewable integration and distributed resources are increasing grid complexity. AI is creating part of the challenge, but it can also be part of the solution. Utilities that recognize both sides will be better positioned to support economic growth while maintaining reliable, resilient and affordable service. Watch Planning the grid at the speed of AI: From interconnection queues to grid readiness on demand to hear experts from Siemens, NVIDIA and Dominion Energy discuss how utilities can prepare for AI-driven load growth.
