artigo.texto: Advait Battery Ecosystem Private Limited, a subsidiary of BSE and NSE listed Advait Energy Transitions Limited, has entered into a Master Supply Agreement with HiTHIUM for the supply of lithium iron phosphate battery cells. The agreement will support Advait’s planned 2.5 GWh annual capacity cell to container Battery Energy Storage System assembly facility in Gujarat. HiTHIUM to supply 314 Ah LFP cells Under the agreement, HiTHIUM will supply its 314 Ah lithium iron phosphate prismatic cells to Advait. The arrangement is structured to support cell offtake of up to 1 GWh over the next year. It is expected to create a high volume supply framework as Advait scales domestic BESS assembly for utility scale, commercial and industrial and renewable energy applications in India. The cells will form part of Advait’s planned capabilities covering module and pack assembly, container integration and system commissioning. Advait building domestic BESS manufacturing capacity Advait’s 2.5 GWh BESS cell to container assembly facility is under development in Gangad, Gujarat. The facility is scheduled to begin commercial production soon. The company said the plant is being developed to serve grid scale energy storage, commercial and industrial applications and renewable energy integration projects. The Hithium agreement will provide a supply framework as the facility moves towards commercial production and volume manufacturing. Partnership strengthens integrated energy storage platform Advait said the agreement is part of its strategy to build an integrated battery energy storage manufacturing ecosystem in India. The company has also entered into a strategic collaboration with Adaptive Engineering for engineering design, Energy Management System architecture, PLC and SCADA systems and integration capabilities. With the latest agreement, Advait aims to combine cell sourcing, engineering, module and pack assembly, container integration and system commissioning under its domestic BESS platform. Advait Energy Transitions expands clean energy portfolio Advait Energy Transitions is a Gujarat based power and renewable energy company. Its portfolio includes battery energy storage manufacturing, green hydrogen project development, electrolyser manufacturing, fuel cell manufacturing and clean energy EPC services. The Hithium agreement supports the group’s wider expansion across energy transition technologies and related infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Another data center developer is eyeing land just outside of Lincoln By Maddie Ames , Reporter Sept. 25, 2026, 6 a.m. · More than 560 acres on the edge of Northwest Lincoln are being optioned to a Nevada solar and data center developer, according to records obtained by Nebraska Public Media News. It's the latest in a string of purchase options taken out by data centers in Lancaster County. There’s Monolith and Stark Power data centers just outside of Hallam in southern Lancaster County. And there’s the Google data center near Interstate 80 and North 56th Street that is operating, but still under construction. The most recent purchase option lists Larry Coffey of Lincoln optioning his property to “Coffee Grounds Data LLC.” And while that LLC's name is vague, the purchase option lists Ricardo Graf, the chief development officer for Arevia Power. There’s a similar listing like that in Mayes County, Oklahoma. In a purchase option from December 2025, the grantor “Rock Creek Land & Cattle” optioned land to “Rock Creek Data LLC.” Graf’s name is mentioned there, too. Arevia is a utility-scale solar developer. It’s also gotten into data center development – including the proposed 3,700-acre data center outside of Boise, Idaho. Its subsidiary company, Rhea Data, is looking to build Idaho’s largest data center, with around a 600-megawatt capacity. Coffey confirmed the option with Nebraska Public Media News, saying he was approached earlier in the year about his land. He added that the developers are eyeing the land for a data center. In a response to Nebraska Public Media News, Graf said the company "Coffee Grounds Data LLC" is evaluating the property as part of an "early-stage site diligence process." "Given how preliminary everything is, there isn’t much additional project-specific information we can responsibly provide at this point," Graf said in his statement. He added that this early in the process, a development plan hasn't been determined. An option is essentially an agreement that gives the buyer the right – but not an obligation – to buy the land within a certain timeframe for an agreed-upon price. This option is for four years. The land option comes after a long silence among Lancaster County Commissioners on data centers. They only spoke up recently, after concerns continued from Hallam residents about Monolith’s and Stark Power’s plans. Initially, commissioner Matt Schulte proposed a moratorium while studies are done to examine future data centers in the county. However, the board halted plans to vote on a potential moratorium after learning that Bold Education — or Bold Nebraska, a political advocacy group founded by Nebraska Democratic party chair Jane Kleeb — had applied for a zoning code text amendment that would address the issue. Now, the board is creating a data center task force to mull possible regulations. It’s set to give its recommendations by the end of December. County Commissioner Sean Flowerday said earlier this month that any land will need to be zoned as industrial to get a permit to start data center development. And as of right now, that isn’t possible in Lancaster County. “The truth is there already is an effective moratorium in Lancaster County because you only build these things on industrial land…The actual truth is that there's very, very little, there's very few spaces where you could pull a data center or much of anything that was currently zoned industrial out there,” Flowerday said during a Sept. 10 County Board staff meeting. Eighteen counties in the state currently have moratoriums on data center development.

artigo.texto: Em 2026, os parlamentares poderão deixar de cumprir certas regras fiscais ao proporem ou analisarem projetos que concedem benefícios tributários para Data Centers, programas de apoio a pessoas com câncer e com deficiência, áreas de livre comércio da Região Norte e resseguradoras brasileiras. É o que prevê a Lei Complementar 237, sancionada no dia (15.09.2026) pela Presidência da República, com um veto, e publicada no Diário Oficial da União. Criação de exceções às regras fiscais para setores determinados teve apoio do Executivo Entre as regras dispensadas para as propostas que reduzem tributos, estão: Criação de metas para o incentivo fiscal; Avaliação de seu custo-benefício; Limite em 2% do PIB. Várias dessas exigências haviam sido criadas em 2025 para frear o avanço de renúncias fiscais (cortes de impostos) e outras vantagens específicas para certos setores. A nova lei tem origem no Projeto de Lei Complementar (PLP) 74/2026, relatado no Senado pelo senador Camilo Santana (PT-CE). No relatório, Camilo diz que a medida é necessária para o “atendimento de demandas setoriais legítimas”. Ele lembra que tais incentivos fiscais devem estar previstos no Orçamento e que serão considerados para a meta do resultado primário — cálculo que monitora a saúde das contas públicas. Regras dispensadas Ao analisar os incentivos, os parlamentares poderão desconsiderar a vedação de ampliar isenções fiscais (prevista na Lei de Diretrizes Orçamentárias de 2026) e o limite de 2% do PIB para o total de benefícios tributários federais. Para 2026, o teto equivale a cerca de R$ 274,2 bi, segundo cálculo de 2025 do Planalto. Os senadores e deputados também ficam dispensados de: Estimar o impacto orçamentário-financeiro; Reavaliar a receita prevista na lei orçamentária; Prever a arrecadação do mesmo valor de outra forma, como compensação; Estimar a quantidade de beneficiários, entre outras normas. A maior parte das restrições flexibilizadas estavam previstas na Lei Complementar 224, de 2025, que determinou um corte linear de 10% em benefícios fiscais federais. Ela é fruto de discussões encabeçadas pelo Executivo para rever os valores que deixa de arrecadar. Em 2025, a Receita Federal projetou que os incentivos fiscais poderiam chegar a R$ 612,8 bilhões em 2026. Beneficiadas A norma viabiliza o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), sancionado nesta quarta-feira (16.09.2026) para estimular a instalação desses estabelecimentos no país, principalmente os que tenham como foco a computação em nuvem e a inteligência artificial (IA). Os Data Centers (locais que guardam os sistemas de computação de uma empresa) são considerados estratégicos e cada vez mais demandados no mundo, segundo especialistas ouvidos no Senado. As novas regras também abarcam os seguintes incentivos fiscais: do Programa Nacional de Apoio à Atenção Oncológica (Pronon) e do Programa Nacional de Apoio à Atenção da Saúde da Pessoa com Deficiência (Pronas/PCD). Criados em 2012, os programas permitem deduzir doações do Imposto de Renda; às empresas habilitadas nas áreas de livre comércio, atualmente localizadas no Acre, Amapá, Amazonas, Rondônia e Roraima. Com menos impostos, o regime tributário busca impulsionar a economia de cidades fronteiriças; às resseguradoras locais (sediadas no Brasil), com relação à desoneração de Imposto sobre a Renda das Pessoas Jurídicas e da Contribuição Social sobre o Lucro Líquido. A resseguradora é uma empresa que funciona como “seguro das seguradoras”, assumindo parte dos riscos de seus negócios. Veto O governo federal vetou trecho que livrava municípios de até 65 mil habitantes de comprovar que não havia atraso nas suas dívidas com a União para receber transferências voluntárias de recursos federais. Atualmente 90,5% dos 5.570 municípios se enquadrariam na regra, segundo estimativa de julho do IBGE. Para o Planalto, a medida desincentivaria a boa gestão dos recursos públicos. artigo.texto: Rússia ataca maior operadora de telefonia móvel da Ucrânia e atinge data centers Cerca de 100 mil residências em Kiev tiveram os serviços interrompidos Internacional|Da Reuters LEIA AQUI O RESUMO DA NOTÍCIA Produzido pela Ri7a - a Inteligência Artificial do R7 A Rússia atacou neste domingo (27) a sede da Kyivstar, maior operadora de telefonia móvel da Ucrânia, informou a empresa à mídia local, enquanto Moscou seguia com bombardeios a data centers e infraestrutura de comunicações ucranianos. A Kyivstar informou à agência de notícias Interfax Ucrânia que sua sede em Kiev havia sido atingida, mas não houve vítimas. O Ministério da Defesa da Rússia também informou neste domingo que atingiu um data center pertencente à Vodafone Ucrânia, segunda maior operadora de telefonia celular do país. A Vodafone Ucrânia não respondeu a um pedido de comentário. O presidente ucraniano, Volodymyr Zelensky, afirmou que a Rússia atacou um data center em Kiev duas vezes na manhã deste domingo, ferindo duas crianças e um adulto. Veja Também Moscou também atingiu data centers pertencentes a provedores de internet ucranianos na semana passada, causando interrupções no serviço para cerca de 100 mil residências em Kiev e na região circundante, de acordo com o Ministério Digital da Ucrânia. “A Rússia tem como alvo os principais data centers ucranianos, buscando interromper o fluxo de informações. Alertas rápidos sobre ameaças de mísseis e drones são essenciais -- eles salvam vidas”, escreveu o ministro das Relações Exteriores da Ucrânia, Andrii Sybiha, no X na quarta-feira. artigo.texto: Arcadis innovates with sustainable solutions for data centers: engineering that transforms digital infrastructure. The company is embracing advanced technologies and energy efficiency to build sustainable data centers, reducing environmental impact and driving global digital transformation. São Paulo – As demand for digital infrastructure grows, data center energy consumption and environmental performance are receiving greater attention. With the goal of creating innovative and efficient solutions, Arcadis, a global leader in sustainable design, engineering, and consulting, is adopting technologies that combine sustainability, energy efficiency, and high performance in its projects. With the acceleration of digitalization, data centers can consume up to 50 times more energy than commercial buildings of the same size, accounting for up to 3% of global electricity consumption, according to industry data. Arcadis sees the transition to more sustainable digital infrastructure as both an environmental imperative and a smart business strategy. The company believes it is possible to combine high performance with technological innovation while reducing carbon emissions. “The growing demand for cleaner and more resilient digital infrastructure has driven a true revolution in data center design. At Arcadis, we combine our expertise in engineering and sustainability to support clients in building more efficient, future-ready solutions with a lower environmental impact. Arcadis’ approach to data centers takes a systemic, one-stop-shop view, which also addresses the challenges of electrical connections, water supply, and fiber,” says Isabel Rando, head of industry solutions at Arcadis. Innovative solutions for energy efficiency Arcadis has implemented various technologies to increase data center efficiency and minimize environmental impact. Key solutions include: - Energy and water optimization: Both are fundamental resources for data center operations, particularly in the pursuit of sustainability and net-zero goals. As major priorities for clients in the technology sector, the efficient use of these resources is becoming increasingly essential in data center deployment projects. - Smart environmental monitoring: Technologies that expand the thermal operating range of equipment without compromising durability, in accordance with American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE) guidelines. This approach helps reduce energy consumption in cooling systems. - Use of battery energy storage systems (BESS): Replacing diesel generators with energy storage batteries contributes to data center decarbonization while providing greater efficiency and energy autonomy. Independent and strategic engineering for data centers In addition to technological solutions, Arcadis offers specialized independent engineering and owner’s engineering services, ensuring that projects meet clients’ technical, timeline, financial, and operational objectives. Through a strategic and impartial approach, the company helps protect the owner’s interests while treating sustainability, health, and safety as non-negotiable priorities. It also supports the minimization of technical and financial risks, strategic schedule management to meet project milestones, and alignment with industry best practices and client quality standards. A prime example of how Arcadis applies its innovative solutions is SINES DC in Portugal. With a capacity of 1.2 GW and 100% renewable energy, SINES DC is one of the largest data center campuses in Europe. The facility uses seawater cooling systems, taking advantage of its strategic location on the Portuguese coast to optimize energy efficiency and reduce its carbon footprint. “Arcadis is at the forefront of the transformation of data centers, delivering sustainable and innovative solutions to the challenges of digital transformation. With projects across various regions, such as Latin America and Europe, Arcadis leads the way in creating more efficient, resilient, and environmentally responsible digital infrastructure,” concludes Isabel. Accelerating a positive future for the planet.

artigo.texto: BTR New Material Group Co., Ltd. Leading global supplier of natural graphite anode materials for lithium-ion batteries. According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Natural Graphite Anode Material market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global natural graphite anode material (NGAM) market is positioned for transformative growth over the 2026-2035 forecast period, underpinned by the relentless expansion of lithium-ion battery megafactory capacity for electric vehicles and grid-scale energy storage. As the primary active anode ingredient in most commercial lithium-ion cells, NGAM sits at the core of the energy transition, and its demand trajectory is tightly linked to battery production volumes. China currently hosts over 70% of global NGAM processing capacity, spanning spheronization, purification, and carbon coating, creating a pronounced supply concentration that is reshaping trade policy and investment incentives worldwide. Prices for coated spherical graphite fell 30-40% during the 2023-2024 correction, resetting the pricing base for 2026 and compressing margins while opening volume demand from cost-sensitive battery segments. The market is bifurcating into standard-purity CSPG for LFP batteries and premium grades for high-energy NMC cells, with the former growing faster in tonnage. Environmental compliance costs and synthetic graphite substitution remain key challenges, but the overall outlook points to robust expansion through 2035. The baseline scenario for the natural graphite anode material market anticipates sustained double-digit growth through 2035, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of approximately 18% in volume terms. This outlook assumes continued global EV adoption, supportive government policies, and the gradual diversification of supply chains outside China. Demand will be primarily driven by lithium-ion battery production for electric vehicles, which account for the largest share of NGAM consumption, followed by stationary energy storage systems. The market is expected to see a shift toward higher-purity, coated spherical graphite as battery manufacturers demand improved performance and consistency. Supply-side constraints, including permitting delays and capital intensity for new purification plants outside China, may tighten availability in the short term, but ongoing investments in North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific are expected to alleviate these bottlenecks by the late 2020s. Pricing is forecast to stabilize after the 2023-2024 correction, with gradual increases as demand outpaces supply. The market index, with 2025 as the base year (100), is projected to reach 450 by 2035, reflecting a 4.5-fold expansion. Key risks include accelerated synthetic graphite substitution, slower-than-expected EV adoption, and geopolitical trade disruptions. However, the fundamental demand drivers remain strong, and the market is poised for significant growth. Electric vehicle batteries represent the dominant end-use sector for natural graphite anode material, accounting for the majority of global demand. As automakers ramp up production of EVs to meet emissions targets and consumer demand, the need for anode materials surges. Natural graphite, particularly coated spherical graphite, is favored for its cost advantage and improving performance. Through 2035, this segment will expand as new gigafactories come online in North America, Europe, and Asia. Demand-side indicators include EV sales volumes, battery pack sizes, and the mix of battery chemistries (LFP vs. NMC). The shift toward higher nickel chemistries may slightly reduce graphite intensity per kWh, but overall volume growth remains robust. Major trends include vertical integration by OEMs, localization of supply chains, and the development of fast-charging batteries requiring advanced anode materials. Current trend: Growing rapidly. Major trends: Rapid EV sales growth in China, Europe, and North America, Increasing battery pack sizes for longer range, Shift toward LFP batteries in entry-level EVs, boosting natural graphite demand, Localization of battery supply chains driven by policy incentives, and Development of fast-charging batteries requiring high-performance anodes. Representative participants: Tesla, Volkswagen, General Motors, Ford, BYD, and Hyundai. Grid-scale energy storage systems are a fast-growing end-use sector for natural graphite anode material, driven by the global transition to renewable energy and the need for grid stability. Lithium-ion batteries dominate this segment, and natural graphite anodes offer a cost-effective solution for large-scale storage. Through 2035, demand will be propelled by utility procurement of storage capacity, government mandates for renewable integration, and falling battery costs. Key demand indicators include renewable energy capacity additions, storage duration requirements, and policy support. The segment favors LFP batteries, which use natural graphite anodes, due to their safety and cycle life. Major trends include the rise of long-duration storage, the use of second-life EV batteries, and the development of specialized anode materials for stationary applications. Current trend: Accelerating. Major trends: Rapid growth in renewable energy installations requiring storage, Government auctions and mandates for grid-scale storage, Declining battery costs making storage economically viable, Shift toward LFP chemistry for stationary storage, and Development of long-duration storage technologies. Representative participants: Tesla, Fluence, Sungrow, BYD, LG Energy Solution, and Samsung SDI. artigo.texto: O Grupo Greenvolt, através da Greenvolt Power, a sua área de negócio de energias renováveis utility scale, iniciou a construção do sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) de Siedlce, na Polónia, com uma capacidade de 600 MW / 2,4 GWh. O projeto será a maior instalação BESS do país e um dos maiores da Europa, estando o início da operação comercial previsto para o final de 2027. Siedlce integra a carteira de projetos de armazenamento de energia em baterias da Greenvolt que conta atualmente com 4,6 GW, incluindo cerca de 2,4 GW na Polónia. O armazenamento de energia em baterias está a assumir uma importância cada vez maior na estratégia de crescimento da Greenvolt, abrangendo tanto projetos de grande escala como soluções behind-the-meter para clientes comerciais e industriais em vários mercados europeus, através da Greenvolt Next. “Com Siedlce, estamos mais uma vez a passar dos planos à concretização. O mais importante é construir ativos, criar valor real e reforçar as infraestruturas necessárias para integrar mais energia renovável no sistema. A Polónia é um mercado estratégico para nós e o armazenamento de energia em baterias está a assumir uma importância cada vez maior no nosso crescimento”, afirmou João Manso Neto, CEO do Grupo Greenvolt. Com 600 MW de potência e 2,4 GWh de capacidade de armazenamento, Siedlce proporcionará uma maior flexibilidade ao sistema elétrico polaco, armazenando eletricidade durante períodos de elevada produção de energia renovável e disponibilizando-a quando a procura aumenta. Este sistema contribuirá para a integração da produção eólica e solar e ajudará a equilibrar a oferta e a procura de eletricidade. Siedlce dá continuidade ao crescente histórico da Greenvolt Power no desenvolvimento de projetos de armazenamento de energia em baterias na Polónia. Turośń Kościelna, com 200 MW / 800 MWh, entrou em operação em julho de 2026, enquanto Ełk, também com 200 MW / 800 MWh, deverá entrar em operação comercial no quarto trimestre deste ano. Quando os três projetos estiverem operacionais, disponibilizarão, em conjunto, 1 GW de potência e 4 GWh de capacidade de armazenamento. “Estamos agora a avançar com Siedlce para a fase de construção, com os acordos de fornecimento das baterias e de ligação à rede já estabelecidos. A experiência que adquirimos com Turośń Kościelna e Ełk proporciona-nos uma base sólida para concretizar um projeto desta dimensão, e a nossa prioridade é manter este ritmo e colocar Siedlce em operação até ao final de 2027”, afirmou Weronika Nowak, CEO da Greenvolt Power. O projeto contempla 210 contentores de baterias e 105 contentores de transformadores equipados com sistemas de conversão de energia, permitindo o fluxo de eletricidade entre as baterias e a rede. A Greenvolt Power está a trabalhar com a empresa de engenharia e construção P&Q e com a empresa de energias renováveis e empreiteiro ONDE no desenvolvimento das infraestruturas elétricas do projeto.

artigo.texto: Google’s Grid-Interactive AI Data Centers: From Backup to Grid Partner At Data Center World Power, Google’s Tom Garvens detailed how full-stack design, LVDC power, BESS, and liquid cooling are reshaping hyperscale AI while supporting local grids. AI infrastructure is expanding at an unprecedented pace. Google now processes more than 3 quadrillion AI tokens per month, representing a sevenfold increase in compute demand from May 2025 to May 2026. Meeting this velocity requires innovation in energy efficiency and power delivery. Tom Garvens, vice president of advanced technology innovation at Google, outlined this challenge during a keynote at Data Center World Power 2026 in Houston, held Sept. 21-23. He described Google’s full-stack approach to scaling AI, positioning data centers as active partners in stabilizing local grids. Turning Backup Power into Grid Services To bridge the speed mismatch between rapid AI rollout and multiyear timelines typical for utility capacity expansion, Google has developed energy strategies that transform backup assets into grid-supportive resources, streamline operations during peak demand, make load shaping more intelligent, and prevent disruptive power swings – while supporting utility resilience. Beyond these strategies, Google is reviewing and redesigning the entire AI data center ecosystem – from chip to utility. This includes optimizing for liquid cooling, low-voltage direct current (LVDC) architectures, intelligent algorithms, and facility design. A core pillar of this work is publishing standardized power and facility technology specifications through communities such as the Open Compute Project (OCP), enabling the industry to build interoperable, efficient, and sustainable infrastructure. “Google has tightly coupled vertical integration in AI along with close partnerships with energy providers,” Garvens said. “We develop and design our own data centers, chips, servers, and rack designs. By having control of our entire hardware and software stack, we can optimize these things together for sustainability and energy efficiency.” Powering AI at Gigawatt Scale Google is investing alongside utilities to add grid capacity. That assistance is vital as a gigawatt-class data center campus can comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected chips running a single workload. Google’s approach is twofold: work with utility partners to streamline power delivery and adjust its own hardware and software to be more grid-friendly. “Utilities are [setting] different requirements that we must demonstrate that we can meet,” Garvens noted. “Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Nvidia have come together to define an interface spec on how utilities and hyperscalers can interface with each other.” Battery energy storage systems (BESS) have become critical in Google’s campus designs for onsite energy storage and for buffering rapidly fluctuating workloads. Buffering smooths power and voltage transitions. Backup generators remain in use, but diesel does not scale well to campuses at 1 GW and beyond. BESS are increasingly used to provide standby power, supported by demand-response agreements with utilities for peak shaving. “When peak needs are beyond what we've got power for, we can get that from local storage,” Garvens explained. Rather than competing for constrained capacity in saturated markets, Google has been identifying remote sites with ample land and available power. The company is also considering campus developments in small towns where the data center would be a primary employer, he said. Another design change: Google has moved away from centralized Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) systems, favoring rack-level battery backup operating around 54 VDC. Eliminating an extra AC-DC-AC conversion step yields approximately a 1.5% efficiency gain. “We do all of our power conversion at the top of our racks, where we take our AC down to 54 volts, and then we run DC through our racks; our battery backup also runs at that voltage,” Garvens said. Inside the Rack: 54 VDC Today, 800 VDC Tomorrow Google has introduced changes at the chip, rack, and facility levels, supported by software that can intermix workloads to smooth overall load and make it more predictable. Rack density remains a major challenge. Roadmaps anticipate racks approaching 1 MW each over the next year or two. That necessitates liquid cooling for at least the hotter elements within the racks. Delivering the required current at lower voltages would demand bus bars and cabling with significantly more copper. This calls for a higher distribution voltage. Google is pursuing a gradual migration toward 800 VDC for power distribution, which is expected to take a couple of years to mature. In the meantime, Google has implemented “sidecars” alongside its racks – adjacent power-distribution enclosures that house cabling and power gear – reserving the racks for high-density servers. The tradeoff is floor space. When 800 VDC becomes broadly available, those sidecars can be converted to additional AI server racks. “We're working with the industry on bringing solid-state transformers to maturity,” Garvens said. “We are also continuing to improve our power usage effectiveness [PUE]. We can't ever get to 1.0, but we continue to challenge ourselves to get as close to it as possible.” Workload Shifting and Water-Smart Cooling With dozens of data centers in operation and many more in development, Google can be fluid about where it runs workloads. artigo.texto: India's Battery Manufacturing Ambitions Take Shape Through Lohum's Global Mineral Hunt Lohum's nickel mine hunt reveals India's bigger goal: building a domestic battery manufacturing chain to rival China. Image: Internal Indian critical minerals producer Lohum is pursuing nickel mines in Indonesia and the Philippines, but the acquisition drive is really a proxy for a far larger story: India's attempt to build a domestic, mine-to-manufacturing supply chain for electric vehicle batteries, one that no longer depends on Chinese processing. Founder and chief executive Rajat Verma has set out plans to increase Lohum's nickel production capacity tenfold, from 1,000 to 10,000 metric tonnes a year, within 18 months. Crucially, that expansion isn't only about extraction. Lohum currently produces its nickel entirely by recycling, at its Gujarat plant, and Verma has been candid that the target reflects an ambition to build supply-chain scale rather than a finished production figure. Access to a quality overseas mine, he said, could push the eventual capacity even higher. To fund the plan, the company is seeking to raise around 30 billion rupees (roughly $315 million) through a mix of equity and debt, and is already in talks with investors it has declined to name. What makes this a manufacturing story, not just a mining one, is what Lohum is building around the minerals. In Uttar Pradesh, the company is commissioning a 5,000-tonne-a-year cathode active material plant by March, one of the higher-value manufacturing steps in the battery chain that has historically been dominated by Chinese firms. Alongside it, Lohum is constructing a rare earth magnet plant with 1,200 tonnes of annual capacity, addressing another link in the chain where China's grip on refining, rather than raw deposits, gives it outsized global leverage. The company is also scouting for rare earth sources across Southeast Asia to feed that facility. Lohum's ambitions extend beyond nickel and magnets. Earlier this month it became the first Indian company to ship lithium ore from an overseas asset, having secured rights to ten lithium mining blocks in Zimbabwe with estimated reserves of 30 to 40 million tonnes. The plan is to process that ore into lithium sulphate on-site before shipping it to India, where it will be refined into battery-grade lithium carbonate, again pushing value-added manufacturing onto Indian soil rather than exporting raw material for processing elsewhere. A lithium-ion battery-recycling plant under construction in Sharjah, in partnership with the UAE government, rounds out a strategy that spans extraction, processing, cell-material manufacturing and end-of-life recycling. The timing is pointed. India is racing to expand renewable energy and EV adoption to sustain its economic growth, and is acutely aware that its manufacturing ambitions could stall without secured mineral inputs. That vulnerability has been thrown into sharp relief by recent turmoil in Indonesia's nickel sector: authorities there have sharply cut this year's mining quota for Weda Bay, the world's largest nickel mine, while a fatal fire at a separate Chinese-owned smelter has raised fresh questions over the safety and stability of Indonesian supply. Shanghai nickel futures climbed on the back of the quota cut, underlining how tightly Southeast Asian mine output and Chinese processing capacity remain intertwined, precisely the chokepoint Lohum and, by extension, Indian industrial policy are trying to route around. Beijing, meanwhile, is tightening its own grip. China has unveiled a two-year plan to consolidate its non-ferrous metals industry, aimed at curbing price wars domestically and pushing producers toward higher-value output, a move likely to reinforce, rather than loosen, its dominance of critical mineral processing in the near term. For India, the calculus is clear: owning mines abroad matters less than owning the manufacturing steps in between. Lohum's push into cathode materials, magnets and refining, not just raw nickel and lithium, signals a bet that the real prize in the battery supply chain lies in processing capacity, the very stage where China's advantage is hardest to dislodge. Whether Lohum can secure financing, close mine acquisitions and hit its construction timelines will be an early test of how quickly India's broader industrial strategy can translate mineral access into manufacturing self-sufficiency. artigo.texto: Chillicothe — Mayor Luke Feeney discusses the data center issue and the city’s powers concerning it, as well as other considerations about developments at the former paper mill, in an interview. With concerns about data centers in the news – and friction over allowing the “data hall” proposed by Alignment Engine Inc. on the “Chilpaco Innovation Campus,” I asked him for a sit-down interview. This was an offer to respond to Portia Boulger, founder of “Appalachians Against Data Centers,” who had confronted Feeney and other city officials over the February letter the city sent to the developer of the proposed “data hall.” Feeney declined that response, and instead he and I spoke about the data center and the city. Our interview is below, in three parts. He also soon produced a Facebook Reel video where he more thoroughly explained the city’s powers regarding zoning and other regulations: “This short video lays out the facts and timeline as clearly as possible. My goal being to provide the public with accurate information, explain the process, and make clear the difference between a discussion or inquiry, a zoning interpretation, a formal application, an approval, and actual construction. “Relevant documents can be found at this link.” Chillicothe Council will be meeting in the Main Annex of the Chillicothe and Ross County Public Library, behind 140 South Paint Street, at 7pm on Monday, September 28th. - He won’t comment on stories, but will comment on the process - Developing the “Universal Development Code (UDC, which replaced zoning and other powers) was a 19-month process - Regretfully, the process did not touch on data centers - 2025 was a “roller coaster of a year” - The “zoning certification letter” regarding the possibility of a data center - It was not zoning approval or permission to proceed - Such question and letter is almost always a first step - He wishes the data center issue was as big then as now, because they would have considered it in the UDC - The state was still giving out incentives for data centers, until May 2026 - The city did not get any other communications on the proposed data center between February 20th and the July 2 announcement - The city hired legal counsel to advise them, then created the moratorium - He wishes the moratorium had gone to committee for further review - There are still no formal communications about the proposed data center - There was only the email question from the developer - That means the city can’t say yes or no - City’s rules still cover industrial zones: setback, sound, etc. - The February letter is a typical hypothetical request, the start of a conversation - The Universal Development Code was meant to be updated, and has been once already - No matter what happens, data center regulation will go into the UDC - The February letter was very generic, and was sent in an email so it was dated by the email - Again, not want to address Portia Boulger’s statements - What is his perspective on the proposed paper mill development, including restarting The Chief? - The legal procedurals should be looked at completely separate from community impact by actual proposed development - The city has an absolute obligation to apply zoning rules - There are lots of proposals at the paper mill – he is excited about any opportunity to being back jobs - The proposals are speculative, and can’t be guaranteed - The city needs to be responsible about zoning, but also be supporting about jobs and business development - Zoning is city-wide – rules should be applied the same everywhere; can’t spot zone - Could there be a better solution than what has happened and is proposed? - Considering the speed of purchase, moving equipment in, the energy, conversations – better than expected - April 15th, 2025: his birthday, and paper mill closing announced - Across Ohio, paper mills have been closed for decades - His role is to be excited, supported, enthusiastic, and trust…but verify - He must budget for next year – but can’t budget city revenue on income tax from proposed jobs - 350 more people would mean more income tax – but can’t bet on - The city must be reserved, needs to see receipts - But what about claims of backstage deals and corrupt officials? ; ) - Data centers have been controversial – other than covid, he has not seen anything evolve so quickly - The state was incentivizing data centers through May - Similar to the seeming overpopulation of solar fields and windmills? - There is no solid data – only a presentation – is a proposal, a promise - We are all here to do the best for the city - This topic been so confusing, has created confusion, and challenges in communication has added to the confusion - The goal of the moratorium was to slow down the process and listen to the community - There is excitement around the paper mill redevelopment, but uncertainty around the data center - And then my camera battery died

artigo.texto: A Rússia bombardeou a sede da Kyivstar, maior operadora de telefonia da Ucrânia, e data centers da Vodafone e de provedores locais em Kiev. Os ataques causaram ferimentos em três pessoas e deixaram cerca de 100 mil residências sem acesso à internet. O presidente Volodymyr Zelensky confirmou os impactos na infraestrutura de comunicação, enquanto o governo russo alega que ataca infraestrutura militar e de dados para interromper o fluxo de informações ucraniano. A Rússia atacou neste domingo (27) a sede da Kyivstar, a maior operadora de telefonia móvel da Ucrânia, informou a empresa à mídia local. O ataque ocorreu enquanto Moscou seguia com bombardeios contra data centers e infraestrutura de comunicações ucranianos. A Kyivstar confirmou à agência de notícias Interfax Ucrânia que sua sede em Kiev havia sido atingida, mas não houve vítimas fatais. Ataques à infraestrutura de dados O Ministério da Defesa da Rússia também informou neste domingo que atingiu um data center pertencente à Vodafone Ucrânia, a segunda maior operadora de telefonia celular do país. A Vodafone Ucrânia não respondeu a um pedido de comentário sobre o ocorrido. Impacto nas telecomunicações e alerta internacional - Alvo estratégico: A sede da Kyivstar, líder do mercado de telefonia ucraniano, foi atingida em Kiev. - Vítimas: O presidente Zelensky afirmou que o ataque a um data center feriu duas crianças e um adulto. - Queda de serviço: Cerca de 100 mil residências em Kiev ficaram sem internet após os bombardeios da semana passada. - Segurança digital: O chanceler ucraniano alertou que interromper data centers busca silenciar alertas de mísseis que salvam vidas. - Contexto: Moscou alega atacar infraestrutura militar, mas críticos veem uma ofensiva contra a conectividade civil. O presidente ucraniano, Volodymyr Zelensky, afirmou que a Rússia atacou um data center em Kiev duas vezes na manhã deste domingo, ferindo duas crianças e um adulto. Moscou também atingiu data centers pertencentes a provedores de internet ucranianos na semana passada, causando interrupções no serviço para cerca de 100 mil residências em Kiev e na região circundante, de acordo com o Ministério Digital da Ucrânia. A Rússia tem como alvo os principais data centers ucranianos, buscando interromper o fluxo de informações. Alertas rápidos sobre ameaças de mísseis e drones são essenciais -- eles salvam vidas, escreveu o ministro das Relações Exteriores da Ucrânia, Andrii Sybiha, no X na quarta-feira (23).

artigo.texto: Os carros estão se tornando mais caros, complexos e dependentes de componentes eletrônicos de alta voltagem. Essa combinação pode criar um problema que ameaça a longevidade dos veículos, segundo um alerta de Rupert Hoellbacher, chefe da Bosch Mobility Aftermarket. Ele afirma que manter os carros em circulação por mais tempo dependerá da viabilidade econômica dos consertos, especialmente com a transição para os veículos elétricos. Leia Mais - Comprar um elétrico usado barato é bom negócio ou cilada? - 5 cuidados essenciais antes de comprar carros elétricos usados - IA promete aumentar vida útil da baterias de carros elétricos A lógica é simples: um carro pode durar décadas, mas seu reparo precisa fazer sentido financeiro. Quando um componente principal custa mais para ser substituído do que o valor do próprio veículo, a tendência é que o proprietário o descarte em vez de pagar pelo conserto. Nesse cenário, as baterias dos carros elétricos ganham destaque, pois são o componente mais caro. Embora uma falha não signifique a necessidade de trocar todo o conjunto, os custos podem se tornar proibitivos em um veículo mais antigo e fora da garantia. A própria Bosch destaca que muitos problemas podem ser resolvidos com o reparo de módulos individuais, em vez da substituição completa do pacote de bateria. O mercado de reposição, com oficinas independentes, desempenha um papel crucial. Se essas oficinas puderem diagnosticar e reparar componentes individuais da bateria a preços razoáveis, um carro elétrico pode se manter útil por muito mais tempo. "Se não conseguirmos tornar o reparo ou a substituição da bateria mais atraente financeiramente, a resposta é clara: sim. A expectativa de vida dos carros diminuirá", afirmou Hoellbacher. Ele acrescenta que isso representaria um retrocesso para práticas de negócios sustentáveis, já que muitos componentes são projetados para uma vida útil significativamente mais longa. Manter os carros funcionando deveria ser o objetivo A abordagem de reparar em vez de descartar oferece um benefício ambiental evidente e também um argumento financeiro básico: continue consertando o carro que você já tem. Isso se torna cada vez mais relevante à medida que os preços dos carros novos continuam subindo e a tecnologia embarcada se torna mais cara. Um veículo não se torna inútil apenas por ter centenas de milhares de quilômetros rodados. No entanto, se a bateria ou outro componente principal tiver um custo de substituição muito alto, sua vida útil econômica pode terminar muito antes da mecânica. A questão central é que a eletrificação não deveria significar a criação de carros descartáveis. • Assista aos vídeos do VRUM no YouTube e no Dailymotion!

artigo.texto: Mercado para empresas de data centers que buscam IPOs fica mais desafiador Apesar da pressão, a empresa de dado DayOne segue planos de abrir capital em novembro, após o adiamento do IPO da SB Energy e notícias de uma disputa envolvendo Oracle e Blue Owl A operadora de centrais de processamento de dados DayOne segue em frente com seus planos de abrir capital já em novembro, segundo três fontes a par do assunto, mesmo com o aumento dos juros e os contratempos em outras áreas do ecossistema ameaçando reduzir a janela de oportunidade para as empresas acessarem o mercado de IPOs. A empresa sediada em Cingapura desenvolve e opera centrais de processamento de dados para clientes de computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial. A companhia planeja tornar público seu pedido de registro junto à SEC (Comissão de Valores Mobiliários dos Estados Unidos) em meados de outubro e abrir o capital em novembro, disseram as fontes. A DayOne se recusou a comentar. As intenções de IPO da DayOne surgem após dois contratempos para operadoras de data centers nesta semana: o adiamento do IPO da SB Energy e notícias de uma disputa envolvendo Oracle e Blue Owl, que pode atrasar um grande projeto de centrais de processamento de dados no estado americano do Novo México. O contraste destaca como o mercado de infraestrutura de IA está amadurecendo. Empresas com clientes diversificados e maior visibilidade da demanda ainda podem atrair interesse, enquanto projetos que dependem fortemente de um único cliente de IA ou exigem grandes quantias de capital inicial enfrentam um cobranças maiores dos investidores. “A linha divisória está em saber se a demanda já foi contratada e está em operação, ou se é apenas planejada”, disse Ke Yan, chefe de pesquisa da Shenton Research, empresa de pesquisa de investimentos com sede em Cingapura. Com a energia sendo agora a principal restrição ao setor, os investidores preferem operadoras com fornecimento de eletricidade garantido, uma grande parcela da capacidade contratada já em operação ou em fase de conclusão e contratos “take-or-pay” de longo prazo, disse ele. As exigências dos investidores estão se intensificando à medida que um número crescente de empresas se encaminha para os mercados de capitais, com desenvolvedores e operadores de data centers, incluindo Switch, Vantage Data Centers e CyrusOne, explorando IPOs. Oferta mais diversificada A diversificação geográfica da DayOne e o fato de possuir data centers em operação, e não apenas em desenvolvimento, ajudaram a diferenciá-la de alguns concorrentes aos olhos dos investidores, disse uma das fontes. A empresa, apoiada por investidores como Coatue e Hillhouse, levantou US$ 4,5 bilhões em uma rodada de financiamento série C encerrada em junho. Ela poderia buscar levantar até US$ 5 bilhões na IPO (oferta pública inicial de ações), com uma avaliação de cerca de US$ 20 bilhões, segundo reportagem da Reuters. A companhia garantiu cerca de 2,1 gigawatts de reservas de capacidade e opera na Ásia-Pacífico e Europa, incluindo Malásia, Hong Kong, Japão, Finlândia e Espanha. Enquanto isso, a SB Energy, apoiada pela SoftBank, adiou os planos de divulgar formalmente seu IPO nesta semana, enquanto trabalha para esclarecer questões adicionais da SEC. Também há preocupações dos investidores quanto à avaliação que a empresa busca e à sua dependência da OpenAI como principal cliente, segundo uma das três fontes familiarizadas com o assunto e outra fonte. A SB Energy busca ser avaliada em cerca de US$60 bilhões, acrescentou uma delas. A SB Energy se recusou a comentar. Houve várias negociações entre SoftBank, SB Energy, OpenAI e Nvidia, fornecedora de chips da OpenAI, nos últimos meses. A Nvidia concordou em fornecer uma garantia de até US$ 105 bilhões para ajudar a OpenAI a alugar o data center no estado norte-americano de Ohio que está sendo desenvolvido pela SB Energy, além de investir US$ 1,5 bilhão na SB Energy. A SoftBank, que apoia a OpenAI, está recebendo pedidos de investidores para uma operação de dívida no valor de US$10 bilhões, denominada em dólares, para ajudar a financiar seus investimentos na OpenAI. A empresa já havia obtido um empréstimo garantido pela participação na OpenAI. Invetidores mais exigentes O custo do financiamento da expansão da IA está sob maior pressão. Taxas de juros mais altas tornam mais caro financiar instalações cujos retornos podem levar anos para se concretizar, enquanto os investidores exigem maior visibilidade sobre os clientes e os fluxos de caixa que sustentarão esses investimentos. Para desenvolvedores que dependem de dívida, a receita contratada de clientes com boa capacidade de crédito é crucial para o pagamento dessa dívida, já que eles financiam instalações caras preparadas para IA, incluindo racks de alta densidade e sistemas de resfriamento líquido, disse Neil Bear-Hetherington, diretor de mercados de capitais de data centers para a Ásia-Pacífico da CBRE. Para os desenvolvedores de data centers, isso torna a identidade e a solidez financeira de seus clientes cada vez mais importantes para os investidores que avaliam projetos que podem exigir bilhões de dólares em investimento inicial. Para empresas que se preparam para abrir capital, um mercado de IPO menos tolerante e um maior escrutínio sobre a infraestrutura de IA criam um incentivo para agir rapidamente enquanto a demanda dos investidores ainda existe.

artigo.texto: Situado em Évora, no eixo entre Lisboa e Madrid, e com 1 MW de capacidade instalada, o centro pertencia à portuguesa Decsis, entretanto declarada insolvente, revelou uma fonte contactada pela Lusa. “A aquisição marca a entrada formal da NxN em Portugal, e representa um novo passo no desenvolvimento da sua plataforma de centros de dados” na Ibéria, adiantou a operadora em comunicado, esclarecendo que este centro “presta atualmente serviços a clientes em Portugal e a sua incorporação permite à NxN iniciar a sua atividade no país com base numa infraestrutura já existente e com atividade comercial”. “Évora permite-nos iniciar a nossa atividade em Portugal com base numa infraestrutura já existente, numa localização privilegiada”, afirmou Sergio Riolobos, CEO da NxN Data Centers. No mesmo documento, a NxN partilhou o objetivo de reforçar “a sua estratégia de crescimento a longo prazo em Portugal”, tendo sob análise “novas oportunidades de investimento e desenvolvimento”. “A nossa intenção de investir até 100 milhões de euros nos próximos três anos em Portugal reflete esse compromisso e a nossa confiança no potencial do mercado português”, afirmou Javier Salas, também presidente executivo da NxN Data Centers. No entanto, o investimento anunciado não está associado a um projeto específico, estando a operadora a “analisar novas oportunidades de desenvolvimento e aquisição em Portugal, com o objetivo de expandir progressivamente a sua rede de centros de dados”. Segundo o comunicado, a empresa pretende ampliar a sua plataforma através de novas infraestruturas digitais, desenvolvidas de acordo com os mais altos padrões de sustentabilidade e eficiência da NxN. Fundada em 2023, a NxN tem em desenvolvimento uma rede de centros de dados em Espanha e Portugal, preparada para responder à procura por capacidade de armazenamento e computação, incluindo aplicações de inteligência artificial. A plataforma tem já confirmados dois centros em Espanha, nomeadamente um centro de dados em Madrid que deverá entrar em funcionamento no final de outubro, e um outro projeto em Valência, atualmente em construção. A estes junta-se agora o centro de Évora, o seu primeiro ativo em Portugal. Imagem cedida pela NxN Ddata Centers

artigo.texto: Chery iCaur V27 Long-Range Edition confirmed with 51.2 kWh CATL battery and 300 km EV range Chery has officially disclosed technical specifications for the upcoming iCaur V27 Long-Range Edition ahead of its September 30 market launch in China. Known domestically as the iCar V27, the mid-to-large boxy SUV will use a 51.2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery supplied by CATL, delivering a CLTC-rated pure-electric range of 300 km (approximately 215 km WLTP). The current lineup sells across three variants priced between 169,800 yuan (25,193 USD) and 196,800 yuan (29,200 USD): the rear-wheel-drive Falcon 500 at 169,800 yuan (25,190 USD), the all-wheel-drive Falcon 500 at 182,800 yuan (27,120 USD), and the flagship Falcon 700 at 196,800 yuan (29,200 USD). Battery expands range and charging capability The 51.2 kWh battery represents a 49.3% capacity increase over the 34.3 kWh pack used in existing models. Current trims deliver 210 km CLTC (approximately 150 km WLTP) for rear-wheel drive and 200 km CLTC (approximately 145 km WLTP) for all-wheel drive. The 300 km CLTC rating increases claimed pure-electric range by 90 to 100 km over those versions. Chery states the pack supports 30% to 80% DC fast charging in 17 minutes, while vehicle-to-load (V2L) output increases from 3.3 kW to 6.0 kW. EREV powertrain and existing chassis carry over The range-extended electric vehicle (EREV) retains its dual-motor all-wheel-drive setup, producing 335 kW (449 hp). A dedicated 1.5-litre turbocharged petrol engine serves as the onboard generator. Chery claims peak brake thermal efficiency of 45.79% and a fuel-to-electricity generation rate of 3.71 kWh per litre. The Long-Range Edition retains the V27’s existing dimensions. Built on a unibody chassis, it measures 4,909 mm in length (5,055 mm including the exterior spare wheel), 1,976 mm in width, and up to 1,894 mm in height, with a 2,910 mm wheelbase. Off-road specifications include a 24-degree approach angle, 23-degree departure angle, 600 mm water-fording clearance, and 32,186 N·m/deg torsional rigidity. The cabin continues to use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P cockpit processor with 30 TOPS of AI compute and a voice assistant integrated with DeepSeek AI models. The Falcon 700 retains a roof-mounted watchtower LiDAR and Horizon Robotics Journey 6P computing chip with 560 TOPS for urban and highway pilot navigation assistance. Sales decline precedes Long-Range Edition launch. The battery upgrade arrives as V27 retail sales continue to cool in China. After the SUV rolled off the production line in January and entered the market in March, deliveries peaked at 4,184 units in April before falling for four consecutive months to 1,609 in August. Monthly volume was 3,456 in May, 2,219 in June, and 1,764 in July. The model’s share of total iCar brand deliveries fell from 63.8% in April to 39.3% in August, according to China EV DataTracker. In China’s boxy hybrid SUV market, the V27 competes with Changan’s Deepal G318 (179,900 to 229,900 yuan / 26,690 to 34,110 USD), Jetour Shanhai T2 (159,900 to 209,900 yuan / 23,720 to 31,140 USD), and BYD’s body-on-frame Fang Cheng Bao Bao 5 (179,800 to 239,800 yuan / 26,80 to 35,580 USD).

artigo.texto: A Weg informou que ampliou o projeto de sua nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), em construção em Itajaí (SC). Segundo comunicado ao mercado divulgado nesta sexta-feira (25/9), o investimento total estimado é de R$ 330 milhões e a capacidade anual projetada é de 4 GWh, com início das operações previsto para o segundo semestre de 2027. A companhia afirmou que o projeto, anunciado em fevereiro, foi atualizado para incorporar maior nível de automação e ganhos de eficiência industrial, o que permitirá ampliar a capacidade produtiva. A Weg também citou a expectativa em torno do primeiro Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade de Armazenamento Nacional, previsto para dezembro de 2026, como parte do contexto de expansão do mercado. No comunicado, a empresa destacou que sistemas BESS têm papel relevante na integração de fontes renováveis, como solar e eólica, ao permitir armazenar energia quando há maior disponibilidade e entregá-la quando necessário, contribuindo para estabilidade e eficiência do sistema elétrico. Por Luísa Laval *Conteúdo elaborado com auxílio de inteligência artificial, revisado e editado pela Redação do Broadcast, sistema de notícias em tempo real do Grupo Estado

artigo.texto: While one 25th Assembly District candidate calls for change from the state, the other believes he should return for another term. Incumbent Paul Tittl and Challenger Chris Able debated yesterday on WOMT 100 and WCUB about several topics like data centers, education, and public safety. One question concerned data center tax exemption through the Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation (WEDC) for “projects that involve buildings constructed or rehabilitated to house a group of networked computer servers to centralize the processing, storage, management, retrieval, communication, or dissemination of data and information.” Able said he was concerned about the tax incentives because while data centers bring construction jobs, there aren’t as many career options after a project is completed. “It would be a shame, depending on the size of the incentives, overly large incentives really are just costing us more in tax revenue than they are going to create,” he explained. “So I would want to see what the Legislative Fiscal Bureau projects as the costs of those based upon the size before I would be supportive of them.” Tittl says while in the state assembly, he had voted for a data center tax credit bill for when data centers purchase building materials. He also says data centers can bring a lot to the table. Tittl stated, “They may not bring a lot of high-paying jobs, but they will bring tax revenue to your local communities.” He mentioned a story from the State of Virginia in which he says a community is thriving after getting a data center. Moving to education, both Tittl and Able were asked about Governor Evers changing a number in a previous state budget to fund education for 400 years. Both candidates agree that’s not how it should have been done, and don’t believe any governor should have that power. Tittl spoke out, saying, “I would be in favor of getting rid of that. It was very creative what they did. Let’s just say that. But I don’t like it. It’s not right to tax the people for the next 400 years. Able added, “What we need to do is to figure out exactly what the state share per student would be. The local government then has to make up the rest, and if they want to make up more than that, that’s their choice under local control.” While both agreed, Able said he was not in favor of a constitutional amendment question on the November 3rd General Election because of how it was written. Another question the candidates answered involved Wisconsin’s State Surplus and what should be done with it. Previously, Tittl voted in favor of a deal made with Governor Evers that would have included no tax on tips, special education funding, and rebate checks. “I believe that it was responsible,” he reflected. “Would I want it to go all back to the people, yeah, in some form. It’s going to go back to the people no matter what.” He also added that the state cut taxes and still has surplus while adding to the state’s rainy-day fund. Able sees the surplus differently, saying it’s not that the state collected too much, it’s that the taxes aren’t being spent as intended. “We have allowed the Knowles-Nelson fund to deplete completely,” he commented. “So we haven’t been doing a good job on stewardship of our natural resources. We have underfunded the Department of Natural Resources, so that people have to, when they leave, we can’t even afford to replace them.” On education, when asked about the state’s voucher school program, Tittl said he supports it, adding that it shouldn’t be the government’s job to tell a student where to go. “Above anything else, parents can op for the right school for you,” he mentioned. “They know you better than anyone else as a child. “And the other thing is, the voucher program is not just open to everybody who wants to get in it. It is open to people of a certain poverty level based upon how many people in your family.” Able says he supports the right to school choice and likes private schools, but there needs to be a new way. Able replied, “I think it’s a funding mechanism that has to end. We need to find a better way to do things. And public money should be transparent to everybody in exactly how it’s being used.” You can find the full 25th Assembly District debate between Paul Tittl and Chris Abel at SeehaferPodcasts.com. We will host another debate on October 8th between 9th District State Senate candidates Amy Binsfeld and Christian Ellis.

artigo.texto: AURORA | Colorado will receive $250 million from the U.S. Department of Energy to upgrade a key power transmission connection between Colorado and Texas, state and federal energy officials announced from Aurora yesterday. The grant is part of a U.S. Energy Department project spending about $2 billion to try to squeeze more electricity out of the nation’s aging and stressed power grid, as President Donald Trump’s administration steps up efforts to avoid blackouts amid skyrocketing energy demand spurred by artificial intelligence data centers. The $2 billion will go toward 31 projects across 26 states that are expected to produce more than 23 gigawatts of additional electricity capacity — enough to power 16 million homes, according to federal officials. “This means lower costs and fewer outages for Coloradans,” Gov. Jared Polis said in a statement. “By strengthening Colorado’s electric grid and expanding our ability to share power with other regions, we can better protect families and businesses during extreme weather and periods of high demand while continuing to save people money.” The local funding will support the Colorado-to-Texas Western-Eastern Intertie Modernization Initiative, known as CO2TX, a project state and regional energy officials say will strengthen the connection between the Western and Eastern power grids. The nation’s electricity system is divided into large regional grids with limited ability to share power between them. The Colorado Energy Office is partnering with Xcel Energy on the project, according to state officials. The total CO2TX project cost is $1.2 billion, with the federal government providing $250 million and Xcel providing an 80% match, according to the release. The Colorado portion of the project will shift the main transmission connection from Lamar to a higher-capacity May Valley substation in southeast Colorado and link it directly to the Colorado Power Pathway transmission network. One terminus is in southeast Aurora at the Harvest Mile Substation. State officials said the upgrades will vastly increase the system’s capacity to move electricity, reduce strain on the grid and improve reliability during periods of high demand and extreme weather. The project also is expected to give consumers access to electricity from a larger pool of sources. “By strengthening Colorado’s electric grid and expanding our ability to share power with other regions, we can better protect families and businesses during extreme weather and periods of high demand while continuing to save people money,” Polis said. The project will upgrade existing equipment and power lines rather than build entirely new transmission corridors, officials said. That approach can increase capacity while limiting construction costs and land-use impacts. Tim Walsh, assistant secretary for environmental management at the Energy Department, said federal investment will continue to support grid and power improvements for Colorado and the broader Western United States. Energy Department trying to squeeze more electricity from the aging power grid The $2 billion in federal money will go toward 31 projects across 26 states that are expected to produce more than 23 gigawatts of additional electricity capacity — enough to power 16 million homes. The projects will use new technologies such as sensors to measure real-time weather conditions to ensure safe transmission or direct power away from congested paths, the department said. The upgrades could improve power reliability and lower electricity costs for about 100 million Americans, officials said. “This is a quick way to lower electricity prices and increase reliability: using fibers that are already in the transmission lines to analyze what’s the temperature out, what’s the wind out, how can we use this transmission line to distribute more power, but safely and only in the right conditions,” Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a news conference promoting the grants Thursday at a PPL Corp. facility in Allentown. The eastern Pennsylvania electric utility says two data centers in its territory came online this year and six more are under construction, with enough other data centers in the advanced planning stages that its peak electric demand could quintuple by 2032. PPL said it is receiving $71.5 million to modernize an existing high-voltage transmission line across roughly 30 miles in northern Pennsylvania. The announcement comes amid warnings that AI’s voracious demand for power is threatening to overwhelm U.S. power supplies, as massive new data centers come online faster than new power plants can be built. It also comes as electricity bills rise faster than inflation in many parts of the U.S., blamed in some areas on demand from data centers. The snowballing opposition to data centers in communities across the country has thrown a wrench into the plans of the world’s richest companies and transformed the midterm election landscape. Trump continues to stick up for data centers, even as politicians from both major political parties criticize them and many communities try to block them. In the meantime, Congress and some states are trying to push utilities to expand their use of new technologies to make grids more efficient and to lessen the need to build new power plants. Julia Selker, the executive director of the WATT Coalition, a trade association for grid-enhancing technologies, said both the projects and the scale of the investment are significant. Utilities in the U.S. are lagging places like Europe in adopting the technologies, despite federal investment in the past to develop and test them, Selker said. Still, Drew Maloney, CEO of the Edison Electric Institute, a trade association of for-profit utilities, said America’s electric utilities are making a “significant investment” every year in new technologies to strengthen the grid and reduce outages. artigo.texto: Data center cooling is changing. The engineering fundamentals are not. As AI accelerates the need for data center design, the focus tends to gravitate toward what goes along with this: new challenges, structural limitations and cutting-edge technologies like next-generation chips and increasingly sophisticated controls. But, beneath these advances is the infrastructure that determines whether they perform reliably and efficiently. Back to basics: Engineering fundamentals Consider advanced liquid cooling. By transferring heat more efficiently than traditional air-cooling methods, liquid cooling can support higher-density computing environments while, in many designs and depending on facility, local climate and nearby heat demand, reduce reliance on energy-intensive chillers. It can also create opportunities for waste heat recovery and reuse, along with wastewater treatment and recycling, returning water to the closed-loop environment, and supporting progress toward net zero water usage in data centers. These benefits have created a surge in adoption, with liquid cooling penetration for high-end AI chips surpassing the 50% threshold in 2026, according to recent analysis. While liquid cooling is often framed as a new innovation, the principles behind it are rooted in one of the foundational concepts of heating and cooling design: hydronics. Long considered the backbone of HVAC heating and cooling applications, hydronic systems are directly relevant to data centers. Just as every component in a data center functions as part of an interconnected ecosystem, a hydronic system relies on the seamless interaction of its individual components. Every balance valve, fitting, connection point, heat exchanger, tank and pump must work in harmony throughout the cooling loop to ensure continuous performance. And whether heat is removed through a chilled-water system, rear-door heat exchanger or direct-to-chip loop, the underlying task remains the same: move thermal energy from where it is generated to where it can be rejected or reused. That requires more than circulating fluid through the system. Designers must account for things like flow, pressure, temperature, system, redundancy and equipment balance, which all help determine whether heat can be moved efficiently from the chip to its ultimate point of rejection. Back to where it all began In 1954, Xylem’s Bell & Gossett engineer Gil Carlson developed the concept of primary/secondary pumping, which became the standard technique adopted by contractors, engineers and boiler manufacturers alike. In this piping arrangement, two separate water circulation loops are employed so that the equipment loop and building distribution loop can operate somewhat independently. Today, this same concept directly informs many liquid cooled data center designs, whereby primary and secondary loops work together to move heat from IT equipment to heat rejection systems and illustrating an inherent hydronic principle: connected cooling loops operate most effectively when they maintain hydraulic independence yet remain thermally linked. When densities are high, the stakes are higher AI densities are creating intense heat loads that are changing the way facilities respond to these shifting dynamics and as new computing comes online. In response, cooling loops must scale in accordance with the capacity required to manage high-density AI networks. Hydraulic separation can support this flexibility. Instead of designing every component around a single, fixed operating point, for instance, engineers can create circuits that accommodate additional cooling capacity as racks and data halls are deployed. But hydraulic independence does not mean the loops operate without affecting one another. Rather, they remain thermally connected. If secondary flow exceeds what the primary side can effectively support, recirculation and mixing can increase the temperature of the fluid supplied to the load. If the primary side circulates more water than necessary, the system may consume excess pumping energy and compromise its intended temperature differential. Similarly, decisions made at the rack can affect everything from piping and pumping to heat rejection, water use and power demand throughout the facility. Hydronic infrastructure is designed with this compounding efficiency in mind, knowing that each individual piece of equipment has an important role to play toward the performance of the greater whole. The intelligence of any cooling system begins with sound hydronic system design, all around a common objective to deliver the right flow, temperature and pressure at the right time. The technology may evolve, but performance is ultimately determined by engineering fundamentals, practical application and the expertise of facility managers, engineers and operators who bring these systems to life. About the Author Steven Lucente Steven Lucente is a business development manager for Xylem’s Applied Water business, where he leads data center business development and turns customer infrastructure challenges into scalable growth strategies and win-ready solutions. For 110 years, Bell & Gossett, a premier Xylem brand, has engineered industry-leading equipment including pumps, valves, heat exchangers and accessories for hydronic HVAC and plumbing systems. artigo.texto: Rússia atinge maior operadora de telefonia móvel da Ucrânia e centros de dados O Ministério da Defesa da Rússia também afirmou ter atingido um centro de dados pertencente à Vodafone Ukraine Atualizado A Rússia atingiu a sede da Kyivstar, maior operadora de telefonia móvel da Ucrânia, neste domingo, informou a empresa à imprensa local, enquanto Moscou mantinha os ataques contra centros de dados e a infraestrutura de comunicações ucraniana. A Kyivstar informou à agência de notícias Interfax Ukraine que sua sede, em Kiev, foi atingida, mas não houve vítimas. O Ministério da Defesa da Rússia também afirmou neste domingo ter atingido um centro de dados pertencente à Vodafone Ukraine, segunda maior operadora de telefonia móvel do país. A Vodafone Ukraine não respondeu a um pedido de comentário. O presidente ucraniano, Volodymyr Zelensky, disse que a Rússia atingiu duas vezes um centro de dados em Kiev na manhã deste domingo, ferindo duas crianças e um adulto. Moscou também atingiu centros de dados de provedores de internet ucranianos na última semana, provocando interrupções no serviço para cerca de 100 mil residências em Kiev e na região ao redor, segundo o Ministério da Transformação Digital da Ucrânia. “A Rússia tem como alvo os principais centros de dados ucranianos, buscando interromper o fluxo de informações. Alertas rápidos sobre ameaças de mísseis e drones são essenciais — eles salvam vidas”, escreveu o ministro das Relações Exteriores da Ucrânia, Andrii Sybiha, no X na quarta-feira.
